Summary

"Do you have work for me, or are you simply gawking like the rest?"

Work. Monsters to be vanquished or demons to fight. One doesn't hire a witcher unless they're desperate.

Phainon shivers. "Not work," he says, watching the witcher blink, breathe, study him. From his mannerisms alone, he reminds Phainon of a half-tamed animal. Alert, keenly aware of everything. They say witchers can smell fear. What, then, does he smell on Phainon? "But I have another request."

"Speak, then."

He inhales, swipes his tongue over his lips to taste the rainwater on them. "When you set off," Phainon says, "take me with you."
|
Mydei just wants to fight monsters, collect his paycheck, and move on to the next miserable village and the next miserable client with something to slay. Phainon would do anything it takes to grow stronger and escape his past, even follow a witcher around. Neither of them was ever meant to fall in love.

chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.html:
It's late, and Phainon is still bleeding by the time he gets back to the inn. It smells like stew and sweat and beer, and it's hot where outside it had been frigid. There's a bard playing, armed with a lute and a voice like sour milk, and it's not a home, not even close, not even a fair substitute on the road.

The flimsy strip of bandage Phainon has pressed to his torn calluses has already soaked through, and now it's threatening to drip from his cupped palm. It's been a long night, and he's already overstayed his welcome. One more day, maybe two, however long it takes to scrape up enough coin to make it to the next village, and then he'll be off.

He heads back to his room first, despite the way the smell of food makes his mouth water and his stomach roll with hunger. He's spent the last few days as a hired hand, hauling and chopping wood, shoveling manure, fixing leaks and holes in walls. Usually this goes well enough, but tonight he'd swung his axe in exactly the wrong way, ripped the calluses right off his palm, and been sent away with the gloves he'd ruined instead of coin as payment, even though they were already worn and can't have been worth half of what he's due.

It's with a sigh that he starts to clean himself up. He'd love a bath, but he'd hate to pay for it, so he settles for wiping himself down with a rag and a pitcher of water, taking extra care with his wounded hand. It hurts to move, more to touch. He has to peel the callus off, lest it snag on something and tear open further. The whole process is done with unsteady fingers and the inside of his cheek pulled between his teeth.

When he's done, clueless as he is about anything medical, there's more blood and his hand stings like he'd shoved it in salt. He curses as he digs through his bag with one hand for his bare bones supplies, trying not to spill and getting red drops on the wooden planks of the floor regardless.

By some miracle, he manages to bandage the wound, wash, and dress himself. He finds himself with only one functional hand, though at least the injured one isn't his dominant. He's not sure how much work he'll be able to do like this. How much worth he'll have as a hire to the unhappy, stingy people here. He wonders if there's any use in lingering after all.

He sits for a little while after that, exhausted from the day or the work or the dull throbbing in his hand. And then his stomach grumbles and he remembers how hungry he is, how parched, and he drags himself up on sore legs to head downstairs for a meal.

The stairs creak beneath him, worn and wooden. It's strange that he hears that as much as he feels it. The music and chatter from the inn have stopped. He pauses at the entrance to the hallway, scanning the tables, the stools at the bar, the group gathered around the fireplace, the bard at the front of the room, fingers frozen on his lute.

They're all looking at a man in the entryway, the door groaning shut behind him, each of his footsteps audible as he heads toward the bar. He's tall, perhaps Phainon's height. His hair is ragged, messy and stained red like blood at the tips, blond at the roots. His face is unsmiling and severe, though he has little reason to play at pleasantry with a reception like this. His hands and legs are armored and he wears a sleeved robe on one arm but not the other, and perhaps the most notable thing about him, the thing that draws stares to him like moths to flame, are the markings on his bared skin, down his arm and up his neck, creeping over his chest and back.

Phainon's breath stills in his throat. 

"A drink," the witcher says, tossing a coin onto the counter. The sound of it is crisp and clear, cutting through the silence as it lands. The innkeeper doesn't even look at it.

"We don't serve your kind here," she says, bitter, though her voice trembles. The witcher's chest rises with an inhale as a man sitting on a stool rises and spits at his feet. It lands on his boot, and when he turns his gaze, the man stumbles a step back.

"There's no work for you here, freak," he gets out, terrified and still foolish enough to provoke.

The witcher looks down at his armored shoes. Phainon waits for a fight or an argument, but there's only an exhale.

"It seems not," the witcher says, and turns his attention back to the innkeeper, pushing the coin closer to her. He takes the man's stool, and it seems spitting is as far as his courage extends, because he doesn't utter a word in protest, just opens his mouth and closes it again. "A drink," the witcher repeats, firmer this time, and there's a long pause before the innkeeper furiously snatches the coin. But she gets the witcher a drink, setting it down with enough force that some of it spills, and no one is brave enough to say anything else.

Watching him sit there and drink, Phainon finally unfreezes, taking a breath and heading to a table with a couple of young men he'd worked alongside the day before. They're not quite friendly—none in this town are—but they've been nice enough, even if they won't laugh at his jokes.

"What is a witcher doing here of all places?" Phainon asks, pulling a chair out and taking a seat.

One of the men looks up, idly stirring his stew and glancing in the direction of the bar before he quickly looks away. Another makes a face like his stomach is upset. "I haven't the faintest idea," he says. "I just hope it leaves soon."

Phainon is reminded of his hunger. His stomach growls, but he's not sure asking for a bowl will be productive at the moment, with everyone on edge. "Do you ever get monsters here?" he asks instead. "Ghouls and stuff?"

"No," the last occupant of the table scoffs. He's older than the rest. Angrier too. Phainon has never been to such a rotten town. He'd have left after his first day here if he weren't worried about his finances. "We don't get monsters here, and we certainly don't need a monster to clear them out. What happened to your hand?"

"Ah." Phainon looks at it, bandaged and resting on the table. "Just an accident chopping wood; I'm alright." The look he gets gives him the sense that he wasn't be asked out of concern. He laughs a bit awkwardly, tangling the fingers of his good hand in the hair at the back of his neck.

It's still so silent. The bard never picked his music back up—not that Phainon is complaining—and conversations take place in hushed tones. It's strange. He knew people hated witchers. He understands the fear, but this...

"I'm... going to see if I can get a bowl of stew," he tries, standing. A hand grabs his wrist.

"Are you daft?" the oldest of the group says, halting him. "You want to walk over there?"

Phainon glances over his shoulder. A broad, muscled back, those red markings converging at the spine. The witcher isn't covered in blood and gore, and he doesn't wear bones or trophies from his kills or anything else to make him seem monstrous. He isn't even carrying a visible weapon, just a satchel at his side, a belt with a dozen pockets, and those gauntlets. His head tips back as he drinks deeply, uncaring about the disturbance he's caused.

"I guess not," Phainon concedes, hesitating and pulling his wrist free. He sits back down, not quite certain if what he's feeling is fear or awe or desperation at the sheer opportunity in front of him. He needs to talk to the witcher, but it wouldn't do to approach him now and earn the ire of the entire town. At least, not until he's had a chance to fill his stomach.

So he lingers a little. Tries to make small talk with this group of men who seem allergic to small talk. He observes the witcher the whole while, watching him down two beers, a slab of roast lamb, and a bowl of stew. He doesn't seem to care about the eyes on him. And are there eyes; the entire time he's watched by half the inn, like they're all scared he'll get up and start a slaughter. But he doesn't, and he seems long used to this kind of attention, disdain, terror. Phainon realizes he's part of the problem too.

A few more minutes pass, his stomach grumbling all the while. He picks at the bandages on his hand as he listens to one of the men telling some alleged story about a witcher bleeding babies for potions. Then there's the rough scrape of a stool on the ground as the witcher stands up. The room goes silent again, all eyes turning warily toward him. But the only things he does are leave his dishes and push his stool back in before he leaves without a word. The door brings a breeze as it shuts. It stays quiet for a dozen heartbeats before tables erupt in conversation.

Phainon smiles tightly and sets his hands on the table. "Well," he says, "I suppose I should be safe to get a meal now?"

They don't laugh. One man spits. "Good riddance to the witcher."

Phainon gets himself a bowl of stew, regretfully parting with some of his scant savings to pay for it. But a hot meal is a hot meal, and he's spent too many days on the road sustaining off of stale bread, dried fruit and meat, and whatever he manages to forage or hunt, so it's difficult not to allow himself a small bit of indulgence. The way it warms him through is worth it, even if the taste is nothing special. They haven't reached winter yet, and he keeps warm in the day with hard work, but the nights have been getting cooler and cooler, and the rains they've been having soak a person through and steal heat straight from their bones.

He eats far too fast, and then it's gone, and his stomach is still rumbling, and he'd rather not fork over the money for a second bowl.

Conversation is unsuccessful, and the sour milk sounding bard starts to sing again, so he heads back to his room. It's late enough that he could sleep. His body is certainly tired enough for it. Or, he thinks as he bends to peer between the window slats, he could look for the witcher.

It's long since grown dark outside, and while he's heard that witchers have some level of night vision, even they need to sleep. He'll probably camp somewhere tonight and set off to find work in the morning.

The problem is this: Phainon doesn't have the faintest clue where he might go to build a camp. Somewhat far from the town for sure, so he won't get harassed, but close enough to be convenient.

Phainon reaches for his coat, discarded on the bed, stained with mud and bloody at the end of the sleeve where he'd torn his hand open. He'll just go out and look a bit. There's a decent chance the witcher will come back in the morning for another meal before he sets off, or to ask around a little more for work.

There might be some. He could see people hiding it, pretending there's nothing because to go up and ask for help with a hundred disdainful eyes on you might as well be social suicide. Because for all the lives they save by hunting down the monsters any regular human couldn't handle, witchers are treated like dirt more often than not. Phainon has always found this strange. Most people find his views—his destination—stranger.

He struggles into his coat, closes the shutters on the window, and heads out. No one says a word or spares him a glance, so he steps into the night with a lantern, finding it colder than he expected it to be. Perhaps he's just used to the warmth of his bedroll at these hours, or he's unadjusted after being spoiled by the fireplace inside, but he pulls his sleeves as far over his fingers as he can and tucks his injured hand into his coat pocket.

It smells like rain out here, sweet and sticky. The cobbled pathway leading to the entrance of the inn reflects the light of his lantern with wetness, though it's dry under the eaves of the building. He's the only one out here. The sound of music bleeds through the shut door behind him. A breath, his exhale fogs the air. He sets off, following the path without so much as a plan as to where he'll even look.

Stone turns to packed down dirt, mud in places where water has had a chance to accumulate. The further he gets, the more the music is replaced with the soft sound of rain, falling so gently he barely feels it. Maybe it speaks of more to come, maybe not. Either way, it'll soak him soon enough. Not even five minutes into this, he's already starting to regret it.

What is he even going to say if he manages to find the witcher? He tries thinking it through, playing out a handful of different scripts and scenarios in his head. He can't remember what the witcher's voice sounded like. He imagines it raspy and deep and pissed off, and it makes him laugh, just softly, just to himself. He shivers in his coat. Holding his lantern out, he hasn't the slightest clue where he's even headed. Just walking, it seems. It's too dark to make much of anything out.

Cold and tired now, he turns back, retracing his steps through the mud until the inn comes back within view, spilling light from its windows, plumes of smoke from the chimney. He's well aware he's a bit of a fool at times. Now especially. He should've gone after the witcher when he had the chance, but now he just looks forward to being warm again and getting a good night's sleep. The rest, he'll worry about later.

Dirt turns to stone. A twig snaps, and Phainon puts his hand on the knife at his waist, whipping around and circling the hilt before he remembers his injury, pain stabbing through his palm. Quickly, he trades his knife and lantern to opposite hands, half aware he's likely being paranoid as he scans the darkness, but he's been paranoid for a long time now, and he doesn't know how to stop.

A moment, two. Nothing but the sound of rain, a little heavier now, weighing down the ends of his hair. Phainon lets out a breath, and when still nothing comes, relaxes. He turns back to the inn, tucking the knife back into place, hidden in his belt.

"It's dangerous out," comes a voice, deep and gravelly. "Or did you already know that?" The hair on the back of Phainon's neck stands on end. He fits the hilt of his knife back in hand, and finds himself face to face with the witcher. In the dim glow from Phainon's lantern, his hair is wet and blood red at the tips. His markings seem to reflect the light back, that or they glow by themselves. Same with his eyes. He'd seemed so close to human from afar, but up close it's clearer that he's a little bit off.

"I know," Phainon says. He stands tall, as best as he can. He isn't afraid, not quite, but he'll admit to a bit of wariness. Awe that translates into caution. Still, he holds the witcher's gaze, finding them a shade of amber near to gold. A witcher's eyes are always a sickly, wolfish shade of yellow in the stories, but these aren't that. He doesn't smile, but no one here seems to smile, and after seeing the way he'd pushed in his chair and ignored provocation, Phainon doesn't think he has a thing to be afraid of. "But I like to think I can handle myself."

A slight cock of the head. He watches the witcher breathe in, bare chest rising, and isn't he cold? Damp and half naked, he must be, but perhaps his constitution means he isn't bothered. "I've felt your eyes," he says. "Do you have work for me, or are you simply gawking like the rest?"

Work. Monsters to be vanquished or demons to fight, protection to be given. One doesn't hire a witcher unless they're desperate. And Phainon, well... He hardly has a few pennies to his name and, despite his trying, has yet to encounter anything more dangerous than a particularly angry cow. Recently, anyway.

He shivers again. His fingers grow numb, and the lantern puts just enough pressure on his hand to send the slightest ache through his wound. He leaves his knife in its sheath at his waist and switches the lantern to his other hand, tucking the injured one back in his pocket.

"Not work," he says, watching the witcher blink, breathe, study him. From his mannerisms alone, he reminds Phainon of a half-tamed animal. Alert, keenly aware of everything. They say witchers can smell fear. What, then, does he smell on Phainon? "But I have another request."

"Speak, then."

He inhales, swipes his tongue over his lips to taste the rainwater on them. He's nervous. This could be the opportunity of a lifetime, a shortcut to every goal he has, something he's unlikely to find anywhere else. Witchers are few and far between. "When you set off," Phainon says, "take me with you."

For a moment, the witcher just looks at him, incredulous or expecting a joke. And then he laughs, loud and rough and... not what Phainon had been expecting at all. "You want to travel with a witcher?" he asks. "Are you out of your mind?"

You're human like the rest of us, Phainon doesn't say. You aren't some scary monster. "Maybe," he admits, unable to help folding his arms around himself as he shivers. His hair drips into his eyes. He's sure he looks like some wet rat, hardly a worthy traveling companion, but it doesn't matter. "But I'm strong, and I can hunt and fish, and I have some knowledge in foraging. I wouldn't be a burden."

The witcher's gaze lands on Phainon's left hand tucked into his pocket. "You're injured," he says.

"It's barely an injury at all," Phainon tells him, despite how much it bled, despite how much it hurts to so much as open and close his fingers. It's new, so of course it's painful. He's always healed fast. "I'm still capable of all of those things regardless."

"And do you have the strength to journey as I do? I don't walk slowly, I don't stop often for breaks, I walk well into the night and rise with the sun. You would only slow me down."

"I can travel as you do," Phainon insists. He might have a taste for small luxuries, but he's well accustomed to living without them. "You underestimate me."

"You're shivering," the witcher says, like an accusation. "Right now, there's little you'd rather do than return to that inn where it's warm."

"So I'm capable of feeling discomfort," Phainon agrees, "But I'm good at enduring it, and I won't ask you to accommodate me."

He seems to study Phainon more thoroughly now. The set of his shoulders, the way he straightens up for the appraisal. His build isn't obvious beneath the coat, but Phainon has always been strong. Perhaps he can't compare to the bulk of a witcher, but he's far from weak.

The cold bites. The rain grows heavier, puddling in the cracks between the cobbles, dancing in the dim lantern light. "My work is dangerous," the witcher says. "I am dangerous. What makes you so certain you can handle yourself?"

"I'm trained in the sword," Phainon answers.

"And yet you don't carry one."

"...I had to sell it, but the moment I can afford another..."

Something like a laugh. "You're better off with a caravan to get wherever you're trying to go," the witcher says. "You wouldn't be able to keep up with me, human."

"Phainon," Phainon corrects him. The witcher merely blinks, cocks his head to one side. Phainon swallows around a dry throat. "My name," he explains, finding himself far more angry than afraid. "It's Phainon."

"You wouldn't be able to keep up with me, Phainon," the witcher amends. His nostrils flare. His gaze turns to something over Phainon's shoulder. "My answer is the same."

"There's no need to wait up if I slow you down," Phainon says. "But you'll find that I won't." Far behind him, the door to the inn swings open, bringing a thin stream of light and a round of laughter and bad music. The witcher takes a step away.

"Head back, now," he says. "You wouldn't want to be seen talking to a witcher."

"'A witcher,'" Phainon repeats, lips growing numb, hair wet enough to paste to his skull. A drowned, frozen rat. He barely feels the cold, growing more and more frustrated. "Don't you have a name?"

"You have know need to know it," is the reply he gets. The door shuts, taking the light with it. Phainon can hear the drunkards stumbling home. The witcher turns away, and Phainon thinks that if he lets him out of reach, he'll never see him again. He catches the witcher's wrist. A dangerous move. He can feel the tension under his hand, the way he could end up thrown so easily, but he doesn't care. 

"Humor me, if we're going to travel together," he says.

"We aren't," the witcher says, pulling his wrist free. "Go."

It climbs up Phainon's throat. "Please," he tries, and earns a strange, unsettled expression, and then a sigh.

"Mydeimos," the witcher finally says.

"The Undying," Phainon breathes. He cracks a smile, as wide as he can muster. "It's a pleasure."

Narrowed eyes, a pinched mouth. Behind, drunken laughter. Mydeimos' gaze lands back on him, considering, contemplative. Nervous hope settles in Phainon's chest, but, "You'd best go," is all Mydeimos says.

He turns his back to Phainon as he walks away, soaking wet and still somehow imposing. Phainon needs this, but it wouldn't do to chase him down again and again. Phainon wants to grow on him, not plague him. So instead of making a fool of himself and begging, he just puts on a smile and says to Mydeimos' shrinking back, "I'll see you in the morning, then, Mydeimos. I'll be up early, so there's no need to wait around!"

Not a word of acknowledgment. The feeling that stirs in Phainon's stomach is like a sickness. Maybe he'll never see Mydeimos again, and he'll be back on his own, trekking without a soul for company and nothing but a small handful of coins, those ruined gloves, and the shoes on his feet. He turns back to the inn, nearly shaking with the cold as he pushes past those drunkards to make his way back inside where its warm. It's so helplessly human of him. He thinks of the witcher in the cold. His socks squelch in his shoes as he heads back up the stairs to his room.

No hot bath awaits him, but he towels off and changes into his last set of clean clothes. The rest he'll have to launder before he sets off. He doesn't see himself getting much sleep tonight anyway. He dresses and wraps himself in his blanket, extremities half frozen and his nose running as he struggles to change the bandages on his hand with stiff and clumsy fingers.

His stomach growls. All his bones still ache. He has a feeling this is going to be a long night.

△

He barely sleeps. By the time he's done washing his clothes and hanging them to dry, packing up what scant amount of stuff he has, and worrying, the night has gone by. He lays in bed, wrapped in blankets and staring at the ceiling until the first hint of sun breaks the horizon, and then he gets up.

It's strange, the mix of bone-deep tiredness and nervousness. He's restless but he wants to rest. Should he somehow find Mydeimos today, then conquer the slightly more impossible task of convincing him to take Phainon along, he's hardly in ideal shape for a hard day of traveling. He's certain he's stubborn enough to do it, but he doesn't enjoy suffering. He can only hope the witcher was exaggerating how roughly he travels. 

All this assuming Phainon even sees him again.

Downstairs, he orders a bowl of porridge as something like a farewell to this rotten town. He spends a bit extra on sugar and raisins—though he probably shouldn't—and finds himself about half as hungry when he's done as he was before he started. That is to say, still very hungry. He returns his room key and heads out to town for provisions. He's setting off regardless of whether he's alone or not. Still, he keeps a close eye out because he's certain Mydeimos isn't going to come to him.

It's still chilly this morning, still early enough that the sun is only just properly rising, painting the sky with red and orange and pink. His coat is still a bit damp, not having had enough time to dry overnight. He shivers, but it isn't windy so it isn't too bad, and the clouds have gone so he's safe from the rain.

The town is already busy with people heading to work. The air is clean and fresh when Phainon takes a breath, still humid from the rain the night before. He has to take care to avoid puddles as he walks, and when the cobbled pathway turns to dirt, he finds it churned to mud by wagons and feet and hooves alike. He's careful not to sink too deep into it and ruin his boots as he makes his way to the market to buy some supplies. More bandages, for one. More long-keeping rations. A small bit of cord to replace the one he'd lost to the wind when he'd tied up his tarp for a makeshift tent. Little by little, his savings drift away. All because he hadn't been paid for the work he did yesterday. On the bright side, he manages to barter a bit, seeming to have charmed the young woman working at the general store.

Pack full but not so heavy as to be a problematic burden, Phainon walks a lap around town. He follows the whispers of witcher, and monster, and bad luck to have one of them here, and finds... Very little. The lap yields nothing. So does asking around. Everyone claims to have seen him, no one seems to know where he went.

Mydeimos the Undying. The Blood Crown. They say he killed the king Eurypon and slaughtered a dozen other men with his bare hands. Phainon has never known what to make of the tale. Perhaps there's some truth, twisted and warped into something not quite right. Perhaps it's all true. Perhaps none of it is at all.

As he heads back in the direction of the inn, he spies a man on horseback. He watches, feet aching from all the walking he'd done before he stopped in town, muscles aching from all the work he'd done since he stopped in town, and imagines for a brief moment how nice it must be to have a horse. Sure, there's care involved, but he wouldn't have to carry his own bags, and he could alternate riding and walking depending on what part of him hurts. He could never save up for such a thing, though.

He watches a little longer, the horse and rider in no hurry, hooves clomping rhythmically. The horse is a reddish-brown creature, well groomed and strong, muscles rippling as it walks. Phainon's gaze trails up to its rider. Well built, armored from the thighs down, gauntleted, basically bare from the waist and covered in deep red markings. His hair looks dipped in blood, and even from here, it's obvious he hasn't smiled in a long while.

Phainon starts running, feet slipping in the mud, the cold and exhaustion forgotten until he comes to a stop, and then a fast walk alongside Mydeimos' horse when he shows no sign of slowing. "Hey," he tries, and finds himself breathy despite barely having run more than a few dozen meters.

One gauntleted hand tugs softly on the reins, the horse turning to block Phainon's path, forcing him to halt, foot landing in a particularly muddy spot. Amber eyes gaze down. Mydeimos' mouth turns into a frown. "You again," he says. Exasperatedly, so exasperatedly. His horse gives a huff and flicks its mane.

"Me again," Phainon confirms. He offers a smile, wide as he can muster. He's nervous suddenly. Not so suddenly, considering the way he'd spent the entire night tossing and turning. Mydeimos glares down like he hasn't the slightest idea what to do with some stranger dead set on following him. But uncertainty means it's possible to wheedle a yes out of him. Phainon can be quite convincing, when need be. He pulls his foot free from the mud and stands tall, squinting a little through the sun shining over Mydeimos' shoulder.

"I'm ready to set off whenever you are."

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

He's stubborn. So strangely stubborn, this smiling, white-haired man. His eyes are very blue, he's pale skinned and tall, perhaps as tall as Mydei himself. He wears a leather choker on his neck. His heritage isn't obvious. Neither are his motives. 

He doesn't smell like fear, is the strange thing. He reeks of something. Some odd concoction of sweat and blood, but none of the sour tinge of fear. He's nervous, clearly, based on the shiftiness of his gaze and the bobbing of his throat. He's desperate for something, or he wouldn't have come, wouldn't insist on following the worst possible person to follow. But he isn't scared. Not of Mydei, it doesn't seem. Nor does he spit or scorn. But what does he want? What does he have to be desperate to follow Mydei for? If not a monster he needs hunted, then what?

"So?" the man called Phainon asks, shifting from foot to foot the longer Mydei is silent. He's squinting against the sun, bringing his bandaged hand up to block it. His coat smells wet; he's obviously cold again, and his eyes are underscored with dark circles. Cold and tired and still smiling. Desperate. But why?

"You're not coming with me," Mydei tells him, nudging Strife to start walking again. Her tail whips Phainon as she complies, and he isn't certain it's an accident.

After a brief moment of spluttering, footsteps come from behind. Phainon, speed walking to keep pace, clumsy as he does so, one boot caked in mud.

"You act like a bit of company will kill you," he says, struggling to balance the words with his breath. "I'm not going to hold you back, and I won't make you provide for me or break earlier, if you're so insistent on traveling like you're being chased. I'll be an asset to you, even. I can hunt, fish, and forage. I can cook and tie knots. We can take turns keeping watch if you're worried about bandits or monsters at night. There are so many advantages to traveling together rather than alone."

He's panting from the pace, flushed red in the face from the chill or his frustration. Mydei ignores him, nudging Strife to walk a little faster, though he won't have her trot with all the people in the road. Still bargaining, Phainon falls into a jog, uncaring of the attention he garners, stuck to a witcher's side. Mydei spares him a glance, glad not to find those luridly blue eyes on his.

Phainon keeps talking, talking, talking. They make it to the end of the town, and Mydei turns Strife onto the main road. He'd taken the time to gather supplies and go through his potions. This town has been far less friendly than most, and he'd had a difficult time bartering. Hence why he'd been so slow to leave. Hence why he has this still rambling man following him. It's been ten minutes and he hasn't shut up, and since they're on the road and he's all packed up, it seems Mydei has inadvertently given him what he wanted.

They're close enough to town that he won't have any issues finding his way. Mydei considers for a moment, two, and then spurs Strife into a run.

"You—!" Phainon's words are lost to the wind whistling in Mydei's ears as he folds himself over the neck of his horse. He doesn't run her like this often, especially not at the start of a long journey, with how heavy he and his armor and supplies are, but he figures losing a burden is worth a longer break and a few extra oats.

A minute passes like this, then two, three. Strife gallops for maybe a mile and a half before Mydei slows her down and dismounts, letting her rest. The road behind them bends, wreathed sparsely in trees and vacant as far as the eye can see. When Mydei listens, he can't hear a thing out of place, just Strife's huffing and a colored leaf falling the the ground here and there. Without a horse of his own to follow, Phainon will have to have given up and turned back. He gives Strife a few minutes to catch her breath and graze, then guides her on foot by the bridle.

He doesn't mind the monotony of walking, the silence, the slow way it wears the body out. He likes the simplicity, the way it frees up the mind, the way it puts his restless muscles to work without violence. Used to unrest as he is, he's learned to appreciate the peace.

And he gets to keep this peace for all of seven or eight minutes before something sets his senses on edge. A moment, two, there's a sound behind him, growing louder and louder. He pauses. Footsteps and breathing. A little longer, and Phainon breaks into the clearing, hair stuck to his forehead with sweat, mud up to his shins, gasping furiously for breath and stumbling to a stop.

"You—" His chest is heaving. He ran all this way after a galloping horse and witcher of all things. Some scant handful of minutes to breach a gap of a mile and a half, laden with his bedroll and pack, already short of breath from jogging alongside Mydei and talking as long he had.

Now, he sags, bracing his good hand on a nearby tree, trying to breathe and speak at the same time. "You. Absolute bastard," he manages after a moment, and Mydei is shocked enough to give him the time. "What is wrong with you?"

Indignant and reeking of sweat, he paints a picture. Strife huffs and flicks her tail, lifting her head from where she's been chewing on a clump of dying dandelions. Swallowing thickly, breathing not quite evenly, Phainon straightens up. "How hard is it to hear a guy out?" he asks, frowning.

He's one of the strangest things Mydei has ever come across, and that's saying something. "I've already given you my answer," Mydei tells him, "you're the one insisting upon not understanding the word 'no.'"

"All I'm asking," Phainon starts, pausing for another inhale. He seems too exhausted to be properly angry now. "Is that you give me a chance—"

"A chance to what?" Mydei interrupts him. "What business do you have in following me? Do you have a death wish, or are you just stupid?"

But Phainon doesn't react with anger or cursing or spitting. He just says, carefully and levelly, "I have my reasons, but I mean you no harm, and I won't be a burden. All I ask is that you allow me to tag along."

"Why should I agree when you won't even answer my questions?" Mydei asks, taking a step closer to him. "I don't know you, and you don't have work for me. I can't see a single reason why I should bother."

Steady now, pulling his hand off the bark, holding Mydei's gaze, Phainon is still stubborn. So stubborn, but why? Mydei isn't friendly to him, has made it clear that he doesn't intend to be any kind of protector, and his whole purpose is seeking out danger, not avoiding it. And then there's the way Phainon ran to catch up, the way he'll wait around in the cold, the way he claims he'll endure suffering if it means he can only be allowed to follow. It doesn't make sense at all.

Mydei knows all about creatures and monsters and magic and curses, but he hasn't a clue about this. Phainon, lacking an ounce of fear when faced with him.

"I want to get stronger," he says, thumping his bandaged hand against his chest. "I want to have what it takes to protect the things that I care about. I want—"

Mydei swings his fist, intending to punch Phainon in the gut and leave with Strife as he's reeling, but he doesn't connect with flesh. Instead, Phainon catches his wrist and side steps, expression incredulous, then hardening.

"You think I'm some weakling," he says, grip tight. His smile is gone. Mydei pulls free of him and, less out of a desire to hurt and more out of some strange kind of curiosity, throws another punch. Again, he's avoided with practiced motion and solid reflexes. A breath in; it seems Mydei has made him properly angry now.

"And that's fair!" Phainon continues, ducking under a hook and raising his guard. He's still out of breath, but he fights like it matters to him. Strange, stubborn human. "I can hardly compare to a witcher, I'm sure. But I—" A sharp exhale; he pivots on his front foot to kick with his back, and he would have landed it were Mydei anything but what he is. "—Am going to get stronger. And you—" He can't dodge in time; Mydei's armored fist connects with his forearm, but he barely so much as hisses before he throws a counter attack, catching Mydei's shoulder.

He hits with the bandaged hand. Mydei can smell the way it bleeds, torn open for the force or the way he clenches it tight.

"I'll what?" Mydei asks, finding himself grinning. He likes this kind of fight, this kind of show of resolve. He isn't using his full strength, let alone any of his potions or tools or weapons, but Phainon keeps up with whatever Mydei gives him unarmed.

"You'll—" His teeth are gritted. His breath comes in harsh pants. He'd sprinted over a mile with all of his stuff on his back, and he's still good for a fight. He takes a hit to the side, lands one to Mydei's face, uncaring of the way it makes the blood smell stronger. He must be exhausted and in pain, but he's still fighting, still following, and he may be human, but perhaps there's some truth to his earlier words.

So I'm capable of feeling discomfort, he'd said, but I'm good at enduring it. And Mydei hadn't believed him at all.

"—Take me with you," Phainon finishes. That's the moment where he falters, losing his balance after taking a knee to the gut, glaring furiously but not struggling when he finds himself pinned, covered in mud, and so wholly, entirely human. His eyes, up close, are frightfully blue.

"You're smiling," he says.

He's scraped and bruised in places where he'd taken hits. Mydei's gauntlets, one silver and one steel, are anything but soft. He smiles a little wider. "You'd be wise to assume I'm baring my teeth."

But Phainon only laughs. His scent doesn't turn sour. His head falls back. He breathes like he'll never be able to get enough air, and his heart pounds loud enough that Mydei can hear it. "Please," he says, and it comes out much more tiredly now. "Let me try, and if I can't keep up, feel free to leave me in the dust."

Mydei can't wrap his head around him. This man who wants to grow stronger by following a witcher. There's potential there, a beautiful, stubborn kind of resolve. If only he didn't talk far, far too much.

Mydei gets up, dusting himself off without a word and returning to Strife, unbothered and grazing through the whole ordeal. She huffs a small protest as he swings into the saddle, but complies when he takes the reins and guides her back onto the road.

Phainon, left in the mud, calls to them, "Not even an answer this time, Mydeimos?"

He's dirtied and bloodied and sweat soaked and furious. Mydei spares him only a glance, and then shouts, "I thought you said you could keep up!"

△

It might be a mistake. Phainon turns out to be just as much of a talker now as he was when he was tossing out every argument in the book to persuade Mydei to bring him along. Perhaps he's allergic to silence, perhaps he's bored. It makes no difference. A headache starts to build behind Mydei's eyes regardless. His peace is taken from him without so much as a halfhearted apology.

"Your horse," Phainon says, "seems like a very good horse. Have you had it long? I've always wanted one but I've never had the money. Are they hard to take care of?"

"You talk too much," Mydei tells him. Realistically, Phainon talks a normal amount. Mydei's just used to no talking at all. "Her name is Strife."

"Lovely," Phainon says. "That doesn't answer my question."

"I've had her three years now," Mydei says after a long delay, patting Strife's neck. She doesn't react, just looks at him with one glassy eye. "She's seven."

"She's beautiful," Phainon tells him. "Is she a lot of work? What does she eat? And is it really okay to just tie her to a tree at night or something? I've always felt like that's a bit cruel, but how else do you know she won't wander off if you don't?"

Mydei sighs through his nose, squeezes his eyes shut for a second or two. "Does silence offend you?"

Phainon's gaze finds his, too bright a blue. There's a clump of mud in his hair, streaks of it up the back of his neck and all over his trousers, despite his futile efforts to clean it up. He's lost the coat at least, after sweating so much and the sun coming up. His tunic beneath is clean enough, but he still looks like he's spent a few days on the road rather than less than a few hours.

"No," he says, not quite smiling. "Does conversation offend you?"

"When it's as meaningless as this, yes."

A laugh, but Phainon goes quiet, at least for the next stretch of road. There's only his footsteps, slightly labored breathing, and Strife's hoofbeats to accompany them. The woods are patchy, some trees with fewer leaves than others, but they block out some of the sun, so Mydei doesn't have to squint against it. The earth starts to dry, though the air still carries the fresh scent of rain. A thin breeze blows, rustling through leaves, hitting Phainon first, then Mydei. It carries the faint scent of blood.

Subtle, silent, he glances at Phainon. His gaze tipped to the ground in front of him, mouth parted, hunched a little from his burden. He moves his injured hand up to shove his hair aside, and sure enough, he's bled through his bandages and hasn't done a thing about it.

"Are you ever planning on letting that hand heal?" Mydei asks dryly.

Phainon holds his hand out in front of himself like he'd forgotten it was there. "It's not that bad," he says, despite the mess of red. He's scraped in a few places from Mydei's gauntlets too, though those have mostly turned to bruises. "Just tore a few calluses off by accident."

"There are things other than me here that can smell blood," Mydei tells him. "Unless the plan was to attract something that will injure you more. In which case, continue."

A laugh. Phainon picks at the edge of the bandage until it comes undone. "You have a bit of a sense of humor in there, don't you?" he says, freeing his pack from one shoulder so he can dig through it as he walks, somewhat awkwardly juggling the supplies he digs out. "Wait till the world gets a load of this: witchers are funny!"

"I wasn't joking."

"Right, right," Phainon says, "you're the monster expert, not me."

He spares a bit from his waterskin to wet a strip of cloth, cleaning up the wound as best as he can while still walking, a roll of fresh bandages tucked under his arm, bag still hanging from one shoulder. It isn't terrible, so far as Mydei can see. Torn calluses, exactly as he'd said. He's just broken the scabs. It would be easy enough to heal with the Sign of Aquila, but he won't. Phainon might take it for some kind of declaration of friendship.

Still, it would be better if he washed it properly and used some salve, but they're a ways from the river, and Mydei is too stubborn to stop for him, and Phainon is too stubborn to ask. Better to just berate him.

"And yet you want to grow stronger," Mydei scoffs. "I can't imagine how you expect to do that if you're careless enough to get yourself eaten."

"And what, pray tell, is going to eat me out here?" Phainon asks, shoving the bloody rag in his pocket and unwinding a length of the bandage. "You?"

Mydei turns back to watch the road, rubbing his palm over Strife's neck. She gives a snort and slows to a stop when he urges her. Phainon pauses too, busy concentrating as he struggles to wrap his hand.

"Beasts and monsters are indiscriminate," Mydei tells him, dismounting to give Strife a break. He offers her an apple from one of his saddlebags and gives her a moment to chew before continuing on foot. "You're injured, and you don't even have a weapon."

Phainon laughs. It's an airy thing, and too easily given. He stumbles as he makes to follow again, barely regaining his balance before he can fall flat on his face and hurt himself some more. He seems to think nothing of it, even when Mydei gives him an unimpressed stare and continues on. "I've traveled on my own quite a bit, and I've never had any problems," Phainon calls, jogging to catch up. "I appreciate the concern, though. Are you worried about me?"

"Anything you attract becomes my problem by proximity only," Mydei reminds him.

"Right," Phainon says, finishing with his bandage, "I'll be careful to never bleed ever again to spare you the trouble. Tell me, is it true that a witcher's blood is gold?"

And there, as soon as a couple of words are exchanged, Phainon takes it as permission to open the floodgates. Mydei sighs. "What business is it of yours?"

"None, I suppose," Phainon admits. Walking like this, they're about the same height. He's quite tall for a human. Mydei's half certain he'd only grown this tall because of the mutations he'd been forced to go through, but here Phainon is, the same height and wholly human. "I'm curious, though. Humor me; isn't it a good idea for us to get to know each other a bit anyway? It's a long journey to... Where exactly are we headed?"

Mydei presses his lips together, hoping to stifle his laugh before it can come out. Oh, but he fails, and Phainon's eyes turn to him like moths to flame, shocked by the sound, delighted by it, though it's at his expense. "You insist on tagging along and you don't even know?" he asks. 

"I was preoccupied with other things," Phainon defends himself. "It's not like it matters anyway; it's nearing winter, and you're a witcher. You're not going to get too far away from Castrum Kremnos."

A twig snaps underfoot. Mydei looks at him, that streak of mud still on his neck, the way he struggles to shove his supplies back in his bag. "What does Kremnos have to do with this?"

The mock offense and mirth slips from Phainon's expression. "Well," he says, wetting his lips, "that's my destination, after this little stint is over. I want to learn from you, and then I want to learn from them." He's nervous now, like he thinks Mydei will leave him behind just for this absurd, audacious request.

"What makes you think you're welcome?" Mydei asks lowly.

"That's the thing," Phainon says, swallowing. "I don't think I'm welcome. But I want to get stronger, and I'll prove myself however I need to. I'll do whatever it takes."

So resolute, so stubborn, so sure of this. His mouth is a hard line. He's already half proven his strength and his drive. A begrudging seed of respect grows its roots. Mydei looks away.

"And if you get killed along the way or left in the cold to freeze?"

"I'll survive," Phainon says, certain of it. "But if not, then so be it. Where to?"

"Okhema," Mydei answers. "The Holy City."

△

Their first day on the road is fairly uneventful. They walk some more, though Mydei gets to ride Strife when he's tired. Phainon doesn't complain once about how his feet must hurt and his shoulders must ache from carrying his pack. He doesn't slow Mydei down, as promised. He's a fast walker and willing to push himself.

When they break for lunch, it's in a tidy clearing close to the river. He disappears for a while as Mydei hitches Strife, letting her drink and graze as he picks the crusts of mud off his sabatons with a stick. It's nice to sit for a while. Mydei doesn't care much for luxuries, but the weight off his feet and a tree at his back is always a welcome relief. He listens to the water, the wind in the trees. That sweet, blissful silence he's recently found himself robbed of.

He gets to keep it for all of twenty minutes before Phainon comes back, snapping twigs and disturbing rocks. "I got lucky," he says, a smile in his voice. When Mydei looks up, he has a clump of oyster mushrooms in one hand and a hare in the other. "Didn't even have to go far."

So he hadn't been lying when he said he was skilled in hunting and foraging. There's no need for him to share with Mydei, though; he has his own rations. He gestures vaguely. "Start a fire, then," he says. "I'll be on my way in another half hour, and you can stay behind for some stew."

Phainon gives a too easy laugh and takes a seat, not too close but not far. He lifts the hare. "We'll save this for dinner, then. I'll gut it so we can take it with us."

"It's your kill," Mydei says.

"I'm not going to eat an entire hare," he says, giving Mydei a strange look as he pulls a knife from his waist. "And I'd like to sleep tonight, not stay up trying to preserve it. Besides, I said I'd be useful. Obviously I'm going to share."

A strange feeling in Mydei's chest. He purses his lips.

So Phainon handles the hare, and Mydei has Strife carry it as a compromise. They wash up and eat from their provisions, and then they're back on the road again until the sun sets. Phainon still talks too much, and little of it is of substance. Slowly, the scenery changes from woods to meadows with a handful of autumn-blooming species, though most plants in the area have long since photosynthesized their last.

The temperature starts to drop; Phainon pulls on his dirtied coat. Mydei feels it less than he would have, once upon a time.

Before the sun can disappear behind distant mountains, they make camp for the night. Mydei finds a spot with even enough ground and a spot nearby to hitch Strife. Before they lose the light, they gather firewood and pick rocks off the ground to to lay their bedrolls. As Mydei prepares a fire, he catches the sound of Phainon chuckling. He looks up. "What is it?"

"Nothing," Phainon says, but he smiles a little as he comes beside the fire pit with the meat and mushrooms. "Nothing, just... What happened to walking well into the night? Did you lie to scare me away, Mydeimos?"

Mydei frowns as he arranges logs for the fire. "I won't strain Strife. Your well-being is of little consequence."

"Of course, of course," Phainon agrees, waving his injured hand. He pulls his knife from his belt again, unwrapping the meat and cutting it into smaller pieces as Mydei works on the fire. "I don't have a pot, by the way," he says. "They take up far too much space. So there won't be stew unless you have one. I was thinking we'd have skewers. There's salt in my bag."

Salt is a valuable resource on the road. "Save it," Mydei tells him. "Chances are, you'll have more need of it later."

Phainon hums, a little awkward as he holds the meat in place with the fingers of his left hand hardly bent. "Then I'll buy more," he says. "You're welcome to what I have now."

Stubborn. Strange. Plenty of humans are indifferent or even friendly to him; not every town is like the one from before, cursing and spitting at him. Many respect and fear in equal measure, some celebrate witchers as heroes, but none are this audacious, acting like they're friends. "HKS," Mydei murmurs under his breath, digging for his tinderbox.

Phainon pauses, cocking his head. "What was that?" he asks.

"Kremnoan language," Mydei tells him, striking sparks until the flame catches. "It isn't a compliment."

Phainon steals a couple of the sticks Mydei gathered for the fire and skewers them through alternating bits of meat and mushroom. "No need to worry about me misunderstanding the intention behind the word; I know better than to expect anything positive to come from your mouth. What was it again? Hai...?"

Mydei exhales and doesn't answer, moving a burning twig to the other side of the fire to help it catch too. A few moments and it does, and then the fire is crackling and blazing, if only for a handful of moments until the kindling burns off. The heat is welcome, even if Mydei isn't terribly sensitive to the cold. He's seen the way Phainon has been shivering, though he doesn't concern himself with it. Now, firelight flickers and dances across his face, casting shadows, making the contours of his smile terribly obvious.

"Come on, say it again," Phainon prompts, "or are you worried about hurting my feelings?"

"I wonder how you haven't been killed in a bar fight," Mydei tells him.

"What?" Phainon laughs too loudly for the night, for the kind of company he's keeping.

"With your mouth and your audacity, surely someone's tried to put you in your place?"

Again, he laughs, finished with preparing a skewer and offering it without a hint of a grudge. "Oh sure, they've tried," he says, "but I'm quite capable, you know. Perhaps I can't compare to a witcher yet, but what common drunkard fights as well as I do?"

The fire pops; some of the wood Mydei gathered was still wet from the earlier rain. Phainon's still holding the skewer out. Reluctantly, he takes it. "Yet," he repeats.

Phainon shoves meat onto another stick, smiles. "What, you think I can't do it? I know you went easy on me earlier, but keep in mind I had just run for however long to catch up to you. Besides, I said I was going to get stronger, didn't I? It's not like I'm at my peak."

Grunting, Mydei holds his skewer over the fire. "You assume I won't improve at the same time you do." Quiet, but for the crackle of the fire. Phainon keeps his head tipped down to look at his work as he assembles his skewer. The fire casts shadows, so Mydei can't make out his expression.

"The way you said that makes it sound like you believe me," Phainon says, only looking up when he's done, holding his laden stick over the fire. He shifts a little, planting a hand and foot on the ground to get more comfortable. At his side, there's enough meat and mushrooms for seconds and thirds.

"I've seen your stubbornness," Mydei says.

"My resolve," Phainon corrects. He shifts again, moving the blade of his knife into the fire to sanitize it. Mydei turns his skewer ninety degrees and looks at the fire instead of his ever present smile. "Admit it, you've decided I have what it takes. Why else would you have let me come with you?"

"Don't flatter yourself," Mydei says.

"But I've kept up, haven't I? I might've lost that spar earlier, but I surprised you, I saw it. And I've made myself useful; you didn't even have to lift a finger for this meal. Whatever kind of weakling you think I am, I'm going to keep proving you wrong."

He goes quiet again. The sun has fully set, and they're shrouded in darkness, but for the unsteady light of the flames. Like this, letting silence sit between his words, he's a little bit less annoying than he had been during the day. And Mydei will admit—if only within the safety of his own mind—that he is starting to respect Phainon. Mydei turns his skewer again, listening to the fire hiss as a bit of fat drips onto the logs. 

"Anyone can last a day," he says. "You'd best prove first that you can last when things become difficult. Then we'll see whether you have what it takes."

"And I do," Phainon says firmly. A moment passes, two. He turns his skewer over and squints in the firelight. Their eyes meet. He bumps Mydei's stick with his own and says, "I'm putting salt on this no matter what you say. Are you sure you don't want any?"

And Mydei, pinched and grumbling and uneager to change his mind, also quite likes salt. Phainon awkwardly and one-handedly digs a small jar of it out of his bag, holding it up with eyebrows raised, and Mydei has a difficult time being stubborn about this.

When they're done cooking and Phainon is sprinkling a bit over his skewer, Mydei sinks his teeth into his cheek and holds a reluctant hand out. Phainon laughs and laughs and laughs, and Mydei's face grows hot and embarrassed, but Phainon passes the jar over, and Mydei doesn't speak as he takes it.

The skewers, he has to admit—hunted, prepared, and seasoned by someone else as they are—are not bad. He doesn't have to ask for a second one before it's pressed into his hand. And this time, Phainon does not laugh.

Chapter End Notes

lore concoction volume 1: Instead of medallions, witchers in this universe are distinguished by their markings. They can sense magic through them, and the more they have, the more mutations they've been through and the stronger they are. Regular tattoos are highly stigmatized because of witchers, so Phainon doesn't have the sun marking on his neck.

Also!! Witchers do still have one steel sword (for people) and one silver (for monsters) in this universe, but Mydei is quirky and has his gauntlets instead. Suspend your disbelief about how impractical that is for combat.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

He wakes with some difficulty, sore and aching all over. His feet are blistered, he's bruised from sparring Mydeimos, and as used to travel as he is, it's always rough on the body. But the sun comes up, and he's a fairly light sleeper. Mydeimos wakes the moment they have a hint of light, and he isn't exactly silent as he packs up his bedroll and takes care of his horse.

Phainon doesn't allow himself to linger for fear of being left behind. Not that he's certain he would be. Mydeimos seems to be letting him tag along, after all, as obvious as it is that Phainon wears on his nerves. Still, he shouldn't test his luck.

Three more breaths, cozy and warm and blissfully horizontal, and then Phainon peels his eyes open and pushes himself up.

There are the remnants of last night's fire, the leftover imprint in the earth where Mydeimos' bedroll had been. Phainon forces himself up and slides back into his boots. It takes him more hassle than it should to roll his bed back up, and then he's swishing the gross feeling out of his mouth and going through his pack and pockets to make sure he has all his things.

Back to him, a dozen yards away, Mydeimos brushes Strife. His hair is tied back, and he hasn't put on his armor yet—which sits in a pile by Strife's saddle on the ground—leaving him in simple trousers. Without his gauntlets, his markings reach all the way down to the backs of his hands. In the stories, the more markings, the more mutations a witcher has undergone. Phainon isn't sure how much truth there is to that, but it would make sense. Mydeimos the Undying is all marked up, and notorious for being one of the strongest witchers alive. Not that there are many.

"You're awake," he says as Phainon approaches, not bothering to turn. She's a horse, but Phainon is fairly certain Strife gives him a look. "Good. If you can't rise with the sun, you have no business traveling under it."

"'Good,' he says, almost like a little part of him would be sad if I proved not to be able to keep up," Phainon teases. Mydeimos turns to him, not impressed at all. Phainon offers a smile. "I'll grow on you like a fungus, Mydeimos. You'll have to be careful if you want to maintain your mysterious aura."

"A particularly stubborn fungus," he sighs. "I hold no fondness for your persistence. I'm leaving in twenty minutes. Do with that as you will."

"We're leaving in twenty minutes," Phainon corrects. "Let me take a leak and I'll figure out breakfast." He's careful not to limp on his way into the trees, feeling Mydei's eyes on him. He'll get used to it, but now he's stiff from sleep and all of his pains feel especially prominent.

He takes care of his business, and when he comes back, Mydeimos has disappeared somewhere, though he's left Strife—groomed and re-saddled, the armor pile gone and presumably but back on—so Phainon isn't worried that he won't come back.

As he waits, he takes care of his hand, cleaning and re-bandaging it with a bit of salve, testing the way the scabs pull at his skin when he flexes his hand. It still hurts, especially since he'd ripped it open again, but it's better than the day before. 

He's quick with everything else he does to prepare himself for the day, mindful of the time limit Mydeimos set that he isn't interested in testing. When he's ready and still waiting, he heads back into the trees for a couple of late season elderberries he'd spotted on his trip to relieve himself. They won't be able to cook them or have them as any kind of substantial snack without getting an upset stomach, but a few here and there won't cause any problems. And they're sweet, a bit of a luxery on the road.

They return to camp at the same time. Phainon gets barely a glance as Mydeimos goes straight for Strife, unhitching her. "We're leaving," he calls. Phainon is quick to follow.

"We're," he repeats, "you said we're leaving. It looks like I really am growing on you."

Mydeimos glances at him out of the corner of his eye, and maybe it's the way the sun hasn't finished coming up, but Phainon could swear he smiles a little. "I meant Strife and myself," he says. "You're welcome to come along, if you want."

"Even then," Phainon says, wrapping his arms around himself against the slight morning chill. "Since when was I welcome? I think you really do like me, Mydeimos."

There's no reply. Mydeimos double checks his saddlebags and hoists himself onto Strife's back. He's off without another word, Phainon scrambling to get his pack on his shoulders as he keeps up. "Mydeimos," he says, jogging a bit. He has Strife walking a bit fast, if only to make it uncomfortable for Phainon to keep pace. "Is that what you usually go by? Or is there a nickname you use with friends? Deimos? De? Or...?"

A sharp glance. This one doesn't hold a shred of humor, and Phainon wonders if he's somehow stumbled upon a sore spot. But then Mydeimos sighs and faces the road ahead again. "Mydei," he says, "if you must shorten my name, call me Mydei."

"Mydei," Phainon repeats. "It has a nice ring to it."

A grunt. Mydei seems content to leave the conversation there. Phainon lets him, if only for a while. Speed walking as he is, some warmth makes its way back into his muscles. With each step, he gets a little more used to the soreness, though the bottoms of his feet are still tender and he finds himself a bit out of breath.

A little longer. "Do you like elderberries?"

Mydei replies without looking at him, "They'll make you sick."

"Only if you eat a lot. Look, I found some earlier, and you've insisted upon taking off before breakfast. Would you care for a couple? They're sweet."

The silence that comes is a long, long one. And then Mydei holds out a hand, slowing Strife to a pace Phainon can comfortably walk alongside. Phainon tries very hard not to laugh, breaking a cluster off and passing it over. "Don't eat too many; weren't you just worried about getting sick?"

A scoff. Mydei sits back in the saddle, plucking a couple of berries. "There is no word for 'sick' in the Kremnoan language," he says. "I regularly drink potions that could kill a man in seconds flat when I fight monsters; what is a handful of elderberries going to do to me?"

"Nothing I suppose," Phainon concedes, this time failing not to laugh a little. "I'm sure your mutations will protect you, but I can't say the same for a fragile human like me."

Mydei doesn't seem amused by this, but he's never amused by anything, so Phainon doesn't take it personally.

"Say, what business do you have in Okhema anyway? Is there a job waiting for you?" he asks after a while.

Mydei turns to him, frowning. "That's my business," he says, signaling an end to the exchange.

Phainon sighs. "'My business,' he says," he murmurs under his breath. Mydei hears. Obviously, he hears.

They walk on. Strife stays at a slow pace, and his muscles have finally warmed up enough for him to fall into a steady rhythm that only hurts his legs and feet a little. But he's good at enduring, so he doesn't say a thing.

The sun comes the rest of the way up. The road ahead angles into an incline, veering farther away from the main river, though there shouldn't be any shortage of small streams for them to get water from. A breeze whistles through colored leaves and stalks of dying grass. Phainon takes a deep breath and gets nothing but horse. He wrinkles his nose and resigns himself to another day.

△

"How about we play a game to pass the time faster?" Phainon asks later. It's midday now; the sun hangs high overhead, and it's warm enough that he's shed his coat. Mydei is... unclothed as always. "I ask a question and you answer, and then you ask a question and I do."

"What part of that makes it a game?" Mydei asks. Just yesterday he likely wouldn't have replied at all. His response to no response ratio is getting much better the more Phainon wears him down. Now, he only ignores him about half the time, instead of all of it.

"We can reward points for interesting answers, or for interesting questions. At the end of the game, whoever has the most points wins."

Mydei is walking now, having dismounted Strife earlier to give her a rest and to stretch his legs. His armored feet are loud on the dirt road. He gives Phainon a look. "And who makes the score? It's hardly fair if we do it ourselves, and there's no point in winning. No, HKS. You're not asking to play a game, you're asking for a conversation."

He has to laugh, incredulous and irritated both at the thorough, brutal criticism. "You caught me! I wanted to converse with my traveling companion, how unthinkable! Honestly, don't you get bored of the silence? Don't you ever have fun?"

Were Phainon on his own, he'd be singing to pass the time, or creating scenes in his head and narrating them aloud in dramatic voices. Somehow, he doesn't think Mydei would appreciate this. He's been trying, as best as he can, to respect the peace, to respect Mydei's space and silence. He'll let the air sit empty for hours, but now and then he wants to talk, to get to know and learn from this person he's scrapped his plans—however flimsy they were—to follow. It's frustrating that this is the response he always seems to get.

Mydei looks at him, and almost seems to hesitate for a moment. And then, "No," is the reply.

Phainon exhales, defeated. "Really?"

"Really."

He goes quiet, watching his feet on the road, boots covered in dust. A glance at Mydei shows him staring resolutely ahead. Phainon follows the markings from his arm to his shoulder, beneath red-tipped hair. He wants to be friends, Titans above. It feels like it's been so long since he truly had one of those.

"Do you never get lonely?" he asks next without thinking.

A branch snaps beneath one of Strife's hooves. Mydei is quiet long enough for Phainon to regret asking. It came out too serious, not like he was joking or teasing. He's talking to a witcher. A witcher that has come to tolerate him and maybe even respect him a little, but certainly doesn't consider him a friend, let alone some kind of confidant. It's a weird thing to ask anyway. But then Mydei speaks.

"Is that your first question?"

"Is that..." Phainon trails off when the realization hits. He doesn't comment or make a big deal out of it, though he wants to. Three days of knowing each other has been enough for him to know that Mydei will take back any olive branch offered if made to regret it even a little bit. Phainon clears his throat. "Yes, it is."

"No, then," Mydei says. "I don't get lonely."

The road starts to angle back toward the river. Strife huffs, and the timing makes it seem like a reaction.

"I don't believe you," Phainon says. "And it sounds like Strife doesn't either."

A glare. "She's a horse," Mydei says. "Horses do that."

Again, Strife huffs, tossing her head a little this time. Phainon laughs. Mydei scowls.

"Well, it's your turn to ask a question," Phainon offers instead of pressing, because again, he's aware he's walking on a fine line. It's a miracle Mydei has even agreed to this at all. The fact of it makes him forget the pain in his feet.

Mydei is quiet for a while, and Phainon gives him his silence until he finally asks, "Why are you so determined to get stronger?"

Phainon hums. "Good question. That's one point for you," he says. Mydei grunts. "Do you want the long story or the short one?"

"The true one."

Phainon kicks a pebble, watches it skitter. He offers a smile. "Childish fancy. I've wanted to be a hero since I was a boy, but a hero needs strength if he's going to save anyone."

"The true one, HKS," Mydei says. "Childish fancy dies the moment your back hits the dirt."

"There are layers to any story," Phainon says. He watches Mydei's eyebrows knit, then lets his gaze float over the dry, trampled grasses fringing the edge of the road. "I didn't lie to you. Look, your horse agrees."

"I repeat," Mydei says, reaching to pat Strife with his hand wrapped in her lead. "She is a horse. Unless you fancy yourself some kind of lunatic who can speak to animals?"

"That would be a wonderful ability for the hero in a storybook," Phainon muses. "Which I desperately long to be." He finds himself smiling a little at the unimpressed stare it earns him, both from Mydei and the horse. His chest gives a soft, bittersweet pang. How he misses his town. How he misses his people. Play pretend with the children and preparing for the fall harvest with his parents, ruminating on dreams and divinations. But all of those things are gone now, and he can never have them back.

"So you've trained yourself to fight and endure harsh conditions so you can what? Rescue damsels in distress and slay dragons in towers?" 

"I'm hardly at dragon slaying level yet, though I appreciate the confidence," Phainon laughs, much to Mydei's obvious frustration. "But like I said, there are layers to any story. Perhaps another question could scope them out. But alas, it's my turn."

"Ask, then," Mydei says. "You've earned no points from me."

"I'll accept the loss if I must. For my next question... Why don't you ever hide your markings? Wouldn't it be easier to just wear a big robe into town so you can stop to rest and restock before you look for work? I imagine it's much easier if they can't tell you're a witcher, based on our last stop."

But Mydei's answer is simple. "I've no interest in being treated kindly by someone who would take it back the moment they know who I am."

Who, he'd said, not what. Phainon looks at him again. The markings, the gauntlets, the hardened set of his face. "Another point," he says. "I like your answer. What use does good will have if it comes from a place of insincerity?" He picks at his bandages, thinking about that old village full of bitter souls. A prickle of leftover anger. He's still mad about that wood chopping incident.

"Is that hand bothering you?" Mydei asks.

"Huh?" Phainon looks at it, but the bandage hasn't bled through or anything. It's a bit dirty, stained in elderberry juice and browned in places where he'd touched a rock or a tree or something else. "Oh, no, it's fine. Just a bit inconvenient, is all."

But Mydei is kind of glaring at him, a furrow forming between his brows as he sighs and brings Strife to a stop. "Hold it out," he says.

"Uh. Pardon?"

"Hold it out," Mydei repeats, turning to face him fully. "Otherwise it'll get infected and you'll only become a liability."

Tentatively, Phainon holds his injured hand out. "And what exactly are you planning to do to prevent that? 'Cause it's a bit late, really, ah—!" Mydei snatches Phainon's hand none too gently, the metal of his gauntlets poking unpleasantly and scraping as he undoes the bandage. Phainon fights himself not to wince, shoulders up to his ears. "I'd love an explanation, if you would."

"Quiet," Mydei says, shoving the bandage out the way until the mess of scabs is visible, cracked and ugly but hardly debilitating. And then he forms a shape with his fingers and murmurs something under his breath, and the wound starts to knit itself back together, itching horribly in the process. Phainon yanks his hand back, and Mydei lets him go.

"What..." He holds his palm up in front of him, turning it over as it continues to tingle, the scabs falling away to reveal plain, albeit lightly scarred, skin. He glances at Mydei. "How did you do that?"

"The Sign of Aquila," Mydei tells him. "It heals small wounds." Uncaring of Phainon's confused awe, he resumes walking, patting Strife on the neck before he tugs on her lead. He turns his head when Phainon falls behind a handful of steps. "Do you want to be left there?" he calls out. Phainon swiftly jogs to catch up.

"No," he says, still gaping at his hand. "No, I'm just very confused, but... thank you. Why did you do it?" And why didn't you do it earlier? he doesn't ask. He closes his palm, opens it again, and finds not an ounce of pain.

"So you won't become a liability," Mydei says, and it's a flimsy excuse at best. Phainon had already given him permission to leave him behind if he proves unable to keep up, and a tiny thing like that wouldn't take him out, even if it did get infected. Most likely.

"I see," Phainon says, though he doesn't. He balls up the old bandage and buries it in his pocket, still baffled by the way he can move his hand without any discomfort. He lifts his gaze to Mydei's back, his tattoos converging in the dip of his spine. "Thank you," he tries, wondering why Mydei had done it at all, after everything from the two days before.

Behind as he is, he can't see Mydei's face. There's no real reply, just a noncommittal grunt, and Phainon jogs a little more so they can walk side by side. There's an odd silence, the air awkward now. Phainon clears his throat. "You know... it's your turn to ask a question."

△

It's maddeningly monotonous, walking for hours on end, but Phainon is used to the physical suffering of it and has a mind capable of keeping itself entertained. For the most part. Mydei serves as a conversation partner at times, and not at others. He shuts it down quickly the moment Phainon decides to sing a bit, because apparently having fun is a crime. So he alternates between thinking hundreds of thoughts that stay in his head and gambling with the odds of getting a response to the ones he decides to share aloud.

Slowly but surely, that ratio gets better and better. Now, Mydei answers to more than half of the things he says, and it feels delightfully like progress.

As they break for lunch, he chews on a slightly stale butt of bread and watches Mydei eat on a rock a dozen meters away. How can I make you like me? he wonders, a twisting feeling in his gut. What will it take to be your friend?

It's only been a few days. Mydei healed him, Mydei answers more often, Mydei has stopped making it sound like he's going to leave Phainon behind if he takes an extra minute to piss behind a tree before they take off. But... this is the closest he's ever come to his goal. Without Mydei, he doesn't have the slightest clue how to get to Castrum Kremnos. No one does. And the odds of Phainon finding another witcher willing to let him tag along are slim to none.

He needs, desperately, to be liked. He doesn't know how to cope without it. Maybe he's being irrational, especially now that they've evolved into something close enough to friendly, but he can't shake the feeling.

Several more long hours of walking, and they break for the night.

There isn't much cover where they are. The landscape has shifted from woods and meadows to sparser plains, populated with grasses and shrubs and what would be beautiful swathes of wildflowers were it spring. Instead, it's mostly brown and wilting, and Phainon struggles to forage, though he manages to dig up a fistful of dandelion root and catch a dove.

Mydei, again, builds the fire. As the sun sets, it turns cold again, and even with his coat, Phainon feels the chill. As he comes back, he passes Strife hitched nearby, a blanket thrown over her back. The flames are already roaring, and it's a relief to come back to the warmth. He drops the dove in Mydei's lap and finds his things on the ground, leaving the roots in a safe spot as he starts picking through the dirt and grass for rocks things that might poke him when he lays down in his bedroll for the night.

"You don't need to share if you're going to hunt," Mydei says, though he's begun to pluck the feathers from the bird so it can be cooked.

"Mhm, and I take it you don't want any salt on your portion either?" Phainon asks, standing and wiping his hands on his pants when he's satisfied that he won't be terribly uncomfortable in that spot. He spreads his bedroll out, careful not to get his boots on it.

There's no response, so he looks up. Carefully, Mydei watches him. "You never learned to take care of yourself first, did you?" he asks, but it doesn't quite sound like a question. Phainon frowns.

"You make it sound like generosity is a bad trait. I have enough provisions to get me to the next town; hunting is only saving me a bit of coin. It's not as if I'm sacrificing my own well-being in any way."

"It's foolish," Mydei says anyway, though he turns his gaze back down and continues plucking feathers. The fire dances on his face, deep shadows filling the furrow in his brow and the downward tilt of his mouth. "I can provide for myself."

Smoothing out the wrinkles, Phainon finally sits, stretching his cold hands to the heat of the flames. "Think of it as a debt repaid, if you can't accept a favor between friends." he says. "For allowing me to tag along, and for healing my hand. And no, I'm not trying to bribe you in hopes that you'll teach me to fight and take me to Castrum Kremnos. I intend to prove I deserve those things with my strength, not petty favors."

"I see," Mydei says, and looks away. Phainon watches him a little longer and sighs, dropping his hands to his thighs when the heat of the fire becomes too much. As Mydei starts preparing the meat, he looks for a couple of suitable sticks to cook it on.

They feast on salted dove, dandelion root, stale bread, and the last few elderberries in Phainon's pockets. All things considered, it isn't the worst meal Phainon has had on the road. He'd been hungrier than he thought, anyway.

His gaze keeps finding its way to Mydei, lit by the firelight. Respect the quiet, he thinks to himself. He opens his mouth to speak, remembers, and closes it again.

"If you have something to say, just say it," Mydei says without looking up. At Phainon's inhale, his silence, he sighs and lifts his head. "I can smell it," he says, gesturing vaguely, "whatever inner turmoil it is that you're experiencing right now."

"Ah." Phainon purses his lips. "Well, it's nothing. Do you think we'll make it to town tomorrow?"

Mydei's eyes narrow, but he doesn't press. Phainon can't imagine a world where he does. "We should make it by midday," he says. "Assuming you don't fall behind."

"Still on that, are you?" Phainon asks. "Haven't I proved myself well enough?"

The fire crackles. Mydei's eyes look like molten gold. "We'll see."

Chapter End Notes

Lore concoction volume 2: Witchers are born human and then undergo trials and mutations throughout childhood. Only the strongest survive and come out as witchers. Castrum Kremnos is where this takes place, and where witchers go in the winter—Kremnos is Kaer Morhen if you know the source material. Witchers have gold blood, while humans (*cough* Phainon) bleed red. I've also given Mydei high cold/heat tolerance so he can be half naked all the time as he's meant to be.

Signs are simple spells witchers can cast. In the source there are 5 basic ones, but this is my au and I make the rules so there's one for each Titan!

more on Signs

All of this will be included in later chapters as each Sign is used if you want to learn about witchers as Phainon does, but here's what each Sign does. How powerful they are depends on the strength/magical ability of both the caster and the
casted-on. Mydei is pretty weak on the magical front; most of his strength comes from brute force, not Signs.

Aquila: Heals small injuries. Casting it on a large wound can help in some capacity but repeated use has no greater effect.

Cerces: Clears the mind, but without meditation or other techniques, the thoughts can come right back.

Georios: Essentially Quen; forms a protective shield to block attacks from the user.
