Janus: Works as a tracking spell if you have something with a connection to whatever's being tracked and are within a few miles of them/it.

Kephale: Provides a temporary strength boost.

Mnestia: Charms someone to make them feel calm and happy.

Nikador: Mydei's red crystal things that canon never explained. Works to create an emergency weapon by drawing on the user's energy to make a sharp crystal.

Oronyx: Immobilizes whatever it's used on for a short time.

Phagousa: Counters charms and illusions.

Talanton: Creates a "law" both the caster and casted on have to obey. Something like "this can not be spoken of again" would swear both to silence. The less likely both parties are to follow the "law" the less effective it is.

Thanatos: Takes the pain away from something on the brink of death.

Zagreus: Makes someone more likely to believe whatever you're saying. Usually used for lies, but can also enforce the truth.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
chapters.html:
They make it to town on schedule. Phainon wakes the moment Mydei does, and they pack up camp and have breakfast as they walk. It's a few hours of travel, and the closer they get, the more people they start to see. There aren't nearly as many as there will be on the road to Okhema, as this is just a small town on the way, but there are some. Most steer clear as they spot the markings on Mydei's body, but none express any kind of hostility, which makes him think this village might be a bit more welcoming than the last.

Phainon is quiet at times, and not at others. It's a blessing and a curse, what with the way he's terribly annoying and makes the time pass faster all the same. What with the way Mydei likes the silence to hear his own thoughts and yet finds himself wondering when Phainon will deign to fill it next. He smells odd during these spells when he's quiet. Not like fear but something faintly anxious. Mydei does not ask him about it.

"You go first," Mydei says as they approach the gates, slowing Strife. But Phainon slows too, and turns to him with a frown.

"What do you mean, I should go first?"

Mydei frowns back at him, his dirty hair and road-worn clothes, blue eyes squinting against the sun. He's so wholly, obviously human. One look at Mydei, and he's anything but. "It'll be easier for you," he says vaguely, and dismounts so he can walk Strife to the stables. His feet meet the earth with a metallic sound from his armor. Phainon is still standing in place, eyebrows furrowed. Mydei sighs. "HKS. Don't you want a bed and a warm bath? Just go."

"And have you sneak off to the Holy City without me? Oh no, I think not," Phainon says. He sticks by Mydei's side as he resumes walking, too stubborn for this own good. Even if this town is nicer than the last, standing too close to a witcher is unlikely to make him any friends. But what does it matter.

"There might be work," Mydei says, "I'm staying at least a day."

"Yes, and you're taking me with you."

Another hundred meters. A man with a wagon comes through the gate, and already they get a long, lingering stare. Phainon doesn't seem to care about the attention. Mydei sighs, feels a headache coming on. "Suit yourself."

Inside, the town is small and busy, the day's activities in full swing. They pass people hanging laundry, churning butter, children playing in the street. All stop and look, the same as they do anywhere. Mydei knows he's conspicuous, armor catching the light and clanking softly with each step, gauntlets sharp and menacing, torso half bare to show the markings labeling him as something other than them. Mydei has long since grown used to it. Phainon, however, has not.

"I hope my hair looks alright," he says. "They're all staring; is this how you're usually received?"

Mydei's mouth quirks at the corner. "Sometimes with cheers, sometimes with stones, but yes, always with stares." He glances at Phainon, finds his hair a mess, a couple of sections standing up as stubbornly as him, and feels the urge to laugh. "They're not looking at you."

"Oh they most certainly are," Phainon says. "You know I went to school in my hometown for a while. I was debate champion; with all these eyes on me, I'm reminded of that."

Strife snorts, aware of the attention too. Mydei pats her neck. "I told you it'd be easier if you went ahead," he says, sparing Phainon a glance and finding him already looking back.

"And I'll have you know I'm quite alright with being gawked at," Phainon says, "so long as my hair looks alright. Did you say you're sometimes greeted with cheers?"

"Rarely," Mydei admits, "but some places teach that witchers are heroes." He hesitates. "I had wondered if you came from one."

Dozens and dozens of eyes. Phainon keeps nodding and smiling at everyone who looks at him, acting like this is some kind of parade or festive homecoming. It's almost funny. Tentatively, a young boy waves back, hiding behind his father's leg.

"I didn't," Phainon says. "We never had any witchers come around where I'm from. The topic didn't come up much, but when it did, it wasn't particularly positive. I remember playing pretend with a couple of my friends as a boy; I was a Chimera, one of my friends was a priestess of Oronyx, and the other wanted to be a witcher, fighting monsters and such. When his mother caught wind of the game, she dragged him home by the ear and he wasn't allowed to play for a week."

Mydei is quiet, listening to this. It's hard to imagine children playing pretend as witchers, hard to imagine after being forced to go through all the trials and mutations himself. He probably hadn't been much older than the boy from Phainon's memory when he'd been cast out by his father, forced to fight day after day, fevered and drugged up on alchemical concoctions, forced to sit and watch his own body and senses change while he didn't have a choice in the matter.

It's always kids, plucked away to be turned into witchers. The thought of some, safe and happy and healthy in their loving homes and villages, role playing children turned into men turned into monsters... He barely remembers his own childhood. All that's left of it sits in the form of a yellowed piece of parchment tucked into one of Strife's saddlebags. A letter from his mother. The purpose of this whole detour before he returns to Kremnos for the winter.

"There's nothing fun about being a witcher," Mydei says, grip tightening on Strife's bridle. He keeps his gaze firmly ahead, catching sight of what looks like an inn with a stable. "His mother was right to scold him."

"Maybe," Phainon muses, dropping his hand after waving to a cluster of whispering teenagers. "He was a kid, though. What kid doesn't like to play pretend at saving cities and beautiful young priestesses? A witcher's job isn't too far off, when it comes down to it."

He's looking at Mydei as he says this. His eyes are a clear sky blue. "I suppose not," Mydei concedes, and turns away.

"You, mister, are you a witcher?" comes a voice, an out of breath man running up to them, clothe splattered in dirt. He wears a hat, which he takes off and folds to his chest as he stops in front of them, halting their progress toward the stable. Mydei cocks his head, leveling the man with a stare.

"I am," he says, and watches as the man sighs with relief.

"Good," he says, still catching his breath. Again, "Good. We've a need for your work here. There's a devil haunting these parts!"

"A devil?" Mydei repeats, eyeing the dirt streaked across the man's clothes. Less like a rough day in the fields, more like someone had thrown balls of mud at him.

"Yes, sir," he confirms. "It's been playing pranks and stealing and wreaking havoc. Not one of us can chase it out; it's got all the powers of a devil and more! We'll pay for your services, of course."

At his side, Phainon looks between Mydei and the man, eyes wide, entire body perked up. "A devil?" he asks. "Devils are real? And there's one here? Has anyone been hurt?"

The man turns his attention to Phainon, a flicker of confusion in his face before he deigns to answer. "Hurt? No, not quite, but dozens are going hungry and more have had their most precious possessions taken from them! Something needs to be done right away before the situation can get worse!"

"And how do you know its a devil?" Mydei asks. "Has anyone actually seen it?"

This makes the man splutter. "It's an elusive creature!" he says. "It might not have shown its face, but we'd recognize the work of a devil like this one. Trust me when I say that's what it is, Sir Witcher."

Mydei grunts and rubs along the back of Strife's neck as she sniffs at something on the ground. "My horse needs to be stabled," he says. "I need a meal and a bath." The man opens his mouth to protest, but Mydei raises a hand. "Where should I go to discuss business when I'm finished?"

The man hesitates, conflicted but desperate enough and afraid enough not to fight Mydei on this. "You'll want the mayor's house," he says. "She's two blocks down this road to the left. Big white building with lots of flowers; you can't miss it."

Mydei nods, bids him a good day, and guides Strife along past him without another word. Phainon is quick to keep up.

"Shouldn't you treat this with a little more urgency?" he asks, frowning. "He said people are starving; can't a bath wait while you take care of the devil?"

"Devils aren't real," Mydei says simply, and brings Strife to a scared-looking stablehand who keeps their exchange to as few words as possible, if only because anything out of his mouth comes out as a stutter. Mydei passes over a few coins, and when the stablehand takes Strife's lead rope, she snorts, and he jumps even at this, as if a horse could somehow have witcher powers too.

"Well, whatever it is, it's bad enough for them to call it a devil," Phainon says. A pause, during which he practically radiates disapproval. Mydei makes his way to the entrance of the inn. The footsteps by his side come to a halt. It's a mistake to turn, but he does anyway.

"Do you really not care, Mydeimos?" Phainon asks, the deep lines of his frown etched into his face. "Isn't this your job?"

And somehow he actually manages to make Mydei feel a little bit guilty. And for what? He sighs. "I care, or I wouldn't help at all," he says. "This creature is playing petty pranks and stealing trinkets, all of which are likely easily recoverable wherever they've taken up residence. No one is in any real danger, and I need a bath. If you're so worried, feel free to find the mayor yourself."

He hasn't bothered with trying to be convincing. Still, Phainon's expression softens with something like understanding. "You're not worried at all," he says. "No, I'm sure you know all about stakes with your experience. What makes you so sure this isn't more dangerous than it sounds?"

"It isn't hard to narrow the possibilities down when you've encountered as many monsters as I have," Mydei tells him. "Whatever this is, if it hasn't hurt a soul so far, it won't. And whatever damage it does cause is reversible enough. Besides—" He laughs roughly. "—There's no way a little town like this is going to pay me enough to rush out without so much as a meal."

△

"You are not to kill her under any circumstances," says the mayor, seated across from him in a white, upholstered armchair. She'd been tall when she greeted them at the door, with green eyes and neatly curled blonde hair. She dresses in white and gold, similar to the aesthetics of her home, surrounded in crisp white autumn roses, wooden floors covered by intricate, pale toned rugs, accents around the place painted as close to gold as one can get without the accompanying wealth.

There doesn't seem to be a single servant in the house that Mydei can spot signs of, and a large loom on one side of the room suggests that she'd woven the rugs and the tapestries on the walls herself. Mydei finishes appraising the place and returns his attention to her, the mayor who introduced herself as Aglaea at the door.

"That's the first I've heard gotten request," he says. "I don't tend to kill when it isn't necessary, but what does it matter to you whether this 'devil' lives or dies, when either way is a means to an end?"

She smiles slightly. It's a strange smile, a cold smile. "Perhaps I've grown fond of the creature," she says blandly. "All I ask is that you chase her away, unharmed if possible. The townsfolk here and I have put together a fund to pay for your services. Will fifty balance coins be enough?"

"Fifty?" Mydei laughs. "This creature is dangerous and stubborn, you've said, and has stolen hundreds of coins worth of precious heirlooms, and all your entire town can scrape together to solve the problem is fifty balance coins?" He leans back on the stiff sofa, arms crossed. "I'm sure you're stretched thin, just like everyone else, but fifty coins is an insult to my profession."

"Wells, then—" Aglaea smiles tightly "—I apologize if I've offended you, but fifty coins as payment was tradition amongst witchers at one point, was it not? This town is far from wealthy and behind on the times; we're unable to muster up much more than that."

"Fifty was customary once, sure," Mydei tells her. "But that was generations ago, when it didn't cost half as much as it does now to buy a cup in a tavern. No, since I understand this is a difficult time for all of us, I'll be content with a hundred."

Her smile grows thin. She smooths her fingers over her skirt, one leg crossed over the other. "A hundred balance coins is two or three weeks work for a man here," she says, measured. "I don't imagine you'll need more than two days to take care of our problem."

"My work is difficult, hard to find anywhere else, and will save your people from far more than two weeks of suffering."

They hold each other's gazes for a time, and then Aglaea sighs. "Seventy-five pieces is the best we can do," she says.

"Seventy," Mydei tells her, because he's never been an unreasonable man. "But I'd like you to call in a favor. For tonight at least, I sleep for free."

"It seems we've found a generous witcher," Aglaea says, and stands delicately, offering a hand to shake like people so rarely do. There isn't a hint of fear in her scent. Most everyone else is at least a little bit wary. But not her, and not Phainon. "We have a deal."

"Indeed," Mydei says, and shakes on it. Her grip is surprisingly firm, and despite her elegant appearance, her hands are not soft. "Show me the spot, and I'll take care of it."

△

Entirely unsurprisingly, Phainon is waiting outside when he's finished in the mayor's home, busying himself by talking to a couple of children. He's squatting to be level with them, smiling in a way that scrunches up the corners of his eyes, and it makes sense that he likes children, what with how much he's like one. Cheery and excitable and overly prone to pouting. These children, at least, seem to like him too.

Mydei catches a bit of their conversation. Something about how not everything that looks scary actually is scary. When Phainon sees Mydei, he pats the children on their heads and sends them off, to a chorus of protests. Mydei waits a handful of paces away, arms folded, until they leave.

"I thought I told you to wait back at the inn," he says.

"You did," Phainon agrees, straightening up and wiping his hands on his trousers. He's different after a bath. Less pungent, for one. Neater, brighter, hair mostly cooperating with him. He could pass for handsome. "But you'd have to walk a ways to fetch me before going off on your little adventure, so I figured I'd save you the trouble."

He's a bastard and he knows it, based on that gleam in his eye. Mydei can't even be mad. Can't do much more than give a dry laugh. "How generous of you," he says. Phainon's smile is triumphant as comes to Mydei's side, all but ready to skip off into the distance.

"That's me," he says. "Always generous, never getting in the way..."

"You're aware you could get hurt, yes?" Mydei asks, turning down the right street. Their destination is a barn at the far edge of town where the 'devil' has taken up residence, much to the frustration of the barn's actual owners. He's already packed his belt and satchel with potions and things he might need, but he isn't worried, since he just plans to scope the place out first. Still, with Phainon coming along... He's capable for a human, sure, but Mydei has never seen him up against magic, and he's loud and unarmed and might have all of the wrong instincts.

"Yes, I'm prepared for that," Phainon says, sobering. "But I need to learn somehow; it's the whole reason why I wanted to travel with you. And I can tell you don't think this 'devil' is particularly dangerous. Seems as good a starting point as any, don't you think?"

Mydei glances at him. A fresh long sleeved tunic to combat the slight chill, his same sturdy boots, covered in dust from the road to contrast his clean clothes. There's a choker around his throat that Mydei hasn't noticed before. Perhaps the collar of his other shirt is higher. Perhaps he's just usually wearing his coat. Mydei isn't sure why he notices at all. He watches Phainon swallow, notes that he'd shaved too.

"Just don't get in my way," he says.

A laugh, nervous now. "I wouldn't dream of it," Phainon says.

"I'm not going to protect you."

"Then it's a good thing that I'll just be... standing and observing this time."

Mydei lifts a brow. "Are you sure you can handle that?"

Phainon frowns. "I'm hurt by your utter lack of faith in me. I've proven myself these past days, have I not?" He finishes the sentence and almost trips on a rock. The timing is unfortunate enough to make Mydei laugh as Phainon clears his throat and dusts himself off though he'd gotten nothing on him.

He's such a fool, but... Anyone else, and Mydei wouldn't even consider allowing them to tag along, regardless of his perceived lack of danger for this particular job. Any number of things could happen. Any number of things could go wrong, and there are any number of ways to get hurt. With Phainon... perhaps he'll show his grit. Perhaps he'll have some sense knocked into him and he'll give up on following Mydei like some lost dog. Perhaps nothing will happen at all. Mydei finds himself strangely invested in the result.

"We'll see," is all he says. Phainon stinks like determination.

△

They make it to the barn without incident. It's simple and nondescript, tall and wooden, a few bales of hay stacked on one side beneath an attached roof. The doors are pulled shut, and the cobbled pathway is covered in random splatters of mud, wet and dried both, and Mydei is reminded of the man who had approached them for the job, dirtied from head to toe. Aglaea had said that their 'devil' hasn't responded well to the villagers' attempts to chase her out, though she hadn't mentioned the exact method of retaliation. Mydei's lips curl up.

He pauses as they approach, extending a hand to halt Phainon as well, tasting the air for any sign of danger and straining his ears for sound of it. He likely wouldn't catch much unless the air was reeking with blood or magic he'd feel through his markings first. As it is, he catches nothing with his nose, and though he strains his ears, there's nothing but wind and the soft sound of Phainon's breathing.

"If you're just watching, you might find a place to hide," he suggests, not sparing a glance as he continues forward, intending to examine the outside of the barn before he goes in. Footsteps come right alongside him.

"You think I'm going to hide?" Phainon asks, seemingly incredulous. "How am I supposed to learn anything peeking through the bushes? No, I'll risk a little action, thank you."

"Suit yourself," Mydei murmurs. "Just shut up and stay out of my way."

There's really nothing special about it. The barn doesn't bear any signs of damage aside from normal weathering. There are no magical traces to be found, and he doesn't smell blood or rot at any point around the building. Phainon follows with his arms crossed around himself, starting to shiver the moment they're out of the sun and in the shade of the barn. He seems to regret forgoing his coat, but he doesn't complain. Mydei's blood has been running hot for a long time, and he barely notices.

"What exactly are you looking for?" Phainon whispers. He's actually quiet about it, which is surprising for some reason. A regular human wouldn't have heard him, even this close, but he's aware that Mydei's senses are stronger.

Mydei shouldn't answer. Shouldn't make him feel like he's somehow part of this operation, shouldn't make him think that Mydei's willing to teach him what he wants to know, but...

"Signs," Mydei answers, pausing to check one of the muddied splotches on the ground. "Everything leaves them, and I've yet to decide exactly what species we're working with." We're, he'd said. If Phainon notices, he doesn't say anything.

"Magical signs?" Phainon asks, crouching beside him, watching as Mydei scrapes a bit of mud up with the sharp tip of one gauntleted finger. He smells it, senses it, and finds nothing out of the ordinary.

"Magical or non-magical," Mydei answers. "Anything that doesn't look like it was done by a human."

There's a pause, stretching. He wipes the mud from his finger. Phainon takes a breath. "Have you ever been asked to take care of a monster, only to find that it was human all along?" he asks.

Mydei looks up. Finds a faint shadow in his eyes. A flicker of movement. "I've killed humans, yes, if that's what your asking," he says carefully. Phainon's mouth parts, and he gets the sense that it's not. He watches, carefully still, as a hand reaches into one of Phainon's pockets. "Any kind of creature has the potential to be a monster. Sometimes humans are the most monstrous of all."

Phainon is frowning, but Mydei doesn't get the sense that he's upset by the admission that Mydei has killed men. No, it seems like something else. It always seems like something else, another layer behind every question he asks and smile he forces.

And then he gives a dull laugh and straightens up, that hand swiftly withdrawing. "I suppose you're right," he says. "I've certainly known some pretty monstrous individuals. Not that I've... well. Killed any, but I imagine the people you've had to deal with have been a measure or two worse than the ones I have. Big difference between... I don't know, murdering and refusing to pay a hired hand as promised. Not that... Mydei?"

He ends up as collateral damage. In the next instant, that hand comes back, silent and sneaky, attempting to dip back into Phainon's pocket after being startled by his movement. Mydei forms the Sign of Oronyx, which freezes them both in place so Mydei can launch himself at the thief. She's strong, though, and breaks free from the Sign in time to jump away before Mydei can grab her.

A Dolosian, judging by the feline ears and tail. Her hair is a gray mess, her short, hooded cloak tattered and stained, her gaze half feral. In one long-nailed hand is a something small and rectangular she must have stolen from Phainon, still frozen under the Sign as Mydei shoves past him to catch the withdrawing thief before she can get away.

She's fast, though. Terribly fast and shrewd and far more familiar with this area than Mydei is. She pulls ahead, unimpeded by the uneven terrain while Mydei's armored feet catch on stones and divots in the earth. She's too far for him to use another Sign on, so he uses the Sign of Kephale on himself, ignoring the strain of using the magic in the wake of the increased strength in his muscles, letting him push ahead that much faster.

Breathing hard, armor clanking, slowly gaining on the Dolosian, he stretches out one hand and catches her by the tail, yanking hard and sending them both crashing to the ground, rolling in dirt, grappling with each other. She shrieks sharply, scratching at him with her claws and drawing blood by his neck, teeth bared.

"Off," she hisses, trying to knee him in the groin, her back against the earth. Her eyes, clear blue, fill with a mix of terror and fury. "Get off!"

Mydei catches one of her wrists, then the other, pinning them hard by her shoulders. His own blood—spilling from the stinging scratches at the base of his throat—drips gold onto her already dirty robe.

"Give it back," he growls. "Whatever it is you've stolen. All of it. Give it back, and leave this place, and I'll let you go alive."

"You'll let me?" She laughs, smiling furiously, showing pointed teeth, squirming against his strength, slowly losing the enhancement from the Sign. He's still stronger, though, keeping her firmly in place. His head pounds from the fading magic. The Dolosian reeks of fear, but she spits in his face. "Who do you think you are?"

"A witcher," he tells her, wiping her spittle on his shoulder, squeezing her wrists harder until he's sure it's painful. Ignoring the throb in his head, he forms the Sign of Zagreus against her skin. "Hired to kill, but merciful enough to consider otherwise. I'll ask again: return everything you've stolen from these people and leave."

The scent of her terror grows, and though her squirming ceases, her anger does not. "Liar," she grits. "You'd use the power of Zagreus against me? Don't you know what I am, Witcher? And yet you're still fool enough to try. You won't kill me, whatever I do."

Still, it's clear the Sign worked on her, or she wouldn't smell so afraid. Heavy footfalls and rapid breathing approach. Phainon, released from Oronyx's Sign, finally catching up.

"What in the name of the Titans was that?" he pants. "One moment you've frozen me in place and the next you're running like your life depends on it. Is this how a witcher's hunt usually goes?"

The Dolosian's struggling redoubles; she bucks and writhes until he loses his grip on one of her arms, letting her attempt to slip out from under him until he catches her by the inside of one leg and kneels hard on her tail.

"Off the tail!" she screeches. "Off, that hurts!"

Mydei shifts, putting his weight on her leg instead. She gives up on struggling, but she glares at him fiercely. Phainon catches his breath, coming to a stop a few paces away, clearly terribly confused.

"Are you the one that's been stealing stuff and tormenting everybody?" he asks.

"Phainon," Mydei says in warning.

"I believe you have something of mine," he continues. "I'd appreciate it a lot if you'd return it to me. Mydeimos, do you need to sit on her so crudely?"

"Mydeimos," she echoes, and laughs. "You're Mydeimos the Undying, and you'd have me believe you'd kill me?" She grows louder now, more hysterical, flopping down until her back hits the grass, arms splayed out, tail whipping, uncaring as Mydei still sits on her leg.

"You're so sure I wouldn't?" Mydei asks, cocking his head, curious.

"You have a reputation amongst us 'devils' and 'monsters,'" she says, laughing again, folding her arms behind her head like she's relaxing rather than pinned by a man who might kill her. "You don't kill us if we're smart, if we're sentient, if we don't kill first. No, you're an honorable witcher, and the fact that you felt you needed to cast Zagreus' Sign means I have no reason to believe you when you say you'll kill me."

"No one's going to kill you, Miss..." Phainon hesitates.

"Cipher," the all too amused Dolosian supplies.

"Cipher," Phainon repeats. He takes a step closer. "Mydeimos, how about you get off of her and we can all have a nice, civil discussion. Without killing or chasing each other. Doesn't that sound nice?"

"She's dangerous," Mydei says, to another bout of laughter.

"Sure," Phainon agrees, setting a hand on his shoulder as though he might hold Mydei back. It should bother him, but he's caught on the coldness of Phainon's fingers. His gentle, placating expression. "And so are you."

"I'm not going to run," Cipher says, wiping a tear from where it had fallen into her hairline. "You've made my leg go numb anyway."

And Mydei's head just pounds. The whole job is ruined anyway. Without Phainon here, he'd have found some way to make the threat successful. He'd already have Cipher returning whatever she'd stolen and running for the hills, and he wouldn't even know her name. But as it stands, here they are. Why not? Why shouldn't they have a civil conversation? It's so absurd Mydei could laugh. And at the end of it all, if Cipher runs or they end in a stalemate, he can always use his gauntlets as intended, just enough to scare her away.

He gets off of Cipher's leg, sitting in the dirt beside her, though he keeps one hand around her ankle just in case. "Sure," he says, smiling dangerously. "Let's have a civil conversation."

Phainon joins them on the ground, brushing a spot of dirt from one leg of his trousers. "Terrifying smile aside, let's," he says. "Miss Cipher, you stand accused of stealing quite a few heirlooms and such from the townsfolk here, and just now you've taken something important from me as well. We'd all appreciate it if you could give those things back and stop playing pranks."

She listens to this, and when he finishes, she laughs and laughs and laughs. "And what a kind soul you are," she says, and reaches for something in one of her pockets. Mydei tenses, but it's just what she'd stolen from Phainon, which turns out to be bit of paper, crumpled from her run. "Is this it? Some treasured heirloom you can't live without? Take it back, Deliverer boy. It's worthless to me anyway."

Silent now, smile slipping, Phainon takes it, attempting to smooth out the creases. He looks at it for a moment, turning it over with hands far more carefully than Cipher's had been. His sigh, barely audible, is shaky. A blink, and he forces himself to smile. "Yes," he says tensely. "Yes, this is it. I thank you for its return, though I do wish you'd been a bit more careful with it. What about the rest? Would you return all of that too?"

"I don't think I will," Cipher says. Her tail lashes the earth. Tension returns beneath Mydei's hands.

"And why not?" he asks. "Need I remind you the position you're in? Perhaps I won't kill you, but I haven't sworn off harm."

"Terrifying," she breathes. Her next laugh is weaker. She throws an arm over her face. "Do you know what I steal, Witcher?"

"Food and heirlooms, handmade odds and ends, I'm told. I've heard complaints of families going hungry and mothers weeping from precious memories stolen away."

"Exaggerations," she hisses.

Mydei hums. "I would imagine so."

She throws her arm off her face and pushes herself up to sit properly. "What?" she says, incredulous. "You believe me?"

"I do, yes," Mydei says. "And I believe you have reasons for stealing whatever you actually did. Regardless, you've caused a problem, and I've been asked to solve it."

"I need it," she says, expression twisting, leg jerking free from Mydei's grip. Something tells him she won't run, so he lets her go, witnesses her fury. "Everything I took, I need far more than the person I took it from does."

"Why?" Phainon asks. "What makes you so sure of that?"

She seethes, glaring at them each in turn, and stands. "I'll spare you the sob story," she says. "If Aglaea wants me gone, I'll be gone. Just tell her that whatever I took couldn't be recovered. Maybe I destroyed some of it, maybe it was too well hidden to find after you chased me away." She makes to go, but Mydei catches her by tail, yanking until she kicks out and screeches and crashes right back down.

"That isn't the deal."

"We never had a deal," she hisses. "And we won't. Let me go!"

"Miss Cipher," Phainon says, crawling on his knees to lay a cold hand on Mydei's shoulder again. "Mydeimos, would it hurt you to be a bit gentler?" Mydei grunts, but lets go of her tail when he's sure she isn't about to run again, furiously settling cross-legged in the dirt. All three of them are covered in stains from it. Not unlike that village man who must've crossed Cipher and been pelted because of it.

"Miss Cipher," Phainon tries again, "we'd like to hear your story, that way we can come up with a solution."

Only now does she really seem to see him. "Hah." She tugs on the ends of her own hair. "Don't you ever get tired of being so polite? Really, who even are you? What are you doing, following a witcher around?"

"We're friends," he says, simply, strangely, easily. He still has the crumpled paper in his hands, holding it so delicately. A card of some sort, though Mydei can't see it well. It's painted with the shape of a knight or some kind of hero, creased and worn now. "And I do try to be kind to everyone I meet; it costs me very little, and I find that to many it's worth quite a lot If you'd rather I treat you cruelly I certainly can."

She laughs, flicking her tail and then folding it into her lap, perhaps to keep it away from Mydei. She picks at a crust of dirt stuck in her fur. "So there is a temper in there after all," she says. "Wonderful."

"We'll be coming to an agreement whether you like it or not," Mydei tells her. "Start talking if you'd like it be somewhat on your terms." It isn't much of a threat. She seems past the point of caring. Dolosians are said to be tricksters by nature, but he's never known one to be malicious. He's certain she has her reasons. Hearing them just isn't usually his style. Not with the nature of his work. But with Phainon here as some strange kind of middleman... He's killed off any intimidation factor Mydei might have had anyway.

Still, Cipher glances between them, and it's clear she recognizes a threat when she sees one. He watches her swallow, watches her put on a smile faker than the last. "There's not much to tell, Mr. Witcher. I've been living in this place in secret for years now, taking what they won't notice to get by. But then one day they noticed me, started counting their stores more carefully and calling me a devil. I figured I'd stop bothering to be sneaky about it, is all, if they're going to chase me away regardless."

"But do you really need so much?" Phainon asks. "You've stolen enough to feed a family for months."

"Stores for the future," Cipher supplies, waving a hand.

Mydei studies her expression, made carefully blank. "And the heirlooms? Children's toys and handmade blankets, what do you need all of those for?"

Now, there's a flash of something in her eyes. "Petty revenge," she offers. "Simple greed. I wanted those things, and I wanted them to feel the loss, so I took them. I'm sure a witcher knows all about my kind, isn't that right? We Dolosians are notorious for coveting and wanting, are we not? I'm just like the rest."

All three of them are quiet for a spell. Mydei holds Cipher's gaze until she breaks eye contact. Phainon is the one to speak first. "What's in the barn, Miss Cipher?" he asks. A breath. In one swift motion, she stands up and bolts. "Well, that's not good, is it?"

"Titans above," Mydei curses, scrambling upright and taking off after her. Again, she's terribly fast, faster than him and far more agile, but after a bit of rest, he can cast another Sign without to much strain. He wipes at the dried crust of blood at his throat and and forms the Sign of Kephale, feeling strength fill him. Behind, Phainon's footsteps beat against the earth, falling farther and farther behind as Mydei pushes his enhanced body to run faster and faster.

It's a mad dash to the barn. Ahead, Cipher deftly leaps over a wheelbarrow, not slowing even a bit. Mydei swerves around it and loses a bit of ground on her. His breath comes fast. He casts the Sign of Kephale again, ignoring the spike of pain in his head. After casting so many Signs, it's less effective, and he can't stop to down a potion to make up for the fact.

He comes close, she flicks her tail out of reach. His breath echoes in his ears. Three sets of footsteps—two, Cipher's are silent as a cat's. She curves around the building with unfair ease. Forced to take it wide or slow down, Mydei loses ground. There's the clatter as she leaps inside through a window. Mydei curses under his breath as he fails to stop himself in time, having to backtrack to follow, and not half as graceful as her as he hits his head climbing inside.

It's dark inside, but for puddles of dying daylight spilling in from the windows. Shadows fill the spaces between and behind bales of hay stacked high and tall beams supporting the loft and roof. The ground is soft and cushioned with escaped straw. The air smells of sweet earth and grass, and a perfunctory scan yields not a thing. He slips a hand into his belt for a potion he quickly downs, straining his ears for anything other than the sound of Phainon's hard breathing as he struggles to climb inside and falls into a pile of hay when he makes it.

"Titans is it dark in here," he says, brushing the pieces that cling to him off as he gets himself upright. "Where'd she go?" He's squinting. Mydei's darkvision from the potion starts to kick in, and he angles himself away from the window so the light source won't hurt his eyes.

"Quiet," Mydei says. "That's exactly what I'm trying to find out."

He checks the ground for footprints or some kind of sign pointing to the direction she'd gone in, but a Dolosian's step is light, and he can't find a thing. He isn't even remotely surprised he'd lost her. Regardless, annoyance settles in his chest at the same time as a frown takes his brows. He can't resist saying, "This is your fault, you know."

"Mine?" Phainon asks, incredulous. "Sure, because threats of murder are always the way to solve problems! If you weren't so incapable of anything even resembling diplomacy, I'm sure we could have worked something out ages ago. Now listen to your own advice and shut up so we can look for her."

"You can't see a thing."

"...And you can?"

Mutations have made his eyes stronger than most by default, but with the potion he'd taken, he can likely see far better than even Cipher herself can. "Yes," he says simply, rather than explaining. He takes a step, hopeless to keep it light, what with his armor and lack of skill in stealth. "Light a match or something; check the loft."

"You think I brought matches? I—" Mydei tosses his tinderbox in Phainon's direction, and he cuts off, fumbling as he catches it. "Well. Thanks, I guess."

They begin their search in earnest. Mydei heads deeper into the barn, checking every corner he comes across, steps slow and soft as he can make them.

He finds hay. More and more hay, endless piles of it. Farm tools tucked away in storage, plows and hoes and shovels and wooden troughs. When he reaches one end of the barn, sacks of grain and bundles of other food, some of it half eaten. He finds a crust of bread, a jar of preserves, a bit of cheese. Too much for one. Far too much for one. He makes his way to the other end of the building.

Phainon's flame flickers. He climbs down from the loft one handed, ladder creaking, feet landing in the straw. "No one there," he whispers. Mydei turns his gaze away from the tiny light, made overly sensitive by the potion.

"I found some of the stuff, though. Quilts and blankets piled on the floor like they've been used for beds, dolls and carved figures left about like they'd been played with..."

"How many blankets?" Mydei asks.

"Not sure. Three piles of them, with at least two each. Six or more." Mydei grunts. Phainon hesitates. "Do you think she has children? Or younger siblings? People she's caring for?"

"Every creature has its reasons," Mydei murmurs, not meaning for Phainon to hear.

It seems he does anyway. "And do you usually care to listen to them?"

"No," Mydei admits. "No, I do not."

They search the other side of the barn. Nothing but more hay, more things tucked away in storage. In one spot, the straw seems messier than everywhere else. He sweeps it aside with his foot, curious, and comes up with nothing. He clears a wider area, and thinks of it.

"Check the ground," he says to Phainon, still keeping his voice soft. "There could be a cellar."

And so they check the ground, sweeping the hay aside aside with their feet until they finally find it. Until Phainon finally finds it, which irks Mydei for reasons unknown. Perhaps it's the triumphant sound he makes, snapping his fingers and saying, "bingo!"

Mydei follows him to a hatch in the ground, hastily cleared. He squints against Phainon's match, burnt nearly to his fingertips.

"Put that out," he says, crouching and brushing aside a bit more straw.

"I remind you that I can't see the way you can," Phainon tells him.

"So stay behind. You'll set everything on fire if you get spooked and drop that, and it's hurting my eyes. Don't mess this up." Phainon opens his mouth to protest, but Mydei cuts him off before he can. "You said you'd listen to me. You promised not to get in the way. Unless you'd like to see what happens when you break a promise to a witcher?"

A dull laugh. "So you're threatening me too, now?" Phainon asks, but he's honest to a fault, and whatever this is means far more to him than it does to Mydei. "Fine." He blows out the match. "Fine, then. Go on. I'll wait here."

It leaves an odd, bitter taste in his mouth. He doesn't want Phainon to think of them as friends, but... Well. Why doesn't he want that? Aren't they, after days stuck with each other? But Phainon isn't someone he's known and suffered with, isn't someone who gets it. Gets Mydei or gets what it's like to be a witcher, or gets anything else. But he's trying, isn't he? And he's stubborn, determined, strong. Titans above.

"This is my work," Mydei says, meaning to soften the blow, however poorly he manages it. "There comes a point when you shouldn't get involved."

"I understand," Phainon says flatly. He takes a couple of blind steps back. "I won't get in your way."

He shouldn't say more, doesn't say more. Just purses his lips and pulls the hatch open. Down below, it's pitch dark. He climbs carefully down and lets the latch fall shut so there isn't an easy exit. Habit from a hundred other, far more dangerous jobs. Better he die than let something loose.

It isn't a particularly large cellar. He reaches the bottom, makes out the shape of one central hallway and walls lined with shelves of canned goods, sacks of potatoes and seed for the next crop, barrels and kegs of who knows what. It smells earthy here, the air cool and dry, and when he takes a long, deep breath, he catches thick, sour fear scent.

"Spare us both the trouble and come out," he says, chancing a step forward. He's careful, prepared for the possibility of an ambush. He isn't sure if Cipher will try to fight him. So far, all she's done is run, and the only thing she'd done to the townsfolk is throw mud, but now she's been cornered, and flight isn't an option.

Another step forward, and she comes out, hands up. "Alright," she says, and her voice trembles. "Alright, you've caught me." A soft sound like a hiccup or a sniffle. She moves forward, and he isn't certain the sound came from her.

"Just take me away, oh big bad witcher," she continues. "I'll go, I'll be out of your hair and you can collect your paycheck, alright? Just don't..."

"Don't what?" Mydei asks. A step forward. The fear smell grows all the stronger. Subtly, she positions herself between him and one corner of the room, and he gets it. Tasting the air, he takes a step back, two, giving her more space. "Do you think I'm some kind of monster who's out to hurt children?"

Her laugh lacks any sort of humor. It's nervous. "Could you really blame me for worrying?"

"No," Mydei says. "But you're wrong to. Come out. All of you."

Without much choice, she exhales and half turns toward that corner, keeping her front facing Mydei. "It's okay," she says. "You can listen to him. He won't hurt you." The last part is to him, no doubt. A warning, though she's helpless to threaten him with any real impact.

Slow and hesitant, two children rise from behind a pair of barrels. Dolosians, by the shapes of them in the dark. Mydei can't see them well enough to make out features, but he can make out the feline ears atop their heads, both half hiding behind Cipher. They reach her chest height, too old to be her own children. They're strays, most likely. They wouldn't be the first Dolosian kids to be abandoned, whether by choice or not. A sick feeling turns in Mydei's stomach.

"I won't," he says. "You were right to laugh at my threats before. I follow a code, and I don't harm intelligent creatures."

"You might follow a code," Cipher says, putting an arm around both children. "But some of your kind don't."

"Perhaps," Mydei agrees. "Still. I promise, if a witcher's word holds any weight to you." He waits for a breath, but she stays silent. Neither child offers a word. "Let's take this into the light," he says, pushing the hatch back open and climbing out. He ignores Phainon's curious stirring in favor of holding it open as Cipher reluctantly follows, helping each of the kids out in turn.

With a bit of dusk light coming in from the windows and the potion he'd taken, Mydei is able to make them out now. There's Cipher, dirtied as ever. The children look nothing like her, one with dark hair, one with light, both with different noses and eye shapes and facial structures from her, though they all share the same ears and tail characteristic of their race. The light haired one seems to be a boy, the dark haired a girl, each dressed in clothing as nice as anything, if covered in straw. Stolen, no doubt.

"Explain," Mydei says.

Phainon lights a fresh match, cupping his hand around the flame, his expression far from a smile.

Cipher's ears pull back. She tucks the boy's face against her hip, though the girl pushes away before she can do the same with her. "Aunt Cipher isn't a bad person," she says, standing as tall as a child can. "You can't hurt her! You can't take her away!"

"Serena," Cipher hisses. Firelight reflects off the girl's wide, fearful eyes, and she stops pretending to be strong. Cipher tucks her close and addresses Mydei. "Whatever you're thinking is probably right," she says. "First it was just me, and then I found them and I took them in too. They don't steal, they don't play pranks. Leave them out of this."

Phainon looks like he wants to speak, but Mydei shakes his head, and thankfully, he listens.

"So you've been keeping them secret?" Mydei asks.

"They call me a devil," Cipher says flatly. "Do you think they'd be any kinder to a devil's children?"

"Return what you stole, and no one has to know a thing."

"It's not like you're giving us a choice." She laughs. It's a terribly dull sound. "You have us at the ends of those sharp gauntlets of yours, little witcher. What more can we do?"

△

"Seventy balance coins, as promised," Mayor Aglaea says, pushing a heavy pouch across the table to him. Mydei takes it and peeks inside, but doesn't count. "I trust your accommodations have been sufficient?"

"Yes. Thank you," Mydei says. He'd taken a second bath after returning last night, washed his clothes, ate his fill, and slept for a long time in a soft bed. His stuff is still hanging to dry, and Phainon found a bit of work patching holes in an elderly couple's roof for a bit of coin, so they won't be taking off again until midday.

Across the room, Cipher sits in an armchair in one corner of the mayor's house, washed clean herself, hair combed and braided on one side. She glares when Mydei glances her way, and breaks eye contact first.

"What a nasty devil that was, kidnapping women and children. I trust you've recovered, Miss Cipher?" he asks.

Aglaea turns to her knowingly. Far more shrewd a mayor than Mydei would expect to find in a town like this. Cipher shows her teeth. "I have, yes," she says. "The mayor here has offered me and the children a place to stay, as well as honest work to earn our keep. I owe both of you my thanks." Her tail beats the edge of her seat.

"Yes," Aglaea says, smiling thinly. "If only you'd have come to me sooner, before you'd ended up in the hands of that thing, none of this would have happened."

One of Cipher's ears flicks. Her eyes narrow, her smile is strained. "Indeed," she says, and stands up. "Well, I suppose I should help the children. There're a lot of things to sort through and return that the 'devil' stole, and they don't know the town well."

"Of course, Cifera," Aglaea says. "Do let me know if you need anything at all."

A tight smile. Cipher shuts the door behind her.

Aglaea turns to Mydei. "You've done me a service."

"You're certain no one will notice?" Mydei asks, tucking the pouch of coins into his satchel. "They don't exactly pass for humans."

"This may be a village of fools, but not one of us is cruel, and few care about the distinctions between the intelligent races." Aglaea assures him. "I wouldn't be surprised if few have even heard tale of Dolosians before. As far as anyone will know, Cifera and the children as victims the same as they are. They'll fit right in."

"And you aren't worried she'll continue to steal, or cause some other kind of problem down the road?"

"Consider how Cifera sees the children," Aglaea says. "Lost, abandoned or orphaned... I used to feed her, you know. When she was a handful of years younger than she is now. She can provide for herself, but I still care for her as if she was my own. Whatever comes, I'll accept it. You've done great work here, Mydeimos. The townsfolk will sing your praises."

"Well," Mydei grunts, "anywhere I'm not met with stones is a welcome place to be in my book."

She tips her head to one side, lifts the cup of water on the table in front of her as if to toast. "To kind comings and goings, then," she says.

He lifts the cup she'd given him as well and nods. "To kind comings and goings."

△

He leaves Strife in the stables a little longer as he looks around the market to restock his provisions. Hard rye bread, a bag of walnuts, oat cakes, dried plums. Aglaea had been right; the people here are kind to him once they learn he'd solved their 'devil' problem, some offering him discounts, however small.

Once he's stocked up, he finds the house Phainon is supposed to be working at, figuring they'll sit down for one last meal at the inn, gather up their dry clothes, and head out.

He's there, as expected. Bundled up, flushed from the early winter chill finally starting to settle in. His breath fogs up in the air, and he seems surprised to see Mydei when he gets there, standing with his arms crossed, watching Phainon lower his hammer and climb off the ladder on which he's perched.

"Hurry up," Mydei tells him. "I'd like to get in a few hours of travel before we lose the sun."

"You waited?" Phainon asks, and it creates a strange sensation in Mydei's stomach, the way he smiles, triumphant-like, all too proud and pleasantly surprised. He looks like he's going to laugh and call Mydei 'friend' again like it's the easiest thing in the world.

"Yes, well." He looks away. "You did make me swear I would."

The next night, they camp with their tarps strung up and tied down as a makeshift tent to protect them from the weather. It rains a little bit, and there's just enough wind to be an annoyance. Phainon falls asleep to the sound of raindrops splattering against waxed canvas and wind making it flap. Not far, Mydei lays in his own bedroll, quiet and still and unobtrusive.

It's the closest they've been to each other this entire time, and Phainon is more worried than he needs to be about bothering Mydei. He's too conscious of his tossing and turning, aware that if he moves too much, he might bump into Mydei, and if he breathes too loudly, he might keep him from sleep. He's not sure exactly how strong a witcher's senses are. He's not sure how lightly Mydei sleeps. Being so conscious of it only makes him want to toss and turn even more, but he lays there, stiff and itchy, a little bit cold, listening to the storm and hoping it's loud enough to block out all of his sounds.

He does fall asleep eventually, thinking about the day, wondering about Cipher and those two children and whether or not they'll find a way to fit into that town. The way the mayor Aglaea had seemed to care so much for this person the rest of the village labeled a devil.

Mydei had told him about it later, after he'd healed himself up and a bit of prodding, and he hadn't said it in so many words, but he let on that he wasn't upset by Phainon's intervention, though he made sure to say that Phainon could've gotten both of them killed had the 'monster' been, well, an actual monster.

It's fair. Phainon has always been a little bit too trusting or naive or optimistic. Even after everything, even after watching his own town get scorched to the ground, it's a habit he hasn't quite been able to break.

His dreams are a blur and not quite pleasant. There's fire, so much fire. The tattered edge of a black cloak. The helplessness of being frozen, from fear paralysis and then that Sign Mydei cast on him. That Sign... He'd been cold, his body wouldn't listen to him no matter how he'd tried. Now, there's a sword tip to his chest, a masked face, and he's frozen in fear, frozen under a spell, and—

Abruptly, the dream is cut short. It twists into something else, and he sees that Sign again. That Sign, the twist of Mydei's fingers to form it. The cut on his neck from Cipher's nails bleeding the gold blood of witchers. He'd healed it later with Aquila's Sign, grouchy with headache and eyes dilated huge and light sensitive from a potion he'd taken. He'd used it on Phainon too, tingling and itchy and weird. He replays the rest of the day with details blurred and made strange all the way until he lays down to sleep, and then the rest of the night is dreamless or forgotten.

He wakes to Mydei shuffling out of his bedroll, fabric rustling, the tarps crinkling. The wind and rain have died down, but when Phainon shifts, he feels the lingering cold in the air and smells the sticky petrichor scent of it.

Tired from poor rest and still half asleep, he cracks his eyes open. There's Mydei, kneeling beneath the low ceiling of the tarps and pulling his armor out of his bedding piece by piece so he can roll it back up. He sleeps with it in the blankets with him to protect it from weathering and potential thievery by creatures with an affinity for shiny things. Phainon still finds it funny, nights after seeing him do it for the first time.

Now, Mydei's hands are bare and the rest of him unarmored. His markings continue to about an inch above his knuckles, and he must be feeling cold, because he's pulled both of his sleeves on, though his robe is still open at the front.

Perceptive as ever, his gaze, gold as first light, lands on Phainon. He sweeps a bit of dirt from his bedroll and begins folding it into thirds. "Get up if you're awake," he says, voice low and raspy as it always is in the morning. It's a small thing, this observation, but it ends up filed away with a dozen other things in Phainon's carefully kept catalog of information about witchers—this witcher, Mydeimos the Undying, impossibly allowing Phainon to tag along, and, as of the day before, only a little bit begrudging about it.

Grumbling and mourning the loss of warmth, Phainon sits up and slides reluctantly out of comfort and into the cold, stretching as best he can with the tarp in the way and kneeling on the ground to straighten out his bedding and roll it up so they can set off. Not for the first time, he laments his lack of a horse of his own. Despite the recently positive trajectory of their relationship, he can't begin to imagine Mydei allowing him turns on Strife, not in a million years, so all he's left with are his two tired feet.

Mydei pauses for a moment, his eyes on Phainon with weight to them, a tangible kind of attention he takes care to ignore. And then Mydei speaks after some hesitation, voice still rough. "We can spar, if you're fast," is what he says, entirely unexpectedly, and Phainon's fingers twitch, covered in the dirt he'd been sweeping clean from the bottom of his bedroll as he rolls it up.

Phainon stills, something buzzing and hopeful taking root in his chest, and clears his throat. "Can we?" he asks, careful not to sound too excited.

Again, Mydei says, "If you're fast."

So Phainon is fast, buckling the straps on his bedroll and setting it aside to help Mydei, armor moved into a neat pile in a dry spot outside, take down their makeshift tent. He's perhaps more thrilled than a person ought to be at the prospect of sparring with a witcher, but he's here to get stronger, to learn to fight, and he remembers the way they'd fought before, with tooth and nail and beautifully, and he knows Mydei went easy on him but he still has the bruises and he wants the chance to prove himself. To be strong, to be respected.

So after they've packed everything up and once again find themselves on wet, muddy, post-rain ground, he's grinning. And the strange thing—though perhaps this should be expected, filed away from the last time they'd fought and Mydei had that look on his face—is that Mydei seems almost as excited as Phainon is, though he tries harder to hide it.

"Does this mean you're willing to help me get stronger?" Phainon asks. Maybe he shouldn't test his luck, but he's found, after testing it over and over, that Mydei isn't quite as stony as he makes himself out to be.

"I'm willing to spar," Mydei corrects him, and shows his teeth. "Whether you learn and grow stronger from it is up to you."

"Wonderful," Phainon says, stretching a bit, still stiff from sleep and the cold. He's sore all over, as he is more often than not, and still tender where he's bruised, but he knows better than to ask Mydei to wait. It's mercy enough that he keeps his gauntlets off and hasn't wriggled back into his leg armor. He's a little less scary like this, and the stakes aren't quite so high as last time, so Phainon looks forward to it. "I'll take whatever I can get."

"Show me, then," says Mydei, sinking into a fighting stance, as comfortable with it as he is with breathing, "the strength of an ordinary human."

"Sure," Phainon says, matching him, raising his hands to form his guard, planting his feet. He smiles, anticipation building in his stomach. "Just... keep in mind that I'm much better with the sword."

A rough laugh. "That doesn't matter when you're unarmed, unless you'd like to stay helpless until you can scrape up the funds for a new one?"

"I'm hardly helpless," Phainon tells him, liking the taste of the challenge, taking a full breath to prepare himself.

"We'll see about that."

Mydei makes the first move, a swift lunge, fist flying out. Phainon ducks away from it, attempting to retaliate and finding himself easily blocked. He tries a kick, a jab, a hook; Mydei blocks or avoids them all, natural and stable. His muscle memory is better than Phainon's, his foundation is better, his technique, his power, but Phainon has far less experience in a fight and has always been a fast learner.

He raises his arms against a blow aimed for his face, feeling the sting of the impact against his wrist, and notes that blocking isn't sustainable when Mydei hits this hard. He'll have another bruise there, a string of them as he's forced to deflect another, put on the defensive. He loses ground, gritting his teeth against the sting of the strangely satisfying kind of pain that comes with a fight.

Gradually, he learns to avoid the blows instead of taking them, though he makes quite a few errors. Mydei is fast, but he isn't without his tells. Phainon ducks and dodges and slips beneath his fists, but then Mydei goes for a kick to the body and he isn't able to react fast enough, too focused on his hands. He takes it, crushing against the top of his hip, throwing him off balance and right into Mydei's hand, catching him by the back of the head and yanking him forward, right into his knee.

The pain is dizzying. He sees stars for a moment, tastes the copper tang of blood in his mouth, and when Mydei lets him go, he goes crashing right into the earth, unbalanced and dazed and pinned in an instant.

He hadn't been hit that hard in actuality, but his cheek throbs viciously and he'd bitten his tongue, and by the time he regains his senses, it's clear he's been beat, Mydei restraining his arms and pressing one knee into his chest.

"Well," he says, and turns his head to the side to spit red in the dirt. His chest strains beneath the weight Mydei puts on it, so his words come a bit breathless. "I'd say it looks like your victory, doesn't it?"

Mydei frowns down at him, and it was inevitable that he'd lose, human and inexperienced and pitched against a witcher of all opponents, but the longer he's scrutinized, the more he can't help a twinge of shame that he hadn't lasted longer, done better, recovered faster. Has he failed to prove himself? Was Mydei, somehow, expecting more from him than this? His hip aches where he'd been kicked, his cheek where he'd been kneed, his shoulder and forearms where he'd been punched.

A moment passes. The pressure on his chest eases as Mydei climbs off. He's pressed right back down when he attempts to sit up, and then there are fingers twisted in front of his face and the pain in his face turns to this terrible, ticklish tingling and then disappears altogether. The Sign of Aquila. Mydei unmakes it and stands, offering Phainon a hand, and that—despite all the previous scrutiny—makes the shame dissipate. Because that—Mydei's offered hand, his healing—doesn't seem like the sort of thing offered as a consolation prize.

Phainon reaches out and lets himself be hauled upright, spitting another bit of blood from his healed tongue to the side. "Thank you," he says, embarrassed by the pleased surprise in his own voice.

Mydei only grunts and plants his feet again, that feral, frightful smile pulling at his mouth once more. "Another round," he says, "unless you're too weak now that you've been beaten into the ground to try again?"

His hip and wrists still ache. He's still out of breath from the fight, but Titans damn him if a grin doesn't stretch across his face. He settles back into his stance, raising his guard and already figuring out the things he can do better. "Not a chance," he says, and this time, he strikes first.

△

They spar for four more rounds, and Phainon loses every single one of them. He ends up covered in mud and bruises, but each time he lasts a little bit longer, he learns a little bit more, and he tries out new strategies to some success and some disaster. But each time he loses, Mydei casts the Sign of Aquila on the worst of his wounds and helps him up.

It's clear the spells take a toll on him, but when Phainon tells him he doesn't need to do it, his only reply is that, "you were hurt by me; you'll be healed by me too." So he takes care of anything that bleeds, and Phainon is left with nothing more than a handful of bruises and scrapes. And by the end of it, he earns the closest thing to a compliment he's yet to receive from Mydei. Two words, and a firm nod. "You're learning."

He tries his best not to be obnoxiously pleased with himself, if only so Mydei doesn't decide never to spar with him again.

After it all, they travel on, packed up, rested somewhat, fed, and armored in Mydei's case. As the sun settles in the sky, they forget the chill of the morning. Phainon loses his coat, finding the long sleeves of his tunic and the exertion of walking uphill enough to keep him warm. Mydei drops his right sleeve again, a mile of marked skin exposed to the air. Even when it's somewhat nice out like this, Phainon can't understand it.

"Do you not get cold?" he asks, but the only reply is a grunt that explains nothing at all. Phainon laughs a little and sighs at once.

They end up following the river after a mile or three. It's about forty meters wide and deep enough to be deceptively slow and smooth. There isn't a bridge for another half day, where they'll cross and continue along the road for a day after that to get to the next town.

Phainon's never been in these parts. Everything on this journey is new to him. Every step takes him farther and farther away from home. Faced with the river on one side and a dormant plain of tall grasses and sparse trees on the other, he misses the ocean. He misses golden fields of wheat and a forest full of sunny clearings and years of childhood memories.

He glances up at Mydei, riding Strife with his gaze forward, hair spilling around his neck, hands curled loosely around the reins. Mydei, who'd waited for him. Mydei, who'd sparred with him. Mydei, who doesn't seem to mind Phainon quite as much as he had days before. Still, he isn't exactly an open book.

"Where do you call home, Mydeimos?" Phainon asks, not really expecting an answer and so used to being ignored at this point that he's almost surprised when a considering gaze lands on him.

"Castrum Kremnos," Mydei answers after a breath. "It's the same for all of us."

Us, being witchers. It's the place where they're made, the place where they winter. Adjusting the straps of his pack, Phainon asks, "And before that?"

"There is no before."

The sound of Phainon's footsteps, Strife's hooves, the faint creak of Mydei's armor as he shifts on her back. Wind through dead and dying grasses like wheat.

"Isn't there?"

Silence. Phainon decides not to press any further.

△

They break for lunch and continue along until they cross the bridge. After that, they walk another hour or so before stopping to set up camp. It's another long day. Phainon takes off his boots and massages his sore feet by the fire, fingers stiff with cold, eyes stinging from the smoke and how close he sits. Mydei watches, silent, firelight dancing across his face and reflecting off his eyes.

The sky is clear and cloudless, and the wind has stilled, or they wouldn't have risked the flames. After a dinner of fish Phainon caught with his hands because he doesn't have a pole, decently fresh bread bought from the last town, and sweet, gummy dried plums, they let the fire die and set up for the night.

With no chance of rain and the air still, they don't bother with the tarps. Mydei disappears to string up their food in a tree, and Phainon sets up his bed by the still warm ash of the fire, doubling up his socks so his feet won't go cold.

It's terribly silent. No crackling fire, no wind to rustle through the foliage, no footsteps or hoof beats. Strife is hitched with space to graze and rest without getting in their way. Mydei is still gone. It's too late in the year for crickets. Alone in the dark, however briefly, Phainon remembers the way it felt to leave home, to walk miles and miles with nothing but his own blistered feet and aching shoulders for company, and he feels... lonely, maybe. There are so many people he wishes he could come back to. So many people he wishes he could tell, hey, I traveled with a witcher! But those people are long gone, and he has to make peace with it.

Mydei comes back as he's shifting his clothes to the front of his pack so he can use it as a pillow. He isn't quiet, can't be with all the armor he has yet to shed. He doesn't speak as he squats to roll out his bed, doesn't say anything though he knows Phainon watches.

The routine of it is a little bit soothing. The silence between them something like companionship. He hopes Mydei thinks so as well, that he can be a little bit of a comfort, even if he isn't quiet and compliant and whatever else Mydei might prefer him to be. Humans are social creatures. Phainon doubts that could have been mutated and trained out of witchers too.

Mydei removes his armor next, metallic and a little bit too loud for the night. Gauntlets first, then the pieces on his legs. They're bulky and most certainly difficult to travel with, but he has a way of fitting the pieces together, the small pieces nesting inside the larger ones like dolls, then all of that fitting somewhat neatly by his feet in his bedroll. He'd only shrugged when Phainon noted that it must be cold and uncomfortable, but he must be used to it the way he's used to baring half his body to the elements like it's nothing.

Phainon redoes the ties on his pack once he's done arranging stuff, Mydei shoves his armor down into his bedding, and side by side and silent, they prepare for bed. They're almost as close as they had been the night before, lacking space and huddled under the tarps. The first night they'd slept on opposite sides of the fire, as far away from each other as they could get. Now, he couldn't reach out and touch Mydei, but it's a near thing.

"Goodnight," Phainon says, laying down, turning his head to watch as Mydei does too.

There's a grunt, a rustle of fabric, and then for once, Mydei says it back, low and rough. "Goodnight."

Phainon wraps himself up, tight and warm, pillowed on his lumpy pack, and tries to sleep. Seconds stretch to minutes. Minutes to an hour, maybe, or more, or less. He rolls onto his back and opens his eyes.

The sky is still beautifully clear, ink black without the sun. The moon isn't out, but the stars are, hundreds of them, thousands, all twinkling softly, sharing what tiny amount of light they can. He'd been taught constellations as a child, and he maps them out now, this sky that's the same wherever he lays beneath it. Here or Aedes Elysiae or anywhere else. As a child, he'd lay in the wheat fields and watch the stars at night or the clouds in the day.

He pulls a hand free from his blankets and stretches it out above him, finding sharp, cold air, and fitting the three stars marking Talanton's scales between his fingers. He searches for Phagousa's goblet, Aquila's eye, Nikador's lance, mapping each one out, sparing a steady, even breath between each. Sometimes it helps him to fall asleep, sometimes it doesn't. Right now, he wears loss and nostalgia and loneliness like another coat keeping him warm.

His exposed fingers grow cold. He tucks them back close to his body and sighs. Somewhere to the side, Mydei rolls over, a vague, shadowed lump. Phainon turns to face him, listens for his breath, and tries desperately to fall asleep.

△

The next day is, not unexpectedly, a lot more walking. It's oddly warm once the sun comes up, so Phainon finds himself shedding his coat and rolling his sleeves over his elbows. He's starting to want a bath again, though he'd washed up at the river bank before they left it behind the day before. Dirt and sweat and his own oils settle into his skin and hair, and Mydei reeks of horse, and the both of them are visibly road-worn and dirty from the spar they'd had this morning too.

Two rounds rather than five, but Phainon had lasted longer in each of these than he had in any the day before. Still, he'd ended flat on his back in the dirt both times, with fresh bruises alongside old ones, purple and brown and tender and blotchy. Phainon doesn't mind them though. They speak of the accomplishment of testing himself against a witcher, and he finds that he's rather proud to have them.

He's proud too, of the approving nod Mydei gave him after their last spar. Short, terse, and without a word to accompany it, but it felt to him the same as those words from last time had. You're learning, it said. You're stronger than the man you were yesterday. He'd taken Mydei's offered hand after and let himself be pulled up, easily and with nothing to it.

And now they walk. And walk. And walk some more. Mydei alternates riding and walking. Phainon doesn't. Maybe one day, if he can get Mydei to like him enough, and if he can scrounge up enough spare apples to earn Strife's favor too, he might be allowed a turn. For now, he suffers on sore feet until they break for lunch and he can sit down, and again after, the sun already sinking as the days grow shorter and shorter the closer to the cold season they get.

When, finally, they reach the next town, the sun is only a handful of minutes from setting and the chill has returned enough that he's pulled down his sleeves and put on his coat, fingers wrapped in his sleeves and tucked in his pockets. He's more than looking forward to a bath and a warm bed. Mydei dismounts to walk Strife through the gates and the rest of the way to the inn—there's only one in this tiny, tucked away little town—and then they're handing her off to a gaping, simultaneously awed and horrified stablehand, and then—

"I've no room for a witcher," says the innkeeper, thin-lipped and frowning, with a weathered face and a sour disposition. "You'll scare away my guests."

Mydei barely reacts, hearing this. He'll have heard it before, tens of times, dozens of times. Phainon remembers him that first night they'd met. Quiet, calm like this, even as he'd been spit on and yelled at. He thinks of the way he'd tucked in his stool and set his dishes neatly after, and feels something hot and indignant in the pit of his stomach. His hands curl into fists.

"What guests?" Phainon laughs, but it comes out furious. "Pardon my rudeness, sir, but your town is small and out of the way. There's us and what, a couple of other travelers? A handful of locals stopping by for drinks? Who is he going to scare, asleep behind a shut door?"

"Exactly them," the innkeeper replies tightly. His faces turns more sour. "I'll rent you a room, but not the witcher. I don't run that kind of business, and it isn't up for debate."

Hot angry floods from his chest to the rest of him, settling in his clenched hands, asking him to hit something. Instead, Phainon takes a breath, uncurls his fists, and tries a smile this time. At his side, Mydei is still silent, used to this, enduring this injustice as he probably always does, and Phainon hadn't thought about it, really. He'd watched it happen before, watched that man spit on Mydei's boots, and somehow he hadn't thought about it at all.

"I understand you're worried about... rumors, or... something," he says, voice carefully level, forcing that smile. "But we've had a long journey and need a place to rest. We aren't going to make a commotion or cause any problems. We're just looking for a place to sleep for the night. Times are hard on all of us, aren't they? No one needs to catch wind that there was a witcher here at all, unless you want to tell them."

A long moment passes, the innkeeper continuing to frown, looking between them, Mydei still silent, Phainon fuming and trying his best to hide it. The innkeeper sighs. "I'll rent him a spot in the stable."

"In the stable?" Phainon repeats, slamming a hand down on the counter. "Does he look like a horse to you? What do you—!"

Four balance coins, the price for a room for the night, land on the counter. Phainon turns, mouth open, to Mydei holding the innkeeper's gaze, withdrawing after he sets the coins down. "I'll be gone in the morning," he says, and leaves, leaves.

"Mydei," Phainon calls to his back, "you can't seriously be fine with this. Mydei!" But he doesn't say anything else, just pulls the door open and shuts it behind him, soft as a whisper, not even upset enough to slam it. The anger cools in the wake of confusion and disbelief.

The innkeeper clears his throat, reaching for the coins on the counter, and the fury comes back. Phainon slams his hand over two of the coins, looking the innkeeper dead in the eyes. "He's not paying full price."

△

Later, cold and frustrated, a bucket of clean water and rags in one hand and two bowls of the meal for the day—mashed root vegetables and too thin slices of roast goose, all doused in a mysterious thick brown sauce—balanced in the other, he kicks open the stable door, greeted with the stench of horse and manure, and checks each stall until he comes near to the end and finds Mydei there, set up for the night.

"You weren't even going to argue for a meal?" Phainon asks, and he means for there to be some fight in the words, but there is none. Just resignation.

In the dusk blue barely light, Mydei cracks his eyes open. It's hard to see their color. They hadn't even been given a lantern. "I have rations," Mydei says.

"Yes," Phainon says. "Rations for the road, for the sad moments when fresh, hot meals aren't available to us." He moves into the stall, nudging Mydei's leg until he moves over, making space on the bed of mostly clean hay. He sets one of the bowls beside Mydei's leg, the pail out of the way of either of them, and sits down with an unhappy grunt. "Your coin bought this, by the way. How could you pay the full price for a room when they gave you this?"

There's wood siding dividing the stalls. Phainon shrugs off his pack and leans his back against it, drawing up his knees, setting his bowl in the space between them and has torso, trapping the heat from the hot food that he stirs furiously with his spoon. Mydei sits up, metal creaking, fabric rustling. He reaches for the other bowl, sparing it a glance and a sniff before he stares at Phainon some more than he already has.

"Did you get a room for yourself?" he asks, calm and level and no doubt noting all of Phainon's stuff tossed into the hay and how he's settled, however discontentedly, here in the stinking stables.

"No," Phainon laughs, indignant. "No, are you kidding? I fought for a meal and a bucket of water and I came out here. Not a chance is a bastard like that seeing any of my coin."

"...So you used mine."

"Yes," Phainon says, finding himself angry again every time he calms down, "and I procured you a meal you wouldn't have advocated for yourself with it, so I don't think a debt is in order." A bite. The mash is creamy and savory and delightful, even if they'd skimped on the meat, even if the smell of the stable ruins some of his appetite. He chews, swallows, warmed from the belly, and finds himself fuming again. "Titans above, that bastard. How do you deal with people like that all the time?"

Mydei is still quiet, still studying him, still looking at Phainon like he's some strange, alien creature for being here at all, and that's frustrating too. Why shouldn't he stay? Why can't he? Why are passive acceptance and outright hostility the only things that don't make Mydei look at a person like that? It's ridiculous, it's unfair, and Phainon's so furious that it took him this long to see it.

"I'm used to it," Mydei says. "There's no need for you to be out here too, unless you're really that short on coin."

"I know you're used to it," Phainon says, ignoring the insult, sagging, kind of sulking now. He's so tired. Titans, he's had a headache from squinting in the sun all day and his whole body is cold and sore and aching. "That's exactly the problem, don't you realize?"

Nothing else is said about it. They eat in silence, wash up with the rags and water in silence, lay out their bedrolls in silence. They're close again. Enough to touch, this time. At least the bed of hay makes a softer place to sleep than the ground. Phainon lays down in the dark and listens to Mydei polish his armor.

He's more comfortable than he thought he'd be, now that he's used to the smell. That, or he's just exhausted. Cloth on metal, rhythmic circles. The huffing of horses and the swishing sounds of their tails. Strife, the next stall over, peeks her head over the siding, snuffling. Mydei's soft murmur, "You have your own oats, I don't know what you're coming to me for."

Then, "Phainon."

He's falling asleep easier than he has in a while. Maybe he's just that worn out. Maybe he's had too many distractions today to spare a thought toward the things that usually keep him awake and watching the stars. He tries to reply, to grunt at least, but his consciousness is slipping, and he might not manage. 

His shoulder is cold. Something else is said, but he doesn't catch what. A sigh, maybe. Fabric rustling like wheat in the wind.
