He can see it there, golden wheat like golden eyes, and this is his favorite dream, grain tickling his legs, a gentle, blue ocean, and his fingers around smooth, cool glass. A young version of him tosses out a message in a bottle, filled with all his dreams. He watches it get carried away by the waves.

Distantly, in another world, a cold, hard real world, someone pulls his blanket back over his shoulder where it had slipped down. He's not cold anymore, not in the dream, not in life. For once, easily, he sleeps.

△

They don't linger in the morning. They pack up early and refill their waterskins from the well. Mydei takes care of Strife, Phainon takes to the market to buy a couple of things—lest Mydei get refused service—and argues hot porridge with preserves for breakfast from the still sour and increasingly less tolerant innkeeper.

They eat fast, and then they're off, heading for the second to last village standing between them and the Holy City. It's a cold morning, and it doesn't grow much warmer later in the day. Mydei pulls his other sleeve on. Phainon buries his hands in the pockets of his coat.

They don't have a long way to the next town, just half a day's walk on a side road, not the main—too populated so close to Okhema and a rampant place for harassment and hassle—at Mydei's behest. Mydei doesn't say as much explicitly, but Phainon can pick up on his reasons easily enough.

Their trip is quiet. Peaceful, with calm winds and a thin layer of frost over everything, shimmering in the sun until it melts later in the morning. It's beautiful, the first of it he's seen in the season, and while it's a harbinger of rougher travels, he's warm enough now and in an odd, optimistic mood. For once, Phainon is happy to let the silence sit and linger between them, listening to the sound of their footsteps, Strife's hooves, the metallic noises from Mydei's armor.

It's why he's surprised when Mydei speaks first. "Do you dream?" he asks. A strange question, coming from him, but saying so would only discourage him from opening up a conversation like this again, so Phainon just considers instead.

"What kind of dream do you mean? Do I dream when I sleep? Or do you mean hopes and wishes?"

"Both," Mydei says. "Either."

"Well..." Phainon looks down at his boots. Worn leather on the gray-brown pebbles and dead grass of the earth. He adjusts the straps of his pack on his sore shoulders. "Yes, then," he says. "To both of those things. I don't tend to remember my dreams at night, though. Sometimes I do, but not often." They aren't pleasant most of the time, but he doesn't say that. "And as for my wishes... I want to get stronger. I want to be able to defeat monsters and protect people who can't protect themselves, but you already knew that."

Why do you want to know? he almost asks, but stops himself. Mydei's expression tells him nothing at all. Anyone else, and he'd assume this is just idle conversation. With Mydei, he isn't so sure. It's the first time he's shown interest in this, in knowing Phainon, in... he doesn't know.

"What about you?" he asks instead. "What do you dream of?"

More quiet. Their walking feet. "I don't dream anymore," Mydei says after a long while. "Not since I was a kid."

"Which kind of dreaming?"

A rough laugh. "Both," Mydei tells him. "Either."

It's easy and odd at once, whatever this is. They've talked plenty. They've spent so much time in each other's company the past several days that it's inevitable. They've discussed the weather in depth, they've discussed food, monsters, battle, told stories that don't give away anything too personal. Rarely do they touch on the past. Rarely is Mydei willing to divulge anything about how, why, what it is to become a witcher.

"You don't dream of... I don't know, triumphing over the strongest monster you've fought yet and earning a whole bag of gold and the renown of an entire city?"

He looks at Mydei, a near perfect match in height, side by side like this. This whole time he hasn't been able to pinpoint who's taller. Mydei, maybe, but he has the advantage of a slight incline, and his boots, now that Phainon is looking, have a heel. Maybe Phainon is the taller one after all. For some reason, he feels inappropriate for noticing.

"No," Mydei says, and Phainon's gaze follows the markings on his arm down to where they disappear beneath his gauntlet before he looks away, feeling inappropriate for this too. There are clouds today, thin, long hazes of them that turn the sky blue and white in blurry swathes. The sun is veiled but still terribly bright, the horizon blocked out by trees here and there, some vivid with fall color, some entirely bare. "There's nothing triumphant about taking a life."

Phainon cocks his head and finds that he's denied eye contact. He watches Mydei's profile instead, his sharp jaw, the tension in it, his ragged hair. "You realize you kill by trade, don't you?"

"By trade," Mydei agrees. "Not by choice."

"But you enjoy sparring, tests of strength," Phainon notes. He never sees Mydei grin so much as he does when they fight, rolling in the dirt, playing tricks, trying desperately to get the upper hand. Just thinking about it... Perhaps he'll have to ask to spar again when they break for lunch, if his feet don't hurt too terribly.

"Yes, because I always kill when I spar," Mydei says dryly. "I'm sure you would know, having been killed by me a dozen times by now."

Phainon laughs. "A joke!" he exclaims. "Since when were you capable of such things?"

Mydei laughs too, though it's a small thing. "Expect stupid answers when you ask stupid questions."

"Fair enough," Phainon says. Slowly, his smile slips and fades. They crest the tiny hill they'd been climbing, walking on a decline now, slow and steady, each half in the grass because the path is narrow and unworn. A question, maybe stupid, waits on his tongue. "Hey, Mydeimos?"

A grunt, but a warmer grunt than it might've been another day. Mydei seems in a somewhat good mood. Phainon might ruin it. He hopes he won't. "Were you made a witcher against your will?"

He's heard the stories of children stolen away from their parents or sold by them, forced to endure things no child should have to endure, coming out unfeeling—undreaming—monsters. He can't be certain how true the stories are. He's certain that, like all rumors, they're exaggerated to some extent. Mydei isn't a monster, isn't unfeeling, but he's been through something to make him into what he is, and there are so many things that are unfair about it.

"I don't see how that's any of your business."

"I'll admit that it isn't. Don't feel pressured to answer, if you're insistent upon remaining mysterious and unknowable," Phainon tells him. "I'm just curious, what with all the false rumors surrounding witchers. I want to know the truth."

"Fool," Mydei says, soft, and doesn't answer his question.

Phainon sighs, laughs a little. "I suppose I'll take that as you remaining mysterious and unknowable, then."

But, "Yes," Mydei says. "It was against my will, as it was for most, if not all."

"I wondered," Phainon says, instead of something he doesn't think Mydei would appreciate, like I'm sorry.

They walk on. Endlessly, they walk on, five minutes stretching to ten, to twenty. They break for lunch in a copse of trees, their backs against bark, Phainon talking about antique vases and other things Mydei probably doesn't care about between bites. He doesn't end up asking for a spar, finding the feeling of sitting down much too good after a long morning of walking.

They set off again, not too far from the next town. An hour or two at most, somewhere beyond a thick line of trees. The chilled air smells faintly like smoke, like campfire, and after a time, Phainon grows tired of his own mind and their silence.

"Your Signs," he tries. "Like the one you use to heal and that other one, the one that froze me, what are they exactly?"

"Aquila's," Mydei says, "and Oronyx's."

"You've said." He thinks of the twist of Mydei's fingers, but he can't remember the shapes of each. "Do the powers come from the Titans? Are there others? One for each?"

"Yes," Mydei says, and adds nothing else.

"...To which question?"

Mydei, tilting his head to look down on Phainon from Strife's back, gives an unimpressed stare. 

"Most people explain when they're asked a question, you know," Phainon tells him. He lifts a hand, silencing Mydei, who wasn't about to speak. "If it's a trade secret, that's your right, I suppose, but really, what harm can come of me knowing?"

"What good comes of you knowing that a witcher can freeze a man in place with a wave of his hand, among other things?" Mydei asks. "My job is hard enough as is without rumors like that going around."

Sarcasm again. It's terribly rude and delightfully new. "Oh, come on," Phainon says, "they already think you bleed babies for your potions. A rumor like that is barely a drop in the bucket. And who am I going to tell anyway?"

"People talk," Mydei says, though he seems a little bit less tight-lipped. "I imagine you'll insist on entering town with me, as you do. You'll be seen, and later, when you're looking for someone to chop wood for or whatever it is you do to busy yourself, you'll be asked questions."

He kicks a pebble out in front of him. It doesn't stir up dust because of the recent rains, just tumbles a bit and comes to a stop for him to kick again. He gives up on that to look at Mydei again, a laugh held back on his lips slipping into his next words, "And you think my answer to those questions will be what? 'Oh, yes, ma'am, he's very dangerous, he bleeds babies and freezes men in place with a wave of his hand'?" He laughs. "You'd only have to ask for my lips to be sealed."

"Infant's blood isn't even a useful alchemical ingredient," Mydei scoffs, reaching out to pat Strife like she's taken offense to this too. All she does is snort and toss her head, continuing to walk.

"Right," Phainon says, squinting against the sun to look at him, "so why not lend me truths, that way I can help correct some of those nasty rumors?"

Mydei doesn't have a response to this. He's quiet for a moment, thinking about it, maybe. Or just thinking, or done with the conversation. He's still hard to read, as best as Phainon tries. But they haven't known each other long, and that'll come with time. For now, he lets the silence be, listening to the sound of their footsteps, Strife's hooves, the breeze shaking the dying leaves. Phainon can't help but smile slightly when Mydei speaks again, because—

"You're right," he says.

"I'm..." Phainon studies Mydei's face, pinched and begrudging, and grins. Mydei only frowns and turns away, shadowed with the sun to the side. "Can you say it again?" Phainon prompts. "I'm not sure I heard you."

Mydei ignores him. "The Titans know why you're so nosy today, but ask, if you must."

"Really?" Phainon asks, perhaps more incredulous than he should be. "I can ask, and you'll answer?"

"HKS," Mydei grumbles. "Ask."

Phainon laughs, almost tripping on a rock, and asks, "your Signs, then. How do they work? What do they do?"

A sigh. "There are twelve," Mydei answers. "One for each Titan. They're simplified spells for combat. Nothing like what a sorcerer can do, but strong enough."

"Can anyone learn them?" Phainon asks.

Mydei tips his head down to look at him. "What, like you?"

"...Or anyone else."

"Do you have an affinity for magic?"

"Not that I know of," Phainon admits.

"Then it isn't likely," Mydei answers.

And then it's silent again. Mydei doesn't offer any more information. Not about whether he'd had the affinity naturally or if it's something mutated into him or otherwise forced, not about what the other Signs do at all. Twelve of them, one for each Titan, with powers ranging from small healing to freezing a man in place. He can't even imagine what the other Signs might do. And they're simple, Mydei said. Phainon has never met a sorcerer; just what can they do, if those are simple?

"What other powers do they give you?" Phainon asks.

Mydei huffs a laugh. "Trade secret," he says.

Phainon chuckles, kicking a pebble, kicking it again when he comes upon it a few steps later. "You're such a bastard," he says. "And what if I catch you using them, what then? What if I end up collateral damage again like when you used Oronyx's?"

"Make your observations and learn," Mydei says, unapologetically. "Isn't that what you've decided to follow me around to do?"

There's a sharp, cold breeze. Phainon shivers, pulling his sleeves over his hands buried in his pockets. He gets another whiff of smoke, like they're downwind of someone's campfire or chimney. Perhaps they're closer to the village than he thought.

"You make me out to be some kind of dog," Phainon says. "I have goals, you know. I'm not following you around, I'm following the opportunity to get stronger."

"Right," Mydei says. His reply takes a moment and comes out distracted, which strikes Phainon as strange. He turns right as Mydei brings Strife to a stop, pausing and breathing deeply, scenting the air and scanning the road, the trees, the spaces between them. Around them, it's silent but for the breeze through senescing leaves, the soft sound of them falling now and then, their own quiet breath.

This happens now and then. Mydei will sense something and go full witcher mode, searching for it. A half-tamed animal, like the first time they'd met. Though, Phainon has started liking comparisons like that less and less.

"Is something wrong?" he asks softly, watching Mydei's gaze shift, Strife snorting and stamping her hooves anxiously.

There's no reply. Mydei only presses a hand to Strife's neck, and then she doesn't calm, forms a Sign Phainon hasn't seen yet that has her relaxing. His gaze turns toward the sky and sticks there. Somewhat reluctant, Phainon shifts closer to see through the canopy and turns his gaze up too.

Smoke. Tall, billowing columns of it marring the sky, distant but close enough to explain the smell. Phainon's breath stills. His blood goes cold.

Only now does Mydei look at him, gaze as gold as anything.

"That one," Phainon says, and his voice is unsteady, "that you used to calm Strife."

The horse is still calm and silent, head dipped to graze at the grasses on the ground. "Mnestia's," Mydei says.

Phainon's exhale is shaky. His hands are sweating. There's a familiar dread waiting in his chest like an old friend he'd rather not see again. Seeing those lines of smoke, smelling them, his mouth has gone dry. He feels sick.

Still, he forces himself to nod, head tipped up to meet Mydei's eyes, forcing himself to be strong. Not just some scared, lost boy, haunted by his past. "Right, then," he says. "I suppose we should go check that out, whatever it is."

Fires, screaming, bloodshed. His hands curl into fists in his pockets, tight enough for his nail to dig in. Mydei's attention lingers on him for far too long before he nods and takes the reins, Strife reluctantly giving up her grazing to carry him along at a much quicker pace, Phainon jogging along until—

Until they reach the place where they path bends and eases out of the forest and into the huge clearing that houses the village. It's here, perched on a slight hill, looking down at the framing of trees, the pond, the field that must be full of wildflowers in the spring, that earth that must serve to grow crops in the summer, that they see it.

The town, buildings collapsed and scorched and turned to ash, some still smoking.

Chapter End Notes

and thus enters the plot

chapters.title: Chapter 6
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

They search for survivors, calling out and picking through rubble in case anyone might be trapped beneath. The smell is overwhelming up close. Burnt wood, stone, flesh. There's no shortage of bodies, many that look like they tried to run, most showing stab wounds alongside gruesome burns. There isn't even the slightest chance this was an accident, then.

Phainon had been frantic at first, charging into the still smoldering ashes of the village—just a tiny thing, really, probably with a population smaller than two hundred—but with every fruitless cry of is anyone there? we're here to help, he grows more and more haunted, desperate but not disillusioned, like he knows there's no one left and wants nothing more than to be proved wrong.

Mydei grabs his arm, watches him whirl around—eyes wide and red-rimmed from the smoke or emotion or both, mouth and nose hidden away beneath his tunic held up as a filter—and says, "Phainon."

A hard exhale. Phainon knows what he's going to say. He yanks free, and the smoke is thick but Mydei thinks he can smell him, sour with fear and cold sweat, but maybe that smell is leftover from the fallen.

"There's still a lot of this place we haven't checked," Phainon says. His gaze is wild, flitting around, never lingering in one spot longer than a moment. Briefly, it returns to Mydei's face, similarly covered by the shoulder of his robe. "People could be trapped, or they don't have the breath to yell, or they're scared we're with whoever did this. We need to keep looking."

Around them, burnt rubble still smolders, crackling softly. Between the two of them, there's hardly a sound, just charred earth and blackened bodies and crumbled houses. Mydei is familiar with this kind of carnage. He knows what it looks like as it happens, endlessly loud and stinking, a torrent to all the senses, overwhelming and horrifying and—

Phainon isn't breathing well. Too quickly, too shallowly. Mydei takes a half step forward. "Can I calm you with Mnestia's Sign?" he asks. "Like I did with Strife?"

"What?" Phainon asks voice muffled through fabric, eyebrows furrowing, and then he shakes his head. "No. No, I... We need to keep looking."

Looking at him, seeing effort he makes now to at least appear calm—Evening out his breath, leveling his voice, stilling his shaking, Mydei doesn't protest. They keep looking, and Phainon proves himself remarkably good at keeping himself together. Mydei is careful to keep an eye on him, wondering if this is his first time seeing this kind of carnage. If somehow it's not.

Every inch of the rubble is searched until their hands and gauntlets are stained with soot. Still, for a hundred bodies they check, not one is alive. After a point, Phainon straightens up, pulling his shirt down, wiping his nose on his sleeve as he continues to walk, expression tormented and glassy.

At the far edge of the village, right where the char stops, he sinks to the ground like a stone.

Mydei hesitates. Phainon is quiet, listless. There's no easy smile waiting as Mydei approaches, no laugh, no unfunny joke about how slow Mydei is to have fallen behind.

His shoulders are bowed. He doesn't look up as Mydei's armor creaks all the way to him, when a twig snaps beneath his foot. His head stays down when Mydei drops into a seat beside him.

Mydei has always been most comfortable in silence. He doesn't care for company, he doesn't like most people, not those that aren't his brother and sister witchers, forged in blood the same as he was. Phainon... is an exception. He always seems to make an exception of himself. He's proven again and again to be someone with potential and worth and a strange abundance of determination and anger and kindness all at once. Mydei respects him. Mydei... cares for him. In a way. To some extent. They're companions, at least.

"Are you alright?" he asks, perhaps too gruffly. But he's never been adept at comfort. He's never been taught gentleness.

A sniff. Phainon presses the heels of his hands against his eyes, itchy from smoke or emotion, Mydei doesn't know. He's not sure what he'd do, if Phainon were to cry.

"Yeah," Phainon says. Tired more than sad. Again, his voice breaks on the word, "Yeah. I'm alright. This is just..." A lot, he might say, horrible, terrifying, a tragedy. He might say any number of things, but what he picks after a brief silence comes as a surprise. "...Too familiar."

"Familiar," Mydei echoes. He looks at Phainon now. Ash settling in his white hair, soot smeared beneath his nose where he'd wiped it, eyes red-rimmed but dry, downcast and without their light. He smells—beneath the sickening torrent of scents—like cold sweat and stale, tired fear. There's no reply.

Too familiar, he'd said. His own town or another he'd run through. Mydei has wondered, but a part of him has always assumed Phainon lived some dreamy, happy life untouched by hurt before they began traveling together. He smiles so often, so widely. But a happy life never would have made sense. If Phainon were happy, he wouldn't avoid talking about it, he wouldn't toss and turn with nightmares, he wouldn't be following Mydei at all.

There are words for this. Mydei doesn't know know them. "Are you sure you don't want me to calm you?" he tries instead.

"I'm sure," Phainon says, and his voice is quiet "I'll be fine. I'd rather if my emotions remained my own."

"Cerces' Sign, then," Mydei offers. "It clears the mind. Paired with focusing techniques or meditation, you can learn to keep certain thoughts from coming back."

A weak laugh. "No," Phainon says again, but he musters a half smile. He reaches a hand to Mydei's armored knee, sooty glove removed, fingers red with cold. Softly, "Thank you."

His skin against metal. Mydei can't feel it, shouldn't be stuck on it. There doesn't seem to be a thing he can do to help, so he doesn't say anything else, just sits. Stays and doesn't push to keep moving, like he would have were he on his own. And Phainon—stubborn, resolute, strong Phainon, who jumps at the chance to spar, who doesn't have a care about what Mydei is, who slept beside him in the stables rather than letting him suffer the indignity alone, who... probably deserves to be called a friend by now—seems to appreciate it.

Metal against skin. Phainon pulls his hand back, playing with the blackened, already bloodstained gloves in his lap. His fingers must be freezing. This, Mydei doesn't comment on either. He just waits, and Phainon breathes for a while and then stands up, dusting himself off to no avail, not quite smiling, 

"Alright," he says, exhales, burying his hands in his pockets. "We should go. We can..." He nods, more to himself than to Mydei. "Yes, we should go."

Slowly, Mydei stands up too. "You called this familiar," he says.

"Yes, well..." He won't meet Mydei's eyes. His throat bobs when he swallows dry. "...It seems there is no shortage of monsters ready to slaughter and torch down an entire village. I'm not the first to have a story like that, and I won't be the last. Let's go, before..." His breath hitches. He clears his throat, blinks, turns away so Mydei can't see his face, only his back, only his normally strong shoulders. "We'll need to send word to the next town if someone else hasn't already."

So they set off, cutting back through the edge of the scorched town to get to where he'd hitched Strife away from the smoke. On the way out, Mydei pauses. There, stuck to a post of a scorched, half-standing fence, is a scrap of thick, tattered black fabric. He takes it, rubs it between his fingers, frowning. A faint twinge courses through his markings. Magic. He tucks the cloth into his pocket before Phainon can see it.

△

The fire crackles softly when they make camp for the night. Phainon sits, bundled up on a fallen log half rotted and eaten by insects. The light flickers over his face, eyes downcast, mouth a straight line. His hands are outstretched, and maybe it's the cold, or the dark, or the silence that makes one's own breath sound so much louder, but he's quiet. He'd caught a couple of squirrels, cooked, salted, shared, and ate them in silence, and now, belly full, is silent now too. Days ago, Mydei would have been glad for it. Now, he finds that he isn't.

Maybe Phainon notices the attention, maybe he's been thinking about it for a long time, because he looks up, meeting Mydei's gaze and sighing softly. "I think we should take turns keeping watch tonight," he says. "Just in case..."

Mydei nods. "Agreed."

A pause between them. Phainon adds a couple of sticks to the fire. A few moments, they catch, the blaze popping. A embers rise from the flames, glowing red and dying as fast as they'd come up. "Do you think it was a monster that did that?" Phainon asks.

The black scrap of cloth, traced with magic. The wounds on the villagers, stabs and burns both. If it were just the flames, he'd call it an accident or perhaps the work of an elemental lifeform, but an elemental would have left traces leading to a den, and wouldn't have blades to stab its victims. No, more likely this is the work of a group of men. Deserters or starving militants or invaders from another land, thinking to burn and plunder.

"Men are just as capable as monsters when they stand to gain something," is what he says instead, watching the way the light dances on Phainon's face, painting him with a mosaic of light and shadow. The scent of the smoke burns his nose. Familiar, he thinks. In Phainon's voice, too familiar.

"You may be right," Phainon replies. "I wish you weren't."

Mydei grunts, leaves it be, despite his questions. A cool breeze blows between them. Mydei pulls on his other sleeve, closing the front of his robe to keep the cold out. Phainon watches him do it and exhales, speaking again.

"I know what that looks like. My hometown was torched down by a black cloaked swordsman. He came out of nowhere and just..." He gestures vaguely, shadows forming on his face as he clenches his jaw. "...Destroyed it all. Razed the buildings and the fields and killed anyone who tried to run right." His hands turn to fists in his lap. His voice shakes, not with sadness but with fury. "And yet somehow I was the only one who got away. The only survivor, in a town of two or three hundred."

He makes an odd sound, distress and frustration and something else. "Worst of all is that he..." He pauses, exhales, shakes his head. "That's why I want to get stronger, because I was young then, and powerless and afraid, and I don't ever want to feel that way again." A pause. He clears his throat, sniffs, wipes at his face with the back of one hand, gaze anywhere but Mydei. "And, well. You've expressed some curiosity as to why I'm so... stubborn. I figured now is as good a time to explain as any. Sorry if that's more than you cared to know about me. I'm sure most people have backstories like this anyway."

A small laugh. He scrubs at his face some more, and Mydei doesn't have the slightest idea what to say. "No," is what he settles on. "Most people do not have backstories like that."

"Well," Phainon says. He smooths his hands over his thighs, curling in on himself a little tighter. "You're probably right. Look, um. Listen." He clears his throat. "Would you use it now? Cerces' Sign. I can't help thinking about things I'd really rather not think about right now, so if it isn't too much trouble...?"

"Those thoughts will come right back if you can't find something else to focus on instead," Mydei says, but he stands up and circles the fire until he comes to Phainon's side, gesturing for him to scoot over on the log so Mydei doesn't have to sit on the rotted part.

"You said you had techniques," Phainon says, moving over.

"Sometimes we use mantras, sometimes I recite historical texts in my head. Have you ever meditated before?"

"No," Phainon says when Mydei sits.

Wonderful. Mydei hasn't the faintest idea how to be a guide for that sort of thing. "The Sign will clear your mind, but it's your job to keep it that way," he says. "Imagine peace. Focus on your breathing. Are you ready?"

"Imagine peace," Phainon repeats. He sucks in a shaky inhale and shuts his eyes. "How very specific."

But he goes quiet for a handful of moments, preparing a space for himself, though his hands knot in his lap and his posture is weary. Mydei raises his hands and forms the Sign.

Immediately, Phainon reacts, sitting a little straighter. "Whoa," he whispers, eyes peeling open.

"Focus," Mydei reminds him, though he's intimately familiar with the effects of this Sign, the sudden clearheadedness it provides, something that stays sweet and peaceful with proper cultivation.

"Right," Phainon says, shutting his eyes again. In the firelight, his eyelashes look far too long. "My mind has just never been so quiet before."

Mydei drops his hands into his lap and looks at him, watching him struggle to keep his mind clear. Mydei has never known a witcher to manage for than a minute on their first try. He'd probably only lasted a handful of seconds before his torrent of thoughts came right back his first time, but Phainon still seems to hold onto something other than memories of fire and slaughter. "Breathe deeper," Mydei reminds him.

"Ah, but it stinks like smoke," Phainon says, eyes still shut. "I've... imagined myself a wheat field, like ones back home. We were by the sea so the breeze always smelled a bit like earth and salt."

"Your home," Mydei notes. Now, Phainon smiles faintly. It's a real smile, tired as it is. "Is that not counter intuitive?"

"You might think," Phainon says, "but strangely enough, no." His hand slips into an inner pocket of his coat, producing a small, wrinkled square of paper and that he turns between his fingers and rubs his thumb along the creases of. "Say, aren't you not supposed to talk to someone as they meditate?"

"Whatever you're doing is more like daydreaming," Mydei tells him, looking up from the paper and finding his all too blue eyes. They're kind of close, aren't they? There's only so much unrotted space on this log. "That's what the Dolosian stole from you, isn't it?"

"Cipher," Phainon corrects him. He looks down at it, lips curling up slightly again. "But yes. It's a divination card from an old friend. She was going to be a priestess of Oronyx, and when she'd do her readings, I would draw this card every time." He chuckles, more air than sound. "I'm not sure she didn't cheat somehow, but... she gave me the card after a while, since I was the only one who ever pulled it anyway."

He holds it out. Mydei takes it, careful as he can be. The Deliverer, it reads along the bottom. On it is painted a hero with a greatsword, the rising sun at his back, Kephale's symbol at the top. It's all blue and white and fading details foiled in gold. 

"So that's why Cipher called you 'Deliverer boy,'" Mydei notes. He'd wondered, passed it off as nonsense.

It's quiet as Phainon continues to meditate, or some poor imitation of it. "This friend," Mydei starts.

Another laugh. "No," Phainon says, "If you're about to ask what it sounds like you're about to ask. She was always just a friend."

"I see," Mydei says, handing the card back. He nods to it. "And this?"

"I forget the exact meaning," Phainon says, shifting on his sit bones, exhaling. It's hard to see in this light, but his fingers must be bright red and frozen. He'd washed his gloves in the stream to get the soot out, and they're still wet and won't be any help against the cold. "Something about how I'm destined to be some kind of hero." He laughs a little, fond as he looks down at the card. Mydei gets the feeling that they're sitting too close.

"They're memories," he says, standing before Phainon can turn to look at him. He returns to his side of the fire, finding his waterskin from the ground where he'd been sitting and taking a swig like he needs some kind of an excuse.

"Sure," Phainon says. "Yeah, they are." A little longer, he's quiet, but he doesn't seem as haunted as he had been. Those thoughts will likely come back again, but for now he seems alright, bittersweet. "Hey, Mydeimos?"

Mydei meets his gaze through the fire, hums an acknowledgment.

"Thank you," Phainon says, and tucks the card away again. He clears his throat, rubs at the back of his neck. "Just... Yeah. Thank you. For that just now, and for... I don't know. Sorry. I know we're not friends and you don't really want me here, but. You've been kind."

Titans above. Mydei has to say it, doesn't he? He can't just leave it to their spars and shared meals and how close their bedrolls are at night. His tongue feels thick. A lump forms in his throat, and the fact that he finds this embarrassing makes it more so. He isn't warm and easygoing and friendly like Phainon is. His only bonds have been forged through necessity, bloodshed, and shared pain.

"Do you really think you'd still be here if I didn't want you to be?" he asks, and bites his tongue on the insinuation. I want you here, he's saying, if Phainon can read between the lines to hear it. I want you here, he's saying, and Titans above, it isn't untrue. "Don't be so presumptuous as to assume you could force me into anything against my will."

Firelight. Phainon's gaze dips down, and he's daft, certainly, but it seems he understands this much. He smiles faintly. "I suppose not," he says, "but if I may be a different kind of presumptuous... Can we be friends, Mydei? More than me using you as a learning opportunity and a ticket to Castrum Kremnos, and more than me simply taking some of the discomforts of the road on your behalf, or being... I don't know, some form of entertainment."

"I've never agreed to take you to Kremnos," Mydei reminds him, but his mouth pulls into a traitorous smile.

Phainon grins back, the most himself he's been all day. "Yes, well, there's still time to persuade you," he says. "So what'll it be?"

"Yes, Phainon, Deliverer, wannabe hero," Mydei sighs. "We're friends."

△

Mydei takes first watch after the fire burns out. His senses are far keener than Phainon's anyway, and he isn't the one dead on his feet, so it isn't a decision that takes much arguing.

Mydei is well aware that Phainon has trouble sleeping. It would be hard not to notice, sharing space with him night after night. He tosses and turns, though it's clear he tries to restrain himself for Mydei's sake. His breathing takes a long time to settle—he'll sigh now and then, like he's frustrated at his own inability to rest. Sometimes he'll roll onto his back and stretch his hands out to the sky like he's mapping out constellations or trying to give himself frostbite. Tonight, though, he settles down and falls asleep fast.

Mydei listens to the silence, the soft breath, the wind and distant river and the sounds of insects. Here's his peace, as he cleans and polishes his armor. Here's his peace, as he sorts through his potions already sorted through for the hundredth time, as he checks on Strife, asleep a short distance away. Here's his peace, as he sets himself up on his bedroll, watching the silhouettes of trees in the dark, the stars overhead, Phainon beside him, only a meter away, little more than a tuft of white hair visible for the way he bundles himself up to stay warm.

Mydei's gaze sticks to him for a long, long while.

He slips that scrap of fabric out from his pocket, faint strands of magic still clinging to it, sending sparks through his markings as he touches it with bare fingers now. A black cloaked swordsman, he remembers Phainon saying. It doesn't feel like a coincidence. He tucks the cloth away and does another scan of the place. Wind, water, insects, nothing.

Phainon stirs slightly, murmuring something. Mydei turns to him, waiting, watching. It wouldn't be the first time Phainon has spoken in his sleep. He gets nightmares often. Perhaps of his hometown—where had he said that was again? Perhaps he hasn't said at all.

"No," Phainon says, so softly not a person would hear if they didn't have senses like Mydei's. He shifts again, slightly, and Mydei watches on for only a moment longer before he forms the Sign of Cerces and banishes the dream. It wouldn't be the first time for this, either, but Mydei knows better than to tell Phainon something like that.

He watches Phainon settle back into dreamless sleep, and settles in to wait out the rest of his watch.

△

Phainon is back to normal the next day. In the morning, they spar to warm up their stiff, cold, poorly-rested bodies, and he's grinning and taunting and learning the same as he always does. He even manages to pin Mydei for a couple of seconds before he gets thrown off and ultimately loses, but it gets closer each time. Phainon learns Mydei's fighting style, his weaknesses, his bad habits, and he picks up more and more tricks and techniques every day that make it difficult to predict him. He also has a habit of fighting dirty, flinging handfuls of soil, aiming for the genitals, head-butting; he lacks any sense of propriety or manners when it comes to a fight which... admittedly, makes him fun to fight against.

Mydei doesn't go easy on him anymore, aside from not using potions or magic or his gauntlets. One of these days, he might not even be surprised if Phainon wins one of their spars.

When they break for lunch at midday, they find themselves by the river under a break in the canopy, the sun on their backs warm enough for something like a bath. They wash their dirty socks and underclothes, leaving them to dry on a rock, and then Phainon is peeling off his trousers and shirt and stepping into the shallows for a wash, hissing and cursing over how cold the water is.

It isn't the first time they've bathed in proximity—privacy is inconvenient on the road—but Mydei has never really looked, not so much out of respect as out of indifference. But he's looking now, and without all of his modest layers, Phainon is built nearly as well as Mydei is. His back is broad, contoured with muscle, arms and legs showing the strength Mydei has noticed in his kicks and punches.

It isn't surprising, it shouldn't be surprising, but for some reason Mydei's gaze still sticks. The knobs of Phainon's spine as he bends to scoop water in his hands, the slight jut of his shoulder blades.

Mydei looks away after a moment, wrestling out of his own clothes and armor, leaving them in a neat pile by the bank of the river rather than a strewn mess as Phainon had. It is cold when he steps in, frigid enough that it's unpleasant even to him, with how hot his blood runs. The cursing and shivering make sense, and this— Well, it could be something friends do. He's spent hours soaking in hot springs with fellow witchers; this could be akin to that.

He washes quickly, methodically, with a bar of plain soap he's been using for a season, scrubbed down to a scrap no bigger than his thumb. Phainon's has some faint kind of floral scent to it, forsythia or something else, such an unreasonable thing to splurge on, and every now and then Mydei will catch it on him before it gets lost to the scent of the road and his sweat.

Now, he watches Phainon splash water in his face, not caring as it gets in his hair, scrubbing with his eyes squeezed shut and his breath probably held. He splutters when he's done, shaking out his limbs like some kind of dog, scrubbing his armpits and splashing himself with some more water before he straightens back up and dances out of the river, arms hugged tightly to his chest, spouting a fresh round of colorful language.

Mydei laughs at him, running his soap up his arms, looking away for only a moment before there's a violent splash and a shout. His first thought is that Phainon must've tripped back into the frigid water, but the splashing doesn't stop, nor does the shouting, and when he looks over, there's a ray-like creature with beak-like mandibles and a long tail wrapped around Phainon, gray skinned and tipped with crimson and wet, trying to pull him into the river where it will then drown and eat him.

Phainon is thrashing with the creature when Mydei gets to him, holding it by what might pass as its throat and trying to shake off its grasp, but it's slippery and strong, Mydei knows, drowners always are, and it keeps trying to snap at him, forcing him to constantly adjust to avoid losing a chunk of an arm or a leg.

"A little help?" Phainon says when he notices Mydei standing there, voice kind of shrill, barely sparing a glance because he can't afford to divert his attention.

"Consider this a test of strength," Mydei says, watching a little longer as Phainon gets the thing off of himself, panting and unsure what to do with it, still struggling and still slippery, flopping like a fish out of water and still attempting to wrap fins and tail around him before Mydei hauls the thing back with fingers jammed into its gills, tossing it back into the river. Mostly bare and without his gauntlets, he casts the Sign of Nikador for a weapon instead, feeling the power course through him, drawing from his body and his blood, manifesting as hard, sharp crystal he swiftly jabs into the drowner's neck as it comes back for another attack. He yanks the crystal out and kicks the corpse away, where it collapses in the current.

Phainon sits up a ways away, still in the water and thoroughly soaked, catching his breath, and shivering, and says, "Well. That'll be a first for me."

"You've never seen a drowner before?" Mydei asks, dropping the crystal with a splash and offering a hand to help Phainon up. He takes it, fingers frigid, smelling like forsythia and drowner slime, and Mydei realizes he'd lost his scrap of soap somewhere in the river during the chaos.

"No," Phainon says, wrapping his arms tight around himself again, voice strained and breathy. He's staring at the corpse, limp and unmoving now, face down in the water a few paces away. His gaze lifts to Mydei's, eyelashes wet and clumping, the ends of his hair dripping into his face. With them both barefooted, he might have half an inch on Mydei, and it feels strangely unacceptable. "No, I think I'd have remembered such a thing if I had."

"They're rather common as far as monsters go," Mydei explains, stepping away. "They're Phagousa's corrupted titankin, and they tend to hunt in groups, so there will be more."

"Delightful," Phainon says, skipping out of the water as quick as he can. He sounds shaken. "Wonderful, that's just wonderful."

Mydei watches him wrestle himself back into his clothes, still wet and shaking. "Are you scared?" he asks, more curious than anything else. All their time together, and he's never seen Phainon scared before, aside from the day before, but that... that wasn't fear, that was bone-deep, long-standing horror, and this...

"Scared?" Phainon repeats, looking at him, balancing awkwardly on one foot as he fights his way back into his pants. "Oh, no, not scared. Upset, though? Absolutely! I've just realized I'm a a complete, useless fool when it comes to the real dangers of the world, and I..." He exhales. "Okay, maybe I am a bit scared. That thing came out of nowhere!"

"Yes, they're rather adept at that," Mydei says, and hesitates when Phainon's frustration stays, and grows as he struggles with the sleeves of his shirt, fabric clinging to his wet arms. "You fared well against it," he offers.

"Sure," Phainon says, bitterly now, raking his wet hair off his forehead. "Yes, let's go with that, like I wasn't about to die just now."

"You wouldn't have died," Mydei says, bending to fetch his own clothes from where he'd left them on the bank.

"No," Phainon agrees. "Because you're here. Which... thank you for the rescue, but you have to understand why I'm frustrated to have needed it at all."

Mydei is quiet, considering this angry, self-critical version of Phainon. So obsessed with strength, being strong, getting strong, but without the patience to allow himself time to get there. A weakness, perhaps, that Mydei hadn't recognized as one. Boundless potential that comes with boundless self expectation.

"What you need," he says carefully, "is a sword."

A laugh, bitter as everything else. Phainon viciously pulls on his coat. "Oh yes, because I have loads of money for that."

"You'll find work in Okhema."

"Maybe," Phainon says. "Maybe, but enough work in whatever handful of days you're planning to stay to pay for a sword? A proper sword, actually suited to me, that won't break or go dull after a few stabs? Mydeimos, have you ever paid for a sword before?"

He doesn't bother continuing this line of conversation, sensing that Phainon is just in the mood to argue. His armor goes back on, piece by piece, and he says, "Very well, then. You'll continue fighting with your hands."

"But you'll teach me," Phainon says, jamming his feet into his boots. "You'll actually teach me. You'll tell me what I'm doing wrong and how to get better, and you'll tell me about these common monsters so I won't fill up my waterskin one day and end up dead."

"You've never been worried about this before."

"Yes, well, I've never been about to die while casually taking a bath before either."

"You wouldn't have died," Mydei says again.

"You won't always be there, Mydeimos."

He shakes his head, straightening up once he's fully dressed, and says it once more. He brings them face to face, and Phainon's restless movements still. "You wouldn't have died, Deliverer, whether I was there or not."

"You can't be sure of that, given the way things played out just now."

He's frustrating, making Mydei says things he doesn't want to say. He pokes Phainon's chest, steel right over his heart. "I've tested your strength. I know what I'm up against during our spars, and if a drowner isn't a tenth as strong as I am, then the Titans know why I've had even a little bit of trouble against you."

Phainon's gaze flicks between Mydei's eyes. His mouth parts—reddened and chapped—for a breath. "You think I'm strong," he says, a bead of water dripping down his face from his hairline. His mouth curls into an insufferable smile. "Genuinely, you think I'm strong."

Mydei presses his hand flat to Phainon's chest and shoves him away. "HKS," he grumbles. "Don't grow some kind of ego."

He laughs like the sun. It's faintly nauseating. Mydei hikes back up to where Strife is hitched, beating her tail against a couple of stubborn flies. Phainon, as always, jogs to catch up, still wet, still smiling, still far too bright for a dreary journey like this.

△

"Not too far now," Phainon says as they set up camp for tonight with the last bits of dying sun. "Just one more village standing between us and the Holy City, and your..." He leaves a pause that Mydei is probably meant to fill, but doesn't. "...Personal business. Are you ever going to tell me what that is, by chance?"

It's windy again, and might rain or even snow, so they're stringing rope between two trees to make a tent with their tarps. It means they'll have to sleep close tonight, not for the first time and probably not for the last. Close enough to touch, to share warmth if they burrowed just a little bit closer to one another. Phainon will be weird and conscious of his breathing and shifting around, and Mydei will be good enough at tolerating this encroachment upon his personal space because it's based on necessity.

And then he thinks, not of this, but of before, of Phainon sleeping beside him in the stables not born of necessity at all. Of his anger on Mydei's behalf. Fool, he thinks to himself, remembering the softness of his sleeping face. What a fool.

"It's personal," Mydei says blandly, securely knotting the cord as Phainon wrestles with a sheet of waxed canvas. "I've already told you all there is for you to know."

"Is it work?" Phainon asks. "A special commission, perhaps? A beast of legend or a cursed maiden or—"

"I didn't invite you to play a guessing game," Mydei interrupts him, but his reply comes out far less harshly than during the other myriad times Phainon has brought up this particular question. Phainon goes quiet, but seems to note this. Together, in a quietly coordinated kind of dance, they set up the tent, just wide enough to lay their bedrolls side by side, barely tall enough for either of them to sit up inside.

When they've staked down the corners and brushed the dirt off their frozen fingers, Phainon straightens up and says, "I want to know about you." At the look Mydei gives him, he stumbles over his tongue to continue. "If we're friends, I want to know about you, not like... I don't know, like I'm some kind of weird witcher fanatic."

Mydei lifts a brow at him, can't help a laugh when he glowers back, both of them struggling to set up their bedrolls. And Phainon, with the way that he is, can't help but laugh back.

"just..." He visibly fights for the words. "If it's some kind of life-ending, state-threatening secret, don't tell me. But if it's about you, I won't claim any right to know, but I want to. I want to know about you."

"You're assuming there's anything to know at all."

"Don't even try to convince me there's not. Look, you like deals, don't you? Something of mine for something of yours?"

"You're assuming I want to know about you, Deliverer."

Now, Phainon laughs like he's said something actually funny, bending to slide his bedroll into the tent, shoving it right up against one side so there's room for Mydei's on the other. "Well, don't you?" he says, and Mydei can't refute it. "And what's this with calling me 'Deliverer?' Are you making fun of me?"

"Deliverer," Mydei repeats like he's trying it out on his tongue. "A nod to that card you carry around. Wannabe hero. It suits you well."

"Prospective," Phainon corrects. "Prospective hero sounds far nicer."

Mydei sinks to one knee, half smiling as he shakes his head and sighs for show, shoving his bedroll into its spot. Then he sighs again, a real one this time, and says, "I'm going to Okhema because there's someone there..." A pause. He thinks of the letter tucked into the side of one of Strife's saddlebags. The decades that have passed since it was written. "Because there might be someone there that I need to find."

"An old friend?" Phainon asks, blue with dusk, head cocked to one side.

"You could say that."

A breath. Phainon hesitates now, straightening up and pulling away to the fire they haven't yet built. "A lover?"

This, Mydei laughs at in earnest. "Titans, no. Not a lover."

"You're not giving me much to work with here," Phainon points out.

"No," Mydei agrees. "But that's as much as you'll get. Take it or leave it."

"So cruel," Phainon says, making a ring with the rocks they'd gathered earlier, sectioning a space for the fire. He caught another hare, so they'll have meat. It's nice, as much as Mydei will never admit it. He likes that he doesn't have to worry about the hunting. He likes that Phainon is so willing to share his salt. He comes to set up the other side of the fire pit. 

Phainon's head stays down. He sniffles and wipes his nose on his sleeve, presumably running from the cold. "It's your turn to ask me something."

"You're awfully fond of this game, aren't you?" Mydei notes, laying down the last stone. Next is the firewood, piled haphazardly off to the side.

"Sure," Phainon agrees, "I find that making it into an exchange like this—a game, as you called it—makes it much easier to open up, does it not? It's all fair in the end, if we're both sharing vulnerable information. Looks like it's my turn for a question now, isn't it?"

"HKS," Mydei murmurs.

Phainon chuckles, wedging handfuls of kindling into the pockets beneath the structure Mydei creates with the largest pieces of wood. "I'm kidding," he says. "Ask something interesting, won't you?"

He has a lot of questions still, but not many that he wants to voice. Fewer that he thinks are good and fair like this game is supposed to be, the second time they find themselves playing it. "Your hometown," he settles for. "I don't think you ever mentioned what it was called."

"Aedes Elysiae," comes the answer, and the way Phainon says it is full of longing. "It was a small farming town on the coast, golden with wheat fields and never without the warmth of the sun."

"Phainon of Aedes Elysiae," Mydei says, softer than he means to, just to test the words.

Phainon still doesn't look up, shadowed more and more as the sun fades fully, but the corners of his mouth curve into the faintest hint of a smile. "That's me," he says, and sits back on his heels when he runs out of sticks within reach. "My turn now?" Mydei inclines his head, so he makes a show of thinking about it. "What was it like, becoming a witcher?"

"Painful," Mydei replies, trying to keep the bitterness from his voice, "terrifying, agonizing, like being ripped apart again and again just to be put back together. Having to watch other kids die because they couldn't handle the toxic concoctions or the training or the monsters we were pit against."

Phainon is quiet, speechless or something else. "Is it that terrible?"

"I think it's my turn for a question."

"Right." Phainon swallows audibly. Mydei digs for his tinderbox. "Go right on ahead."

"Your black cloaked swordsman. What did he look like?" Mydei asks, striking sparks over a bit of waxed cotton until it catches.

"He was tall," Phainon starts. "His face was completely covered with his hood and some mask made of bone or metal or something. He had a huge, crooked sword, and his cloak was in tatters, and he..." Mydei doesn't look, but he's certain that haunted expression comes back. "I don't know," Phainon finishes. "I didn't get a good look, and it's been a while, but. He wasn't pretty, that's for certain. Do you hate being a witcher?"

Some of the kindling catches, blazing bright, hopefully enough to catch the wood on fire too. "No," Mydei says. "I wouldn't wish it on anyone, but no. It's been long enough that I can't imagine myself as anything else."

"You were robbed of a normal future," Phainon says, like he should be furious about that, and he used to be. He remembers a spear in his hands, a chest caving beneath it, fury so hot he'd been blinded with it. A destiny fulfilled. But then he'd just been cold, and tired, and he knew he'd done the right thing but he didn't feel accomplished at all.

Now, he just shrugs and says, "so were you."

"And I'm so furious over it I can't think straight," Phainon whispers. It sounds like a confession. He doesn't wear his fury on his sleeve the way he does with everything else, but Mydei has seen it. He knows it burns deep, the embers of it ever smoldering.

The fire crackles as it establishes. Mydei watches the glow until it leaves imprints in his vision when he looks up. "Do you know where the swordsman went?"

"No," Phainon says. "And I hope I never see him again. Or that if I do, I'll be strong enough to slay him with my own hands."

It makes sense, he makes sense. His determination, his resilience, his desperate need to get stronger. Phainon isn't really some wannabe hero with dreams of glory. "You want revenge."

"I want justice."

"Call it what you want," Mydei says, using a stick to prod at a log that hasn't caught yet, pushing it closer to the blaze. A moment of silence. When he looks up, Phainon is contemplative and frowning. He wonders if he's upset him somehow. "...Don't forget about the rabbit. Or were you planning on letting it rot and going hungry?"

"No," Phainon exhales. "No, you're right."

Chapter End Notes

Lore concoction volume 3: Drowners are actual monsters from the Witcher series thought to be born from "scoundrels who ended their wicked lives in the water," but I've turned them into those fish enemies in Styxia. A lot of the monsters in the Witcher come from vengeful spirits after death; for the most part they'll be corrupted titankin in this fic instead. Someone dying horribly can be the source of that corruption, though :)

chapters.title: Chapter 7
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

do let me know if there are ever tags I need to add :)

There's blood everywhere, everything is bleeding, burning, hurting. There's pain, agony, heat, so much heat, flames so bright they're blinding, smoke so thick it's suffocating. He can't move, can't claw with raw, torn, bloody fingers to safety. This isn't the aftermath, the post-burning, when everything is an ashen husk so far removed from what it once was.

This is the burning as it happens. It's hoarse, torn throats screaming for dead friends and lovers and family. It's the tear-stained faces of children, the stench of burnt blood, the buildings collapsing on top of people, the sword embedding in the chests of anyone trying to run, the resistance as it goes in, the squelching sound, the glassiness of their eyes, the feeling as the blade comes back out.

Phainon sees it, sees it all, every death, every atrocity. He sees it, he feels it, he is it. He is the child crushed under rubble, the woman with the sword in her chest, the man who can't breathe in the smoke filled air. And then those hands are his, gauntleted in dark steel and stained in blood, starting these fires, slaughtering these innocents. He feels pleasure and purpose, and then horror and fear and pain, because now he is the woman kneeling over her bleeding sister, the boy covered in burns and trying to run, the man being stabbed, impaled and lifted, fingers closing around the cross guard of that huge sword, blood running down the blade, over his fingers as all he feels is pain, pain, pain, so much of it, and then the sword is yanked free and he falls right to the scorched earth, burning, bleeding, hurting.

This, he thinks, is what it must feel like to die. He's known the already dead, the dying, the killer, but he isn't ready at all. He has a wife, children, things he'd still like to do, and he—

He's himself. Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, standing here in this scorched village, scorched like his hometown had been, like the last village had been, like this one is too, and this is the aftermath, the post-burning, when only the last embers smolder and the whole place is turned to ash.

The man is there, the man he's never met. The man who had been him a moment ago. Him, but also his son, brother, father, husband, friend as he'd been everyone else in the village too. A cobbler, skilled in his work and dead now, stabbed right through the chest while he'd been Phainon, while Phainon had been him. And Phainon had also been the one to stab him, the black cloaked swordsman full of pain, so much pain but also pleasure, purpose, like every time he hurt and killed, something in him sang that it was right.

He's shaking. Phainon is shaking, no one else. He remembers, remembers, remembers. What it felt like to kill, what it felt like to die, to be dying, and he wonders if now—

"It isn't your time yet," comes a voice, deep and gravel-like, stone on stone, cutlery on china. "You can't die here, because you aren't done suffering."

No, Phainon thinks. No, no, no.

The black-cloaked swordsman stands in front of him. Tall and towering and faceless, and Phainon can't move, paralyzed with terror or something else, and there's Aedes Elysiae, there's his beautiful home, his friends, his family, his livelihood and his future dead and gone and—

"You're never safe," says the swordsman, stepping closer, stepping right on the dead man's face. "Wherever you go, all you bring is ruin."

No, Phainon thinks, but he can't say it aloud. His tongue has gummed up in his mouth, he's nauseated by the smell of burnt town and scorched flesh. He tries to shut his eyes but he can't even manage that, helpless again, powerless and paralyzed and weak and too useless to do something, anything, and he hates that feeling, hates the way he's trained so hard and so long just to keep it from ever coming back, and here he still is. Cold with terror and unable to do a thing.

"You brought this," the swordsman tells him. Again, Phainon sees it, feels it, is it. The suffering, the horror, the ruin. He cries out but his voice doesn't make a sound and then he's back, frozen in place again as this man, this monster looms over him, bending so they'd be eye to eye if it weren't for the swordsman's mask. "You did this. This is your fault."

No, he thinks again, tries to say it. He fights himself to do something, to fight, to run, to anything, but he can't. He's nothing but an insect pinned to a board, every sense flooded with panic, terror, sickness. No, no, no. Please.

"Aren't you curious who I am?" that horrible voice asks, and he finds himself looking down at his hands, covered in blood, and he remembers being stabbed, he remembers being the one stabbing.

He looks up, and sees the swordsman's face, his—

"—liverer. Phainon. Snap out of it!"

He blinks, and the swordsman is gone. The rest is still there. The charred earth, the embers, the broken buildings and broken bodies of this town, the final one before they make it to Okhema, razed to the ground just like the last.

His gloved hands are covered in soot, but they aren't bloody. His coat is still intact where he hadn't been stabbed. His gaze lands on that dead man, a couple of paces away, charred nearly beyond recognition. But Phainon recognizes him, though they'd never met, though he shouldn't know who the man is at all. Pavlos, a cobbler with a wife named Daphne and two sons, Leander and Paris. He remembers their deaths, their pain, their terror. 

He exhales until his chest caves in, realizes there are tear tracks leading down either side of his face. His nose is running from the cold or the leftover haze of smoke. His legs hurt where he's been kneeling on them. It's so quiet. So, so quiet.

"Phainon," Mydei says a second time. His fingers are twisted into another Sign Phainon hasn't seen before. He only drops it when their eyes meet, and it's strange, the thick, palpable relief that moves across his expression.

"You stepped into a spell," he says, and his voice is strangely calm, carefully, soothingly level, like it is sometimes when he speaks to Strife. "Illusory magic or something like it. I've used Phagousa's Sign to break you out of it. What did you see?"

"I..." Phainon's voice comes out a croak. His gaze finds the dead man again. Pavlos, who he's never met, who he knows so deeply. Everyone here, every destroyed structure, he knows its history. Mydei moves to block his view of the body, so he finds his eyes tracing red markings instead, following them up ridges of muscle, up the side of a throat, up to a frowning mouth and furrowed eyebrows and eyes gold like amber.

He's worried, somehow Phainon has made Mydei worry about him. What a sight he must make, steel gauntlets covered in blood and cloak tattered and soaked in it, with sword as—

Clarity, blissful clarity. The thoughts, the horrible memories that don't belong to him, the face of the black cloaked swordsman all disappear, and there's Mydei, forming the Sign of Cerces.

"Breathe," he says, "or whatever that was will just return."

And already, he feels his thoughts circling back, so he breathes as Mydei tells him to, shutting his eyes and inhaling as much as his lungs can fit, exhaling it out as slow as he can.

"Sorry," he says. "Sorry, I..."

"You saw this, didn't you?" Mydei asks, gesturing vaguely at everything. So much worse; Phainon felt it, knew it, was it, but he just nods tightly, not trusting his voice if he were to speak.

A soft curse. Mydei pushes himself upright and holds out a hand, a steel gauntleted hand, and— Phainon takes it, allows himself to be pulled upright on feet that are steady enough. He catches sight of the man, the man he's never met, who he was, who... He's forgotten his name, forgotten everything about him but the way it felt when he was stabbed. Phainon's nauseous, but he doesn't say a thing.

"The memories you saw weren't yours," Mydei says. "Most of it will fade quickly, but. Whoever— or whatever did this wanted someone to know, and that's never a good thing. Did you see who or what it was?"

Another breath in, one out. Mydei's voice sounds thick, blurry, like he's underwater. It reeks like smoke. Ash crumbles beneath his boots, and he's sick, he's sick and lightheaded at once. He looks at Mydei, his bare shoulder smudged with soot.

"The swordsman," Phainon finally answers, echoing in his own ears. "The one in black, the one who burned down my home." A wave of nausea threatens his lunch, blackness at the edges of his vision threatens his balance. "He's the one who did this."

△

He washes his hands in the river, washes them and washes them until his fingers are tinged blue and frozen so stiff he can barely move them, and he doesn't think about the possibility of drowners until he's already back at their temporary camp for lunch and any potential dangers has long since passed.

He scolds himself for it, curses himself out in his head for being stupid and useless, careless and weak and helpless, powerless, and as he sticks his hands in the pits of his knees and waits for them to warm through, he relishes the agony in each of his fingers, thinking to himself, you deserve this, you deserve pain, you deserve everything that will ever happen to you. And then Mydei offers him half a sweetened oat cake that's supposed to be for Strife but he sneaks for himself sometimes, and he can't reconcile the fact that his train of thought means he must deserve this too.

"Thank you," he says, and takes it with still painfully tingling fingers.

Mydei sits beside him this lunch, which he so rarely does. It makes him realize he must be acting like some traumatized, pitiable thing, and the thought makes him angry. It makes him furious that he might be— That he might be broken, scared, and vulnerable as he'd been that day, even after everything, after how hard he's tried, after every tiny bit of suffering he's forced himself to endure in the name of getting stronger. He hides his free hand beneath his thigh and curls it into a tight, painful fist.

A little longer. None of the feelings fade, not the boiling beneath his skin, not the pain in his hands

"We should spar," he says, turning to Mydei, who he finds already looking at him. Closer than he'd thought, expression impassive, and why is he looking at all? Heat crawls up Phainon's neck. He tries again, "We... should spar."

"Alright," says Mydei, low and kind of quiet. Phainon takes a bite of the oat cake, chews and swallows and finds it sweet and sticking in his teeth.

"Wonderful," he says to the air, to the fallen leaves, rather than to Mydei himself. "Great, I'll just finish this and then we can pick a suitable spot."

Mydei doesn't reply, but he starts working his gauntlets off, silver and steel, one a bit darker than the other, for monsters and for men. The rest of his armor stays on, but he's more of a puncher than a kicker, so Phainon doesn't mind. He finishes the rest of the oat cake, trying to tongue the leftover bits out of his teeth as Mydei gets up. 

He watches his back, his markings that converge in the dip of his spine, the drape of his robe, stained in places with dirt from the road and soot from two burnt towns. Phainon's hand is still clenched, fist white from the tension. It takes time for the color to come back when he opens his fingers, sucking in a deep breath before he follows Mydei into a break in the trees.

He rocks on his feet as they check the place for unseen dangers—holes covered by fallen leaves, hidden stones they might trip over or bash their heads on if they take a tumble.

When it's clear, Phainon straightens up. It'll be good, sparring. Walking wears him too slowly, doesn't give him the rush he needs, the brutal physicality. Walking leaves him with too much time to get in his own head, to think and remember and see and feel and be and—

He settles into a fighting stance. Mydei does too, and he thinks to himself that this will be good. It'll feel good to fight. It'll feel good to hurt, when inevitably he loses. He throws the first punch, rushing forward without a moment's hesitation, connecting with Mydei's guard. His knuckles sting. It's good, the impact, the blur of motion as he throws himself into the fight again, kicking this time, connecting, punching before Mydei hits back.

Phainon takes hits to his forearms, a knee to the ribs, a scuff to the jaw. It's good. He throws himself into it with a shout, forcing Mydei to retreat a step, two, only to retreat a step of his own when Mydei remains on the offensive. A fist glances off his forearm, bruising, aching, and he lifts his leg to kick when he's finds himself tumbling to the ground from a well-timed shove, back hitting the earth, scrambling to catch himself, to move before he can be pinned, but it's too late. Mydei immobilizes his arms against his chest with one hand, the other forearm coming to his throat, kneeling with his legs locked around Phainon's knees to keep him from finding any leverage. For a moment, Phainon struggles and thrashes, but with stronger pressure on his throat, he goes limp.

A dull throb settles into all the bruised, tender parts of his body. His arms, his hands, his mouth where he'd taken a stray elbow on their way down. He's out of breath, struggling to breathe beneath the weight and pressure of Mydei forcing him still. It's good. He hurts and he's tired and some of that restless energy is finally gone.

He wets his lips, peels his eyes open to Mydei above him, a section of his hair braided and dangling between them. It's good, all of this is good, and then something hot and furious roars back to life.

"Again," he says, wheezes against his lack of breath. Mydei frowns slightly, but after a moment of consideration he stands up, offers a hand, and hauls Phainon to his feet.

"You fight hand-to-hand like you have a sword," he says, stepping back into the center of the clearing. "Your center of gravity is different; accommodate for that. I can unbalance you far too easily."

Phainon settles into a stance, considering, shifting his weight slightly. "You're right," he notes. "Why didn't you say so earlier?"

But there's no reply. This time, Mydei makes the first move, lunging toward him swift as anything, immediately testing his new footing with a shove. Phainon is left to stumble and compensate, fighting him off and shifting his weight, trying to find where he's the most centered and stable.

He's quick to learn, but slower to remember, relying on concentration swiftly broken by the blur of battle rather than muscle memory. He's pushed on the defensive as he figures himself out, focused on dodging, ducking, and redirecting Mydei's blows, keeping his feet firm beneath him, looking for openings to fight back.

His body stings and aches and grows hot from exertion. There's no room to think about anything else.

And then he's in the dirt again, the wind knocked from him yet again because he'd slipped on leaves or failed to notice something Mydei had done. His breath comes in harsh pants. He stares up at the sky through the bare canopy, only the last lingering leaves still on the trees, the sun peering through branches, soft white clouds painted on a blue backdrop, and he laughs. A couple of tears stream down his temples, and he looks at Mydei, perched above, flushed and frowning, and holds out a hand.

"Again," he says, and Mydei gets off and helps him back up, palm warm and callused, and they spar again, and again, and again until Phainon's head is quiet and he's forgotten everything but the pleasant throb of his bruises and the proper position his feet should be in and Mydei's tendency to leave himself open for half a second after a right hook. He claims no victories, but he does manage to topple Mydei to the ground and maintain the upper hand for a precious few moments before the tides are turned and he winds up with his face in the dirt, an arm wrenched behind him.

It's the best he's held out yet. The closest he's come to beating Mydei, and it bubbles within him, burns, and that last time he's helped up, he notices a wary kind of respect in Mydei's eyes. Like he knows that had things gone the slightest bit differently, Phainon might've won.

After, they sit side by side on the ground, catching their breath, both sweating, bodies still singing with adrenaline, and he says, gruffly, reluctantly, begrudgingly, "You're improving."

"I'm certainly trying to," Phainon agrees. When he turns, he finds Mydei looking at him, gold-eyed and bitten-mouthed and...

"Thank you," Phainon tells him, "for mentioning my stance."

A grunt. Oddly, so oddly, Mydei doesn't look away.

△

When they make camp for the night, he watches the fire for a long time. It's the same as every night, just there for warmth and to cook whatever they manage to scrounge up for a meal. But Phainon can't help but stare, watching it flicker and dance, forming a hundred different shapes at once, all gone and changed in an instant. Controlled like this, it eats away at their logs so slowly. It's bright enough to leave imprints in his vision, blurring anything else he tries to look at, so his gaze keeps wandering back here.

He's quiet, and Mydei is too. They listen to the crackle of the flames and the somewhat distant river and Phainon remembers old songs he used to sing with his family. Sometimes they would burn the fields after harvest to clear out the dried stalks and restore the earth. He'd been scared as a child, so his parents taught him songs they would sing as the fires caught. Since then, he'd always likened it to a sunset. The blaze, the darkness after, of soot-stained fields, and then the brightness of a new day as the soils recover and foster new, healthy growth the next season.

He's forgotten most of it now, the things he'd seen in that vision, illusion, trap—whatever it had been. He's forgotten the pain and the names and faces and lives of everyone in the village, so maybe the burden is lighter. But he still... He still...

What are the words for this feeling? This haunting, these memories that keep surfacing. He looks into the fire, and this time it's Aedes Elysiae that he sees. Aedes Elysiae, fields scorched not from a controlled burn, but from their razing, and there's a swordsman standing amidst the embers, tattered cloak flapping in the wind, iron gauntlets curled around a crooked, massive sword, and when he turns, his face is—

"A question, Mydeimos," Phainon says, still watching the flames. There's a grunt in reply; Mydei so frequently replies to things with a grunt. His eyes will be molten gold as they always are if Phainon looks up. He won't smile, because he rarely smiles, but he won't scowl either, like he might've once. He'll be steadfast and tolerant and a dozen other things that Phainon doesn't deserve.

"Are there monsters that can take on the shape of someone else?"

"There are," is the reply. "Dopplers and changelings. They're more mischievous than dangerous, though. Witchers don't hunt them."

"And what else?" Phainon asks. "Are there stronger creatures that can do it? Dangerous ones?"

There's a long pause after this. Phainon keeps watching the fire. The spots of wood glowing with bright, undulating orange.

"Nothing you're likely to come across," Mydei finally says. "Is there a reason why you're asking?"

"No," Phainon breathes. "None at all. I'm just curious."

△

The main road is packed, busy, and frantic when they get onto it the next day. Mydei pulls his sleeve up and closes his robe, covering his markings if only to avoid unnecessary attention where possible. It's cold and noisy and they're boxed in by wagons and groups on horses and solo travelers alike, refugees and returning Okheman citizens and people from neighboring towns fleeing or on business.

Many, it seems, have heard of the decimation of those two towns. None seem to know of the swordsman, though there are dozens of different rumors going around. Phainon floats from group to group, person to person as they all travel the same worn road, seeking safety or help in Okhema, and finds that many are wary of strangers and distrustful in a time like this, but from them he hears theories of madmen and monsters, but also that no third town has been razed, no third population of innocents rendered extinct.

It's a foreboding kind of relief that he feels, because everyone he asks shares a common question: where will the monster responsible strike next?

"Were there survivors, do you know?" Phainon asks the man leading a caravan of a half dozen wagons pulled by donkeys. A young girl clings to the man's hand, peering up at Phainon through messy bangs.

"None as far as I know," says the man, sheltering his daughter behind his legs. "I heard from my brother who rode through and found the place in ashes, and he found not a living soul."

"Were there survivors?" Phainon asks a woman traveling with her wife and elderly parents. She gives him a pitying look, face soft and wrinkled and sad.

"My wife is the one who saw, not I. But she didn't mention survivors, no. My guess is that they'll have already fled, if there are any."

"Did anyone survive?" Phainon asks a group of tired-looking men, one with his son on his shoulders.

"No," one says, and the others just nod.

"Was anyone left?" Phainon asks an old farmer, a young woman, a family of four, a pair of hunters, a retired sorcerer. All answer with uncertainty or a negative, and Phainon wonders.

Someone must have made it out, right? Someone must have run away and actually made it. How could he be the only one that swordsman failed to kill? The only one to get away? What about all those others who tried to flee? Why him and not someone else? Why him and not anyone else? Why him?

Mydei rides up to his side on Strife, who snorts and turns her head to look at Phainon with one big, glassy eye before Mydei pats her neck and directs her forward.

"Okhema's gates may be shut," Mydei says, angling his head down, though he doesn't look at Phainon. "Overheard it from a group a ways back."

"Shut," Phainon repeats, "already?" He's sure everyone within two week's journey of the city will be wanting to make it inside once they get the news, if only because of that question everyone's asking: which town is next? Okhema is a city with towering walls and defenses even a Titan would struggle to topple, while all these small towns and farming villages scattered around might as well be paper cards in the wind.

Aedes Elysiae hadn't had a single warrior within its weathered wooden fences. Others might have small forces for defense, but nothing to keep the swordsman at bay, no one strong enough to be anything more than another body to impale on his crooked sword and crush under his boot.

Memories flash, mostly forgotten. A sword through his chest. A sword in his hand through another's chest. That strange, pleasurable and sickening feeling of purpose. The swordsman's face beneath his mask, his eyes, his smile, all of it wrong, so wrong, nauseating.

Phainon swallows thickly, hairs standing up on end, and he gives in to the paranoid urge to look behind him, around him, scanning each face in sight, rough and worn and weathered, some old and some young, some plain and some beautiful, all as uneasy as him, and then there's Mydei. Steadfast, strong and resolute, still astride Strife, drawing attention for his armor and confident, powerful demeanor even though he's hidden most of what marks him as a witcher.

"Two towns just burned, only days away," he says. "I'm not surprised the Imperator would call for a lockdown."

"And are they screening who they let in?" Phainon asks. "Or are they genuinely locking everyone out?"

A moment passes as Mydei considers. There's a sick feeling in Phainon's stomach. He listens to the sound of hooves and feet and wheels on the path, of people conversing and grousing and expressing worries or complaining about the pains in their feet.

"Screenings, I would guess," Mydei finally says. "The Imperator has a firm hand, and may be viewed as a tyrant, but I don't believe she's cruel as to completely close Okhema's doors."
