"And will they let you in?" He'd asked before, during one of uncountable hours they've been walking, if Mydei has been to Okhema before, if he knows what to expect. The answer had been a grouchy, reluctant no.

Now, Mydei just says, "That's the question, isn't it."

So they won't know until they get there. Phainon already feels sick. "Wonderful," he says, kicking a loose stone. "Just wonderful."

△

"State your name, occupation, and purpose."

It's loud. They're packed tight, more in a clump than an actual line. It smells strongly like dirt and sweat and people, pungent and thick, the crowd impatient and frustrated and vocal about it. The guards are little better. The one that disinterestedly cleared Phainon's passage turns his attention to Mydei now, bored and irritated both, thick brows low over his eyes.

"Mydeimos of Castrum Kremnos," Mydei says, smooth and strong, standing tall. "Witcher. I'm here for work."

Now, the man snaps awake, straightening and sizing Mydei up. Head to toe, he studies him, gaze settling on the marking on Mydei's cheek, the edges of others peeking out from beneath his collar, promising more beneath.

"A witcher," he says, still appraising. He crosses his arms over his chest. "What makes you think there's work for you here? My orders are to turn away monsters like you. Haven't you heard about the burnings? Or are you hoping you can sneak in and burn the Holy City too?"

Mydei's expression remains smooth. Horrible, practiced, commendable restraint. Doesn't he get angry? Phainon knows he does, and yet he doesn't show it, doesn't bother reacting to things like this. And now Phainon is the one getting angry for him, because he gets it, he does, reacting with an outburst or a confrontation every time someone makes a snide comment isn't going to help his case or reputation or force people to respect him, but it isn't fair. And Phainon knows fairness is such a childish concept, but even so, his hands curl into fists. His blood goes hot, and he isn't like Mydei. He's never been good at holding it all back.

"Are you kidding?" he says, stepping forward. "Isn't a witcher exactly who you should be letting in at a time like this? You can't seriously think he's the one who did it? Have you heard even a single account suggesting such a thing? When has a witcher done anything but keep ungrateful bastards like you safe? When has—"

"Phainon," says Mydei, and it's not his place, he knows. He shouldn't try to fight Mydei's battles for him, but he's not going to fight this one himself, is he? No, he'll take the disrespect and the indignity and he'll stay perfectly calm and civil and somehow get out of this mess that way. But he shouldn't have to, Titans above. It's so ridiculous that he has to, that half of his interactions are like this, with people outwardly taunting and disrespecting him when he could so easily beat them to a pulp.

Too furious to do much else, Phainon wedges himself between Mydei and the guard, putting on the most menacing smile he can muster. "I'm just saying," he says, "I think, it would be more beneficial to let us in than it would be to turn us away. But, of course, it's up to you."

The guard looks between them for a long while, frowning deeply, and then he shuts his eyes in frustration and sighs through his nose. "The Great Imperator will want to see you," he says, and Phainon's mouth parts on an inhale as he realizes.

The Imperator must've wanted a witcher all along. Phainon's smile slips and his blood goes cold, wondering just what they've managed to get themselves into.

Behind him, Mydei laughs roughly. He grabs Phainon by the shoulder and pulls him back so he can address the guard now, calm and confident and level as ever. "So let us inside," he says, and now he's the one smiling, a dangerous, sharp-toothed thing. "I'll be happy to talk."

The guard eyes him warily for a moment, two. Around them, the chatter and shuffling continues as other guards let other groups through. The line behind them is starting to grow more impatient than it already is. The guard lets them pass, only to stop them inside the gate. "Wait here," he says, clearly not trusting them in the slightest. "You'll need an escort."

chapters.title: Chapter 8
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

Apologies for the wait. I've been busy with school, mourning my cat that just passed away, training for a half marathon, and playing a Lot of Resident Evil.

See the end of the chapter for more notes

Their escort does not give her name, just her title. "Dux Gladiorum," she says, expression guarded, a sword at her side. "I am the Imperator's blade." Her hair is long and dark, bangs over her forehead. Her eyes are the color of the sea. She smells of it too, and one glance at what might pass as a shell hairpiece to the untrained eye has Mydei certain that she is not human and not trying particularly hard to hide it.

"Mydeimos of Castrum Kremnos," Mydei introduces himself. "Witcher."

"Phainon of Aedes Elysiae," Phainon adds, and hesitates, gaze flicking between them. Without much to offer by way of occupation, he says, "Traveling companion."

Dux Gladiorum only levels Phainon with her stare, blinks once, and deems him unworthy of attention. "Come," she says, turning back to Mydei. "The Imperator wishes to speak with you."

So she guides them through the grand, golden city that is Okhema, with tall spires and walls painted with murals of the Titans, wide streets swathed with colorful banners and bustling stalls, floods of people hawking their wares and making their way. More than once, they catch the scent of freshly baked breads and pastries, grilled meats, spices and snacks, and Mydei is reminded of his hunger, which will have to wait.

Phainon, keeping pace at his side and scared into silence by their escort, gawks at absolutely everything. Mydei spares a thought to wonder if this is the first time he's ever even been to a settlement big enough to be called a city. Okhema, as a first stop, is certainly an impressive one.

That letter, the only remnant he has of his mother, his reason for coming here, could burn a hole in his pocket.

"I'm getting the sense that we won't be able to afford anything here," Phainon says in a low voice, leaning in so their shoulders brush.

"Perhaps you wouldn't have that problem if you found yourself an occupation other than 'traveling companion,'" Mydei tells him, if only for the satisfaction of seeing the expression Phainon makes, astonished and offended both.

"My apologies," he says sarcastically, "I'm having a hard time finding something to match your wonderful reputation."

"You've yet to hear me complain of lacking funds," Mydei says, fighting off the way the corners of his mouth threaten to turn up. "I, however, hear you on the daily."

They find themselves inside the Holy City's Marmoreal Palace, a place of communion, connection, and cleansing. Sweet incense smoke floats from public bath chambers hot and cold both. They pass by the third, temperate bath, massive enough to accommodate hundreds, populated by families and friends and lovers and strangers. The sound of conversation fills the air, and there are so many people that the three of them, conspicuous as they are, are barely spared a bit of attention.

Phainon goes back to gaping. Mydei goes back to searching for signs he doesn't know how to look for. Dux Gladiorum continues escorting them, silent and stoic, until suddenly they're stopping before a huge set of double doors, and she extends an arm to halt their progress.

"The Imperator has asked only to see the witcher," she says, nodding to Mydei. The her gaze lands on Phainon, cold as the sea. "The witcher's companion can wait outside."

"Ah," Phainon says, and meets Mydei's eyes briefly. A tight smile. "Well, that can't be helped then. I guess I'll... take a look around. Or something. It doesn't seem Okhema is lacking in things to do."

One of the doors cracks open, and out comes a muscled man in a helmet. "Lady Hysilens," he says to Dux Gladiorum. "The Imperator has been notified. She's ready for an audience with the witcher."

Hysilens nods and returns her attention to Mydei. "You will leave your weapons with Dux Fragoris," she tells him. She sets a hand on the hilt of her sword. "Threaten the Imperator's safety, and you will learn the strength of her blade."

At his side, Phainon inhales at this, but he knows better than to interject. Mydei only nods and removes his gauntlets, leaving them in the hands of the helmed man. Next goes the knives in his belt and his boot and his entire satchel full of potions as a show of good faith. Hysilens and Dux Fragoris exchange a look, nod. Phainon watches silently, lips pursed, brows faintly furrowed.

"We'll meet in front of Marmoreal Palace at sundown," Mydei tells him. "I have business to attend after this."

"I..." Phainon frowns harder, but after a glance at their waiting guards—one burdened by all of Mydei's things—he only sighs. "Very well then. We'll meet at sundown."

Phainon hovers. Hysilens pushes open the double doors and enters first to announce Mydei's presence. "Great Imperator, Mydeimos, Witcher of Castrum Kremnos."

"Good," comes a voice, high and strong. "He may enter."

Hysilens nods at Mydei, gesturing him inside. Phainon inhales sharply, but Mydei doesn't look at him, just steps inside and listens to the doors shut behind him.

"Show the Imperator your respect," says Hysilens.

Mydei dips to one knee to bow, gaze lowered, and says, carefully and lowly, "It is an honor, Imperial Majesty."

A sound not unlike a laugh. The click of heeled shoes over stone ground. "Rise, Witcher."

Mydei straightens up and sets his gaze on Sovereign Cerydra, Empress, Tyrant, and Imperator of Okhema. She's shorter than expected, though she stands with the confidence of someone twice her height. Her hair is stark white, her eyes cunning, piercing blue. The crown she wears on her head is deliberately off center.

"I'm sure you've an inkling of why I've called for one of your kind?" she asks.

"The burnings," Mydei says.

"Yes." She nods, paces a slow circle around him. Mydei does not turn, even as he feels her gaze, prickling the hairs on the back of his neck. Behind him, she says, "My people are under attack. Something is burning my towns, whether man or monster, it remains to be seen. But, I trust, with a sword for each, a witcher is exactly the right person for the job."

"Gauntlets, Imperial Majesty," Mydei corrects her. Hysilens' stare grows hard. Cerydra stops in front of him.

"Pardon?" she asks.

"I am no swordsman, Imperial Majesty," Mydei says. "I use gauntlets."

She laughs, the sound sharp and cutting through the air. "Gauntlets, I see. Well, I trust they serve the same purpose, do they not? Unless I've somehow stumbled upon the only one of your kind that bothers with the distinction."

"You're correct, Majesty," Mydei tells her, holding her narrowed gaze. "I make no distinction between men and monsters that seek to harm."

"Good," Cerydra says, uncaring as she turns her back to him, climbing a few shallow steps to her throne, adorned with gold and blue velvet. She takes a seat, crossing one leg over the other and reclining. "And you're a witcher, so I assume the right price is enough to compel you into my employ?"

Witchers are a kingless faction. Mydei has little interest in politics or power struggles, and he doesn't particularly care who employs him when there is a monster to be slain. And this black cloaked swordsman... man or monster, he's exactly the sort of thing Mydei was created to combat.

"For a job like this, your assumption would be correct," he says. A glance at Hysilens, stare firm, hand on her sword hilt, he adds, "...Imperial Majesty."

"I have little information for you at present," Cerydra says, "but every last one of the men under my command in those two towns is dead. You may have seen the ashes on your journey here. Whatever is causing this, it is dangerous, far more so than any monster I have yet to catch tale of in my kingdom. I would not ask you to handle it alone and risk the life of one of your already dwindling species. No, I ask for your service and your expertise, combined with that of a multitude of other skilled individuals in my employ. Together, with my resources at your will, vanquishing this threat should prove a reasonable task."

"Witchers aren't known to work in teams, Majesty," Mydei tells her.

"Well," she says, resting her chin on her fist, "I suppose you should learn to start. I trust a thousand balance coins is enough to ensure your cooperation?"

Mydei opens his mouth, then closes it.

"Yes." Cerydra smiles. "I thought so. While you're in my service, Witcher, you will respond to the title Dux Sanguinis, is that understood?"

"Yes," Mydei says. "Yes, Imperial Majesty."

△

Phainon is going to have thoughts about this. He's going to want to get involved, to fight, to take down the swordsman by his own hand. And Mydei, walking through the halls of Marmoreal Palace after meeting with and finding himself employed by the Great Imperator, Empress, and Tyrant of Okhema, can't help but feel conflicted over this fact.

Conflicted, because his concern has long since shifted from he'll get in the way to he might get hurt. Because Phainon, strong as he is, resilient as he is, stubborn and fast-learning as he is, is still human, is still mortal, is just not there yet.

Mydei may not have seen this swordsman with his own eyes, but he's seen the scale of the destruction he's capable of. Razing a village without survivors, leaving magical traps that say he wants to be seen and known and feared. Most monsters kill to feed, or when they feel their territory has been encroached upon, or as vengeance when careless humans destroy their homes or threaten their young, but this... Few things are truly, purely malicious at this scale, with this kind of strength.

Not a single survivor. Not one, but Phainon. Phainon, who wants revenge. Phainon, who hides his rage but carries it deep inside and ever present. Phainon, who will get himself killed if he tries to get involved. Phainon, who... Asked some strange questions earlier, and tried to pass them off as nothing. Something like dread fills the pit of Mydei's stomach. But the sun is far from setting, and Okhema is a large city with any number of places for a person to explore. It'll have to wait. Mydei has other business anyway.

Finding himself outside, one hundred new balance coins in his purse—an advance from Imperator Cerydra alongside a writ guaranteeing him a room in Marmoreal Palace and a promise to have his head if he attempts to go back on his word—Mydei remembers that he hasn't the slightest idea where to go, where to look.

Strife had been taken to the stables the moment they entered the city, but he'd taken a few things from her saddlebags.

First, the letter from his mother, yellowed with age, creased soft and wrinkled and recovered only after Mydei had killed with his father by his own hand, some decades after the letter was written. Second, an old, tarnished pin for securing a cape. He isn't even sure it belonged to who he thinks it once did. He isn't even sure if that person is still alive, after all these years.

Turning the pin over in one hand, Mydei forms the Sign of Janus. A faint sensation in his markings tells him the spell worked, but nothing happens. Perhaps the connection has been lost between this object and the person it once belonged to. Perhaps that person isn't in even in Okhema, is dead, never owned this pin to begin with.

He'll try again in another spot. The Sign of Janus is short ranged. There are any number of reasons why it might not work.

△

Freshly bathed, belly full, Mydei accepts a message delivered to his room. It bears the Imperator's seal; a summons to Dawncloud tomorrow, the city's administrative seat, for the purpose of discussing confidential matters regarding the city's safety. His contract. The team he'll have to work with.

He has a lot to think about, sighing and putting the summons away. He returns to combing his hair, now clean and dry, and redoing his braid. Almost sundown; he'll be meeting back up with Phainon soon. Strange, how silent it's been without him. How much more space Mydei's thoughts are left to fill. He fastens his braid and puts his armor back on before leaving.

Hand on the door, he pauses. Slipping the pin out of his pocket, he casts the Sign of Janus on it again. Nothing happens, so he puts it back and is on his way.

Phainon is already there, waiting just outside the entrance to Marmoreal Palace, bathed in gold light from the setting sun, cleaned up once again. "I see you've also taken advantage of the baths," he says as Mydei approaches. He's freshly scrubbed and shaved, and perhaps it's just Okhema's fragrant streets, but he smells faintly like flowers. Mydei breathes in too deeply before he catches himself.

"Yes," he says, and looking at him, there's this fluttering kind of relief in his stomach.

Phainon's smile slips into something a bit more serious. "And did it go well?" he asks.

He blinks, watching the breeze move Phainon's hair. "...My bath?"

"No," Phainon laughs, "your meeting with the Imperator."

"It went fine."

"Yes, and...?" One pale brow lifts, but Mydei only shakes his head.

"I won't talk about it here."

"Right," Phainon says, nodding. He starts them walking back into the city. "Secret, important business and all that, not to be discussed in public. I suppose accommodations are our next stop, then? I did look around a bit, and while most everything is absurdly expensive here, I did find a couple of inns that look promising. Figured I'd get your opinion before making any decisions, though."

"No need. I have a room already."

"Oh, do you? Something affordable, I hope? Where is it?"

"Marmoreal Palace," Mydei says.

"You— I— Pardon?" Phainon says, halting in his tracks. "Isn't it expensive?" Seeing the shock on his face, Mydei gets the strange urge to smile.

"It's free," he says. "Courtesy of the Imperator. There's a private bath and a balcony."

"You absolute bastard," Phainon laughs, incredulous. "Can I at least see it before you banish me to the slums? I've always been curious what it feels like to be rich."

A thought, unbidden, unwarranted: he'd been willing to sleep next to Mydei in the straw, outraged on his behalf, rather than leave him with the discomfort alone. Maybe he'd only done it to save some coin. It's stupid that the memory sticks. That tiny, ridiculous, insignificant thing. He's less pushy as of late, now that he's realized Mydei isn't about to leave him behind. He looks like he expects Mydei to say no to him even seeing his fancy room, and he looks fine with it, and it's so stupid.

Mydei should be angry with him for trying to fight his battles. It wasn't his place to be upset with the innkeeper than night in the stables. It wasn't his place to fight for meals and water with Mydei's coin. It wasn't his place to stand up to the guards here, and yet. And yet. 

They need to talk anyway. And Phainon will be safer by Mydei's side than anywhere else. So, like a complete and utter fool, what he ends up saying is, "There's enough space, if you want to sleep on the floor."

Something in him squirms at the way Phainon lights up like a new dawn. "You mean that?" he says. "You can't take it back. I don't care if it's only the floor of luxery, Mydeimos; if you're seriously extending the invitation, I will gladly take it." He laughs, delighted, a faintly musical sort of sound, and Mydei sinks his teeth into the inside of his cheeks.

"For free," Phainon continues. "One of the best rooms in Okhema, for free. Can you believe it?"

Titans above. What has Mydei done? "HKS," he mutters. "Maybe I ought to charge you rent."

△

"Wow," says Phainon from the balcony. He's been buzzing around since the moment he'd stepped foot in Mydei's room, enthusing about the artwork on the walls and the vase set on a marble plinth, expressing appreciation for the size of the bath and the softness of the bed and the rugs underfoot. And then he comes here, and he goes quiet.

Mydei comes up beside him, crossing his arms and looking out on the view, blanketed now by the blue of dusk. The sky, wide and expansive and painted with handfuls of clouds. The city below, mountains and forest beyond. It's cold enough this late for their breath to fog in the air. Phainon's knuckles are pale as he grips the balcony railing, still quiet, just looking out.

"Wow indeed," Mydei says, where once he might've just left the silence. Phainon turns to him, robbed of all of his color but blue, blue, blue, and lets out another breath that puffs up in the air.

"Wow indeed," he parrots, nonsensical as it is. "Well, let's hear it. What kind of deal have you struck with the Imperator to score this free of charge?"

The moment breaks. Mydei clears his throat. Hesitates briefly. "I've been tasked with vanquishing the swordsman," he says, and waits for... What, he doesn't know. He wonders if Phainon will be glad for this, or if he'll be afraid, or angry, or any number of other things.

But all he says is, "I figured as much." His grip on the railing doesn't grow any looser. He bends forward now, looking down at the city below, and it's clear that there's something else that he wants to say. So Mydei waits, leaves the silence, the space for him to fill, gaze stuck on the bit of his nape showing beneath his coat collar and wondering what he must be feeling.

But he doesn't say anything else. Doesn't stake claim on the swordsman's life or ask to join the fight or express any kind of emotion, whether that's fear or relief or anger or who knows what else. He just keeps looking out at the city, dusk-colored and weary, and he's so rarely quiet. Only ever when something is wrong.

Cold wind ruffles them both. Mydei steps up so they're shoulder to shoulder, folding his arms over the railing and leaning over them. His breath diffuses in the air. Phainon is still quiet, still not looking at him, not looking at anything at all. "I'm surprised you don't have anything else to say about this."

"I'm thinking," Phainon says without so much as a laugh. "Just thinking."

Strange, the way Mydei is almost tempted to ask him what he's thinking about. Tempted to ask what he's been wondering all day. Instead, he just waits a little longer, leaving another silence he can choose to fill or not. When he doesn't, Mydei exhales and straightens up. "Alright," he says. "Don't hurt yourself."

Now, there's an attempt. Phainon chuckles. "I assure you I'm quite accustomed to the task."

"Sure," Mydei agrees, and makes to go.

"And Mydei?" Phainon calls. Mydei stops, turns back to him. Soft, blanketed in blue, and seemingly so, so tired, Phainon smiles. "I appreciate you letting me crash with you. I'd have thought you'd have been sick of seeing so much of me by now."

"What did I say, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae. We're friends. Companions, you said it yourself. So long as you can shut up long enough for it, it matters not to me how close to me you sleep."

Another laugh, stronger this time. "Sometimes, the way you speak... You'll give someone the wrong idea about us, Mydeimos." He laughs again, shakes his head like he finds something genuinely funny.

Mydei frowns, and otherwise thinks nothing of it.

△

"You can call me Tribios," says the red haired woman waiting in the meeting room at Dawncloud. She's fairly tall, adorned in flowers and gold, with the white robes of a priestess. "Or Dux Fatorum if Cerydra or Hysilens is around. Otherwise, I don't care much for titles."

Her smile is warm. Her eyes are blue. Something about her name is familiar.

"Mydeimos," Mydei greets her in turn, taking a seat at the long but strangely empty table before him. "Dux Sanguinis, though I, like you, have no particular attachment to the name."

The only other occupant of the room speaks last, a girl dressed in red and white, with curled pigtails, a cheery disposition, and a baby unicorn in her lap. "I'm Hyacine," she introduces herself. "Dux Lucens. You're a witcher, right?"

Mydei has once again opted to cover up, rather than draw attention to himself in the streets. Still, some of his markings creep too high up his neck to be hidden by his robe, and there's no hope to hide the one on his cheek without cosmetics. Neither of them appears to be afraid of him, though. He finds that important people rarely are.

"Yes," he confirms. "And you are...?"

"A healer from the Twilight Courtyard," Hyacine says, offering a smile. A sorceress, then, though not one focused on offensive magic. "Damage control in case anyone gets hurt."

Mydei gives her a nod. "Good. Healing magic is always useful." He turns to Tribios, who has a pad of paper in front of her, sketching something with a pencil worn to nothing more than a stub. "And you?"

"Me?" She seems to startle, then collects herself, laughing awkwardly and wiping charcoal stained fingers on her dress. "Right, yes. Holy Maiden of Janusopolis speaking. My strength lies in strategy, intelligence gathering, and..." She hesitates, glancing down at the paper. Mydei follows her gaze, and finds, not notes for the meeting, but blueprints for some kind of contraption? "...Innovation," is how she finishes. Sheepish now, her smile is not unlike Phainon's.

Mydei frowns. "And what is the Holy Maiden of Janusopolis doing here?"

"Ah. Well." She pulls a strand of hair between her fingers. "I suppose you could say I owe Cerydra for some things."

Mydei frowns harder. "...I see." She'll be useful, at least. A priestess with Janus on her side; she'll have powerful magic with a number of uses. Mydei's Signs can't begin to compare to what she'll be capable of. But still, the Holy Maiden of Janusopolis here, serving under the Imperator... Last he'd heard, she'd been imprisoned in Janusopolis for sacrilege.

Another glance around the room. He hadn't been particularly early, though he'd tried not to be late either. Still, in this whole, wide meeting room, with a table to seat three dozen, lit with braziers, floored with intricate rugs, walls trimmed with gold and fitted with red drapery, they're still the only three. "Will the Imperator be joining us?"

"She's very busy," says Hyacine, shaking her head. The unicorn in her lap gives an agreeing little doot doot!

"...I see," Mydei repeats, and doesn't know what to think about this haphazard little group. Hyacine and Tribios seem nice enough, powerful enough, but been expecting a small army, or esteemed military leaders, people of that sort. But this... a healer and a priestess of Janus...

"We're a small team now, but there will be more of us once the right people are found for the job," Tribios says. She twirls her tiny pencil between her fingers and offers another smile. "But I promise you we're quite capable."

"I don't doubt it," Mydei says.

A smile. "Then let's share what we know, shall we? We can come up with a plan from there."

"Yes," Mydei says. "But first, Lady Tribios, a question."

She blinks, tips her head to one side. "I'll certainly try my best to answer it."

"You bear some measure of Janus' power, yes? If you're willing, there's someone who might be a valuable asset to our team that I would ask for your help locating."

"Well," she says, seeming to think. A smile. "Alright."

Chapter End Notes

lore concoction volume 4: Cerydra doesn't have a title for Mydei like she does the rest of the heirs, so I've made one up for him after some research. I do not speak Latin so please correct me if you do and this is wrong, but "Dux Sanguinis" pretty much means "General of Blood"

I forgot to make a note about Strife until now!! The main character of the Witcher, Geralt, names all of his horses Roach. All of Mydei's are named Strife; this one is Strife III.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

It's my birthday! Have an update!

Don't think about it, he tells himself. Don't think about any of it. Nothing here has been burnt to ash. Nothing here will be. It's safe here, safe as anything, as anywhere will ever be.

Okhema is the biggest city, without contest, that Phainon has ever seen. It's tall and grand and protected, and there are enough faces on one block of the market street that it's impossible to meet and know and hope to remember them all. Guards stationed and patrolling, walls sturdy and high, gates protecting everyone under the Imperator's iron rule; Okhema is a city, a fortress, something that isn't remotely easy to conquer. It would be ridiculous to compare Okhema to tiny villages burnt down with barely more than fences for protection, but Phainon is still paranoid, still filled with this ever-present dread, so sticky and persistent he feels like he had after Aedes Elysiae again. Scared all the time, helpless and angry and so full of nauseating feeling.

No one else is worried. The rumors reduce the black-cloaked swordsman to a madman, the Imperator's lockdown just a way for her to flaunt her power, the burning of those towns tragic and forgotten the moment something else comes up. It's better this way, without people panicking and making a mess of the situation, but still. Phainon can't help but notice potential gaps in Okhema's defenses, places where damage could be done.

Finding work hasn't been easy. A large population lends a large workforce. After spending a good part of the morning searching while Mydei disappears for another meeting with the Imperator's anti-swordsman brigade, Phainon finds himself washing and carding dromas wool to be spun for weaving.

It isn't work he's done before, and its far more intensive than he'd been expecting, the fleeces filthy and cumbersome when wet. Carding clean, dry fibers is repetitive and arm-aching. The woman he does it for complains that he's slow and has no sympathy for his hands, frozen from washing with frigid water, his fingers scratched on the rough carding brushes, neck sore from looking down at his work. But she pays him after she pokes at the basket of prepared fibers he presents her with, and she says he can come again tomorrow.

It isn't much, an he isn't sure he's eager to repeat the experience, considering the way he reeks of dromas and his body aches in new and unpleasant ways, but he isn't sure how likely he is to find something else. Already, it's late enough that Mydei is probably back. Picking up a large loaf of rich smelling stuffed bread from a stall as he walks down the market street, Phainon forks over an entire balance coin and finds himself glad that he's rooming for free.

The sun has mostly gone down when he returns to Marmoreal Palace. He offers smiles and nods to people who are far richer than he is as he makes his way to the lavish room with the plush bed and private bath and beautiful balcony view where he will be permitted to sleep on the floor, and he allows himself a laugh over the irony of it. That he would be here, that this would become the life of some village boy from Aedes Elysiae, that he would turn out to be so useless as to spend his day washing and carding dromas wool instead of helping the effort to kill the man (monster? thing?) responsible for setting fire to his future.

Mydei is sitting at the desk when Phainon comes in, a sheet of parchment spread out before him and a pen in hand. He's alert now, as he is always, but after sparing a brief glance Phainon's way to confirm he isn't a threat, he returns to whatever he's working on, head tipped down, the bone at the top of his spine visible, his hair an artful mess. There's a strange feeling in the pit of Phainon's stomach, but he's been feeling strange all day, so he pays it no mind.

"You can write?" he asks instead, pretending it surprises him greatly. He comes closer, setting the bag with the bread down, and what surprises him instead as he peeks over Mydei's shoulder to catch a glimpse of the page, is the neatness of his handwriting, the way each word is carefully assembled with carefully created parts; he notes, from the one word he watches watches Mydei pen down, that he writes slowly too.

And then he's flipping the sheet over with ink still wet before Phainon can read more than a handful of words: mutations, mother, meeting. Mydei's nostrils flare as his eyes meet Phainon's, head tipped up because he's sitting and Phainon is standing, a wrinkle in his forehead, ink stains on his bare fingers, black patterns mixing with red.

"You speak as if you don't have a brain," he says, exhaling audibly, mouth pinching.

"That was in jest," Phainon laughs, hoisting himself to sit on the empty part of the desk. He nudges Mydei's thigh with his ankle, glancing between him and the backside of the page, Mydei's hand pinning it in place. "What're you writing anyway? A letter to someone?" He pauses, considering. "Poetry?"

"HKS." Mydei's stool scrapes the ground as he stands, not bothering to answer. He makes to move away but pauses, frowning deeper as he breathes deeply and fully the way he does when he's scenting the air for danger. He ducks closer to Phainon, too close now, uncomfortably close, making his hair stand on end, and breathes.

Phainon goes entirely still.

"You reek," Mydei says, and takes another breath. "Is that dromas? What were you doing?"

Phainon's throat clicks. As Mydei straightens up, he finds himself aware of his heartbeat. Not afraid, though. He has nothing to be afraid of. "Is this a new stage in our friendship?" he asks. "Where you start sniffing me whenever you feel like it?"

Gold eyes return to him. Mydei scans over his face, his chest, his throat, and then he looks away. "It's normal among witchers," he says, and sounds awkward, almost. "I... apologize."

"Oh," Phainon says, and has this strange thought: this means you're comfortable with me, doesn't it? His mouth goes dry. They're still kind of close; him on the desk, Mydei having never really moved away. "Well, don't. I was just surprised."

Mydei just grunts and steps out from the desk, taking the paper he'd been writing and folding it up, rubbing his thumb over the bit of ink he'd gotten on the desk like he might clean it up even after it dried.

The silence is weird. Phainon tries to fill it. "And if you must know, I found work for a spinner washing and carding dromas fleeces. So. Keen nose."

A hum. Mydei tucks the paper away in one of his pockets. "You reek," he says again.

"Well, luckily we've found ourselves in the city of Okhema. Care to join me for a trip to the famous baths?"

"There's a bath right there," Mydei points out, gesturing toward the private bath set in stone on one side of the room.

"Yes, well," Phainon says, "that one isn't famous, is it?"

△

The water is hot and the air is fragrant with incense, sweet and smoky and floral. Once again, another of Mydei's Imperator-granted privileges reveals itself. They're allowed entry into the Hero's Bath—Phainon only by proxy—reserved only for the most acclaimed warriors of Okhema, the waters glimmering gold with enchantments from a priestess of Phagousa. The moment he sinks into them, he can feel the work of that magic, soothing all the aches of his flesh, quieting that persistent, panicked voice in the back of his mind.

"I didn't even know this place existed," Phainon says, setting into one of the benches built-in under the water, letting it cover him to his chest. Perhaps because of the exclusivity of the place, or perhaps due to luck, they're the only ones here. "Do you think they keep it under wraps so people aren't constantly trying to sneak in for a feel of these enchantments? I've barely gotten in and all of my aches are gone."

"It isn't a secret; you just didn't know about it because you've only been in Okhema for a day. And as for people sneaking in, I doubt it, and I don't particularly care." Mydei settles in a short distance away, arms folded across his chest, eyes slipping shut. He's taken to wearing his robes properly while in the city; somehow Phainon had forgotten about the conspicuous way his markings stand out. He'd be gawked at in the regular baths. Phainon hadn't even considered that, despite watching him be feared and hated by others multiple times on their journey so far. He feels guilt at his own thoughtlessness.

"And if someone were to sneak in right now, would you care then?" Phainon asks, instead of doing something stupid, like apologizing. Mydei's eyes crack open, gaze turning to Phainon, low-lidded and lazy. It's remarkable how little Mydei moves when he's relaxed. How slowly his chest rises and falls, like he needs less breath than the rest of them. The water is hot. Phainon's fingers buzz as they acclimate. His face feels hot too as he finds himself staring at the patterns on Mydei's throat.

"There's more than enough space for them to bathe too," is what Mydei says, and then he's sinking a little lower, eyes falling shut again, head tipping back. Phainon's gaze is drawn back again. To the bump in Mydei's throat, and then to his hands as they unfold and stretch out to rest along the rim of the bath, paler than the rest of him from being hidden by his gauntlets, fingers dripping. "I still wouldn't particularly care."

Phainon allows himself a laugh, turning away so he won't be tempted to look and look and look. "Too tired for it then? What does the Imperator have you doing anyway?"

"Very little, for how much of my time is being wasted."

"Well, the perks seem worth it, at least."

Mydei sighs, shifts in the water. "We don't know enough. I can't kill a monster if I don't know what it is."

A thick feeling in Phainon's throat. A memory behind his eyes, a hand removing a mask, the face behind it. "I see," he says. "And... once you know what that monster is, what then?"

"Then we make a plan," Mydei says. He looks at Phainon again. "Then we kill it."

He doesn't know why the subject makes him so nervous. Why this part of him keeps screaming no, no, no. Why he can't shake the thought that maybe Mydei isn't strong enough. That Phainon himself can't do a thing to help him but sit on the sidelines and try not to get in the way. He wants vengeance. He's been so furious for so long, but— But what, he doesn't know.

He sucks in a breath. "Well, I hope you'll learn what you need to learn soon," he says, and realizes he sounds weird.

"Phainon," Mydei says. Phainon, his name, not one of any number of things he's called Phainon instead to avoid using it. It sparks a sudden panic. 

"Say, what were you writing earlier?" Phainon asks, trying to change the subject, trying not to betray that insistent feeling. "Was it a letter? Do you write to your other witcher friends every now and then, or...?"

Silence. Mydei looks at him for a long while and sighs. "Yes, it was a letter," he says.

"Something for business?" Phainon asks. The only reply is a grunt that doesn't really serve as an answer. "A friend?" he tries, still scared Mydei might circle the conversation back. "A... lover? Or something else along those lines?"

A rough laugh. "No," Mydei says. "If you must know, it's to do with my original business in Okhema. There's someone I'm looking to meet."

Phainon passes his fingers through the water. "The old friend," Phainon says.

Mydei lets out a breath through his nose, smiling faintly. "Yes," he confirms, "the old friend."

"Is this funny to you?" Phainon asks, finding himself frowning. "I'm only curious. We've been travelling together for a little while and I still don't know much about your friends, if you've any family, a long distance lover somewhere in the equation— Why are you laughing?" Phainon asks, kind of incredulous as Mydei barks a laugh, louder than the last. Against his will, Phainon finds himself laughing as well. "What's so unthinkable about it?"

"Your expectations, Deliverer," Mydei says, shaking his head. One more chuckle, he pulls his arms off the back of the baths to cross them over his chest again, exhaling heavily. "Do I seem like the type with a sweetheart back home?"

"I don't know," Phainon says, smile stilling. He tracks a bead of water down Mydei's shoulder, the contours of his arm. Back to his face. Severe features more than capable of softening, eyes as gold as the dawn. It isn't hard to imagine Mydei with someone to hold and whisper sweet nothings to in the dark. He's strong, but he isn't heartless. Maybe he'd fall in love with some village girl he saved from a monster somewhere along his journey, willowy and delicate to contrast his bulk. Maybe another witcher, someone who understands his suffering in a way no one else ever could, someone he's known a long time, someone who's strong enough to meet him blow for blow and guard his back in a battle, someone who—

Phainon realizes he's frowning, tries to school his expression. "I don't see why not," he says. 

Finally, Mydei sobers. His gaze sticks somewhere around Phainon's neck, the choker he hadn't taken off with the rest of his clothes. "I'm looking for a friend of my mother's," he admits after a moment, and Phainon's mouth parts.

"Your mother," he repeats. He knows very little when it comes to Mydei's past, less when it comes to his family.

"My mother," Mydei agrees, and doesn't say any more. Phainon wants to ask, but figures it wouldn't be fair. Not when he's made a point of not elaborating too. The rest of their bath is spent largely in silence.

△

He goes back to the spinner and her dromas fleeces the next day, finds her wrinkled and scrutinizing as she pulls open the door when he knocks. She watches him squirm for a moment, two, long enough to make him wonder if she'll withdraw her offer of more work, but then she pulls the door open wide and steps out of the way to let him inside.

"Two balance coins per fleece you wash, five for each you card," she says, leading him through the home to the back, where there's another door and an outside portion of property where a veritable mountain of wool waits. "Though the ones from yesterday aren't dry yet, so you'll just be washing today."

"I— Not that I'm complaining, ma'am, but that's more than you paid me yesterday."

Her eyes narrow, but she nods. "It is," is her only reply, and then she's running him through her rules again and warning him that she'll be inspecting his work before he sees any of his pay. As she turns to head back inside where it's warm and her spinning wheel awaits, Phainon calls out to her.

"Do you spin all of this yourself?" he asks. he'd worked on maybe four fleeces yesterday; today there has to be thirty.

She barks a laugh. "Hardly," she says. "I have children and a couple of hired girls to help; I run a business. Now you'd best get to work." And then she steps inside and shuts the door behind her, leaving him to sniffle against the cold and roll up his sleeves to do just that.

By the time the sun goes down, after a lunch break and having the spinner poke at each of fourteen washed fleeces hung to dry, Phainon finds himself sore, reeking again of animal, and twenty-eight balance coins richer than he'd been before. It might be the most money he's made in a day, and again he's invited to return. He feels beautifully optimistic.

When he gets back to their room in Marmoreal Palace, Mydei isn't there, maybe still caught up in yet another unproductive meeting, maybe getting dinner, running some kind of errand, or visiting the baths. It feels strange to wonder. Strange to wait for him, strange to come back to him at the end of a long day. They've spent so much time together all at once.

Phainon's stomach rumbles. He wonders if Mydei would expect him to wait; they've eaten just about every meal together since the start of their travels. But Mydei isn't here, and it's early enough into the night that he could still be gone for a number of hours without it being considered late. As it gets colder, the nights get longer.

Titans above, it's ridiculous that he's even thinking about this. It's Mydei. He probably couldn't care less if Phainon eats without him or not.

Still, he smells like dromas and he knows it. He'll take a bath first, and if Mydei still isn't back by then, he'll venture off to find something to eat.

So he takes a bath, basking in the—unfortunately unenchanted—heat after spending so long washing wool in water that might as well be ice. He realizes he's spoiling himself for when they end up back on the road and he's forced to wash up in frigid streams or deal with his own smell between towns, but this is a luxury he'll never turn down. Hot water to soak in dispensed as easily as turning a knob. Back home, back before the swordsman, this journey, all of it, he'd have to heat the water himself, bucket by bucket. Among so many things he misses from home with every part of himself, there's at least one thing he does not.

Mydei does not return by the time he's clean and changed, so he heads out to wander the halls of Marmoreal Palace in search of food, before realizing promptly upon finding it that even if he's managed to make twenty-eight balance coins in a day, it would be entirely unreasonable of him to fork nineteen of them over for onion pancakes.

Pulling his coat tight around him to combat the night chill, Phainon ventures out to the market street instead, still bustling and lit and up down with torches. His breath fogs up. A dozen different scents waft through the air as he walks, and it's different at night, under a darkened sky. He takes an inhale so deep it hurts his chest and spends way too long looking before he decides on a goat cheese pie, if only because the girl selling them, pale haired and blue-eyed and cheery beyond belief, reminds him of an old friend he misses more than anything.

He chats with her and a number of other strangers for a while as he eats, finding himself lonely and comforted and plagued by worries at once, and then returns once again to the room in Marmoreal Palace. Mydei, still, is not back. Phainon entertains himself with this and that until finally the door swings open and in comes the witcher, tired eyed and not even sparing a greeting before he peels out of half his robe and starts stripping out of his armor piece by piece.

"Long day?" Phainon asks. Mydei's armor is dirty. The state of his hair makes it look like he's been in the wind.

He glances up, if only briefly, before continuing to undo the straps holding his armor in place on his legs. "What day isn't?" is the reply.

"Truly spoken like someone who's never had fun."

"Yes, well." There's the opposite of a joke in there somewhere. The space between them goes silent before Mydei slips out of another piece of armor and drops it with a metallic crash. He looks at Phainon again, probably noting the awkward way he stands there, and seems to sigh. "Help me with this damned thing, would you? The buckle is in the back," he prompts, gesturing to his pauldron.

It isn't something he's been asked to assist with before. Mydei always struggles out of his armor alone, perfectly capable of it, having long since figured out exactly the way to do it. It's odd to be asked. Still, Phainon comes closer, and Mydei turns his back to him, lifting his arm out of the way and working on undoing the strap of his other cuisse one handed. It feels, though Phainon knows this is nothing more than the work of squires, an intimate thing. Maybe it's the amount of skin he's presented with, Mydei's half-bare back, his markings, the top of his spine.

Careful, he pulls Mydei's half cape out of the way, black and blood red, made from thick, sturdy fabric. He has to stand close to do this, close in a way that has him conscious of the sound of his own breath, wondering if Mydei can hear it, can hear his heart, can smell the sweat on his palms. Just how strong are a witcher's senses anyway? He's never asked, never felt like Mydei would give him a straight answer.

His swallow sticks in his throat. Why is he nervous? What does he have to be nervous about? The buckle eases undone without issue under his fingers. He takes a breath in through his nose and—

"You smell like smoke."

"Today's task," Mydei says, unclipping the pauldron in the front and pulling it off. "Gathering information where we know the swordsman has been."

"The burnt villages."

"Yes."

Phainon lets go of Mydei's cape, which flutters to the floor now, unsecured. "But how?" he asks, going cold.

"Lady Tribios is a priestess of Janus," Mydei says. The last of his armor undone, he turns, facing Phainon again, smelling of sweat and smoke and just the tiniest bit shorter without the heel of his boots to aid him. "Teleportation spells are well within the capabilities of the Titan of Passage."

"I see," says Phainon, mouth dry. In his head, a hundred questions. A current, louder than anything else, repeating no, no, no. "And what did you find? Any useful clues?"

"More questions than answers," Mydei tells him, tired but level, holding Phainon's gaze, well aware of the way he's suddenly flighty. "An analysis on the site of that spell he cast on you. A couple of new theories."

"So it went well, then. Right?" Phainon finds himself taking a step back, finding the desk behind him, torn between pulling the chair out to sit and gripping the wood for dear life. He's cold, he's sweating, he's gripped by that terror he's tried so hard to shove down since that first village, razed to the ground. Strange, how he could spend so long being so angry and so resolved and so sure he was over that fear, just for it to all come running back the moment he's forced to look his past in the eyes again. And he hasn't even seen the swordsman. Not really, not in the flesh, just in that vision. Just watched him hurt and kill, felt as others were hurt and killed by him, been him as he hurt and killed. Watched him take off that mask and smile and eyes and lips and teeth all too familiar.

"Phainon," Mydei says. Had he seen it too? That vision, those memories, that truth. "There are some answers I need that I think you might have."

"I don't," Phainon says too quickly. "I won't have them, I mean. I know a lot less about him than you might think. I know nothing at all, really, I'm not— He isn't—"

He watches Mydei raise his hands like he might cast a Sign. But then he lowers them, sighs, and Phainon can't decide what makes him feel more like an animal.

Again, "Phainon."

"Mydeimos," Phainon gets out, weird and airy. He's short of breath. He sits down too hard, wants, like a child, to wrap his arms around his knees and hide. "I really don't know anything," he says. It claws up his chest, panic, terror, horror. The swordsman's voice like gravel, you brought this, you did this, this is your fault. That silver mask, the way it felt, his hand around that sword, his purpose, his pleasure, his fingers pulling that mask off. Aren't you curious who I am?

No, no, no.

"Whose face did he wear?" Mydei's voice. Phainon's vision blurs as he stares at his own hands, filthy and bloodstained and guilty, guilty, guilty. "You asked me before about creatures that could wear someone else's face. Phainon, I need to know."

Again and again, the parting of flesh beneath steel. The scent of blood, the flavor of it on his tongue. The cries, the fires, music to his ears, his pleasure, his purpose.

"No," he finds himself saying. He's going to be sick. "No, please." His voice breaks on it. Blood, so much blood. His hands filthy, his sword stuck in someone's chest, his mask—

And then it's gone, and two hands are on the sides of his head, forcing him to look up, vision blurred, and— He blinks. Tears fall and he can see again. Mydei, frowning. Mydei, unarmored and smelling of smoke. Mydei, his friend. "Whose face?" he asks, softer the second time around. "Please, Phainon."

He's kneeling. His hands are hot on Phainon's cheeks. There's nowhere to look but at him, nothing to see but his golden eyes.

"Mine," Phainon admits, broken. "That face he wore, it was mine."

△

"That spell still has its claws in you," says Lady Hyacine, healer, sorceress, and part of the Imperator's team, "but rest assured, Lord Phainon, you'll be rid of its influence in no time."

"Oh," Phainon says. "I'm no lord, Lady Hyacine, just a villager. And thank you, I suppose. Or, I don't just suppose, I'm very grateful to you, also very sorry, and... also very confused."

It's late, late enough to be considered unreasonable now, pitch dark and freezing cold, the markets shut down, no one on the streets. But Mydei had dragged him here to the Twilight Courtyard—the station of Okhema's famed healers—unapologetically waking everyone up in the process, all because Phainon is apparently spelled.

"You're getting along remarkably well, all things considered," Hyacine says.

"Doot doot!" says the tiny unicorn at her side. Phainon's gaze drifts to it, thighs cold on the stone bench he's been perched on for the duration of this examination. He's been poked at and prodded, having his pulse and breathing checked, his pupils examined—you have beautiful eyes, Hyacine had told him, smiling, conjuring a much too bright ball of light to shine into them—his reflexes tested. The moment he'd gotten a hold of himself after being interrogated by Mydei and, admittedly, having a bit of a freak out remembering the things the black cloaked swordsman had forced him to see, he'd been yanked upright and all but dragged here, tears still drying on his cheeks, not one of his questions answered. There had been a red mark on his wrist from all of Mydei's yanking. There's a faint memory of it hurting, but when he looks at it now, there's nothing. He's not sure how it disappeared. Maybe he'd imagined it. Another scan around the room shows that Mydei is gone too.

Hyacine continues talking, Phainon continues being confused. "I was there during the earlier expedition; I'm not an expert on curses, but from the traces we found... you've got a remarkable constitution! Anyone else would've been breaking down left and right, but De says you've barely shown signs of that until tonight!"

"Just to be clear," Phainon tries as she scribbles something down onto a notepad. "You're saying my recent... emotional instability is due to that spell I walked into?"

She nods. "We'll have to get more input and figure out treatment in the morning, but from my understanding, this spell is forcing you to repeatedly experience vivid and unpleasant visions with the intention of inducing as much fear and distress as possible."

Blood, death, pain, pleasure. Phainon twists his own clean hands in his lap, fingers all but frozen, trying to hide a shudder. Vivid and unpleasant might be an understatement. "I... suppose those symptoms do match," he says, a lump in his throat. As of yet, no one has asked him to relate what he's seen, what he keeps seeing. As of yet, no one has born witness to what he'd been forced to confess to Mydei.

"I can't fix it now," Hyacine says, "not when most of our force is asleep, but rest assured, Lord Phainon, you won't have to keep experiencing this much longer."

Faces stuck behind his eyes, twisted in agony, tear-streaked, afraid. You brought this, you brought this, you brought this. Sharp, gauntleted fingers pulling off a mask. His own face staring back at him, something wicked in his eyes. His hands ball to fists, his dirty, bloody, guilty hands. Hyacine says something. He looks up. "Apologies. I don't think I caught that."

She sets a hand on his shoulder. Warm, how is she warm in this cold? Her eyes are pitying, and it turns his stomach. "You're still reliving those visions," she says. "I can't make them go away quite yet, but at least you can get a good rest tonight. Ica?" She straightens up, turning to the unicorn, which lifts itself on tiny wings to float to her side, giving another doot doot when she pets it on the head. "My pin, please," she prompts, and then the unicorn seems to belch something up, which Hyacine catches in her hand and wipes clean on her skirt.

"This is enchanted," she tells him, holding it out. "I'm afraid it's not very strong, but it'll absorb bad dreams, if you have them."

 Carefully, he takes it. A rainbow pin, carved from lightweight wood and lacquered with vivid colors, a fluffy white cloud at the base. "Thank you," he tells her, turning it over to see the metal clasp at the back.

"When it turns gray, the enchantment will have run out," she explains. "I'm not sure how long it'll hold out against a spell as strong as the one on you, but it should get you through tonight at least, and then we'll figure something more permanent out in the morning."

That lump in his throat never quite disappears. "What do I owe you?" he asks, thinking of those twenty eight balance coins in his purse. He has somewhere around forty that he's managed to save up. He has no idea if even that will be enough.

"Oh," Hyacine says, blinking, smiling softly. "Nothing at all. Think of it as a little gift."

△

Later that night, so late it might as well be early, Phainon lays down in his bedroll on the floor, that pin tucked in one of his pockets, gaze stuck on the faint patch of moonlight spilling in from the balcony. This time, Mydei is the one tossing and turning, behind him in the actual bed with its sweet-smelling sheets and abundance of cushions. Phainon is the one who stays still.

He doesn't think about the visions or the bloodshed or the swordsman. Maybe that's the work of the pin, maybe not. He knows little about magic.

He's so tired. A headache pounds behind his temples. He should have fallen asleep the moment he laid down, but here he is. Staring at that light, so faint he can't make out any color. He's comfortable. Bundled as he is, he isn't cold. And yet here he is.

Mydei rolls over yet again, sighing faintly. Phainon remembers the red mark on his wrist, wonders if Mydei healed it without him noticing, if Hyacine did it, if it was never really there at all.

"Isn't it dangerous for me to be here?" he asks, quiet in the night. Neither of them is sleeping, obviously enough. Knowing Mydei, he half expects to be ignored, pulling his hand out of his blankets and stretching his fingers toward that patch of light on the frigid stone floor. It warps over his knuckles. The chill creeps in the gaps he's made.

But, "It's dangerous for you to be anywhere," Mydei tells him, voice kind of rough. "Better here where everything is built out of stone."

"Okhema isn't infallible."

"Nowhere is."

"Of course not."

A long moment passes. Phainon pulls his hand back into his bedroll, tucking cold fingers to his chest. Mydei sighs, an audible thing at Phainon's back. His sheets shuffle. There's a light flick to Phainon's shoulder as Mydei reaches a hand over the edge of the bed. "Move over," he says.

"What?"

"This bed is too soft," Mydei says. "I couldn't sleep last night because of it, and I doubt I'll be able to tonight either. Move over."

Phainon chuckles, mostly air. "Are you really so used to roughing it that you're more comfortable on the floor than in a perfectly good bed?" he asks.

"When the bed makes me feel as though I'll sink straight through it, yes," Mydei tells him. "Now move, or do I need to ask a dozen more times?"

"A dozen more times might help."

"HKS."

Phainon smiles a little. His fingers are still cold. "The floor isn't quite so big as you seem to think," he points out. "Half of it is being taken up by that bath. Unless you're suggesting I take the bed instead?"

"You won't want it."

Finally, Phainon scoots, awkwardly dragging himself and his bedroll until he's all but at the edge of the drained bath. He turns onto his back, watching Mydei's silhouette, little more than a blur in the dark, as he slides out of bed, taking the sheets and one of the pillows with him.

"I didn't think you'd really do it," Phainon says when he's mostly settled.

"Well, I did." His voice comes from just as close as before, but he feels closer without the height of the bed frame. Phainon traces the shape of him in the dark, head turned toward him, though there isn't much to see. He wonders, with Phainon in the patch of moonlight, with Mydei's superior senses, how much better Mydei can see him. It doesn't feel fair. He turns to face the ceiling again, not wanting to be caught looking the way he must right now.

They're both quiet for a while. Phainon shuts his eyes and wonders if he's meant to fall asleep now. Mydei is finally still, not tossing and turning. He doesn't breathe loudly enough for Phainon to hear.

And then, "You'd rather leave, then?" Mydei asks him.

It's cold. Phainon had given up a bit of body heat to the floor where Mydei now rests. "Maybe it would be safer," he tries. "Maybe if I camped out in the middle of nowhere until this was all over..."

"Don't be foolish," is all Mydei has to say.

Again, Phainon goes quiet. His hands ball to fists. "You're right," he says. Cold, quiet. "You called him a Reaver. Have you... fought one before?"

"No," Mydei admits.

Phainon lets out a shuddering breath. "And in the past... There have been others, and someone has to have fought them, right? And won?"

"There was one," comes the reply after a moment. "Known for killing on water, taken down before my time. This one..."

"Is different," Phainon fills in. "Kills with flame."

"He isn't unbeatable. Nothing is."

"You're right," Phainon says, swallowing. "Of course, you're right."

"You're worried." It sounds like an accusation. Phainon folds his hand tight around Hyacine's pin.

"Yes, well. How could I not be?"

chapters.title: Chapter 10
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

It's not a FingerCracc longfic if the summary doesn't get changed at least once

The room is already well lit with pooling sunlight when Mydei wakes on the floor, cold and hard and blocked only by the thin sheet beneath him. His eyes are dry and gummy. He's slept far too late into the day, but he feels like he's hardly slept at all.

Beside him, no farther than an arms length away, rests Phainon, all but cocooned in his bedroll. The sun comes in from the balcony and hits him directly, his hair all but silver, his eyelashes casting faint shadows on the visible half of his face, the other hidden in his blankets.

It feels wrong that he's beautiful asleep. Someone like him, brash, reckless, annoying, angry like him, should drool and snore and have his eyes half open. But here he is, night after night. He kicks, though, so there's that.

A sensation in Mydei's hands, an urge to do something, though he doesn't know what. Sitting up, watching him a little longer, he stretches one hand out so he might cast a shadow over Phainon's eyes. A breath, two, uncomfortable with the sensations in his own chest, Mydei pushes off his blanket and stands up.

Phainon, not a light sleeper, but not a heavy one either, stirs. Mydei hates that he spares another glance to watch as Phainon's eyes crack open, squinting against the sun, bluer than anything.

"You're to go straight to the Twilight Courtyard for treatment when you're up," Mydei says, low and scratchy with sleep, loathing the sound of it, loathing the worry that sticks like pine tar, loathing the serenity of Phainon's sleeping face, loathing the feeling in his own chest. "I have business to attend to," he adds, which is untrue.

A faint sound, acknowledgment or protest, and then Phainon is curling in on himself, hiking the blanket up around his head so it shields his eyes from the sun. Mydei stops looking at him. And unlike any other day, he does not wake Phainon back up.

He washes and dresses quick, and then his hand is on the door if only to breathe, if only to do something other than stare at Phainon as he sleeps in the sun and think to himself over and over, something out there wants nothing more than for you to suffer. Something out there would do anything if it meant making you feel afraid, something out there—

He takes a breath, turns around and pulls the curtains at the balcony shut. Fabric rustles as Phainon stirs again and settles. Mydei doesn't look at him on the way out, shutting the door softly behind him.

A servant nearly bumps into him along the way, scrambling and all but terrified as she catches sight of the markings on his throat and cheek and promptly bow. It turns his stomach, but a letter is shoved in his direction with a high pitched, "A letter for you, Lord— Dux Sanguinis."

He takes it with one gauntleted hand, careful not to touch her. "Thank you," he says, and turns the envelope over to see the seal on the back. The Lance of Fury, the symbol of his parents' fallen house. Mydei exhales, nods to the servant as she scurries off.

He reads the letter over a bowl of yogurt for breakfast, provided to him for free alongside the room as yet another privilege of working for the Imperator. It's sweeter than most things he permits himself, flavored with fruit and honey, but the sweetness of it isn't enough to calm the current of nervousness running through him as he peels the envelope open.

Son of Gorgo, is who it's addressed to, and he never knew his mother, but just that is enough to have the breath stilling in his throat. He starts the letter again from the beginning, though there is little more than a single paragraph to fill the entire page.

Son of Gorgo,

I had long lost hope in the possibility of your survival and return, but after the news of Eurypon's death last year, I had wondered if I would meet you at last. I have waited these long years as I promised your mother I would, and should you have need or want of me, I will fulfill my oath. Name a time and place; I will be there.

Krateros

He'll need a pen and paper to write his reply. For now, calmly as he can, he folds the letter back up, returns it to its envelope, and thinks, you're really real. You're really here, you and your answers.

As your mother, I'm prepared to risk everything and sacrifice my own life, written in Gorgo's neat calligraphy, unfamiliar to him as the rest of her, and yet... You can trust the protection of Krateros. He's my chosen guardian. Mydei lets out a long breath.

△

"You're a siren, aren't you?" Mydei asks outside the Imperator Cerydra's throne room as he waits for her to call him in for an audience. Hysilens only blinks, expression smooth and impassive, from where she guards the door.

"I am the Imperator's most loyal blade," she replies. "Nothing more, nothing less."

But she smells of the sea and carries traces of Phagousa's magic, so Mydei supposes the question is less of what she is and more of why she's here instead of under the sea, and why she's so dutiful. Perhaps a better thing to ask would be what the Imperator has done to earn such loyalty, but it's a question Mydei has no business asking, so he does not.

"A sharp blade at that," he says to her unyielding stare. Silence falls between them. Hysilens seems unwilling to fill it, and Mydei doesn't particularly care. He nods to her, she nods back, and they both wait.

It isn't long before a call comes from the throne room. "Bring in the witcher," bids the Imperator. Hysilens pushes the door open, holding it with her back to allow him inside. Their eyes meet. Her hand is on her sword hilt, a warning left unsaid as Mydei comes before the throne, Imperator Cerydra sitting there, legs crossed, chin propped on her fist.

"Dux Sanguinis," she greets him as Hysilens shuts the door with the three of them on the inside. "Your report. Succinctly, if you would."

"Imperator," he greets her back, inclining his head rather than bowing. She gestures for him to continue. "We have identified the monster responsible for the burnings," he says. At this, she straightens up. "There is solid evidence to believe it's a Reaver, Your Majesty, an extremely rare creature born of bloodshed and strife, bound inextricably to a child born at the exact moment of its creation."

Cerydra's eyes narrow. "Bound, you say?"

"A Reaver does not eat or drink; this child's fear is its only source of strength," he explains. "It grows stronger every time this person is scared, and the moment they've felt enough fear in their life, the Reaver matures and gains the power to become the source of that terror, leading it to terrorize the one it's bound to until they die.

"Any atrocities it commits," he continues, "are with the express purpose of causing that person trauma. Your people have been collateral damage."

Cerydra looks at him for a long while, expression unreadable. "And what happens when that person dies?" she asks.

Now, he hesitates. "It will run free and destroy everything in its path," he says.

"I see." Her eyes narrow. "And this child, this person the Reaver is bound to, the one heralding death to my people through nothing more than their unfortunate presence, who is it?"

The Imperator, Tyrant, Empress, Sovereign Cerydra has never been known for her mercy. Mydei bows his head again to her and hates this, forced, feigned deference, well aware of his own lack of power in this city entirely under her control. "First, Your Majesty," he says, careful to speak calmly, "I would ask a favor."

△

Phainon is gone when he comes back, nothing more than his bedroll haphazardly folded and pushed out of the way to mark his presence. The curtains have been pushed back open. It smells ever so faintly like forsythia soap.

Finally, Mydei writes his reply to Krateros, taking a sheet from the thin stack provided to him by a servant. He spends too long choosing his words despite thinking about them all day, running through potential things to say and how to say them over and over in the moments between other things. He's careful to keep his hand steady. He's careful to keep all of his words neat and legible.

He sends the letter out and has lunch, cheese and olives and rich, stuffed bread. He does not wonder about Phainon, whether he's still stuck at the Twilight Courtyard or whether they're already cured him and he's instead washing wool again and will come back reeking of dromas. He does not worry, most importantly, over the Flame Reaver, plotting and planning how best to make Phainon suffer next.

Mydei's meal turns bland in his mouth. After his next swallow, he takes a breath big enough to make his lungs hurt, holds an image of Castrum Kremnos' hot springs in his head, and casts the Sign of Cerces on himself. The clarity is cool and immediate. He exhales, slow and controlled, and returns to his meal, finishing what's left in a handful of minutes and cleaning up his space.

Back in his room, he moves onto the balcony, breathing the frigid sweetness of the air, feeling the sun, low in the sky and providing the tiniest amount of warmth. He removes his gauntlets first, pausing to leave them back inside on the desk. A cool breeze blows, dries the sweat on his hands as he shrugs out of the right side of his robe, baring his markings to the air. 

A cloud rolls over the sun, diffusing the light. There's enough of them and enough of a chill in the air that Mydei expects it to snow tonight. He casts the Sign of Nikador, energy coursing through his markings until there's a thin, sharp crystal in his hand, red as pomegranate arils or the blood of humans . His finger cuts easily on it and gold wells up, which he smears over his bare arm, following the path of his markings and thinking of home.

As the blood dries, he feels it. Castrum Kremnos, the Stronghold of Witchers, pulling at him, calling back to him. Soon, he feels somewhere deep inside him. Soon.

△

It's late when Phainon comes back, the sun gone, the snow started. He's careful and quiet with the door like he thinks Mydei might be asleep. He isn't. They look at each other.

"The healers at the Twilight Courtyard," Mydei says.

"They took care of it," Phainon assures him, shrugging out of his coat. "It took a while, but I'm no longer cursed."

"Good."

There's melted snow in Phainon's hair. He reaches like he means to remove his boots before he pauses. "Have you looked outside recently?" he asks instead, passing Mydei to get to the balcony, pulling open the curtain. He smells like dromas again. "It's finally snowing."

"I noticed," Mydei says, but he gets up to look anyway when Phainon lingers. They step outside, the two of them at the railing, watching soft flakes float to the city, still lit and busy down below. Their breath fogs. Phainon tips his head up to look at the sky, the line of his throat pale, that leather choker a stark contrast.

"I've always liked snow," he says, and he sounds... optimistic in a way he hasn't in a while. Maybe it's the lack of influence from the Flame Reaver's spell. Shoulder to shoulder, Mydei doesn't want to ask.

"Snow spells hard times," he points out.

"Sure," Phainon agrees. He must be cold since he'd taken off his coat, but he doesn't show it. He looks at Mydei now. "But it's pretty, isn't it?"

And it is, tens of thousands of tiny flakes floating through their air, catching the torchlight from down below, settling soft and lazy on roofs and balcony railings and white hair. Phainon's half smile is soft. Mydei looks away.

"I guess so," he admits. To him, snow has always been a call home. Winter is tough traveling, poor wages from hard off villages, monsters in hibernation. So he goes home to the cold, crumbling halls of Castrum Kremnos, and he spends the snowy season training and soaking in hot springs with his fellow witchers.

They're quiet for a while. Phainon reaches out to catch snowflakes in his palm, watching them melt, frozen fingers folding over the railing when he tires of that, uncaring of the cold that usually has him complaining and burrowing into his coat.

"Aren't you cold?" Mydei asks. A faint laugh.

"I've been washing fleece in half-frozen water for hours; I must've gotten used to it," Phainon replies. It's harder to smell out here where the air is chilled, but Mydei remembers catching it on him as he'd come in.

"I'm saving up for a sword," Phainon adds. "You'd be surprised how much this sort of work earns."

Mydei's tongue feels odd and thick. His gaze sticks on the bit of Phainon's nape that shows beneath the collar of his coat when he looks down at the city below. "Good," he says, and Phainon takes a long, deep breath.

"Listen, Mydei," he starts, and stops, and starts again. "I don't know what kinds of crazy dangerous monsters you've been up against, but this Flame Reaver..." He exhales. "Be careful, is what I'm trying to say."

And like that, the optimistic mood slips out from between them, lost somewhere below. Mydei folds his arms over the railing, leans over them. He gets Deja vu from the night before, them on the balcony, just like this. "You just said you're getting a sword," he points out. "I'm surprised you're not asking for the chance to kill him yourself."

Phainon's grip grows tighter until his knuckles bleach white and his hands begin to shake. "Believe me," he says, low and shaky and furious, "I want to, I do." He exhales, letting go and straightening up, trying to calm himself.

"But I know myself," he continues, "and he... He has too much power over me, and I realize I would only be a liability. I'll leave it to you and the Imperator's team. He gets stronger every time I'm afraid, and then there's that curse he put on me... I don't have magic or enhanced strength and senses like you do. I'm only human, and I'm not..." Strong enough, goes left unsaid.

Strange, how sober he is now. How realistic. Mydei watches him breathe, watches his clenched fists shake, watches him call himself weak. This man, brave enough to face a witcher, strong enough to meet him blow for blow, normally so self-assured and confident, and he's giving all of that up now.

Mydei looks at Phainon's solemn, weary expression, and finds himself angry.

"Then what have you been training for?" he asks. It's hot behind his ribs, growing the longer he looks at Phainon and can't find the strength he knows is there. "Will you just cower and let him cut you down the moment he returns?"

"That isn't— Mydeimos," Phainon says heavily, turning to him, brows drawn together in the dark. "You're misunderstanding me."

"You're only human," Mydei spits. "You're weak, you aren't strong enough, isn't that what you were trying to say?" He has to hold himself back from getting into Phainon's space, from raising his voice for everyone down below to hear. Why is he so angry? "What am I wasting my time with you for, if you won't even bother to fight back?"

"I would," Phainon insists, hands still tight, shaky fists, "I would fight, but I'm not delusional enough to believe I have a chance! My fear makes him stronger, I don't have magic or any other advantage over him! I want to fight, I want to kill him with my own hands, I do, and maybe with more time and training—"

"Time is a luxery no one is afforded," Mydei tells him, and his control is slipping, voice raising in volume, defensiveness, anger, frustration rearing up. Why? He sees the truth in Phainon's words, so why is he so frustrated? "It doesn't matter if you're mortal and magicless—"

"And what does it matter to you anyway?" Phainon shouts, interrupting him. "You want me silent, you want me out of the way, you want me as far as I can get from your business, and here I am, telling you I'll stay away, and now you're angry? You've been driven mad by my pride and arrogance this whole time, I know, and here I am, finally putting myself in my place. Shouldn't you be pleased? Shouldn't you—"

He's stepped into Mydei's space, scent hot with rage, but here he is, still saying all of these frustrating things. "This isn't humility," Mydei tells him. He pokes a finger into Phainon's chest. "It's cowardice. This is the monster that destroyed your home. You said you want justice. I've seen your fury, and yet—"

Hands fist in his robe. Phainon shoves into his space. "Yes, I'm afraid!" he says, voice raising. "Obviously, I'm afraid! I watched my home burn, I lived every moment of that last village's razing in that vision, I was cursed! I know better than anyone how powerless I am, of course I'm afraid!"

Mydei wraps a hand around Phainon's wrist, yanking, squeezing tight enough to hurt when he resists letting go. "So be afraid!" he yells back.

"I'll make him stronger—"

"So be afraid," Mydei repeats, louder, cutting him off, pressing him back half a step. "Train and get stronger and save up for a sword and fight back. This is your fight as much as it is anyone else's, more than it is anyone else's, or did you think the Flame Reaver would show up just because I asked him to? He's bound to you. You're the bait either way, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae. If you're going to snivel and act weak and cower behind your pathetic excuses, I'd rather stop wasting my time on you here."

He can hear Phainon's breath behind his clenched teeth, feel the tension in his fist, shaking in Mydei's grip, creasing his robes. "I never took you for cruel," he says, low and shaky. He shoves his fist back into Mydei's chest hard enough to hurt. "I already know this is my fault. I already know everyone in Okhema is at risk because of me, I already know—"

"Don't put words in my mouth—"

"I want to get stronger," Phainon says, and his eyes, flicking between Mydei's, furious, are wet. Again, he knocks his fist into Mydei's chest. "I want to fight, I want to feel that swordsman's neck snap beneath my own hands, and I want to watch him burn, but anything I do has the chance to make things worse, to make him stronger, to hurt people, and I'm not strong enough—"

It's all wrong, his face, his eyes, the tremble in his voice. "And since when were you weak?" he asks, grabbing Phainon's collar. Phainon grabs his wrist with cold fingers, and they stand there, mirroring each other's positions. "Where's your determination? Where's your strength? Where's your rage?"

A breath. A muscle tics in Phainon's jaw. It's silent down below.
