And then Phainon knees him hard, yanking him forward as together they tumble back inside, a blur of fists and elbows and feet. A hiss of pain, a heavy sound as they collide with the wall, Phainon rears back and slams his fist into Mydei's jaw at the same time as he blocks a haphazard blow with his other arm. Skin tears under Mydei's gauntlet; he's dazed from the punch, but he can smell the blood, hot and metallic. Phainon pays it no heed.

"I don't understand you at all," Phainon is saying through gritted teeth. His fist pulls back again, other hand tangling in Mydei's messed up robes, dripping blood, cold knuckles against cloth against skin. Mydei barely slips beneath his punch this time, sweeping a leg to knock him off balance enough to push him to the floor, where they roll and grapple and slam into the side of the bed frame.

He gets his arm around Phainon's throat, but there's already a hand stopping him from applying pressure, teeth sinking viciously into the meat of his bicep, breaking skin until they're both bleeding, red and gold, hissing from pain and shoving each other away, trying again and again to hit something, fabric, bone, blood-slick flesh. Phainon's elbow meets his shoulder, knee meets his gut, clavicle scraping beneath his metal-tipped fingers.

It's quick, blurry, painful, and then Phainon pins Mydei at last, slamming his back against the ground and weighing heavily across his hips, both hands holding Mydei's wrists down. He's a mess, chest heaving, hair tangled, clothes rumpled. He smells like sweat and blood and fury, heavy and hot, and between breaths he says, "What do you want from me, Mydeimos? Because if it's a fight— If you want me to battle and bleed and die up against that swordsman, despite my fear, despite the fact that I'll just make everything worse, I'll do it. I might not be strong enough to kill him myself, but I'm no coward, and I've been angrier than you can imagine for a long, long time, and I'll get in your way and butt into your business and claim what justice I can for myself, if that's really what you want."

And Titans above, there he is. Blood from his torn arm drips to floor. His chest heaves. His throat rolls against the tight leather of his choker as he swallows. The look on his face is like fire. He doesn't seem to realize it, but it's the first time he's won one of their spars.

Heat—horrible, ill-timed, misdirected and unreasonable heat—floods straight south. Mydei exhales, lets his head fall back against the floor, hard and unforgiving.

"I don't want you in my way, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae," he says, tasting blood in his mouth where he'd bitten his tongue. "I don't want you cowering behind me. I want you to prove yourself, as you have been. I want you to fight by my side."

Phainon's grip on his wrists grows tighter. His weight grows neither lighter nor less insistent, less molten. He swallows, dry enough for Mydei to hear the sound of it. "You don't mean that."

"Come with me," Mydei says.

"What?"

"Come with me to Castrum Kremnos. Train and learn and grow among witchers, where your presence won't put the whole of Okhema at risk and there are wards enough to guard against attack. Come with me and become strong, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, and when the winter is over..."

"You're serious," Phainon says. His blood scent is strong and metallic. Outside, it continues to snow.

"It won't be easy," Mydei tells him. "It'll be the hardest training you've ever experienced."

Again, Phainon just says, "You're serious." He's a solid, firm weight still pinning Mydei down. Hot over his waist and hips, cold fingers tight over his wrists. His bitten arm throbs.

"What'll it be?" Mydei asks. They look at each other, Phainon's eyes flicking between Mydei's. He reeks like blood, sweat, dromas. Cooling rage like a seasoning, beneath that— He's too close, too hot, Mydei is breathing him in too deeply. "Is that a yes?"

A laugh, low and incredulous. "Funny," Phainon starts, pressing hard into Mydei's wrists as he leverages to get off of him, rolling to lay with him side by side, shoulder to shoulder. He exhales like he's still catching his breath. "...How you're pretending this was your idea," he says. "Like I haven't been trying to go to Castrum Kremnos since day zero."

Mydei folds his hands over his ribs now that they're free. In the light of the room's lanterns, he catches the red glimmer of Phainon's blood on the knuckles of his gauntlets. "It wouldn't have made sense before."

"And what changed?" Phainon asks. "The fact that there's a monster after me? The fact that two more villages have burned just because I happened to pass through? The fact that—"

Mydei traces patterns on the ceiling with his eyes. Turns his head to look at Phainon on his back, the part of his mouth, the glimmer of light reflecting off his eye. Mydei's jaw aches from his punch, arm still throbbing from his bite. He surveys the imprints of Phainon's teeth with an odd kind of fascination.

"Quit pitying yourself," he says. "It wasn't you that burned those villages down. The Flame Reaver would have done the exact same thing if it were bound to anyone else. And it would have been worse, because anyone else would have been twice as afraid."

"I'm plenty afraid," Phainon whispers.

Between them, the air seems to calm. Mydei finds his gaze stuck to the shell of Phainon's ear. "I know," he says. "Will you come to Kremnos?"

Another dry, humorless laugh. Phainon turns his head to meet his eyes, blue as dusk in the dark. "You can't take it back," he says. "Of course I'm coming. You're stuck with me, Mydeimos, and you have been since the day you gave up on chasing me away."

"I never tried," Mydei tells him, facing the ceiling again. His heart beats, slow and purposeful, loud in his chest.

"Ha. Didn't you hate me for a while there?"

Here Phainon is, making him say things aloud he'd really rather not time and time again. How much easier it would be to just lie. "I never hated you," he says.

Phainon chuckles. "Sure," he says sardonically.

"Hate is a strong thing to feel," Mydei says, sighing. "Don't think yourself so important. I was confused by you. I found you annoying. I was intrigued by your resolve. I might not have liked you, but I never hated you."

Quiet as Phainon doesn't try to refute him. He's smiling slightly, like he's trying to hide it. "Well," he says, and his voice is a bit weird. "I suppose there's that, then."

"There's that," Mydei agrees.

"Would you... ah, sorry." Phainon sits up, cross-legged beside him, gingerly holding out his torn arm. "Would you heal this? It hurts a bit."

It's still bleeding, red smeared over the whole length of his forearm, three jagged tears through the skin from Mydei's gauntlet. It's the worst wound Mydei has given him. They're even, considering Phainon's bite, purpled and throbbing and leaking gold where he'd broken skin. The injured muscle protests as he sits up too.

"I won't be able to fix it all the way," Mydei admits, reaching for Phainon's arm. It jerks in his grip when he forms the Sign of Aquila, reflex against the tickling sensation.

"Thank you regardless," Phainon says. He's kind of quiet. They both are, in the aftermath. The wounds stitch themselves back together halfway, and the bleeding seems to stop, though it's still a mess of blood already spilled. He'll need a bandage. Mydei realizes he's still holding Phainon's arm and lets it go.

"I'm sorry," he says. The imprints of teeth pulse with the beat of his heart. "For this, and for speaking unfairly to you."

"Maybe I deserved it," Phainon says, crawling to the corner where he's shoved his stuff and dragging his pack over. Out comes some medical supplies, a length of gauze he uses to wipe up the blood.

A moment passes. Mydei feels like he should say more, but he can't find the words. Phainon's blood dries on his gauntlet. He casts the Sign of Aquila on his jaw where he'd been punched. The bite, he leaves alone.

Phainon speaks again. "Did you mean it?" Mydei looks up. "When you said you wanted me to fight by your side?"

"There's still a lot left for you to learn."

"But did you mean it?"

Mydei sighs. "I'm not in the habit of saying things that I don't."

Now, Phainon smiles slightly. "So?"

"So yes, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae. I meant it. If you can keep up."

△

"Sir— Er, ah, Lord— Dux Sanguinis!" comes the voice of the flustered, frazzled servant who delivered Krateros' letter. She's flushed red, but manages to hold Mydei's gaze.

"Yes?"

She takes a breath as if to steel herself. "We've received a couple of complaints from your neighbors regarding a commotion coming from your room last night," she says, recovering from her stutter. Her shoulders square. She holds her ground. "I must remind you that violence is strictly prohibited within Marmoreal Palace, and while you may be a guest of the Great Imperator, you are not exempt from the rules."

Heat rises to his face. He bows slightly. "I apologize," he says.

"As an esteemed guest, you are receiving a warning," the servant says, breaking eye contact now, like she fears he might get angry. "Should such a thing happen again, you will have to search for other accommodations."

"I understand," he says, bowing his head lower. The shame burns his cheeks. "Again, I apologize. It will not happen again."

She hesitates, exhaling. "Well. Good, then. See to it that it doesn't." An awkward pause. "Please, um. Please enjoy the rest of your stay."

△

The snow has settled a couple of inches thick. Most of this will melt in the sun, but Mydei takes it as the first touch of winter. He finds himself breakfast, and then he heads off to meet Krateros at Dawncloud, more nervous than he'd like to admit.

He doesn't know what to expect. Perhaps at one point in time Krateros had held him as a baby, his mother looking on with fond eyes, but to Mydei this is as good as never having met him at all. There's no face to picture in his mind, no sense of the way he speaks beyond his letters, of his voice and personality. And Krateros will have nothing to go off of but terrible rumors and knowledge of the fact that he, like everyone else, was once a child.

The place they've agreed upon is a building with one wall open to the air, two stories high, heated with blazing braziers and people gathered around them chatting. Mydei climbs the steps to get inside, and realizes his lack of a face for the name means he won't recognize which of these strangers was his mother's most trusted friend.

His mother, whom he doesn't know the face of either.

He needn't worry, because after a moment of standing and scanning the room, he's approached by an older man with a scarf redder than blood, and he knows right away. "Krateros," he says.

"Son of Gorgo," comes the greeting. Krateros has a deep, aged voice. His beard is gray to match the streaks in his hair. He's weathered and scarred, silvery tissue beneath a blinded eye, white through the iris. He must be sixty by now, but he still stands tall and strong. He speaks familiarly, fondly, and Mydei realizes he could count the number of times he's heard his mother's name spoken aloud on his fingers.

Krateros comes closer, sets his hands on Mydei's shoulders, studying him with his good eye. "My boy," he says, and though Mydei is covered up against the cold, he must note the markings climbing his neck, the one on his cheek, the obvious signs of what he's become, what he's been turned into. But Krateros doesn't seem afraid or surprised; he's probably known anyway, if not always than at least since Mydei killed his father with his own hands. He just smiles and says, "You look just like your mother."

A tight feeling in his chest. He knows he can't have her eyes, as they've been changed by his mutations. He doesn't ask about the rest. "You've done her a great service," he says, "waiting all these years to keep your oath."

"I always knew there was something to wait for," Krateros tells him, squeezing his shoulders lightly, patting him the way he might pat someone he actually knew. "It's not so easy to get away from Destiny, now is it? The moment I'd gotten word about Eurypon, I'd known it was you. I just wondered if you'd ever get your mother's message and come my way."

Stiffly, he inclines his head. "And you still waited all this time."

"To think you've been turned into a witcher," Krateros says, stepping back, looking over him again. "Titans above, you must've been through hell."

"You're no stranger to bloodshed and suffering yourself," Mydei points out, making an obvious nod to the blind eye. "But it's no use to dwell on the past."

"I'm sure you didn't enlist the Holy Maiden of Janusopolis' help finding me just to reminisce."

"As a matter of fact, I did," Mydei tells him. "I meant to extend an invitation to Castrum Kremnos for the winter, but circumstances have arisen that would make it dangerous and unreasonable. Instead, I would ask for your expertise and cooperation in a job assigned to me by the Imperator."

"I swore my life to your mother," Krateros says. "It would be my honor to lay it down for you, whether that's here, or in Kremnos, or anywhere else."

"You mean that."

"On my honor, Son of Gorgo." Krateros folds a hand over his heart. "I am old and no longer fear death. I have waited a long time to fulfill my oath to your mother. I would be glad to be of use."

△

Yet again, Mydei stands in the Imperator's throne room, Hysilens behind him, hand ready on her sword hilt, Cerydra in front, legs crossed, eyes narrowed at him.

"You're leaving with the source of the threat," she says, "but where is my assurance that you'll eradicate it from my lands completely?"

"When spring has come and we witchers have had time to train and convene, I will return to work with your forces as planned," he tells her. After a moment of hesitation, he removes the plated necklace he wears around his throat. "There is knowledge and equipment in Castrum Kremnos that will better prepare us for this fight, but I understand your concern. As a gesture of sincerity, I will leave this in your care. When the winter is over, Lady Tribios may use it to ascertain my location were I to attempt to escape my duties."

It's a difficult, but necessary gesture to make. Mydei would rather not risk revealing the location of Castrum Kremnos—even if only temporarily—to outsiders. But he needs the Imperator to trust him. Allowing her this much power over him should be worth the trade.

After a moment, she waves a hand. "Dux Gladiorum, if you would."

Hysilens approaches, extending a hand for the necklace. She nods tersely when Mydei hands it over, and it feels suspiciously like approval. The heels of her shoes are loud on the stone flooring as she returns to her post by the door.

"I'll remind you that you won't see a coin from the rest of your payment until the monster is dead," Cerydra says.

"I understand, Imperator."

"That's nine hundred balance coins, Dux Sanguinis," she says, making her point. "Nine hundred balance coins and the rest of your lifetime hailed as a hero."

He inclines his head. Again, "I understand, Imperator."

She sighs, reclines back in her seat. "Very well, then. Go. I will await your return in the spring."

He bows shallowly and turns to go, but pauses when she speaks again. "And Dux Sanguinis?" she calls. He turns to face her again. "See to it that no more of my people are harmed on your journey home."

chapters.title: Chapter 11
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

"So... Krateros, was it?" Phainon asks in the awkward handful of moments when they're left alone together, Mydei busy retrieving Strife from the stables. The older man—graying, covered in scars, and blind in one eye—nods, but doesn't say anything else. Phainon runs his tongue over his teeth. "How do you know Mydei?

Very little has been told to him. Mydei had shown up after his meeting with the Imperator with this man in tow and no explanation, aside from a gruff, this is Krateros. He's coming with us. Looking at him, Phainon realizes he doesn't know how old Mydei is. Maybe Krateros is his father, but this is Krateros, would be a very strange way to introduce one's father. More likely, he's Mydei's "old friend", but even then...

Krateros hesitates, like he's not sure if he should answer, like he might be giving away secrets if he does. But Mydei wouldn't have left them alone out here together—catching whiffs of manure from the barn and watching their breath fog up in the cool air—if he wasn't alright with the prospect of them making some small talk, would he?

Krateros sighs, squints at Phainon in the sun, and says, "I knew his mother."

"His... Oh." Phainon didn't realize Mydei knew his mother. He knows very little about Mydei's past in general, just that at some point in his childhood he was stolen or sent away to become a witcher. But of course there was a before; maybe he was five or six, just old enough to remember his mother's songs and her embrace before being ripped from her arms. Or maybe she was cruel, maybe she was the one who sent him away, maybe... "So you knew him as a child, then?"

Krateros frowns, folds his arms across his chest in a mannerism that is quite like Mydei, and says, "No."

"No?" Phainon repeats, uncertain.

But Krateros doesn't supply him with any answers. "And what about you?" he asks instead, though it sounds less like he's trying to reciprocate the conversation and more like he wants to move it along. "How do you know Mydeimos?"

"I'm his companion, for the time being," Phainon says. "I... met him in one of the villages he stopped at on his way here and we started travelling together."

"He sprinted a mile and a half after my horse," Mydei corrects, coming out of the stable with Strife on her lead rope. "And managed to dodge when I tried to punch him for the audacity."

"I don't like the way your tone implies that those were bad things," Phainon says, holding out a hand to Strife when they come close enough. She snorts and permits him to stroke her muzzle, and in the few days it's been since he last saw her, he wonders if perhaps she'd come to miss him. "Was I meant to just take your fist—gauntlets on, mind you—to the gut and move along?"

"That would have been preferable, yes," Mydei says. His smile is sharp-toothed, and Phainon finds himself pleasantly nauseous with the fact that he can earn it so easily. "Come on."

The three of them make their way to the city gates, where a squadron of at least a hundred trained and armed soldiers waits. "An escort," Phainon notes when it becomes clear that they're here for them. A sick feeling twists in his stomach as he realizes that while he's spent these past days in the safest city in Amphoreus, the moment he steps outside, the Flame Reaver will be free to go after him again. Or worse, go after others. He's not sure how confident he is in these men. "Wonderful."

The squadron's leader signals for the gate to be opened. Outside, there seems to be no one at all; they must've already blocked this area off in preparation for Phainon to pass through.

So many lives in danger just for their proximity to him. He swallows and finds his mouth dry.

Not your fault, he thinks. It's hard, rewiring himself this way, but he knows that the more he hates himself and blames himself and succumbs to the terror, the stronger the Flame Reaver gets. So he tries, and fails, not to feel terrible. It's not your fault.

Flanked by soldiers on all sides, they make it out the gate. Strife seems nervous, Krateros frowns deep enough to etch creases into his face, and Phainon wonders how much he knows, if he's aware of how much danger he'll be in going anywhere with Phainon in tow. Mydei must have told him. He has to have.

The air is sweet. A hundred footsteps fall in sync as they march along. Phainon takes a breath and tells himself, again and again, that everything is going to be alright.

They walk for ten minutes, twenty, thirty, steering clear of the main road, part of the plan to ensure no one will be hurt along the way. From here until they reach Castrum Kremnos, Phainon won't step foot in a single village, and aside from these soldiers, Mydei, and now Krateros, they're going to do their best to make sure he doesn't see another soul.

They'd talked about it the night before, both of them sleepless and exhausted. While Mydei met with the Imperator—Phainon not allowed anywhere near her for obvious reasons—Phainon had gone back to the spinner for a few hours of work before regretfully explaining that he was leaving the city. With all of his money saved up, he could pay for a sword, but there wasn't time to have one forged.

The soldiers leave them after five or so miles traversed without incident, and as he listens to their footsteps fade in the distance, stranded in the middle of a skeletal forest, he feels a bit naked without a weapon. He's gotten used to the security of walls as tall as a dozen of him and guards on every corner.

"Let's go," Mydei says after a moment. Phainon turns back to him, adjusting the straps of his pack with gloved fingers, and watches, incredulously, as Mydei passes Strife's reins to Krateros. "I'll have you ride Strife," he says. "Phainon and I will walk."

Krateros thanks him and mounts in a smooth motion, and it makes sense, really. He has to be sixty or near to it; it would be entirely unreasonable to expect him to make this journey on his feet. Phainon is surprised, is all. He didn't think Mydei was at all open to the possibility of lending his horse.

They walk on.

"So how do you know where we're going, anyway?" Phainon asks. "We don't have the road and the mountains aren't visible through all these trees. Is Castrum Kremnos very close?" Castrum Kremnos. Titans above, after all this time, he's finally going to make it there. If the Flame Reaver doesn't kill them all along the way.

Don't think of that. Don't give him power over you. Instead, he remembers his anger, the promise he'd made to fight and bleed and train and win. He remembers Mydei, golden-eyed and furious, I want you to fight by my side. Come with me to Castrum Kremnos.

He's still bruised. His arm is still scratched up and bandaged where the Sign of Aquila couldn't heal it all the way. He looks at Mydei and wonders if he healed the imprints of Phainon's teeth.

He watches as Mydei removes one gauntlet, then the other, tucking them under his arm. One hand pushes up a sleeve, the other pulls the knife from his waist.

"What're you..." Phainon trails off as Mydei pricks the tip of his finger and smears the blood that wells up—shining gold—over the markings on the opposite arm.

"There's a connection between a witcher and Castrum Kremnos," Mydei says, raising the bloodied arm into the air. His markings seem to glow faintly, and he takes a slow breath. "We should make it there by the end of the day."

Phainon purses his lips rather than comment on whatever ritual or spell he'd just witnessed. "Is the hidden Stronghold of Witchers really so close to the Holy City?"

Mydei lowers his arm after the blood dries, changes their course slightly. "Castrum Kremnos," he says, turning to Phainon, "is a moving city."

"That..." Phainon's mouth falls open.

"That explains the rumors about its whereabouts," says Krateros. "Or, rather, the lack thereof."

"How does it move?" Phainon asks. "And is that what your little ritual just now was? Are you tracking it?" He pauses. "Summoning it?"

"This isn't information we share with just anyone," Mydei says.

"Yes, and it's been a while since I've been anyone, hasn't it? You're taking us there anyway, what would it hurt to tell us?"

Mydei frowns, thinking for a moment. "It's an enchantment," he says, sighing. "I'm no sorcerer; I don't know how it works. But yes, any witcher can ask Castrum Kremnos to move."

Now, it's Krateros that speaks. "Ask?"

Mydei turns to him, soggy leaves underfoot from melted snow, sun catching his cheek through the bare canopy. "Yes," he says. "We can ask, but it doesn't have to listen."

It's awkward. Krateros is quiet more often than not. He answers questions in as few words as possible and never asks follow-ups, never contributes to conversation with Phainon unless directly addressed. Mydei is quieter too, more like he had been the first few days they'd traveled together. Unwilling to engage in banter with Krateros there or just more fed up with Phainon than he usually is.

They're alike, in a way. Mydei and Krateros. Phainon still doesn't understand their history, hasn't been able to glean much out of the handful of scraps he's been supplied with, but they have the same quiet, resolute kind of strength. The same demeanor like they've already seen it all. The same no nonsense kind of attitude.

An old friend of Mydei's, or perhaps not. They're strangely stiff with each other too. Too respectful, like they're afraid of stepping on each other's toes, like they each owe the other a great debt, like... Phainon doesn't know. He's tired. He's uneasy. He just wishes they'd give him something to distract himself with.

Lunch comes and goes, tucked between trees, their backs against rough bark, sitting on fallen logs so they won't soak their pants on the ground. Phainon stays mostly quiet, just thinking. Too much, probably. About the Flame Reaver, about Castrum Kremnos, about training and other witchers, about bruises and the feeling of a sword in his hand, almost forgotten. And then some tiny part of him whispers will it really be safe?

Even now, even here, he wonders. It's been oddly quiet. He keeps seeing dark, tattered cloaks in the shadows and wicked, gleaming blades in things that catch the light. He would be so easy to terrorize here, even in the absence of entire innocent towns to slaughter. But the Flame Reaver never comes. 

"I've been checking, you know," Mydei says between bites of bread.

Phainon looks up, swallows, realizes he's been chewing the same bite for almost a minute. "What?" he asks.

Mydei slips a hand into one of the pockets on his belt, producing a scrap of something. Black fabric, torn and fraying and unmistakable. He doesn't really smell smoke, but he almost thinks he does, a dozen memories flashing at once. "It isn't a strong spell, but the Sign of Janus works up to about a mile away. "Stuck to a fence at that first village," Mydei answers. A pause, his eyes slipping from Phainon's. "I should've told you."

"And this Sign of Janus," he says instead, "is it a tracking spell?"

"In essence," Mydei says, and tucks the fabric away again. Phainon realizes he'd been staring at it until now and looks up. Gold eyes, a faint frown. Krateros watches too, keen-eyed and quiet.

Mydei stands, brushing the crumbs from his robe and pushing his sleeve to the elbow, where dried blood still sticks to his skin. "I'm going to check on Kremnos," he announces to both of them, by which he means he's going to perform his blood ritual again. "We should be close; I'll see if I can get a look." He nods to a tree not too far, tall, with branches low and sturdy enough to climb.

Phainon opens his mouth, but Mydei speaks again before he can get a word out. "There's no point," he says. "It'll be masked to your eyes. I won't be long."

Phainon sighs, but he doesn't protest.

"Be careful, son of Gorgo," says Krateros. Mydei nods to him, firm and sharp, and stalks off.

The wind whistles faintly. Phainon's fingers hurt from the cold, so he wraps the rest of his food for when he can find an appetite and shoves his hands in his pockets. Strife snorts, stamps her hooves, a blanket thrown over her back. Finally, Phainon gathers the strength to meet Krateros' eyes.

"Gorgo," he says. "Was that Mydei's mother?"

"He would have told you if he wanted you to know."

"Right," Phainon says, and tries not to wonder about the past he hadn't been privy too, that Mydei hasn't told him about. He turns to watch Mydei ascend the tree, surefooted and steady and strong. and wonders instead if he could climb it faster. "And what about you? Has he told you about my... predicament?"

"The monster tethered to your soul," Krateros says, nodding. His voice is rough. Every inch of him that Phainon has seen is covered in scars. His posture is terribly tall for someone who must be terribly tired. "Yes, he told me."

"And you've chosen to tag along anyway? Even knowing how dangerous I— how dangerous it is to be near me?"

A sigh. Is he weary? He must be. "I'm not here for you, son. I'm here for him, for his mother, for a promise to myself."

His swallow sticks in his throat. There's an odd, fragile feeling somewhere in Phainon's chest. Not fear, it isn't fear, but something almost like it. "But he told you," he presses, "about the villages. All the people who died just because—" He clears his throat. "—Just because they had the misfortune of being at a stop on my path."

"He told me," Krateros says simply.

"I understand it from him," Phainon says. "He's a witcher; this sort of thing is his job, but you..."

Now, Krateros leans forward, propping his elbows on his knees, finally looking as tired as he must feel. "I'm old," he says. "I've been waiting a long time to keep this promise."

"So it's duty for you too, then?"

A rough laugh. "Duty," Krateros repeats. "Sure, let's call it that."

The sun starts to set. The air grows bitterly cold, their breath fogging up in the air, Phainon's ears stinging. He passes his handkerchief beneath his nose as it runs. They walk on and on until all that's left of the light is a molten glow through the trees and behind distant mountains. When the forest finally breaks and they're left in a wide open valley glowing gold with the dying sun, Mydei brings them to a halt.

"We're here," he says like coming home. 

Maybe there are wildflowers in the spring. Still, even cold and dead and soggy, it's beautiful. Phainon breathes deep, but it's too cold to smell.

The valley, all but empty but for the river at the bottom of the slope. The other half of the forest across on the other side. The mountains to the west, all the shadows to the east. "Where is it?" Phainon asks.

Mydei turns, extends his hand to help Krateros dismount from Strife. And then he removes one gauntlet and pricks his finger as he has a dozen times already today. He smears the blood that wells up between Phainon's eyebrows, unceremonious, and does the same for Krateros, albeit more politely, as Phainon goes cross-eyed and spluttering trying to see it.

He's dizzy for a moment. There's a faint pain in his head, and then the next time he blinks the whole landscape changes. 

A grand city sits, spires tall and gleaming, carved of stone and cast in gold, a sword as tall as a hundred men glowing above it. Nikador's blade, from the legends. Where the valley had been empty but for rushing water and grasses, Castrum Kremnos now waits. Phainon falls speechless with his awe.

"Let's go," Mydei says, taking a step forward. "The sooner we're inside the better."

And Phainon—cold as he is, awed as he is, floored with the realization that the thing he's been chasing all this time is finally in front of him—can do nothing but follow.

The inside is almost as grand than the outside. Where Okhema had splendor and opulence and a sweet smell down every street and corridor, Castrum Kremnos is strong and imposing with banners and braziers, and the air has a faint oily, metallic smell like that of a forge. It's also crumbling in places, disrepair showing in cracked facades and crumbling floors, faded rugs, disintegrating tapestries, and plant life taking over where it shouldn't. 

What handful of witchers there are isn't enough to take care of everything. Still, it's the most awe-inspiring place Phainon has seen. His footsteps echo. His neck hurts from craning it to gape at the high ceilings, the detailing on the walls and windows; lions, weapons, armored warriors. He finds Mydei already looking when he spares him a glance. He's as comfortable as Phainon has ever seen him.

"This is..." He doesn't know the words. Somehow, after all this time, he never thought he'd actually make it here. The one place where he might actually become strong. The only place—protected by the strongest wards and the strongest people—where it might be safe for him to be, where he won't lead to harm just by breathing.

"I know," Mydei says, and there's something proud about it. He's proud of this place, despite what Phainon is sure is a painful history here. Another history he isn't privy to. Another history he'll try not to wonder about.

They walk in silence a little longer. Three sets of footsteps, Strife's hooves clomping along. Phainon gapes left and right, marveling at every pillar taller than two of him, every ornate window, every fire blazing for warmth and light.

Krateros speaks after a moment or two. "Has this place been a good home to you, Son of Gorgo?"

Phainon turns to look at them both, wondering so many things. The place that made Mydei into what he is. The place that took him and changed him into something he never asked to be. The place where he'd experienced more pain than Phainon can imagine.

"My family is here," Mydei says, still proud of this place that must've broken him, even if it also put him back together. "It's home, regardless of the history."

"The other witchers," Phainon says. "Are we going to meet them?"

"Depends on who's here," Mydei answers, but it comes with a nod, his face lit by fire. "It's best you get settled first; we'll find out by dinner."

Before them is a pair of towering, heavy doors. Mydei pushes one open with some effort and holds it for Phainon and Krateros to pass through. Strife comes last, Phainon snagging her lead and passing it back to Mydei. They find themselves in a courtyard, exposed to the air and at least as large as half a block in Okhema. A stone path cuts through the center, leading all the way to the double doors of a massive, palace-like building. To the left is a series of strange wooden contraptions and structures. To the right is a clearing fringed by empty weapon racks, the ground so compacted that nothing grows beneath a thin dusting of snow.

Training grounds. Towering walls set with sconces and indented with doors leading to who knows what. Phainon is awed. He's absolutely awed as Mydei leads them along to another set of doors, these tall and wooden and accompanied by a characteristic smell inside.

It's a stable where he settles Strife, removing her saddle and giving her water and grain as Phainon manages to find himself impressed even by this too. Stone floors padded with straw; the ceiling is high and the stalls are more spacious than he's seen anywhere else. He paces a ways down and finds himself face to face with an adolescent dromas as he pokes his head into one.

"Oh," he says, surprised, and then stretches a hand out for the creature to smell. It makes a soft chuffing noise and presses into his touch, warm where his fingers are still frozen from the journey. "Hello."

"Don't mess with the dromas," Mydei calls.

Phainon opens his mouth and decides against saying anything. Apologetically, he pulls his hand away and wanders back over to Mydei and Krateros.

Their next stop is across the courtyard and into the palace, where it's notably warmer and Phainon gradually regains feeling in his cheeks. "This place is huge," he says as they take a turn down one corridor. It's better maintained here, the rubble cleaned up in any cracked areas, the rugs faded but intact, less dust piled atop surfaces. 

"Yes," Mydei says. He spares Phainon a glance. "There used to be a lot more of us."

Phainon and Krateros are each given a room toward the end of a long hallway. They pass and poke their heads into a dozen or more, finding some with holes in the walls making them frigid and drafty, others with broken furniture or weird smells or no mattresses on the beds.

"We don't get many visitors," Mydei explains apologetically. "Maintaining unused rooms isn't at the top of our priorities."

"It's a bit funny," Phainon says, "the difference between the corridor and all the rooms."

"It's quite alright," is Krateros' reply, lightly clapping Mydei on the shoulder. "I'm used to sleeping in far worse conditions. Any soldier is."

"Well," Mydei says, pushing open the next door, "so long as there isn't a hole in the wall."

This room is missing an entire corner in the back, snow dusted over rubble, cold wind whistling through the cracks. Phainon peers over Mydei's shoulders and finds himself unable to help a laugh. Without a word, Mydei pulls the door shut.

A little longer, they find a suitable room, and after a careful inspection for drafts and mold, Mydei strips the bed of its dusty sheets with a promise of a new set and they leave Krateros to settle in as they continue searching for a room for Phainon.

The longer they walk, the more Phainon starts to notice the cracks in the walls and the places where it must've been patched up. Castrum Kremnos is an old place, Phainon realizes. Still grand despite its age, still strong despite the wear. Their footsteps are muffled on the frayed rugs. Phainon looks at the side of Mydei's face, the bundle of sheets tucked under his arm.

"I'm curious," he says.

"You're always curious," is the reply. A breath, a creak as Mydei pulls open another door and shuts it with barely a glance inside. He sighs. "What about?"

"Your room," Phainon says.

"You're not sleeping there, if that's what you're asking."

He laughs, ignores the slight lump that forms in his throat. "I wasn't," he says. "I know you're sick of me by now." More quiet. The air is weird between them today. It has been. Phainon had attributed it to Krateros' presence, but now it's just them and the feeling is still there. The eye contact they make is brief and accidental.

"I meant I was curious what it looks like. Whether you've decorated it or not, whether you've mounted monster heads on the walls or if you sleep on a pile of furs instead of a bed or something."

Another door, another creak. Mydei lingers a little at this one; Phainon can't see his face, and it's too dark inside to see over his shoulder. "You can see it, if you want," he says. "It isn't much to look at."

"Surely you've done something with it," Phainon says, tipping his head to one side as Mydei takes a step back and shuts the door again. Mydei doesn't really look at him, just continues on. "It's your home, isn't it? You come back here year after year, do you not?"

"I do," Mydei says.

Again, Phainon laughs if only to fill the air. "Alright," he says, and watches as Mydei opens the next door and actually deems this one worthy of going inside. He lights the lanterns as Phainon follows, dumping Krateros' dusty sheets on the ground as he starts poking around to make sure this one is safe.

"This looks good," Phainon says as he pulls the sheets off the bed and finds no signs of mold on the mattress. The dust threatens to make him sneeze, but the feeling fades as he dumps these sheets with the others. 

Mydei faces him after checking the walls and the fireplace. His expression is odd and quiet and Phainon does not ask any of the hundred questions he wants to.

"Get settled," is what Mydei ends up saying. He bends to scoop up the bedding on the ground, stirring up more dust. "I'll be back in a bit with Krateros, and then we'll go for dinner."

"Right," Phainon says. 

They look at each other. That lump in his throat comes back. Why is this weird? Why is he nervous? Why is Mydei looking at him like that? And then he just turns away, all the sheets bundled up and barely manageable in his arms, and this feeling comes like panic. Don't go, it says, and that doesn't make any sense at all.

And yet, "Mydei," Phainon finds himself saying. Mydei stops, turns back, and the feeling almost eases. Phainon finds himself uncomfortably aware of his own heartbeat. "Thank you," he tries, and hopes his voice comes out normal.

Mydei nods tightly.

"I mean it," Phainon tries again. "Thank you. For... letting me bother you all this time. For bringing me here. For fighting this battle with me, even if it's just part of your job."

Mydei's mouth parts on his exhale. "Don't get sappy on me, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae," he says, and smiles a little. "There are worse places to be."

"Worse places," Phainon says, shaking his head, laughing through his nose. "What 'worse places' are there than beside the guy with the monster bound to him?"

"Get settled," Mydei only says again, turning his back. In the lantern light, Phainon watches the reddened tips of his hair as he pulls the door open. "I'll be back."

"Right," Phainon says, and kicks up some dust. The door shuts between them before he can say anything else, chest still tight, heart still beating. He lets out a breath and says to no one, "See you, then."

Fifteen or twenty minutes pass of Phainon trying his best to clean with what limited supplies he has, wiping the dust off long forgotten surfaces with a moth eaten shirt he finds in the wardrobe—opening the window for the airflow despite the chill when he finds himself sneezing half a dozen times in a row—shaking out the curtains, clearing cobwebs out of the fireplace, and failing to sweep the floors without a broom. He works up a sweat and starts to see progress, and then there's a thundering sound as the walls shake and groan and a couple of tiny pebbles dislodge themselves from the beginnings of a crack in the ceiling.

It sends him straight into a panic, plastering himself to the wall, staring into the gaping dark of his open window, straining for sounds in the corridor or the rooms nearby. He wonders if this is it, if the Flame Reaver is going to show himself here despite alleged wards and protective magic and the presence of presumably more than one witcher.

But the creaking stops and Phainon regains his balance, and as long as he stands, listening to the sound of his breath and trying to calm his racing heart, nothing seems to happen. His hands shake. He fumbles in his pocket for Hyacine's charm, the rainbow faded but still retaining a little bit of its color, and somehow he finds it in himself to relax.

He opens the door, slowly and silently as he can, and pokes his head out into the corridor, peeking left and right.

Nothing, no one. Wall sconces lit, windows creaking slightly in the wind. He exhales, shaky, and steps outside.

He doesn't know his way around Castrum Kremnos, so he takes his chances finding Krateros first. Maybe Mydei will already be with him, maybe not, but it's more than obvious that Krateros is military trained and seasoned, and they'll be able to figure something out from there.

"An intruder, is it?"

Phainon whirls, making an aborted motion like some kind of punch before he finds his fist frozen in the air, breath catching in his throat. He finds himself unable to move an inch, and the sensation is so familiar, so sickeningly known to him from every nightmare he's ever had, every time he's set his gaze on the Flame Reaver, and every part of him thrills, screams, cries for him to move, to get away, to fight, to flee, to anything.

The man before him stands with his arms crossed, freezing him in place without even forming the Sign of Oronyx. He cocks his head as he comes closer, studying Phainon. One of his hands is gloved, the other bearing bearing markings, crimson like Mydei's, more on the inside of one forearm where his sleeve is cut to show it. He's clothed up to his chin but for his chest, where there's a hole that doesn't show skin beneath but a window to the galaxy, and he feels— He feels like so much stinging, pressing magic that Phainon can feel it, a headache forming despite his lack of affinity for sensing magic at all.

"Who are you, I wonder?" the witcher asks, because he must be a witcher, he must be, but everything in Phainon is screaming at him to get away, get away, but he can't move, can't speak, can't breathe for the way his head feels like it's splitting.

The witcher takes a step forward, sparing a glance at Phainon's frozen, trembling fist with one eye, a blue so pale it's almost white. "Someone strong, it would seem," he says, voice slow and smooth as the pressure on Phainon redoubles and holds him tightly still without the witcher forming the Sign again.

He can't move, he can't do anything, and the feeling is so cold and static and urgent but he's helpless as he always is, stuck in place as pain pounds through his head and the witcher continues to study him at leisure.

"You've piqued my interest," he says, raising a hand to the patch covering his other eye, starting to peel it back as the pressure grows and grows and the feeling in Phainon's chest claws and thrashes and—

"He's with me, Anaxa," comes Mydei's voice, and the witcher pauses, frowns, slips his fingers out from beneath his eye patch as all of the force eases and Phainon falls to his knees, fingers digging into the faded red rug, gasping for breath.

"Disappointing," Anaxa says, and turns from him. Phainon squeezes his eyes shut and gives the panic a moment to ease before he opens them again, gaze finding Anaxa's boots as he walks slow in Mydei's direction, the patterns on his coattails. "You made it back alive, then?"

Phainon staggers as he brings himself back to his feet, one hand on the wall for support as another rumble rolls through the ground. His breath— he still hasn't gotten a hold of his breath, which comes in rapid, unsteady pants.

"I did. Brought a couple of friends too," Mydei says. "I planned to introduce you, before all this." A gesture made with one hand, the other full with a bundle of fresh sheets and blankets pinned under his arm. He holds out his free hand and Anaxa clasps it like they're comrades, like he hadn't just done whatever he'd done, and— And of course they are.

"Wait," Phainon says, pressing into the wall to stand all the way up. "Just— What is going on here? Who is Anaxa? And why— Why does the ground keep shaking?"

Anaxa turns, looking at him with that one unsettling eye, so pale a blue it's almost white. "You will call me Anaxagoras," he says. "Listen well and learn much while you are here, and perhaps you will gain what it takes to survive your fate, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae." With that, Anaxa— Anaxagoras leaves.

"Hold on," Phainon says, shutting the door, standing there as Mydei passes his forearm over the dresser to clean off the dust and set the stack of sheets there. "A Source? And what do you mean he saw something? And—" A groan rips through the walls again, furniture rattling. Phainon grabs onto the door frame. "—And again, why is everything shaking?"

"Kremnos is moving; the shaking is normal and will stop after it's been going for a bit," Mydei says, pulling a sheet off the stack and unfolding it. It's a red that must've been crimson once, and he shakes it open before tossing it over the bed and working on one of the corners. He looks between Phainon and the opposite corner, clearly expectant.

An exhale, Phainon comes over, finding the corner of the sheet, lifting the edge of the mattress. "And the other stuff I asked?"

Mydei sighs. "A Source is someone with immeasurable affinity for magic, dangerous if untrained. Anaxa is..."

"A Source," Phainon repeats, swallowing, "turned witcher?"

"Yes," Mydei says, and it feels like it hangs in the air. They set the mattress back down, sheet tucked tight beneath the top corners. Three steps toward the bottom; they untangle the rest of the fabric.

"Alright," Phainon says. "And what would he have seen?"

"Your past," says Mydei, lifting the mattress with one hand. "Your future. I don't know."

A chill crawls up Phainon's spine. He pulls the sheet over the corner of the bed as another rumble shakes the walls. "And how would he have seen it?"

"He has visions. I don't know how it works."

Quiet. The mattress falls back into place, blowing a puff of dust. Mydei pulls a blanket off the stack and tosses a case for the flat, dusty pillow to Phainon.

"He isn't going to hurt you," he says, and the tone of it is weird. "No one here will, I can promise you that."

"I wasn't worried." Mydei doesn't reply. Phainon looks at him, the pillow half shoved into the case. He remembers the way it felt to be frozen in place, that cold, considering gaze on him. "I mean it. Whatever that was, it was a misunderstanding. I don't care if he's a Source and a witcher. If he's one of your brothers, and if you trust him, I trust him too. I'm a lot more worried about whatever he saw."

Mydei tucks the edge of the blanket under the mattress, lays a second over the foot of the bed. "He isn't likely to tell you."

"It's my past," Phainon says, tossing the pillow down. "My future."

"I know." Mydei gathers up the rest of the stack of bedding to deliver to Krateros. "But nothing good ever comes of knowing it."

△

Anaxagoras is not there at dinner. Instead, there is an absolute behemoth of a man stirring a pot of something that smells rich and savory and mouthwatering.

"Chartonus," Mydei greets him.

Chartonus looks up from the pot, a helmet hiding his features, though his stature and slate-blue skin mark him as a mountain dweller. "Brought friends, you did," he says with a voice as deep as anything.

"This is Krateros and Phainon," Mydei introduces them. Phainon waves, a bit awkward. Krateros gives a neat bow, which makes Phainon feel like he should have bowed too. "Phainon, Krateros, this is Chartonus, the master of our forge and keeper of our hearth."

"A pleasure, it is," 

"Is he— Sorry, are you a witcher as well?" Phainon asks.

Chartonus shakes his head. "A witcher, I am not. For fighting, these hands are not."

"He watches Kremnos when we all leave," Mydei explains. "He's too important to risk out on the Path."

"I see," Phainon says, nodding slowly. "And... the forge?"

"That reminds me," Mydei says, looking Phainon over, then turning back to Chartonus. "I would ask a favor, if you can find the time for it," Mydei tells him. "Phainon needs a sword."

△

The dining hall in Castrum Kremnos is fit for hundreds, lines of long tables stretching the room, ceilings high, lit with grand chandeliers and braziers at every corner and windows patterned with frost. Phainon is convinced they must keep their fires going with magic. He tries to keep his gaping to a minimum as they walk for what feels like ages down the aisle in the center, passing empty table after empty table.

He can imagine it, rich-looking nobles and dukes with a half dozen different forks talking circles around each other. It's befitting of the atmosphere, the grandeur, the glory that hasn't faded despite the fortress falling into disrepair, but that wouldn't have been right, would it? No, at it's peak, these tables, these rooms, these halls would have been filled with scared, exhausted children forced to live through horrors day after day, night after night.

Phainon holds his tongue. At the end of the hall, crowded around the end of one table out of dozens, are three men. One holds a book, one a lyre, and one has a shield, dented in places, in front of him and off to one side.

Chartonus sets the giant pot on the table, and they all look up from their conversation. One, the man with the shield, long-haired and slighter even than Anaxagoras, with dandelion yellow markings up his arms notices Mydei before anything else.

"Mydeimos," he says, and stands, grinning, extending a hand that Mydei clasps without a thought, pulling him in for an embrace.

"Hephaestion," he greets, grinning back, and it's strange to see Mydei smile like that. Phainon's chest does an odd thing as Mydei lets Hephaestion go and turns to the man with the book, short hair adorned with a laurel, markings a deep forest green patterning his skin. "Ptolemy," Mydei says, and embraces him too. Last is the one with the lyre, elegant as Phainon has ever seen a man, with long, light hair, a stoic expression but for the faintest hint of a smile, and markings a vivid ocean blue. "Peucesta."

"I'm surprised you aren't the last one here," says Ptolemy. His smile is crooked, his eyes are golden brown, and the way he speaks is teasing and familiar. That feeling comes back, twists ever so slightly.

"And with friends," adds Hephaestion, alighting his gaze on Krateros, then Phainon. His eyes are green. His face is thin, almost gaunt, though handsome. Phainon feels strange about this too.

"This is Krateros," Mydei says, gesturing, "the one who knew my mother."

"It is a pleasure," Krateros says, folding a hand over his chest and inclining his head, "to meet the ones who have grown with the Son of Gorgo, and protected him in my stead."

"Finally found him, huh," says Hephaestion, not quite directed to any of them, smiling a little softer. "I'm Hephaestion," he introduces himself. "That's Ptolemy and Peucesta. It's nice to meet you as well." He looks at Phainon then. "And you are...?"

"Phainon," he says. "I'm..." He finds that he doesn't know what to say.

"There's a Reaver on his back," Mydei explains. "I brought him here hoping everyone could train with him, and that we could take the Reaver down before it does any more damage."

Ptolemy gives a low whistle. "A Reaver," he repeats. "You're sure?"

Phainon swallows, glances at Mydei, who just says, "I'm sure."

"Well, then," says Hephaestion, pulling out the empty chair beside him and gesturing to the pot, still rich and hot and fragrant. "Let's all say thank you to Chartonus for the meal, and then let's have a chat."

"Goat and mushroom soup, it is," Chartonus rumbles, and his face is still covered but Phainon could swear he sounds proud of himself. Carefully, he pulls out another chair and sits.

Chapter End Notes

lore concoction volume 5: As I've mentioned before, Castrum Kremnos takes the place of Kaer Morhen in this fic, which is the stronghold of witchers and where they return every winter in the Witcher canon. Kaer Morhen doesn't move and isn't invisible, instead it's just in a very well hidden and isolated location. I've opted for some more made up magic, with Kremnos being able to move (as it can in canon), and the witchers being able to feel it and ask it to come to them because it's convenient and I think it's cool lol.

Anaxagoras my beloved!!! Ohh I have been cooking his character up for so long and I am so excited to introduce him. The witcher Mydei agenda is a no-brainer but... witcher/Source Anaxa hear me out... A Source in the Witcher is essentially someone with a strong and extremely volatile affinity for magic. There are no Source-witchers in canon, and probably for good reason!!

chapters.title: Chapter 12
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Mydei wakes with the sun, light spilling through a familiar, dirty window, the air carrying the scent of metal and leather, mattress just the right amount of stiff beneath him. He slept better than he has in a while, finally back home with his family, Krateros, Phainon.

He presses himself up. The familiar stone walls of his room, the furs serving as rugs, the dresser cluttered with his armor and equipment, the shelf lined with things here and there. A short stack of books, read and reread, a stuffed chimera tearfully and gratefully gifted by a child whose life he once saved, gemstones and trinkets and knives and other random things he's picked up on the Path.

An ornate goblet he'd taken after he killed King Eurypon.

He sets to cleaning his teeth, shaving his stubble, and combing his hair, knowing Chartonus will already be up and making breakfast, knowing Hephaestion and Ptolemy and Peucesta might already be up and training, Anaxa might be working on some fanciful concoction or another, the rest still on their way back as Kremnos follows them across the earth.

Krateros might be awake, stretching out stiff muscles, military routine still ingrained after all this time. Phainon will still be sleeping without Mydei there to force him awake. Maybe he had a hard time falling asleep in the first place, unused to the environment or cold or with a lot on his mind. It's awfully quiet, without him.

Mydei heads down to the dining hall for breakfast. Krateros is already there.

"Good," he says, standing when he sees Mydei. He's sharp-eyed and neat after a night's rest and a chance to clean up the dust of the road. "I wasn't sure where to find you with the size of this place."

"I'll give you the full tour now that you've had a chance to rest," Mydei says.

Krateros studies him, reaches out to grasp his shoulder. One firm squeeze, his hand is warm, rough and callused. "You're a good man, Son of Gorgo," he says, and returns to his seat. "Let's talk."

Mydei pulls out the chair beside him and takes a seat. "I owe you my thanks," Mydei tells him. A pause as he searches for the right words. "And an apology."

"An apology, son?"

"For the chaos," Mydei explains. "For the fact that I've ripped you from your home and put you in a dangerous situation. I planned to extend an invitation here when we met. I wanted you to meet my family, see my home, and have time to share all your stories about my mother; it's why I went to Okhema in the first place, but..."

"I understand," Krateros says. His breakfast is forgotten on the table as he turns in his seat to face Mydei fully. "You're... a witcher." The way he says it is almost sad. "No monster can go unkilled. No man can go unsaved. Besides, you said yourself that I can help keep the kid alive."

"You're willing, then?"

"I may be old, and I may not have magic or the strength of you witchers, but I've been fighting for over forty years, son," Krateros says. "I'd have trained you, had your mother lived to see it. Now, I've waited a long time to make myself useful again. And that boy, Phainon..."

Quiet. Mydei cracks a hint of a smile. "You don't like him, do you?"

"He seems eager and full of potential," Krateros offers, though he's frowning. "But I'm not convinced of his discipline, and I'm not fond of his overly active mouth."

Mydei laughs through his nose. "He's different when he's fighting."

"I'll take your word for it."

"Thank you," Mydei says. "Whatever you can teach him, I can promise he'll learn."

"You have a lot of faith in him."

Faith is a strange thing. Mydei trusts in Phainon's will, his fury, his quickness to learn. Anyone else would have succumbed to the terror by now, anyone else would have given up, would have let the Reaver off its leash and let it burn down the world. "Yes," Mydei admits. "I do."

Krateros takes a long breath, sighs it out. "Alright," he says. "I'll teach him. I'll try to have faith in him too."

"Thank you," Mydei tells him again.

"He's the one who should be thanking me." Krateros picks up his spoon, stirs his food around, and glances back at Mydei. "Go and get yourself a bowl," he says. "We'll talk about your mother."

△

They talk for a few hours as they eat their breakfast and Mydei gives Krateros the whole tour. It's odd hearing stories of his mother whom he'd never met, who loved him more than anything, who gave her life just to give him a chance at his. It's odd, when he tells stories back, watered down versions of what made him who he is today, and Krateros—instead of seeming horrified or disgusted—just seems a little bit sad, and a lot proud.

He squeezes Mydei's shoulder more than once, calls him Son of Gorgo like it's a title that carries weight and honor and that he's more than deserving of. Strange, hearing his mother's name, being able to shape an idea of her. Strange, hearing himself called son of anything, anyone. Strange being assigned belonging, being handed it so easily and without question.

"You really do look like her," Krateros says as Mydei shows him the library, cared for by Ptolemy. "Your eyes are different, and you may bleed gold, but you are still your mother's son."

It has been a long, long time since Mydei last cried. He doesn't, now, but he finds himself tempted to. His throat grows tight. There's a faint pain in his sinuses as he sniffs, says thank you, and brings Krateros to the armory next.

△

Late into the morning, the sun already high overhead, Castrum Kremnos shudders and groans and comes to a stop. Outside, there's a torrent of snow. There's no sign of Phainon. Leaving Krateros to his own devices, Mydei finds Phainon still asleep in his room, threadbare curtains barely blocking the sun, the fire warming the room long since burned to ash.

There's nothing to see but a tuft of his hair poking out from the covers, his side rising and falling with his breath. Mydei looks for a little too long, and maybe it's the way he already feels fragile from discussing his mother. His chest gives a painful squeeze, and then he pulls open the curtains, stirring up dust.

"Phainon," he says. The lump of sheets stirs, but there's no reply. Again, "Phainon." Phainon shuffles further into his blankets, that tuft of hair disappearing, letting out a faint groan in protest.

Still, Mydei's chest aches. "That tired, huh?" he murmurs. "It's midday. Chartonus needs to size you up for a sword. You need to train. There's still a ton of Castrum Kremnos that you haven't seen. What happened to all of that?"

He waits ten seconds, twenty, thirty. Phainon has been stressed, certainly. Physically from all the walking and sparring and everything else they've been doing. Mentally from resurfaced trauma, a monster eager to hurt others to hurt him, a spell designed specifically to terrorize him, a concoction of fear, guilt, sadness, and rage that he carries day by day and has to be weighed down by.

He's gotten up with the sun just about every day for weeks now. He's still mortal and human and soft around the edges where he hasn't been mutated and conditioned into being the perfect killer. But the difference between them is that the people who broke Mydei and made him into this are long dead, and the one waiting to break Phainon is still out there.

A slow sigh. Maybe he deserves the rest.

"You get fifteen more minutes," Mydei says, softer than he means to. There's a wide open spot on one side of the bed, more than big enough for another. He lays down atop the covers after a moment of hesitation, staring up at spiderweb cracks in the ceiling, folding his hands over his sternum. It's cold in Phainon's room with the fire out, which isn't helping the fight to get him up.

"You get fifteen minutes," Mydei repeats to the lump of sheets, close enough that he could reach out and touch and maybe find a little bit of Phainon's lost body heat. It smells like dust, the faint soap they use to wash the linens, lingering notes from Phainon's floral one. An urge arises that he shoves down. "You hear me? Fifteen minutes, and then you're getting up."

Another half-vocalized groan, acknowledgment or protest or anything else. Mydei exhales and watches the light play on the blanket as he waits.

△

The lab where they'd once been poked and prodded and injected with toxins and medicines and all but tortured is Anaxa's now. He's turned it from a place full of nightmares into just another room, though all of the same implements and equipment are still in place.

Now, it's all used for his experiments and alchemy, jars filled with potions and ingredients lining shelves, stoves brewing some concoction or another, tables cluttered with pages and pages of notes. The floor is sticky, and it smells sharp and sulfurous, hinting at a recent spill. Mydei steps around where he thinks the mess is and notes a rack with two vials on the table in front of him.

A glance up. Anaxa is aware of his presence but hasn't turned to face him, busy grinding something with a mortar and pestle, rhythmic and scraping. Mydei returns his attention to the vials. He carefully removes one of the two from the rack. The liquid inside is gold like their blood, warm to the touch though there's nothing to heat it and the air is cold. Perhaps it just came off the stove. He returns his attention to Anaxa.

"What is this?"

Anaxa turns, leaving the mortar and pestle behind. "A mutagen," he says. "I'd advise you to put it down."

"A mutagen," Mydei repeats, an uneasy feeling growing as he studies the gold fluid. It might glow faintly. The warmth might not be leftover from the stove after all.

"I've no intention of torturing children, if that's your concern," Anaxa says, and takes a couple of steps to pluck the tube from Mydei's fingers. "They're for me."

Wary, Mydei eyes the second vial, a shade darker than the last, like old blood instead of new. Of all of them, Anaxa has undergone the most mutations. It wouldn't be the first time he'd given himself more. Every winter, he returns with a sample or two from the strongest things he comes across. Some years they'll work and he'll come out of it with a new strength, others he'll leave himself sick and bedridden until spring.

"Your quest to godhood will kill you one day," Mydei says.

"And I will be glad of it, for I will finally know the secrets of the afterlife." Anaxa slides the tube back onto the rack. Gold. Warm, swirling gold. Mydei has seen any number of colors in Anaxa's solutions, but he's never seen gold. Never a gold so vivid, so like their blood.

"What monster did you take these from?"

Anaxa laughs. "No monsters," he says, and the gleam in his eye is almost manic. "Titans."

"You're not serious."

"Oh, but I am." Anaxa's mouth curls into a wicked smile. "Years of searching, and I've finally succeeded in finding the remnants of their flesh." He points at the vial Mydei had examined, bright, gleaming gold. "Cerces," he says, and points at the other, darker solution. "Nikador."

A cold feeling fills his chest. He isn't sure if it's dread or awe. "You're certain?"

"As I am that the dawn will come," is the answer.

"And if your body rejects them?"

A considering hum. Anaxa taps ringed, marked fingers over the counter. "The pursuit of knowledge is more than worthy of dying for," he decides simply. "Perhaps I will die, perhaps I will become a god. Either way, I will have my answers. Now, did you have a purpose for this visit?"

Mydei lifts his gaze from the vials, pushing down the uncomfortable feeling in his chest. Among all of them, Anaxa is the most morbidly ambitious and dangerously powerful. A Source and a witcher both. A man trying to become a god. The stronger he makes himself, the more he knows about everything, the easier it is to pretend he wanted to be turned into this all along.

Now, Mydei swallows and pulls the scrap of the Flame Reaver's cloak from his pocket. After all this time, it's still stained with magic as he hands it over. "I wanted to ask a favor," he says. Anaxa accepts the fabric, rubbing his thumb along the fraying threads, likely gleaning all there is to know about it just from touch and perception alone.

"That came from the cloak of the Reaver after Phainon. If there's a way you can track it definitively, I ask that you would."

The fingers of Anaxa's other hand slip beneath his eye patch, which he pulls back to look at the piece of tattered cloth. The eye beneath, though Mydei has seen it hundreds of times, still makes him pause.

"He's close," Anaxa murmurs.

"How close?"

Anaxa doesn't reply. He only stares a little longer, and then fits the patch back over his eye, sliding the scrap into his pocket. "I will take care of your request," he says, and returns his attention to his alchemy. "Now leave me, if you would. Many of my ingredients are sensitive to time and may spoil."

"You said he's close."

"I asked you to leave."

Sighing, knowing better than to start this fight, Mydei does.

△

Hours later, he finds Phainon on the training grounds, armed with a wooden sword up against Peucesta. The earth is a mess of churned up mud from their feet and the snow; they're both covered in it, shoes and knees and the backs of their coats. Hephaestion and Ptolemy too, from where they stand aside, watching and throwing out pointers.

Phainon is doing well, all things considered. He's flushed and sweating, clearly working harder than the other three, if only because he's the focus of this training. He's careful and wary; Peucesta is the most lithe and agile of all of them, graceful and quick on his feet. He fights with a sword as well, stepping in for a swift lunge, which Phainon parries, feet slipping in the mud.

There's the dull sound of the training swords colliding, Ptolemy saying, "You're too careful," as Phainon remains on the defensive. He fends Peucesta off once more, twice, and then attempts a counter strike and in a blur of motion, finds his sword knocked from his hand and a blade leveled with his throat. Still, aside from not using his Signs or potions, it doesn't seem like Peucesta held back.

A prickle in Mydei's chest. Phainon still has yet to say anything about the fact that he'd won, back in Okhema. There's a small bit of solace, perhaps, in the fact that he doesn't seem to have noticed how he made Mydei feel.

"Well fought," Peucesta says, lowering the sword and stepping back.

"You're unsteady in the mud," Hephaestion notes as Phainon bends to retrieve his sword. "Practicing your footwork will do you some good. We'll put you on the Pendulum for a bit."

"Did you at least let him eat lunch?" Mydei cuts in.

Phainon turns around, catching his breath, red from the cold and exertion both. "Mydei," he says on an exhale, and lights up like the dawn. "We'll do lunch after this 'Pendulum' thing."

"No." Mydei shakes his head. "The Pendulum is best done rested. You've been at this for hours; you'll only hurt yourself."

A nervous laugh from Hephaestion. "He's right," he admits, rubbing the back of his neck. "We got too excited and overworked you. You just seemed so..."

"It's his own fault," Mydei says, pulling the training sword from Phainon's grasp. His voice comes out too stern. "He's too stubborn for his own good. Never stays down when he should."

"I'm not hurt," Phainon says. "I'm not even that tired. They didn't overwork me. I can—" He's still catching his breath. 

"Good," Mydei cuts him off before he can finish that sentence. I can train longer, or I can still fight. There's no point in running him ragged. They need him strong, they need him at his best. "Then it's time for lunch. You should know the importance of rest."

Luckily, Phainon doesn't fight as Mydei wipes the training sword in the snow to clean off the mud and leaves it in the weapon rack. "Alright," he just says. "I guess I could eat."

"A bath might be in order too," laughs Ptolemy, holding his arms out and gesturing at himself, wet with melted snow and filthy from dirt. "For all of us, I think."

"I'm in agreement," says Hephaestion. Peucesta nods. "Shall we take a trip to the springs after we eat, then?"

△

Chartonus provides them with freshly baked bread slathered in butter, topped with thinly sliced meat, cheese, and the winter greens he grows in his glasshouse at the far end of the stronghold. It's all still warm, and they eat with indecent noises and talk with their mouths full. Krateros joins them halfway through and thanks Chartonus for it, reminding them all to shower him with thanks and praise.

When they're done they make their way to the springs, Hephaestion shouting at empty halls for Anaxa to join them, Chartonus' steps loud alongside them, Phainon and Ptolemy laughing, even Krateros cracking a begrudging smile at the absurdity of it.

Mydei's chest feels warm and awkwardly full, but he says nothing as they make their way down the main hall to the heart of the stronghold, then down a long set of stairs carved into the earth, leading underground to a cave lit with mounted torches and bioluminescent moss. It's warm and humid in stark contrast to the cold outside, four springs occupying the cave, each hotter than the last, with just enough space to walk between them.

Phainon gapes in awe as he usually does, coming up behind Mydei and asking, "why wasn't this part of your grand tour earlier?"

"You'll boil to death in at least two of them," Mydei informs him. Steam curls off the last two springs, the hottest of the bunch. As witchers and frequent visitors of these springs, they've all built up a tolerance for the heat, and even then, they don't dare spend more than a handful of minutes in the hottest. Phainon is wholly human and might not have touched many a hot bath in his life, let alone a hot spring.

"Really," Phainon says, skeptical. He takes a step forward, but Mydei catches his arm.

"You'll start with that one," he says, pointing at the coolest of the four, closest to the entrance. "If, and only if it isn't too hot, you can try the next one. Don't even think about touching the last two." He lifts his gaze and finds Krateros looking at him. Embarrassment brings heat to his face as he lets Phainon go and straightens up. "That would be my advice to you as well, Krateros. The last two pools are extremely hot; even we witchers are careful not to spend too much time in them."

For some reason, Krateros laughs. "Advice taken, Son of Gorgo," he says, and the embarrassment only grows.

"Anaxa," says Hephaestion, "you heard me after all."

From the second pool, where he's already settled and soaking, Anaxa lifts one dripping hand in greeting and replies, "It would have been difficult not to, what with all your shouting."

"How did he get here so fast?" Phainon asks.

"After a point, you learn not to question things when it comes to him," says Ptolemy.

"Uses magic, he does," explains Chartonus.

The group of them goes to the side of the cave opposite the pools, where there's enough space to undress and a few pitchers of water to clean off the worst of their grime so they won't sully the springs too much. Phainon's clothes had taken the brunt of it, but there's mud on his face, hands, hair, and a few odd spots where it must have gotten beneath his clothes. A streak on his back when he strips out of his shirt. Without a word and with all too much ease, Ptolemy helps him clean it off.

When they're clean enough, they head into their respective pools, voices echoing around the cave, unselfconscious of their nakedness. All of them are covered in the scars from their unique battles on the Path and the vividly colored markings from their mutations. Mydei catches Phainon looking, comparing them perhaps. Hephaestion, the thinnest of them with the fewest markings, Anaxa and Mydei with the most, Peucesta with patterns elegant enough to be called beautiful. Ptolemy with modest markings and modest muscle.

"Where did this come from?" asks Hephaestion, lightly touching Mydei's arm. A glance down, the imprints of Phainon's teeth, yellowed and fading because no matter how hard he'd bitten, Mydei heals fast. A feeling like shame or want or both rips through him.

"That..." Mydei trails off. Phainon hasn't noticed. His gaze is stuck on Peucesta's back before he seems to realize he's staring. "It's nothing. Just forgot to heal it, is all."

Hephaestion looks at him like he sees right through him, nut he doesn't say anything else. "Alright," he says. "Should we sit in the cool one to humor your guests?"

And it isn't that it's cool as Mydei sinks into the spring alongside Phainon, Krateros, and Hephaestion. It's still hot compared to the cold he's gotten used to during their travels, it still soaks into his muscles and joints and soothes his aches, but it could be warmer, could soothe him a little more if it were one of the hotter pools. It isn't worth Phainon's inevitable protests and the fact that he'd probably end up hurting himself out of some misguided competitive spirit.

No, this is fine. Hotter than the baths in Okhema, though without all of the enchantments. He settles in, taking a seat on the ledge they'd carved around the perimeter of each spring for the purpose. Krateros sits on his right, Phainon on his left, Hephaestion next to Phainon.

Chartonus goes straight to the hottest pool; as a mountain dweller, he has the best heat tolerance of any of them. Peucesta and Ptolemy join Anaxa in the second. All of them let out a collective sigh, and it's quiet for the entirety of a minute before conversation starts up again. The pools are close enough that they can all still speak if they raise their voices.

Ptolemy breaks the silence, folding his arms over the edge of the spring. "It's good to be back," he says.

A soft laugh. Peucesta doesn't bother to raise his voice. "You've bathed three times down here already since you showed up."

"Yes, and? It's good to be back. I've got my brothers, friends, a hot bath, a good book, everything I need."

"Just say you come back to Kremnos every year to slack off," Mydei calls to him.

"Hey, now," protests Ptolemy. They grin at each other, and then he sinks back into the spring up to the shoulders. "Besides, looks like we'll be having a pretty busy winter this time around, won't we?"

At Mydei's side, Phainon shifts. Hephaestion, the most attentive of them all, seems to notice too. "You've wanted to prove yourself, right?" he says to Ptolemy. "Well here's our chance. The stuff of legends. We'll make history with this. Real history, good history."

"Maybe the girls won't run next time we come around."

"From you?" Peucesta cuts in, cracking a smile.

"And from me?" Chartonus.

"Not from you," says Hephaestion. "Never from you."

Laughter, water rippling. Phainon stays quiet, but he isn't frowning. Firelight flicks over the water gathered on his clavicle. Mydei wants to say something, but he isn't sure what, so he just bites his tongue.

"You're good men," Krateros tells them. "All of you. You don't get the credit you're due."

"You hear that?" Ptolemy, facing away now, throws his arms over the back of the spring and leans back to look at them upside down. "We're good men, brothers."

Hephaestion gives a cheer. Mydei chuckles. He looks at Phainon, who's kind of smiling, but it seems forced. The words still don't come. It isn't your fault, maybe. You've done exactly the right thing in following me here, maybe. This monster would have come around anyway. Bound to someone else, it would have already killed hundreds more. He says none of it. Just keeps his mouth shut and listens to Ptolemy jump into a story from the summer, something about saving some squires as their knights ran off, something that sounds like it came from one of those books he's so fond of reading.

Still, Phainon notices him staring, holds his gaze long enough to look from one eye to the other and back. The lighting makes his irises stone gray more than blue. Talking, laughter. His gaze flicks, down slightly, up, away. He turns to look at Hephaestion as he speaks. And that odd feeling in Mydei's stomach comes back, the one from when he'd watched Ptolemy wipe a smear of dirt from Phainon's back.

He wants to say something, but there's nothing to say. He stretches his arms back over the edge of the spring, over slick rock, fingers almost skimming Phainon's shoulder—pale and bare, bruising on the back, a thin, silvery scar present that Mydei has never noticed up close—before he realizes what he's doing and has to stop himself, wondering why, why, why?

Look at me, something in him wants to say. He's still staring. He forces himself to turn his attention to Anaxa as he says something, Chartonus as he replies, Peucesta and Ptolemy and Hephaestion, anyone but Phainon, who doesn't speak, who usually speaks so much, who glances at him again.

Mydei's used to the temperature of this bath by now, enough that it doesn't feel so warm anymore. He wants one of the hotter ones. He wants Phainon to stop looking at him. He doesn't want that at all.

"And what about you, Mydei?" Hephaestion asks, head cocked curiously, yellow markings crawling up one side of his torso.
