The bones at the top of his chest are just faintly visible; has he always been so thin? "I know you brought back Lord Krateros here, but did you find the answers you were looking for?"

"I..." He clears his throat so his voice won't come out strangely. "Yes, I did."

There's an expectant silence, everyone's eyes on him.

"You don't have to share if you don't want to," Hephaestion says after it stretches on a little too long. "But... your past..."

Mydei spares a glance at Krateros, who gives him a small, firm nod.

"I know the story," he concedes. "Is now really the time to tell it?"

"We're all here," Anaxa says, his way of saying I won't be later.

A long, slow breath. "Correct me if I get details wrong, Krateros," he says. Their eyes meet. Krateros gives him another nod.

"Just after I was born, a sorcerer foresaw a prophecy that I would grow up to kill my father," he starts. A glance at Phainon, who doesn't know this part, who doesn't know any of it. Mydei hesitates. "King Eurypon." Phainon inhales sharply, but doesn't say anything.

"The prophecy drove him mad," Mydei continues. "He meant to drop me in the river and kill me, so my mother challenged him to a duel to save my life and lost."

"She was poisoned," Krateros adds. "She was your father's equal in everything, but in his madness, he became a coward. So before the set time, he poisoned her wine to make sure she would lose, and then he killed her."

Mydei swallows. Everyone is quiet. It's strange, the way this is his story and the way that it isn't. "Right," he agrees. "Then Eurypon dropped me in the river, where Elder Caenis was waiting below at my mother's behest in case she lost. And then she brought me here."

"She wasn't meant to make you a witcher," Krateros says, and it sounds sad. "She was only meant to take you somewhere you could grow up safe."

"I grew up," Mydei says, unsure what he's feeling, feeling too much at once. "And the prophecy fulfilled itself."

"Mydeimos..."

"I tire of this," he says, and hoists himself out of the pool. "I was a child; the past matters not." More silence. He can feel the eyes on him as he finds a towel to wrap around himself, pausing just long enough to gather his dirty clothes off the ground before he steps out.

No one follows him, thank the Titans. Shame burns his cheeks. As he shuts his eyes, he sees Eurypon's horrified face, feels the way it felt as his chest caved beneath Mydei's spear. He'd been so angry. It's a year old memory but he's still angry, even now. He doesn't regret it. It needed to be done; Eurypon was corrupt and horrible and his people were suffering. He was better off gone, even without Mydei getting his revenge. And yet suddenly he still feels shame.

Is it grief for the versions of his parents he never got to meet? Is it frustration at that prophecy, which never would have come true if it hadn't been told? Is it guilt for something he knows could never be a child's fault? He was just that, a child. All of his earliest memories are filled with nothing but pain, and he knows, even as he feels all of these things, that it wasn't, isn't, can't possibly have been his fault.

Still, still, still. He makes it to his room and shuts the door behind him.

△

An hour or two later, which he spent meticulously cleaning and polishing his armor, there's a knock on his door. A breath. Whatever torrent of emotions he'd been feeling has calmed; now there's only the embarrassment of having stormed out like a child. He opens the door.

"Hi," says Phainon, out of breath. "I asked Hephaestion where your room was; I hope you don't mind."

He's wringing his hands, standing awkwardly. Mydei steps out of the way of the door frame, nods sharply toward the inside of his room when Phainon just stands there staring. "Come in."

"I wasn't sure if you'd rather be left alone." But Phainon steps inside without further delay, and Mydei shuts the door behind him. "I tried out the Pendulum."

"Did you now?"

"Yeah." A laugh. Phainon rubs his chest like it's hurting, and his eyes drift around the room, taking in the furs on the ground, the shelves, the desk covered in Mydei's armor. He'd been curious about where Mydei lived. Now he knows. "Fell off a few times too. You were right about wanting to be rested for that one."

"Are you hurt?"

"No, I..." Phainon's gaze lands on him now, blue as bellflower or a robin's egg. "Peucesta healed me after. He's... pretty nice even though he doesn't talk much."

"Yeah," says Mydei. He's still standing by the door, Phainon right in the middle of the room. He's embarrassed. He wishes he wasn't.

"Look, I—"

"There's no need to dance around it," Mydei cuts Phainon off. He comes to his desk, pretending his gauntlets still need polishing if only so he'll have something to do and an excuse not to look at Phainon. "Ask if you have questions. I'm aware I acted like a child."

"You didn't act like a child," Phainon protests.

"Ask. Before I lose my patience."

"You know, I'd rather hear your answers at a time when you actually want to share them with me." Footsteps muffled on fur rugs. "Obviously I'm curious, but I'm not just going to barge in and ask a whole bunch of personal questions when it's clear you don't want to talk about the subject!" Phainon leans against the side of the desk, frowning, not quite in Mydei's space, but closer than he ought to be. His usual garb is replaced by a white undershirt and a fur-lined coat that isn't his. Mydei eyes the familiar embroidery at the collar, and his stomach twists.

"Peucesta give you that too?" he asks, nodding to it.

Phainon looks down at the coat, reaching a hand up to rub his thumb over the stitched word. Perdikkas, written in the Kremnoan script. "Ah, no, Ptolemy did, after I got all muddy falling off the Pendulum. He said it was extra, is it...?"

"Not mine, no," Mydei says. He looks back down at his gauntlets, clean and shining, and pretends to collect dirt from the cracks with his fingernail and a cloth. "It belonged to another witcher."

"Are they...?"

"He didn't make it back last winter."

"He... Oh." Phainon is quiet for a breath, two. "Were you close?"

"Very."

"I'm sorry."

"Don't be," Mydei tells him, and gives up on pretending to polish his gauntlets, pushing them away. "Every time we set off on the Path, we do so prepared to die."

Phainon doesn't speak, so Mydei lifts his head and meets his eyes and finds him not frowning but sad, quietly sad. "I'm still sorry you had to grieve him," he says.

"HKS," said softly, too softly. Mydei bends to grab his satchel, discarded on the floor. He pulls out his knives and sets to polishing those too.

"What was his name?"

"Perdikkas. He was an expert in medicines and alchemy. He had a potion for anything. That—" He reaches out, grabbing Phainon's collar to touch the embroidery. "—is his name, written in Kremnoan."

He looks up, finds Phainon startled, finds him close, fingers folding into a fist with the strange urge to yank Phainon forward before he lets him go.

"I'll commit it to memory," Phainon says.

"You don't need to do that."

"Still." Now, Phainon falls back a step, two as Mydei gives up on cleaning his blades and shoves them back into their sheathes. Phainon bumps into the bed, glancing at it behind him, startled. "Can I sit?" he asks, gesturing.

"Help yourself."

So Phainon does, settling at the foot of the bed, the old wooden frame creaking and groaning. There's something about the sight of him there on Mydei's red blankets, his presence in the room, his scent in the air. As he settles, something makes him smile.

"What?" Mydei asks.

"Of course your bed would be hard as a rock," Phainon laughs.

Mydei frowns. "It's comfortable."

"News to me." But it can't be too bad, because Phainon leans until his back hit the mattress, arms spread out, though his feet are still on the floor.

"I said you could sit, not lay," Mydei says, and gives in to the urge to get up and sit beside him. He finds Phainon's hair stark against the red of the blanket, tossed back and exposing his forehead. His eyebrows are pale. Mydei already knew this. His eyes are so, so blue.

"So sorry," Phainon says, but makes no move to remedy the problem.

"HKS."

"How did you know that Eurypon was your father?" Phainon asks suddenly.

"I thought you weren't asking about that."

"Well. Don't answer if you don't want to, but I figured that might be a little less personal than some of the other things I want to ask."

Mydei sighs, still looking down, Phainon still looking up, folding an arm behind his neck now, settled in. He smells like sweat and soap. It'll stick to Mydei's sheets. "Elder Caenis—the one who fished me out the river, and one of the ones responsible for making us into witchers—would always call me 'Eurypon's brat,'" he explains. "I didn't realize who she meant for a while, but sometimes Anaxa would have visions before he got a hold of his power as a Source. He'd see parts of my past, or the prophecy, and he'd call me a 'child of Destiny' before passing out. It took a long time to piece together what any of it meant."

"Wow," Phainon whispers. He's staring, still looking up, laying in Mydei's bed. "I had hoped you had at least a few years of a normal childhood."

Mydei stares back, thinks of Phainon's quiet sadness by a campfire, tracing his fingers over a his creased deliverer card and missing his home more than anything. His voice, sad and proud and full of longing all at once as he says, Aedes Elysiae.

"Better I didn't," Mydei decides. "This way there's nothing to miss."

Phainon's gaze dips down to Mydei's shoulder, his arm band, his elbow. "And what about the childhood you could have had. Your mother who loved you. You father before he was driven mad. The chance at being a prince. Don't you miss that?"

There's this ache in his chest. Guilt he has no business carrying, grief for people he'd never met, that same feeling that colors Phainon's voice when he speaks of his hometown. "You can't miss what you never had," Mydei says.

Slow, Phainon pushes himself back up. Their shoulders almost brush. His smell is soft and muted from emotion. "Maybe there's a different word for that feeling," he says, quiet, kind of wistful. He's staring into his lap, and Mydei both misses his eyes and doesn't. "Can I hold your hand?"

He still doesn't look. There's just the side of his face, the shadow beneath his jaw, the slope of his nose, the two straps of his choker split against the side of his throat. "Why?" Mydei asks.

"I don't know," Phainon admits. "I just want to."

That ache in his chest. Mydei holds his hand out, hovering over Phainon's thigh, so little space between them. Phainon's folds around it, cold-fingered and callused. He pulls their hands into his lap, and now, their shoulders do press. Mydei's heart beats.

"You don't need to comfort me," he says. "If that's what this is."

Phainon still doesn't look at him as he laughs so softly it barely counts. "You know, I wish I could say that's what this was, but I think I..." He trails off. His throat bobs as he swallows. He squeezes Mydei's hand.

"You...?"

"I don't know," Phainon says again. Again, a pause before the real answer, "I just want to."

"Alright," Mydei says, and squeezes back. When he looks, he catches the faintest hint of a smile, and tries not to think about what it might mean.

△

He can't sleep. That night he lays in his bed, a fire low and crackling in the his hearth, and he can't sleep. Kremnos had come to a stop in the morning, so the halls don't groan and he can't feel the faint sway of motion under his feet. It's dreadfully quiet. He can still smell Phainon on his blanket.

Rather than lay there restless for an age, Mydei gets up. His room is warm enough with the fire, but it'll be cold in the halls, so he throws on his cloak and shoves his feet into his boots before resigning himself to a walk.

It's dark in the halls; the torches stay lit always, but without the tall windows providing daylight, they're dim by comparison.

His footsteps echo. He passes room after room that used to belong to one of his brothers or sisters. But year after year, fewer of them come back until now they've dwindled to less than a dozen, more and more rooms falling into disrepair, being left empty.

It's better this way. Better that their breed dies out. There will always be monsters, but there will never be a good enough reason to do to more children what was done to them.

He's struck with the memory of Phainon's hand in his, but he shakes it off, keeps walking, and eventually finds himself in front of Phainon's door. He stands there, quiet, knowing he must be behind there, hopefully asleep, breathing softly and curled up with all the blankets tucked tight around him. The image is enough. Mydei continues on.

It's good being home again, seeing his family, feeling Castrum Kremnos' welcome. It's good, even if these halls feel so empty.

He walks for what must be a long time. It's late enough that he can't tell the time, and when he steps out into the courtyard, he finds it snowing again, enough already piled up to reach his ankles, thick flakes caught by biting wind. He watches for a while. The snow and the chill makes him think this might be Aidonia. The taste in the air is the same. The cold starts to bite through his clothes, but still he stays, thinking to tire himself out enough to sleep.

But then one of the doors on the other side of the courtyard opens halfway, and a cloaked body slips through, pushing it shut behind them. They're covered in snow, hood drawn over their head, cloak and skirts billowing in the wind. One hand holds tight to the strap of a bag on their shoulder, the other comes up to keep their hood from blowing off.

"Castorice," Mydei calls to her. She hears him, and she looks up, half the courtyard away. Her hood flies off, and her twin pigtails whip through the air with a gust. She jogs over, and he shoves one of the heavy main doors open so they can get out of the cold.

"Thank you," she says, panting when they're inside, untying her cloak to shake out the snow. The wind whistles shrilly through the opening as Mydei pushes the door closed. She's flushed and windblown, shoes and leggings caked in snow that she tries to stomp off before giving up and wiping it off with her hands. 

"It's late," she adds as she straightens up, adjusting the straps of her pack, folding her cloak over her elbow. "I wasn't thinking anyone would be awake."

"Couldn't sleep," Mydei explains. He takes her pack from her before she can protest. "Are you hurt anywhere?"

Sometimes they come back injured. There was one year when Ptolemy had been attacked by titankin on his way to Kremnos. He'd arrived bloodied and exhausted and needed to be patched up and helped to his room, but he'd otherwise been alright. Aidonia isn't known for the kindness of its nature, with cruel weather and wildlife both. Luckily, Castorice only smiles and shakes her head.

"No," she says, smoothing her hair down with gloved hands. "Just tired. I'm surprised you got here before I did."

"Due to some complications," Mydei tells her. "I brought friends, but let's not worry about that for now. Everyone's already here, but for you and Leonnius. He left for Aidonia, did he not? Have you heard word from him?"

With that, Castorice exhales. "He's not—" She pulls her bag back from him, opening one of the pockets and producing a bracelet made from braided cord, a wolf's canine tooth and a piece of amber attached. Leonnius'. "One of the villages I passed by..." She squeezes her eyes shut, brows furrowing together, voice barely steady. "There was a three month snowstorm the moment summer was over. There was an infestation, monsters trying to get away from the cold. The villagers said Leonnius tried to handle it, but there were just too many, and I got there too late, and..." She cuts off as her voice wobbles. A heavy feeling settles in the pit of Mydei's stomach.

He takes Castorice's cloak and wraps it back around her, covering the skin of her arms and shoulders left exposed by her dress. Pulling up the hood to cover her face and neck, he wraps his arms around her tight.

"It's alright," he says. She drops her bag to the floor. "You made it back. That's what matters."

"I wrapped him in red and gave him a warrior's burial," she says with a sound not unlike a sob. Her fingers twist tight in his cloak.

"Thank you," he says. Perdikkas hadn't gotten as much. There wasn't a body for them to bury. "You did well."

She lets out a shuddering breath and pulls back. "I'm sorry," she says. "Thank you, I... It's good to see you, at least." She wipes her eyes with the backs of her hands, sniffs. Again, "Sorry, I just..."

"Don't be," Mydei tells her, and tries to fight off that heavy, pressing feeling. "Get some rest, for now. We can talk about everything in the morning."

Chapter End Notes

lore concoction volume 6: If you've ever spent time in the Witcher fandom, you've absolutely seen the Kaer Morhen fanon hot springs, which even have their own tag on ao3. They aren't canon but we've all collectively decided that the witchers deserve some nice springs after all their suffering, and considering the fact that Kaer Morhen in the winter is absolutely frigid. That extends here :)

Destiny is a mysterious force binding people together and a huge theme in the Witcher. It isn't too important here, but what is a Witcher au without a little bit a Destiny?

chapters.title: Chapter 13
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Castorice, apparently the last of the witchers to join them, is another Phainon has heard tale of before. Where Mydei's notoriety lies in the killing of King Eurypon and his tendency to survive things he absolutely should not, Castorice has a somewhat different reputation.

They call her the Servant of Death, and in the stories she is as ruthless as she is beautiful. Now though, she sits with the rest of them at breakfast—which Phainon is late to—and she seems perfectly friendly.

Her hair is the color of lilacs, kept in tails as long as Phainon has ever seen hair on a person. She wears a white dress adorned with ribbons and floral decals, gloves that reach past her elbows, and white fleece leggings to combat the cold. Her markings, visible where her dress leaves her shoulders and the top of her chest exposed, are pale, patterned like the bones beneath her skin.

"It's lovely to meet you," Phainon says, extending a hand toward her to shake in greeting.

Mydei blocks his arm and pulls him back down into his seat. "Don't."

"Ah... alright?"

"It's no offense to you, Lord Phainon," Castorice tells him, smiling politely. "One of my mutations has made my skin toxic to the touch. Luckily it doesn't linger long on surfaces, but it generally isn't safe to touch me. You'd fall asleep, and if left in contact with me long enough, you'd, well..."

"Oh," Phainon says, and notes the way she sits like she needs to make herself small. His only thought is for what a lonely affliction that must be. "I'm sorry."

"Don't be," she tells him, and her smile is equal parts soft and sad. "It's gotten me out of more than a few scrapes."

"I can imagine." The table is quiet then, everyone just eating in silence, and it feels odd compared to the lively atmosphere of the night before. Phainon wonders if he'd missed or interrupted something, but he can't find it in himself to push past the lump in his throat and ask.

"I've been informed of your predicament," Castorice says after a while. "You're very brave, to come here and train. I can't imagine most people in your situation doing anything but giving in to the terror or trying to flee."

Everyone keeps saying that, but he doesn't feel like it's true. "Anyone would want vengeance," he says. His hand curls into a fist beneath the table, but he keeps his voice level. "I just want to make sure no one else gets hurt, and this seems to be the best place to make sure of that."

"You're right," Castorice says, gently still. Her fingers are slender on her spoon. "Of course, you're right. Just know you have my support as well. All of us... we were made for exactly this sort of thing. We won't allow the Flame Reaver to run free."

"Thank you," Phainon says, swallowing. He looks at her, then each of them in turn. Hephaestion, Ptolemy, Peucesta, Chartonus, Krateros. Anaxagoras, had he chosen to join them. At his side, Mydei. "All of you. I mean it. Even if it's your job, you're still risking yourselves and your home. And I imagine you look forward to the winter for your chance to rest, but now you're spending your time training me and worrying about this monster of legends."

"You'd be surprised by how little resting gets done," Ptolemy cuts in, offering a weak smile. "We run ourselves ragged training every winter. Now, we get to run you ragged and rest a little ourselves. It's not so bad, really."

Phainon gives a grateful laugh. "Still," he says, and finds Mydei's eyes on him. "Thank you."

△

He jumps straight into training when breakfast is through. He spars with Ptolemy, who has a wealth of strange tips and knowledge that he's more than willing to share. Castorice coaches him on fighting against someone wielding basic magic. Krateros is a strict teacher when it comes to swordplay. Hephaestion shows him the safest ways to fall and how to redirect the force of blows he can't avoid. Peucesta spots him on the Pendulum, where he dances between swinging logs on a thin beam, fighting off an imaginary opponent and taking more than a few falls.

Mydei, notably, is absent. Phainon takes a rest after a late lunch, sore and exhausted and yet still with this restless energy in him. He wants to push, to keep training, but at the end of it, he does understand that his body has limits. He does know that overworking himself will do more harm than good.

He finds Ptolemy in the library, sitting alone at one of the tables with a lamp and a large tome spread open in front of him. It isn't quite dark out yet, but the windows here are few, lest the sun damage the books.

"Hi," says Phainon, unsure if he'd been heard as he came in. Ptolemy holds up a finger, continuing to read for the awkward space of a minute before he turns the page and looks up.

"Phainon," he greets. "Hello."

"I'm guessing it's a terribly good book you're reading," Phainon says, coming all the way inside and letting the door shut behind him. The tome really is huge, all tall as his arm from elbow to fingertips and thick enough that he doesn't think he could hold it with one hand.

"Yes," Ptolemy agrees. He pushes out the chair next to him so Phainon can sit too. "One you might be interested in, actually. I'm reading up on Reavers."

"You have texts on that? No, of course you have texts on that; you're witchers," Phainon says, scooting the chair a bit closer so he can see. Ptolemy flips back two pages to the start of the section.

"This is our compendium of monsters," he explains. He points at a heading close to the base of the page on the right. "The section on Reavers starts here; I'm sure you'll find it informative."

"Yes, absolutely," Phainon says. There's an awkward pause as he stares at the glyphs on the page. "Only... one problem. I can't read Kremnoan."

Another awkward silence. "Ah." Ptolemy shuts the book. "Well, that's no problem. We've a translation somewhere. It's only a matter of finding it."

So they look for the translation, Phainon running his finger along spine after spine written in Kremnoan, some in common, some in what he thinks might be arcane scripts. In the end, Ptolemy is the one to find it, pulling another larger than life tome off one of the shelves on the opposite side of the library. They return to the table. Ptolemy opens the cover, flips a few pages for the table of contents, and skims until he finds the right section.

"One thousand seventy-two," he says, flipping a massive chunk of pages to find it. "Just a few more, and... Here." He pushes the book toward Phainon, who pulls it closer, mindful of the age of the weathered pages. Reavers, written in bold toward the bottom of the page. He takes a breath, checks to find the section spans five pages, and begins to read.

It takes him a long time, considering the size of the pages and the fact that he keeps stopping and starting sections over again, reading and rereading to commit things to memory. It tells the story of the only confirmed Reaver in history; the Water Reaver, since the man it was tied to was a sailor, and drowning its preferred method of killing. The Reaver found him on a six-month voyage, and when the ship was far out at sea, his crew got sick, the weather grew bad, monsters attacked and damaged the ship. They asked passing vessels for help, only to watch them capsize and everyone on board drown. The crew got sicker and sicker, circumstances got worse and worse, the sailor grew mad with fear.

Phainon feels sick as he reads. All that over the course of two months. Thirteen ships destroyed, hundreds of men dead. All that, and the sailor made it to shore alive, the Reaver growing stronger and stronger all the while. Two villages were flooded, everyone drowned or killed directly by its hand, but still the sailor survived. He made it almost to a major city before the terror killed him and the Reaver, let off its leash and made powerful by his fear, killed everyone and everything in the vicinity until it ran out of energy and died.

"So that's what would happen," Phainon breaths as he finishes the section. He has to pause and look up, sick to his stomach.

"Pretty gruesome," Ptolemy agrees. Phainon squeezes his eyes shut, takes a long breath, and continues on.

The next section details the origin of a Reaver. If a woman actively in labor dies surrounded by bloodshed, and the baby survives just long enough to see it and die slowly, deprived of milk and their mother's embrace, their spirit might turn into a Reaver, tied tightly to the soul of a happier child born at the exact moment they died, and then they'll spend their growing years searching for that child and devouring every scrap of their fear. Every scare from an unexpected spider or tripping on a root adds up and strengthens the monster-child's spirit, until eventually it's strong enough to become the cause of that fear.

"If there's only been one other, how do you know this?" Phainon asks, disturbed and slightly skeptical.

"There are ways to trace a spirit back to its origins," Ptolemy explains. "The remains of that Reaver were found by the witcher Seliose, who had strong spiritual familiars by her side. They were able to investigate and trace its spirit back to Styxia, where there was a war at the time of the sailor's birth, and— did you even read the footnotes?"

"Ah," says Phainon, finding all of the same information written out in tiny print at the bottom of the page. "No, I did not."

He continues on, finding more and more information. It is thought that Reavers only act with intention to directly devastate the one to which they're bound. Reavers cannot eat or gain energy from any source aside from their host's fear. Only after the host is consumed does the Reaver go on a true rampage, destroying everyone and everything within range. Days after, it will die.

Phainon wondered, though he hadn't dared to ask whether letting him die could stop the Reaver from harming anyone else. There's a faint, guilty feeling of relief at the knowledge that it isn't a viable solution.

"Thank you for showing me this," he says as he finishes the section, rereading the last paragraph three or more times. "It answered a lot of my questions."

"Good," Ptolemy says, smiling faintly. "I think there's more somewhere; I can look for a few other books if you'd like."

"No," Phainon tells him, trying to laugh through the sick feeling still sticking to his stomach. "No, thank you, this is enough. I think I've read as much as I can stomach about this for tonight." Don't be afraid, he tells himself. Don't make it stronger. It's a task easier said than done.

"Fair enough," Ptolemy says. He reaches for Phainon's shoulder after a moment, squeezing. "And Phainon?"

"Yeah?"

"You're doing well. With both your training and with how you're handling the situation. You can trust us, you know? There's no monster the group of us can't beat."

"I know," Phainon says, and tries not to think about the dozens of times he's dreamed or imagined all of them dead or dying because of him. They can't, they won't. Phainon hasn't been afraid of the Flame Reaver for long. It'll still be weak, and every day he grows stronger. "I believe it."

△

The restless feeling doesn't leave, even a day later. Before sundown, he enlists Peucesta's help in running the obstacle course set up around Castrum Kremnos. They call it the Killer, and for good reason. There's climbing and jumping and crawling and a number of things Phainon is not agile or strong enough to do after a full day of other forms of training.

His muscles protest pulling up his body weight, his feet ache from the running, and even with Hephaestion's training, climbing walls just to jump right off of them and take off running is no easy task. Less so when said walls are covered in a thick layer of snow. It takes him an hour to manage the first section with some fluidity after trying and retrying again, though he's far from fast, and he ends panting and covered once more in mud. Peucesta informs him that he only made it about a fifth of the way, and he's just exhausted enough to take that as a sign to stop.

He's voracious at dinner, thanking Chartonus profusely and too busy eating to join the conversation at the table. Mydei, is elsewhere, has been elsewhere for a couple of days now, but Castrum Kremnos is no small place, so Phainon tries to think little of it.

After dinner, he goes straight for the hot springs, washing himself first and submerging in delightfully hot water. It hurts at first; he's still half frozen from his time outside. His fingers and toes feel like they've caught fire, but it's good. He sinks in fully, letting out a pained sound as he adjusts, and realizes he isn't alone.

"You seem comfortable," jokes Hephaestion from the second bath, his arms folded over the edge of the spring. His hair is wet, long and stringy with water, pushed out of his face. He looks as tired as Phainon feels.

"I will be," Phainon tells him. "Just give it a moment."

A slight smile. "I hear you—" Hephaestion cuts off with a cough, deep in his chest. It leaves his arm splattered with gold, but he only reaches for a rag and wipes it and his mouth clean. "I hear you tried out the Killer. What did you think?"

"You're hurt," Phainon says, wet hands on the stone, ready to push himself out of the spring to help. Hephaestion holds up a hand.

"Sick," he corrects. "I have been for a long time. Went through one too many mutations; I'm lucky I survived this long."

Phainon pauses, then settles back into the water. "You coughed up blood," he says. "That can't be normal."

A sigh. Hephaestion sinks a little deeper. "No," he admits. "It's getting worse recently, but there's nothing that can be done, so there's no point in worrying about it. Don't tell the others, if you would. We've just lost Leonnius; it wouldn't be fair to burden them with this too."

"You— Leonnius?" The somberness at meals, the quiet, the way they've all been a little bit more subdued the past couple of days. The way Mydei— Mydei. Castorice must have come bearing bad news.

"You weren't there, that's right." Hephaestion shuts his eyes, rests his head on his folded arms. Tired, so tired. He coughs again, though there's no blood. "He was another of our brothers. Castorice came across his remains in Aidonia."

"I'm... I'm so sorry."

"Part of the job," Hephaestion says, eyes still shut. "We're all ready for it. He died a hero."

But will anyone but them have seen him that way? Phainon bites his tongue, feels this fragile, secondhand grief. "I'm sorry," he says again. "There are already so few of you left."

"It's a good thing," Hephaestion tells him. "May there never be more. Will you keep my secret?"

"I..." He doesn't know what to think. None of this feels fair. "I won't lie if someone asks," he says, "but I won't bring it up, alright?"

"I'll take it," Hephaestion breathes. His voice is rough. He turns so his forehead is on his arms, head down. "Where are you from, Phainon?"

"A farming village on the coast," Phainon answers. "It was called Aedes Elysiae."

"Aedes Elysiae," Hephaestion repeats. He might be smiling. Phainon can't tell. "You're a good man, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae."

△

He sleeps easily, if only because of how much he'd worn himself out training. He pulls his curtains shut and all but falls into bed, and then he's out like a light. He dreams of the Killer, of running it and falling, muscles gummy, moving as if through liquid, and then the images shift to swordplay, Krateros' voice, echoing and disapproving. Phainon as a small child, a stick in his hands, his best friend laughing and joining him with one of her own.

"You're going to be a hero," she tells him. "I just know it."

And then he's older, and she's still a child, and then she's gone and the dream shifts into something else. Sunlight, burning red though his eyelids, too bright, too blinding. A warm hand brushing the hair out of his face.

"Wake up," Mydei says in the dream. There's a dip in the bed at Phainon's side, gold eyes, red, so much red, a glint of something reflective at the end of a braided bit of hair. "You've slept long enough."

Maybe he says something in reply. He doesn't remember as the dream shifts into something else. An exhale, a sigh, a handful of words through syrup. He sleeps and he sleeps, and when he finally wakes up, it's too bright in his room. He squints out the window and finds the sky blindingly white, a thin dusting of snow falling. He stretches his hands out to the cold parts of the sheets and shuts his eyes.

It's warm. He counts down from ten, and then he pushes himself upright, if only because he's hungry.

As he dresses, he considers the window again. The open curtains he was so sure he closed. He heads down for breakfast.

△

"Is it my turn to train you, then?" One pale, considering eye. Anaxagoras labors over a double boiler, something thick and sludgy cooking in a tiny glass bowl.

Finding himself here is something between an accident and dangerous curiosity. Ever since that first day, Phainon has been intimidated and intrigued. The feeling of being frozen in place haunts him. Anaxagoras's voice calling him someone strong, saying, perhaps you will gain what it takes to survive your fate.

"I want to know what you saw," Phainon says, trying to stand tall.

Anaxagoras hums, returning to his work as Phainon comes closer. He adds some kind of powder to the concoction, then mixes it with a silver spoon. "This," he says, "is perhaps the one instance in which knowledge will do you more harm than good. Live your life, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, and you'll learn your truths. You will not hear them from me."

"You said I could survive," Phainon says. "I need to know how."

Anaxagoras's gaze returns to him, if only briefly. He produces a glass jar from a drawer and lays a segment of cheesecloth over it. "So train as you have been," he says, and extinguishes the fire with a wave of his hand. "Prepare yourself, so that when the Flame Reaver comes, you are strong."

Phainon exhales, long and slow. "Please," he tries.

"I would teach you magic, if you had the affinity," Anaxagoras tells him, lifting the glass bowl from the double boiler with a pair of tongs and pouring the contents over the cheese cloth. The liquid that strains out is strangely, vividly gold. "As it stands, there's little I can do to help."

His hands curl into fists behind the table where Anaxagoras can't see them. "And is there no chance that such an affinity could be hidden?"

Anaxagoras's gaze lifts from where he's watching the gold liquid drip into the jar. His eye, cold as ice, studies Phainon. "Would you permit me to check?"

The attention makes him nervous, but he wants—needs—something from this. "Would it harm me in some way?" he asks.

"No," is the reply. Anaxagoras pushes his implements aside, careful with the jar. "Come closer, if you wish for me to look."

Swallowing thickly, Phainon wipes his palms on his pants and complies. He makes his way around the table and comes to stand before the Source turned witcher, shorter and slighter than him but with a hundred times the power. Anaxagoras grabs him by the chin, cold-fingered, rings digging into bone, and peels off his eye patch with his other hand.

Phainon's intake of breath is sharp, his flinch is instinctual, but Anaxagoras keeps him firmly in place, looking at him, through him, into him with this eye that isn't an eye, cracked and haunting and otherworldly, blue and gold and a galaxy or the depths of the sea. There's no pupil, no iris, just this swirling void, and Phainon can't look away, even as this terror grips the base of his spine. He's frozen in place as Anaxagoras probes for something. Magic, like he'd promised. Phainon's very soul, turned inside out and inspected.

"You trust too easily," Anaxagoras tells him. His grip grows tighter, but it doesn't hurt. Nothing hurts, but the sensation has his skin, his insides crawling. He shrinks away from it, tries to peel his mind away from the feeling. "Naive, yet filled with so much rage. Too preoccupied to feel fear, is that it? No. No, there's something else."

He can't pull away, so instead he pushes back, fighting against it, whatever the feeling is, fighting for control of his body, but he's stuck on Anaxagoras's eye, his lack of an eye, his horrible simulacrum of it, but he can't, he's frozen and he's powerless and he—

He wrenches away, gasping, stumbling a step back, squeezing his eyes shut. "What— What was that? What were you doing—"

"Interesting," says Anaxagoras, and when Phainon gets a hold of himself enough to risk another look, he's replaced his eye patch and returned his attention to his little glass jar, the cheesecloth still dripping golden fluid. "That's twice now that you've almost managed to fight me off."

"Why?" Phainon asks, taking another step back, two, his mind still cringing and violated. "In what way was that checking my affinity?"

"A means to an end," Anaxagoras says, strange and cryptic. "I'm afraid you yourself aren't capable of any spells, but you're remarkably resistant to them."

"I— What?"

"I've done as asked," Anaxagoras tells him, raising an eyebrow. "No affinity, high resistance. It seems there are things I can help you with after all. With guidance, you should be able to shrug off the influence of most charms. Bring that cooler here, would you?" He gestures at an icebox and the far counter. Phainon, confused and helpless, grabs it and brings it over, setting it in the cleared bit of space Anaxagoras prepares.

"I don't understand," he says, watching Anaxagoras remove the lid and take a rack of vials out from the snow packed inside.

Anaxagoras sighs. "You fought back when I was poking around your head just now," he says. "And had I not pulled back, you may well have eventually succeeded in pushing me out. It was the same when we met and I used Oronyx's power to freeze you in place."

"And you can train me," Phainon says slowly. "So I can do those things in the future? Against the Flame Reaver?"

"Perhaps." Anaxagoras takes one of the vials from the rack; there are only two, both gold like the liquid draining into the jar now, though in slightly different shades. He compares them, frowning and humming to himself.

Phainon rubs his hands on his pants again, trying to shake off the lingering strangeness in his skin. It felt— Whatever that was, whatever Anaxagoras did, it felt like the Flame Reaver's curse. Something in his head, poking around and settling where it shouldn't. He tries to relax. "But you're willing to try?" he asks. "Please, Anaxagoras."

"Sure," is the reply. "I have the most free time in the evening. Don't come by earlier, unless you'd like to help in my lab. There are syringes in a box in that cabinet. Bring one, if you would."

Quietly, tongue thick in his mouth, Phainon gets a syringe, holding it gingerly and passing it over. Anaxagoras returns the vial in his hand to the rack, taking the other instead, the brighter gold of the two. He removes the cap on the syringe and pokes it into the vial, drawing the liquid up into it.

"If I may ask," Phainon starts, hesitating, "what is that?"

"The solution to a problem," Anaxagoras says. "Presumably." When the vial is empty, he frees the syringe and turns it upside down, pressing lightly on the stopper to expel the air bubble that floats up. At Phainon's helpless stare, he sighs.

"Mutagens," he says. "This one comes from a remnant of the Titan Cerces."

"You— That's— You're serious?"

Anaxagoras sets the syringe down and reaches for the jar, discarding the cheese cloth and poring the contents into an empty vial from the rack. "Yes," he says simply, stoppering the new vial and placing it on the rack.

Phainon knows little of the making of witchers, but somehow he doesn't think they're made with the remains of titans. "Right," he tries. "And what do you intend to do with it?"

"Become a god," is the answer. Anaxagoras replaces the rack into the icebox and closes it. "Eventually, anyway." Phainon isn't certain if he means it in jest or not.

"...I see."

"I will be indisposed for a time," Anaxagoras says, taking up the syringe. "Then, with this divine power, I will reforge the holes in Kremnos' wards, and then we can begin your training." He extends an arm in front of him, aligning the needle with a vein at the center of the arcane markings on the inside of his forearm.

"Wait," Phainon says. "What do you mean by holes in the wards, there can't—"

Anaxagoras plunges the needle into his arm and drains the contents of the syringe into himself with hardly a wince. He inhales as he pulls the needle out, letting it clatter onto the counter, eye squeezing shut as he braces against the edge. Phainon is stunned into silence.

"Yes," Anaxagoras breathes. He folds over himself, shaking. "Yes, this will do."

"Are you... alright?" Phainon asks him, taking a step closer only to hesitate, unsure.

"Leave me, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae," Anaxagoras tells him. "Your training will begin once the wards are repaired."

"I—"

"Leave me."

Phainon swallows, unease only growing, but he leaves as asked.

△

"Holes in the wards," Phainon says. "What does he mean, holes in the wards? Is it wear and tear because the place is old, or do we need to be worried about the Flame Reaver showing up?"

He couldn't find Mydei, can never seem to find Mydei these days, so he settles for the next best thing: Peucesta, blinking up at him from his seat beside the fire, fingers poised to pluck at his lyre. "Did you meet with Anaxa?" he asks.

"I did, yes," Phainon says. "And he looked at me with his creepy eye under the patch, told me there are holes in the wards, and then injected himself with some solution he made from a piece of Cerces, and then he kicked me out after explaining absolutely nothing." He swallows, finding himself out of breath.

Peucesta only sighs and sets his lyre aside. "That certainly sounds like something he would do."

Still no answers. "Well, yes, because he did do it. Now, do you have an idea what any of that means?"

"Kremnos is old," Peucesta says calmly. He has a soft, soothing voice, when he deigns to speak. "It's only natural that it protections would wear thin over time, like the threads in a well-loved shirt."

Phainon hesitates, studying him for a moment. He finds nothing but smooth, shiny hair, ocean-blue markings, and a calm, unworried gaze. Gradually, he calms down. "I suppose that makes sense," he says slowly. "Even so, worn out wards are a vulnerability; is everyone aware?"

"Everyone is aware," Peucesta confirms. "A plan is in place." Still so calm. Phainon nods, letting his worries out with his next exhale.

"Alright," he says. "Alright, good. I guess there's no need to panic then. Sorry about that. Anaxagoras gave me a bit of a scare. That... thing he injected. He said it was a mutagen, and he said he'd be indisposed for a while. Is he...?"

"Anaxagoras makes more mutagens every winter," Peucesta explains. "While we train on the Pendulum and the Killer and spar, this is his chosen method of strengthening himself."

"It just seems..." The way he had to support himself on the table after the injection, the obvious pain in his voice as he'd told Phainon to get out. Mydei described the process of being made a witcher as the most painful thing he'd ever experienced. For Anaxagoras to put himself through that routinely...

He shakes his head. "Nevermind," he says. "I understand. Thank you. I'll. Um."

Peucesta takes pity and takes up his lyre again. "Would you care to hear a song?" he asks.

"I... Yes, please," Phainon says, sinking down into a seat beside the fire. "That sounds lovely, if you don't mind me listening."

"Not at all," says Peucesta gently, and then he begins to play.

△

"You know, I've almost missed you the past couple of days." Here's Mydei in the hallway after dinner, Phainon tailing him like a dog or a duckling, making sure his too sincere words sound like they're in jest. "It seems like you're anywhere, so long as I'm not."

Mydei's head cocks slightly. His throat bobs as he swallows. "You're busy with your training," he says, "I have my own things. I'm not avoiding you, if that's what you're insinuating."

"It isn't," Phainon says, and feels this sticky, embarrassed regret. "I only meant... we haven't sparred in a while. Everyone here has been teaching me quite a lot, and I'd like to test that new knowledge and strength against yours."

A considering him. Mydei returns to walking, Phainon returns to following him. His steps are surprisingly soft without the armor he must've taken off for a bath. His hair had been wet at dinner, though it's dry now.

"Tomorrow," Mydei says after a bit. "I will see your strength only after it's recovered; you're limping."

"I'm not..." Phainon starts, but cuts himself off. He is, actually. He'd been running the Killer for the better part of the evening, and his legs have turned to jelly. "Well, alright. I suppose that's agreeable."

Mydei's door is right up ahead. The conversation tapers into a natural end as they approach, and Phainon supposes this is over. A lump in his throat. An odd feeling like missing someone even though they're right there. They've spent nonstop weeks in each other's company; the least Phainon can do is respect Mydei's space now, but—

Mydei pushes his door open, pauses. Phainon stares at the back of his robes, the unruly way his hair has dried, and waits for a goodbye. But Mydei only pushes the door open and turns his head, looking at Phainon expectantly.

"Oh," says Phainon. "An invitation?"

"You're acting like a kicked dog," Mydei says, and steps inside and out of the way of the door. "Come in."

"I'm just..." He can't come up with an explanation. He's tired, there's a lot on his mind. Maybe Mydei is just the most familiar thing here, and that's why he wants to see him. Maybe... Titans, he knows himself better than that. It's just... Mydei. He's Mydei, and that's why Phainon wants to see him.

"Or stay out there, it doesn't matter to me," Mydei says when he lingers a breath too long. He starts to close the door, but Phainon catches the edge and keeps it from closing.

"Wait," he says, and his voice comes out breathy. "I'm coming, I'm coming."

Silently, Mydei steps back. Phainon comes inside, shuts the door behind him.

It smells like armor polish, all of Mydei's pieces stacked on the top of the dresser and the desk, gleaming in the lantern light. Phainon removes his shoes so he won't track dirt over the furs on the floor as Mydei goes to the hearth to start a fire. It's cold in here, like everywhere else. Phainon is used to it by now. Part of him feels guilty for it, but he still wears Perdikkas' coat.

"I talked with Ptolemy," he says as Mydei kneels and stacks logs in the fireplace. "He showed me your monster compendium so I could read up on Reavers. But also, he mentioned... Leonnius." He watches Mydei pauses, head lifting, though he doesn't turn to look. "I wanted to offer my condolences."

"Received," Mydei says, and reaches for another log.

"Would you tell me about him?" Phainon tries. He's still standing and it feels strange, so he sits slowly at the foot of the bed, trying to keep it from creaking. "Perdikkas had his potions and medicines. What about Leonnius?"

"He was the swiftest runner of any of us. He was the first to offer help to someone who needed it. He was kind."

Phainon waits, but Mydei seems unwilling to share more as he lights the fire and stands, brushing the grit left on his hands by the wood on his pants. Phainon watches his broad back. "I'll commit that to memory too," he says.

"Why?"

"I don't know," Phainon admits. Mydei turns to face him now, so Phainon looks him in the eyes as he says, "I want to. It feels right."

A soft sound, something between a scoff and a laugh. Mydei takes something from his desk, a cloth bag that he opens and takes something out of. He tosses it to Phainon, who catches it out of the air, round and shining and blood red like a gemstone. It's slightly tacky to the touch. When he looks up, Mydei takes a second one from the bag and puts it in his mouth. "Pomegranate candy," he says. "Give it back if you don't want it."

"Candy," Phainon says in wonder. Pure sugar, melted and flavored and cooled. He hasn't had candy since he was a child. He places this on his tongue, finding it sweeter than anything and carrying a rich, fruity flavor. He's never had a pomegranate before, but he thinks he'd like them, if they tasted like this. "Thank you," he says, pressing the candy into his cheek.

Mydei only grunts as he does and closes the bag up. "There are more, if you like them," he says. "Chartonus makes them."

Phainon falls back on the bed and shuts his eyes and gets this memory imprinted on the backs of his eyelids. Mydei's hand in his. Comfortable silence, body heat between them. "I'm glad I met you, Mydei," he confesses, folding an arm behind his head.

"You'd probably be dead if you hadn't."

Phainon opens his eyes to see the ceiling. The cracks feel familiar, the popping of the fire, the smell of armor polish, it's all a new kind of familiar. The closest he's had to a home in a long time. A smile pulls at his mouth. "And you'd be so very lonely, wouldn't you?"

The mattress dips as Mydei sits beside him. An extra blanket is thrown over Phainon's lap. With the fire going, he hadn't realized he was still cold.

"Sure," Mydei says, not caring to fight just this once.

"Everyone here, I..." Phainon trails off, turns his head so he can see Mydei looking down at him, as softly as his face is capable of, the little braid in his hair dangling. Deja vu, familiarity. He hopes, strangely, that they can make a routine of this. "Again, I know it's your job and the Imperator is paying you more than handsomely, but thank you. More than anything, I'm grateful."

"Again with this," Mydei sighs.

The last of the candy disappears on his tongue. "I'll admit," he starts. "I'm training and I'm getting stronger and I'm still so angry, but underneath it all, even though I know it's only making things worse, I'm still scared."

Quiet. He holds Mydei's gaze and twists his fingers tight in his own hair, feeling too many things at once.

A hand folds over his own on the bed, warm, Mydei is always warm where Phainon is so, so cold. He dips his gaze to look, to see their hands together, his own turning palm up, Mydei's fingers slotting with his easily, like they've done this more than just once, like helping each other up after spars and brushing fingers as they pass things to each other counts. Familiar. This touch, the red of Mydei's robes and blankets, the roughness of his voice, even as he speaks softly, "There can be no courage without fear."

"I know," Phainon tries. He's still looking, still caught on the way they fit together, running his thumb over Mydei's. "Thank you."

Finally, he meets Mydei's eyes, finds him close and looking right back, and— would it be fair to call him beautiful? He'd probably hate the word, hate the implication of it from Phainon's mouth. Wouldn't he? Would he?

"Don't thank me."

Phainon wants the word for this feeling, whatever it is. He's still looking, still staring. He can't bring himself to look away. "I'm not allowed to be grateful either, then?"

"I don't care for debts, between us," Mydei says. It plays back in Phainon's head, between us, between us, between us. "if you're truly grateful, then survive. Prove to me that I made the right choice, betting on you."

Faint, curling pleasure. "You've been betting on me?"

A raised brow. Mydei's free hand comes to brush a stand of hair from Phainon's eye. "Since that day you ran after my horse," he says, and the memory is from an age ago and yesterday at once, "what do you think all of this has been, if not me betting on you?"

Their hands still joined. Phainon looks at him, gaze flicking from eye to eye, the cuff at the end of his braid, the markings on his throat. His mouth, not smiling. He wants— what does he want? This, them, whatever it was in Mydei's voice when he said between us.

"Would you mind," Phainon starts, a lump forming in his throat, a fluttering feeling in his stomach, "if I slept on your floor tonight?" Heat in his face. He searches for an explanation, struggles to find a reason like he had that first time he held Mydei's hand, and again, the only thing he can seem to find is that he wants to. Selfishly, he wants to.

"HKS," is the reply. "You're already on the bed. Just... stay, if you must."

Chapter End Notes

lore concoction volume 7: Reavers are not a real thing in the Witcher; this is something I've made up for this story, vaguely based off the Reverend of Empty Words from tgcf for those of you that share that fandom with me too lol.

Please feel free to ask questions if you're ever confused, or share theories if you have them!! I love hearing your thoughts and am so so grateful for all of you kind people reading this. Your comments are endlessly motivating and encouraging to me; thank you all for joining me on this ride so far <3

chapters.title: Chapter 14
chapters.html:
It's far from the first time they've slept this close, but it's different when they're not crammed in together beneath a tarp, trying to stay warm and safe from the weather. Mydei is already familiar with the sound of Phainon's breath, the way he kicks in his sleep, the way he looks, the way he smells.

Something about this feels different. Maybe it's the fact that it's born entirely of choice. Maybe it's the fact that they have to share the blanket, Phainon stealing more than his half so he can cocoon himself like he usually does. Maybe it's the fact that this time, unlike the others, Mydei has has given a name to feeling curled tight inside his chest. Inconvenient as it is, he's certain of it.

They don't touch, though the bed is barely big enough for them both. Mydei lays entirely still, back to Phainon, eyes shut, unable to help the way his senses flood with the scent of skin and forsythia soap, and tries to fall asleep.

In the morning, his half of the blanket is entirely gone, wrapped around Phainon, edges even pinned beneath his body. Mydei isn't cold—he'd elected to wear his robes to bed, considering he's sharing it—but it's still irritating. Still makes something inside of him twist and curl and tangle into knots.

Phainon's forehead presses into his back. His breath creates a warm spot. Mydei stares at the patch of sunlight spilling beneath the curtains and thinks of the body behind him, you, of all people, curling a fist over his heart, as if it ever could've been anyone else.

With a sigh, he rolls out of bed. Phainon stirs, mumbles something. Mydei thinks of the way he's been sleeping late and training hard and decides against waking him up, slipping out instead to wash up and have breakfast.

He runs into Castorice on the way. "How are the wards?" he asks in Kremnoan. 

"Not great," she answers in turn, chewing on her lip. Their language is clipped and unpracticed on their tongues, even after a good chunk of a lifetime spent speaking it. Year after year, winter after winter, they wind up speaking it less and less. "I've made some progress with the holes, but it's as Anaxa said. We can't keep up with the rate they're deteriorating, and now he's gone and injected himself with that mutagen he made from Cerces' body. I brought him breakfast, and he's... this is the strongest reaction he's had to anything. I don't doubt that he'll survive it, but it could be a week or more before he's of any use."

Mydei's stomach turns. He understands Anaxa's idea. He'd already made the mutagen, he didn't have the strength to patch the wards as is. He wants to become a god; it's the obvious solution. But this is incredibly risky. None of them have undergone mutations this strong, not even Anaxa. It's unpredictable. They can't be sure that he'll survive, but if he does, he'll be able to fix the wards and make them stronger than ever, but the trade off of having their strongest out of commission while they're at their most vulnerable...

"And the tracking device he made," he says. "He left it with you, did he not?"

"He did," Castorice confirms. "I checked earlier, and we're safe for now. But he's smart, Mydei. He's shaving the wards down bit by bit; it won't be long before he breaks them open entirely."

A week or more. Anaxa hadn't even discussed other solutions with them. Mydei bites down on the insides of his cheeks. "It's fine," he says, tying to convince himself just as much as he tries to convince her. "So long as Phainon doesn't hear about this and grow uneasy, the Flame Reaver stays weak. We just need to keep him focused on his training."

"A bit late for that," Ptolemy cuts in from around the corner. They all speak in Kremnoan, just in case Phainon might wake and wander down the hall. "Peucesta says Phainon knows about the holes in the wards. Apparently he was even there when Anaxa injected himself."

"What," says Mydei, jaw clenching.

"Peucesta told him it was just normal wear and tear and he seemed to believe it. I don't know what he heard from Anaxa, though."

"So the situation is savable," Castorice says. "We'll keep him busy and not give him any reason to worry, and we'll hold out until Anaxa can fix the wards."

He didn't say anything on the matter, Mydei reminds himself. Last night, talking about Leonnius and his worries and the like, he said nothing about the wards. He must've believed Peucesta, or he would have gotten his fear smell all over Mydei's sheets. Mydei bites sores into the insides of cheeks, thinking about it.

"We need to get Kremnos moving again," he says. "That'll slow the Flame Reaver down at least a little."

"Right," says Ptolemy, bringing a hand to his mouth as he thinks. "But where to?"

"Away from people," Mydei says.

"North, where it's colder," Castorice suggests.

"Things certainly are a bit less flammable with a ton of snow lying around," Ptolemy adds.

"North it is," Mydei agrees, and casts the Sign of Nikador on himself, producing a thin crystal to cut the tip of his finger and beseech Castrum Kremnos to move. The walls groan as he smears the blood over his markings and thinks North, where it's cold and safe and not a soul will find us.

A gentle feeling of acceptance washes through him as Kremnos agrees to his request, the ground shuddering, fresh bits of rubble clattering against the stone floor as the city lifts itself up and begins to move.

△

"So," says Phainon, finding him in the stable brushing Strife. There are a couple of oatcakes in his hand, one with his own bite taken out of it, another that he offers to the horse. He'd roused just after the city started moving, too disturbed by the sounds and the shaking to fall back asleep. He'd come down the hall, confused to find them all gathered, and then they'd gone to get breakfast.

Ptolemy and Castorice are good enough actors; they'd managed to pass of the movement of Kremnos—even after collecting all of its witchers—as its natural inclination rather than something they'd induced themselves. There's no discussion of the wards or the Flame Reaver, and Phainon seems well-rested and in a good enough mood throughout their conversations to reassure Mydei that he has no suspicions.

He'd gone off with Castorice for some more training after, and Mydei had gone about his own business, namely, taking care of Strife and—now his temporary charge—Anaxa's dromas. He'd mucked the stalls, fed and watered them, taken them outside for a time, and now they're here a couple of hours later.

"So," he repeats, running the brush over Strife's side as she snuffles at Phainon's hand for more crumbs.

"I'm rested," Phainon says. "My strength is recovered, and Castorice didn't work me too hard just now..."

His eyes are wide and expectant. Mydei continues brushing his horse. "You want a spar," he notes.

"Well." Phainon wets his lips. "I was promised one." His eyebrows lift as he eats the last of his oatcake.

Mydei tries to sigh, but it ends as a laugh. He gives Strife a few more good strokes with the brush, reaching out to pat her. She snorts, looks at him with glassy eyes. He'll have to take her for another ride around the courtyard later. For now, Anaxa's dromas will keep her company. "I've never met one so eager to throw himself against witchers as you," he says. "Fine, then. Show me what you've learned from my siblings."

Phainon lights up like a match, and this quiet, worried thing in his chest calms. He's safe, it says. He's happy. Strange, what rises up with it is almost like guilt.

"We'll spar inside," he says, putting the brush away and throwing Strife's blanket over her back. She huffs, noting his intention to leave, but he produces a few cubes of sugar for her and receives no further protest.

"Lead the way," Phainon says, rocking back and forth on his feet, obviously excited. Mydei thinks of the last time they fought, fueled by mutual frustration and misunderstanding. Phainon's teeth in his bicep, Mydei's gauntlets tearing flesh. They're both healed by now.

He takes Phainon to what was once a ballroom, though he can't remember it ever being used, even during the time before Kremnos fell into disrepair. It's in surprisingly good shape due to the lack of furniture around to break. One shattered window at the far side of the room, dirt and dust and rubble coating the floors but not too much of an impediment, tables and chairs with tattered cloths along either edge of the room.

The center is a wide open space, which is what he'd wanted. The training grounds outside would do as well, but the sparring grounds have been churned up into muddy slush, and he's tired of doing laundry. The dust on the floors here he can at least brush off for the most part.

"I'm starting to think your earlier tour was lacking," Phainon says. "Is this a ballroom?"

"It was, once," Mydei agrees. There's a long, faded red carpet down the center of the room. Murals on the walls bleached by the sun and losing their shape as the fortress weathers. There were chandeliers once, but they fell with one of Kremnos' moves and have long since been cleaned up. Now, it's lit mostly by natural light spilling in from a dozen tall windows on either side.

"Did you guys throw parties?" Phainon asks, making his way to the center of the room and turning in a slow circle. He looks up to the ceiling as tall as ten or twenty of him, then pauses to survey the murals, mouth parting as his head tips back, that choker stark against his throat.

"No," Mydei tells him. "I've never seen this place used. But it's wide and empty enough for a spar."

"Right," Phainon says. "That spar." Suddenly, he smiles, turns to face Mydei again, hair wet with the snow that poured on them during their brief walk outside to get here. "Do you know how to dance?"

"Is that in jest?"

"You brought me to a ballroom, Mydeimos," Phainon says, coming closer. "Tell me you know how to dance."

"And when do you suppose I would have learned such a thing?" Mydei asks, frowning at him, at his wonder, at the way it makes something in his chest flutter.

"You could have picked it up somewhere," Phainon says, raising one eyebrow. He's close now. Too close, like someone intending to pick a partner at a masquerade. "You're a prince, you know. What kind of prince doesn't know how to dance?"

It's clear he means it in jest, but it falls flat somewhere in the pit of Mydei's stomach. "I'm no prince," he says, and the memory of forcing a spear between his father's ribs plays vividly behind his eyes. His father. It's unfair to call him that. That pitiful man, with madness and terror in his eyes. He was never part of Mydei's family. "And I don't know how to dance."

And maybe he does a poor job of controlling his tone, because Phainon parts his lips and closes them again, frowning slightly, thinking better of whatever he'd planned to say. "A shame," he offers instead, removing himself from Mydei's space and sighing for show. "I was hoping you could teach me. Since we're here. In a ballroom and all."

"It's actively crumbling," Mydei points out, regret in his fingertips, which curl at his sides. He hates that he knows exactly the source of that feeling. Hates that he could almost see it; the two of them hand in hand, pressed close, some kind of music playing. Hates that he's developed the audacity to think of such a thing at all.

"It's still beautiful, and I have an imagination. Really, Mydei, isn't Castrum Kremnos your home? Why are you so critical of it?"

He's odd and irritating. Mydei's jaw clenches. "Did we not come here to spar?"

"Well," Phainon says, perking right back up. "I suppose we can, if you really insist."

"Right, if I insist." Mydei backs up a couple of steps, giving them both space to fall into stance. He kicks a particularly large piece of rubble away so neither of them will trip on it. Dust stirs up; the ground is gritty. No one has bothered to sweep in here since the chandelier incident.

"I am nothing if not accommodating," Phainon agrees. "Anything for you, dearest Mydeimos."

"Incorrigible," Mydei tells him, and makes the first move. His punch is blocked, so is the one Phainon throws back. They fall into a familiar rhythm, matching each other blow for blow, dodging and punching, kicking and sidestepping. Phainon is a hair faster than he used to be, he's learned how to feint, his footwork and stability are better.

Mydei hits the ground with a grunt, struggling to regain control as Phainon tries to pin him, snatching one wrist and scrambling for the other as Mydei tries to buck him off. This becomes more familiar; they roll a couple of times, Mydei wrenching his wrist free, slamming his elbow into Phainon's cheek before they roll again, Phainon back on top, locking his ankles around Mydei's knees, hissing against Mydei's hand shoving his face away. And then the dust that swirls around him makes him sneeze, and Mydei takes the chance to roll them again and pin him quick, securing his hands and pressing a forearm into his throat.

"It looks like my victory," he says, panting.

"I yield," Phainon says with a sigh after testing his hold. Mydei lets up, and Phainon sneezes again. "Titans above. I wouldn't have lost if it weren't for all this dust."

"That wouldn't matter in a real fight," Mydei says, "and so it doesn't here." But quietly, he's rattled and impressed both. Mydei has more skill, but Phainon has talent. There's no other word for how quickly he picks things up, how quickly he improves.

"Again," Phainon says, sitting up. He takes the hand Mydei extends to him, letting himself be hauled up, dusting off his clothes and settling into stance, still catching his breath.

They spar again. Phainon is focused and sharp, and this time Mydei is prepared for how much he's improved. He doesn't give Phainon space to breathe, fighting fast and aggressive, sticking close. Still, Phainon matches him, landing a hit for each Mydei does, blocking and dodging and figuring him out. By a hair, Mydei takes victory again, knocking Phainon off balance with a close kick to his knee and putting him in a choke hold his an arm wrenched behind his back.

"I yield," Phainon grits, pulling on Mydei's wrist. They let go of each other, catching their breath for a moment, too, and then Phainon pushes himself back up, shaking out his limbs. "Again," he says, wiping sweat from his brow, settling into stance.

They spar again. Mydei wins by an even narrower margin as Phainon remembers his patterns and starts applying more and more of his new techniques. One more time, Mydei wins again, and likely only because Phainon hasn't given himself a moment to rest. Now, he struggles upright, brushing dirt and dust off his clothes, wiping away more sweat.

This time, he catches breath, studying the murals on the walls as he thinks, learns, adapts. Mydei can see the gears going in his head as he figures out his strategies, running through what works and what doesn't.

Gradually, his breath slows. He rocks on his feet, testing his sore muscles, and turns back to Mydei. "Again," he says, and smiles. "And I'm going to win this time."

"You've improved by a mile," Mydei says. "I don't doubt it."

That smile spreads wider. "Just wait," Phainon says, and widens his feet. "Just wait until Chartonus is done with my sword."

"I look forward to it," Mydei tells him. They circle each other slow, each covered in sweat and dirt. "Show me your strength, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae. I've been waiting."

So again, they spar, and this time, Phainon is quicker, smarter, more powerful than ever. They're an even match, odds turning against one and then the other. Mydei doesn't hold back, Phainon gives this fight his everything. They're a blur of fists, feet, elbows and knees, ducking and swinging at each other. It barely takes a handful of exchanges for them to end up on the floor, rolling again in the dust and dirt which sticks to them and gets all over their clothes.

Mydei's fingers end up between Phainon's teeth as he shoves him away, Phainon gets Mydei in the eye trying to block with his forearm and swinging his elbow instead. It's messy, as messy as it had been in Okhema, and then Phainon manages somehow to turn the tides and get Mydei on his stomach, kneeling on his back and claiming his victory.

"Finally," he says, breathless, letting Mydei up. When he spits, there's blood it in from a bitten tongue, but he's grinning, dirt all over his cheek where Mydei had slammed him into the ground. He extends a hand, Mydei takes it, and it might be the first time this exchange has played out this way instead of the other way around.

"They've been teaching you well," Mydei tells him, and watches Phainon's smile grow even wider as he gives this bashful, delighted laugh.

"It certainly helps a lot, having teachers instead of trying to figure everything out yourself." Again, he laughs, a little bit giddy, almost infectious. "I can hardly believe it. You weren't going easy on me, were you?"

"You won fairly," Mydei says, cataloging his aches as he attempts to dust himself off instead of looking a Phainon's smile. "Don't insult us both with the insinuation otherwise."

"Right," Phainon says, rubbing the grit from his cheek. A bruise is already blooming there, Mydei's work. It must hurt him to smile so wide. "Again?"

He feels a number of things. Pride, satisfaction, assurance that Phainon is strong, that maybe he can become strong enough. Competitive spirit as his ego bruises against the loss. "Very well," he says, and they settle into their fighting postures yet again.

△

Night comes, and with it, the quiet dark. Mydei returns to his room after dinner and a long, lingering conversation between all of them, sharing more tales from their times on the Path, discussing inane things like which monsters they loathe the most and what foods they desperately wish they could try again.

He likes that, this, when they're all together and the room is filled with warmth and firelight and laughter. He finds himself at ease. He's reminded that, even after everything, even after all their losses and hardships and the way the place is crumbling down around them, Castrum Kremnos is still his home and always will be, until the day it's his turn to not make it back.

They're all at ease, they're all good at acting normal. Phainon is a loud, eager, active participant in the conversation. He spends the whole time smiling, complaining of his soreness from running the Killer, his bruises from sparring any one of them. There isn't a trace of fear in him, at least not here, not now, and Mydei feels himself sink into his seat, belly full, contented, and listens on, cutting in here and there, but mostly just listening, observing his favorite people in the world at rest, happy and nostalgic and aching all at once.

Just for a bit, briefly, their hands brush atop the table. Phainon is slow to pull away.

And then Mydei returns to his room, washing up and changing into his sleep clothes, and he prays for the longevity of this peace. The walls shudder around him, a groan rolling through the fortress as he extinguishes his lamps one by one and lays down for bed.

It still smells like Phainon. Clean sweat and skin and forsythia. Mydei can't seem to escape him anywhere.

He wonders, lying there and trying to fall asleep, if Phainon will come and ask to sleep beside him once more. He thinks about it for a too long time, listening to all the faint sounds in the walls as Kremnos moves. He asks himself, silently, if he wants that, if he wants Phainon to come again, breathing softly and kicking in his sleep, stealing the covers, disturbing his rest. He doesn't come up with an answer before he falls asleep.

△

"Mydei." It's Castorice who wakes him up, too early to be considered morning. Her voice is soft, whispering as she lingers in his doorway, because she knows his senses are strong enough to hear.

Mydei stirs and shakes off the last of his dreams, slow and foggy, pushing himself upright to sit. "Cas?" he asks. He can't tell if it's urgent from the softness of her voice. "What is it?"

"Bad news," is the reply, so he gets up and finds his shoes where he'd left them. It's dark but for the faint light of the moon coming in through the window; Castorice hadn't brought a lantern. But his eyes are strong enough to see, and he doesn't stumble as he laces up his boots, grabs his gauntlets, and meets her in the doorway.

Ptolemy, Hephaestion, and Peucesta are already in the hallway waiting for him when she moves out of the way all still in their sleep clothes, wearing solemn expressions and carrying their weapons. Krateros, Phainon, and Chartonus will still be sleeping. Anaxa will still be indisposed. He doesn't like where this is going.

"Bad news," Mydei echoes, turning back to Castorice. She produces a jar from inside the cloak she wears around her shoulders. A black scrap of fabric suspended in some kind of fluid. It pulses with faint light. Anaxa's tracking device, that light its alarms blaring. A feeling—something between dread and anticipation—fills his stomach. He nods tightly, and the five of them set off.

"It's recent," Castorice says, voice still soft, "but Kremnos is moving. For him to not be getting any farther away..."

"How were the wards, last you checked?" Mydei asks, pulling his gauntlets on, tightening the ties on his clothes so they won't get in the way if it comes to a fight.

"Still failing," she replies, fingers tight about the tracking device. "But enough to hold him off until we can find him."

"Do you think he'll try and get in tonight?" Hephaestion asks, voice just as low. All of them keep their steps quiet, just as much to avoid alerting the Flame Reaver as to make sure they don't wake anyone else up. Chartonus isn't a fighter, Krateros is retired, Phainon... Phainon is doing so well, but he's been promised the winter. He isn't ready. More than anything, they need to keep the Flame Reaver away from him.

"Hopefully he's just coming to finish the wards off so he has easy entry next time, but..."

"He'll be hungry," Ptolemy finishes for her. He glances back at Mydei. "You said he hasn't had a go at Phainon since before Okhema?"

"He had him cursed for a while there," Mydei says. "But Phainon was weirdly resistant to it."

They're all quiet as they walk, following the glow of the tracking device in Castorice's hand. The closer they get, the brighter it grows, barely perceptible. They already know where the holes in the wards are, though, so it isn't difficult to figure it out from there.

"Whatever his plan is," Hephaestion says, adjusting his grip on his shield. "Keeping him away from Phainon is the priority."

The tracking device points them in the direction of the library, where the wall is entirely missing inside a tiny librarian's office and the ward is stretched thin and straining. Outside the door, the tracking device glows bright and hot enough that Castorice hides it away in her cloak again as they all press tight to the wall and listen.

There's the soft sound of a snap opening—a pouch at Peucesta's belt. He produces five vials of potion, silently passing them around, careful not to so much as let the glass clink. Mydei pops the stopper, smells the bitter, medicinal scent of the concoction for enhancing strength and senses. He downs it quick, feeling it burn down his throat, watching the others follow suit, straining to hear any sign of the Flame Reaver as light bleeds through the fabric of Castorice's cloak.

Nothing. They can hear nothing at all, exchanging glances to confirm before Mydei takes a careful step toward the office door, settling his hand on the knob. Scanning the dark behind and around them, straining his ears and still coming up with nothing, Mydei pushes the door open, inch by careful inch.

A frigid, snow-filled gust whistles through the opening. Mydei pushes the door wide as another rumble rolls through Castrum Kremnos, and they're faced with that gaping hole where most of the wall is missing, furniture having fallen away with it or been blown to the side with the door.

The enhanced dark vision from the potion starts to kick in as he scans the room. Dirt, rubble, splintered wood from a broken chair. Warped, ruined books, snow piling on the rough edges of the hole, the floor just inside. His hearing sharpens to catch the breath of the other witchers behind him.

He waits a little longer, feeling Castorice and Ptolemy come up close to survey the room alongside him. Another sharp, chilled breeze whips them across the face, cold and biting. Nothing. Absolutely nothing. Mydei turns to check, and still finds light, even brighter now, spilling from where the tracking device is tucked away in Castorice's cloak.

He steps all the way inside, slow and careful, shoes still crunching against the grit on the ground. Goose flesh forms on his arms from the cold or the knotting feeling in his gut.

"Cas," he whispers, and she comes up, careful not to touch as she brushes by him. She's the strongest of them in terms of magical aptitude, next to Anaxa, and has some training beyond just basic Signs. She stretches a hand out to check the ward, light spilling to the ground at her feet.
