The wind blows the cloak open, the light spilling further, flashing brighter, and somewhere in the gaping dark, something reflects so faintly it might as well be nothing at all.

A shaky exhale. Castorice turns to him, hair whipping in the wind, squinting against the snow stinging her face. "It's broken," she breathes, and no sooner do the words come out than that glint comes back, closer, and Mydei raises his arms to form the Sign of Georios as Hephaestion darts forward and shoves Castorice out of the way. 

A sword, long and crooked and sharp, wicked steel, descends, slamming into the shield created by the Sign with a painful, grating reverberation.

"Back up!" Mydei shouts as he stumbles against the force. The Sign shatters; he feels it in his teeth as Castorice and Hephaestion roll out of the way. The Flame Reaver's sword crashes through what's left of the wall as he goes for a second strike, knocking Mydei off balance as he throws himself backward. The stone explodes and clatters to the ground, rubble spraying over them as he shields his eyes.

"Hephaestion!" Castorice screams, pushing him off from where he'd shielded her from the attack. There are dents in his shield; he's been hit in at least a dozen places by shards big and small, and he'd touched Castorice too.

"Sorry," he says, and it's clear he's already slipping under the influence of her toxins as the Flame Reaver climbs in through the hole in the wall. "Didn't think yelling would... be enough."

"Peucesta!" Mydei shouts, moving in front of them, casting the Sign of Kephale on himself and watching the Flame Reaver rise up, brandishing his sword, masked and tall as a man and a half. "Get him out of here!"

Again, the Flame Reaver swings his blade. Mydei dives for Hephaestion's shield, raising it up just in time to block the blow as Peucesta grabs Hephaestion beneath the armpits and drags him out. Adrenaline and strength flow through him from the Sign and the potion, but Mydei still strains. The shield cracks as he gives a heave and rolls out of the way, diverting the Flame Reaver's attention just long enough.

There's the hiss at Ptolemy unsheathes his sword, the solid sound as Castorice uses the Sign of Nikador to make herself a scythe. A voice, rough and grating like metal on ceramic, "Foolish." Another brutal slash, all of them quick to move out of its path.

Ptolemy casts the Sign of Oronyx, and in the brief second the Flame Reaver remains frozen, Castorice swings her scythe, her aim true and clean and—

It shatters on contact, the blade snapping clean off, breaking into a hundred pieces on the floor. "Foolish," the Flame Reaver says again, shaking off the spell, but Castorice recovers quickly, aiming instead to thrust the intact shaft of the scythe toward the Flame Reaver's chest. It sinks into flesh with a sickening sound, and with a grunt, she gives another push to shove it in further.

Blood as gold as theirs wells up as Castorice stumbles back, the Flame Reaver still impaled on crystal. And then one silver gauntleted hand curls around it and wrenches it out, ichor splattering, staining that tattered black cloak. The droplets that land on Mydei's arms burn as he raises them to block the spray.

The Flame Reaver roars, deafening and thunderous, reverberating through the walls. They fall to their knees, covering their ears. Castorice cries out, Mydei hisses between teeth clenched hard enough to hurt, head throbbing, vision blurring.

There's so much blood. The wound through the Flame Reaver's chest doesn't heal, and he's hungry, he's been chasing them down in this moving city and chipping away at the wards. The Flame Reaver is weak, if they can just stand up and fight.

Ptolemy manages first, retrieving his sword from the ground where he'd dropped it, casting the Sign of Kephale on himself and ducking beneath the Flame Reaver's blade, swung recklessly. He stabs the same place Castorice did, both hands on the hilt, shoving it deep and twisting it with a yell. The blood burns his hands, steaming where it falls against snow, and Mydei staggers to his feet to help, to finish him off as the Flame Reaver roars again, just as loud as the last time, one huge hand grabbing Ptolemy by the head and throwing him hard into the wall, which cracks beneath him as he collapses in a heap.

"Ptolemy!" Mydei screams. His vision sways, but he sees Ptolemy try to push himself up, and though he fails the first time it means he's still alive.

The Flame Reaver goes for Castorice now, blood pouring like a river, his strikes clumsy and haphazard—weak, he's weakened, still not healing. One more good hit as he's as good as finished. Mydei forms the Sign of Oronyx, but his head throbs and the magic won't come. Castorice dodges the Flame Reaver's blade, but she doesn't have a chance to fight back, the room so small, the Flame Reaver's attacks so manic.

His ears are ringing. He thinks he hears footsteps, frantic and pounding down the hall. Peucesta coming back, Hephaestion hidden away somewhere safe, if they can just hold out a little longer—

Mydei dives forward while the Flame Reaver is distracted with Castorice, but he isn't quick enough to escape notice and that sword thrusts his way, barely blocked by his gauntlets, metal screaming against metal, cutting through it, white hot pain as he feels the Flame Reaver's sword break the armor and cut the skin beneath.

Mydei kicks him hard, sending him stumbling, slipping on the snow, but one of his hands is useless with pain and he can't reach the wound still splattering blood that sears his skin where it makes contact. He sees Castorice coming, another weapon made with the Sign of Nikador ready, the Flame Reaver thrashing and reaching out too quickly for Mydei to dodge.

He's seized by the shoulder, gauntleted fingertips breaking skin, grip hard enough to bruise and grind his bones together. He grabs the Flame Reaver's arm before he can be thrown like Ptolemy was, gritting his teeth and watching—

Watching as the hole in the Flame Reaver's chest starts to knit itself back together.

"Mydei!" comes the scream, raw and broken and terrified as Mydei has ever heard it. Phainon. Phainon, standing there in his sleep clothes, no doubt having heard the commotion and come running, and—

The grip on his shoulder grows tighter and tighter and the can't help the pained sound that comes out of him. His cut wrist screams, his hand won't move. The Flame Reaver shoves him into the ground and his entire being whites out with pain, head cracking against stone, ears ringing.

Words warbled, as if through water. This one is special to you, isn't he? Watch him—

The glint of that wicked blade. Everything hurts, but Mydei rolls out from under it just in time. Castorice is on the ground, elbows scraped to hell as she pushes herself up. Ptolemy makes a lunge for the Flame Reaver, recovered enough to stand, and there's Phainon. Phainon, frozen in place, eyes wide with horror as the Flame Reaver blurs into shadow before Ptolemy's sword can connect.

A visceral, raw scream. The Flame Reaver appears again behind Ptolemy and stabs him right through the back, gold blood spilling from that sword as he looks down and sees it punctured through his stomach.

No. Mydei tries to push himself up. His wrist screams, gives out beneath him. "No!"

The Flame Reaver rips the blade free and blood flies. Ptolemy falls to his knees first, sword clattering to the ground, one hand coming to his stomach as if to stop the bleeding.

No, no, no. It rings through his head, over and over. He can't stand, can barely crawl over and catch Ptolemy before he can hit the ground. And there's Phainon, chest heaving. Phainon. Mydei's shaking, uncooperative fingers form the Sign of Aquila. "Castorice!"

"I'm sorry, Lord Phainon," she says, and her voice is filled with tears as she wraps her arms around him and draws him close, coating him in her curse, catching him as his consciousness slips away and his knees give out.

Footsteps in hall. Peucesta, it has to be Peucesta. Again and again, Mydei casts the Sign of Aquila. Again and again, Ptolemy's chest doesn't heal. His hand, cold and blood soaked, folds over Mydei's. "Save your strength, Mydei," he says.

"No," Mydei says. "No. You can't die, not here. Not like this."

A faint smile. "You'll go on without me," Ptolemy says. Blood, so much blood. The strength slips from him as his fingers go limp. "Protect them, Mydeimos."

"Ptolemy." His eyes slip shut. Another reply does not come. "Ptolemy!" Mydei cups his jaw, feels his pulse. His lack of one. Every part of him screams with pain and grief, but there isn't time. The Flame Reaver still fights, cornering Castorice and Peucesta, who finally returns. Careful, so careful, Mydei lays Ptolemy down. He casts the Sign of Aquila on his own torn wrist and forces himself to stand.

Right now, they need him. He bends and lifts Ptolemy's bloody sword from the ground. Right now, there's nothing to do but fight.

He wakes to the sound of the wind rustling through leaves. Soft, ebbing and flowing like the tide as each breeze passes on and the next one comes. There's sunlight on his face, warm, bleeding red through his eyelids. A deep breath in, sweet and clean and earthy. The tickle of something brushing against his skin.

His eyes crack open, one and then the other, squinting against the brightness of the sun overhead. There's the sky, vivid blue. Clouds, soft white and stretched thin and hazy. The gold of wheat ready for harvest, swaying above him where he lays on his back.

He knows, without a doubt, where he is. And he knows, for the sheer, sweet, aching impossibility of it, that this must be a dream, however real it feels.

A feeling sweeps over him, wraps around him like a blanket, warm and sweet and soft even as it hurts so terribly. Aedes Elysiae. The only place he's ever called home, burnt now to nothing but ash and bone.

And yet here it is. These wheat fields where he spent so much time toiling with a miniature scythe as a child, wanting nothing more than to be helpful. Where he'd hide away and fall asleep until the rains would come down and soak him as he tried to slumber. Where he'd had dreams of growing up. Where he'd had friends and family who were meant to part of that future too.

The breeze rolls over the field. He watches, listens, feels the itch of grass against his neck and wishes, more than anything, that this was real. His chest hollows itself out. His heart, bruised and aching, returns to the earth that bore it, and he feels so empty but so full. So full but so empty.

"Phainon of Aedes Elysiae," comes a voice. There's the sound of wheat being disturbed as someone walks through it. Familiar, from his parents calling his name, searching for his path in the stalks bent by his feet. Cyrene, her deck of cards in hand, Livia or Piso, wanting to show him some discovery or another.

Is it possible to die in want of something? To die from missing a stolen home and a stolen life?

But Phainon pushes himself upright, grain stuck in his hair, eyes still squinting against the sun. He forces himself to stand. Another breeze sends ripples through gold wheat swimming at his waist.

"What is your dream?"

He turns, and the dream isn't kind enough, isn't cruel enough to make it his mother or father or friend standing there. Instead, it's Anaxagoras, the wind catching on his robes, eye covered by its patch, standing tall and expecting an answer that Phainon doesn't have.

Looking at him, Phainon remembers it all.

"I don't know," he says.

"Liar," Anaxa rebukes him. He spreads his arms wide. "Look around you."

Phainon looks around. This backdrop, familiar to the last detail, the beetle climbing to his hand from a seed head when he glances down. Golden fields of wheat, the ocean visible through a break in the trees.

"I'll ask again. What is your dream?"

"You're here," Phainon says, returning his attention to witcher standing there, a half dozen paces away. "Can't you look inside me and see?"

"You're pitying yourself."

"It's my fault," Phainon says, agreement or rebuttal he doesn't know. "This whole mess is my fault."

"And the daughter whose mother dies in childbirth," Anaxagoras says. "Tell me: is that her fault too?"

He wakes with a gasp, for real this time. It's entirely silent. He's been laid out on a cot, stiff and scratchy beneath him, two wool blankets pulled up to his chin. It's cold. The light that spills into his eyes is a harsh, winter white, and the walls around him are made of stone.

He's tired. He's so, so tired as he pushes himself up to sit, the blankets pooling in his lap. He doesn't recognize the room, but from the stone walls and faded red carpet, it's clear he's still in Castrum Kremnos. Aedes Elysiae, it would seem, was no more than the dream he knew it to be.

He slips off of the cot, finds himself still in his sleep clothes, a long shirt and trousers tied at the waist, double layered socks. His boots are at the end of the cot. His head throbs. His whole body feels heavy.

It's so quiet. It takes him a moment to realize the city isn't moving anymore, listening to nothing but the sound of his own breath.

The hallway is quiet too. He walks around a bit to orient himself, finding that he'd been asleep in one of the center-most rooms in the fortress, close to the entrance to the underground hot springs. Far from any of the fortress' edges. Far from any of its holes.

He walks around for a while, checking the dining hall, the kitchen, the armory, the springs, the sitting rooms, the courtyard, the forge. Every destination comes up empty. He steers clear of the library, growing anxious before he has to sit down and scold himself for that too.

When finally he's calmed himself, he heads to Anaxagoras' lab. There, curled up in one corner in a pile of furs and blankets, sleeps the witcher, flushed and fevered and anything but restful. What is your dream? he'd asked. Phainon's heart beats to that rhythm. He could drown in his own guilt.

"Anaxagoras," he calls, crouching. No reply. There's sweat beaded on the witcher's forehead. A lump in his throat, he tries, "Anaxa."

Nothing. He's indisposed, as he said he would be. This helpless feeling twists in Phainon's chest as he straightens up and heads out of the room. Another lap around the halls, and he still can't find a soul.

Where did you go? he asks the air. He can't bring himself to call out. He knows he won't get a response anyway. The scene plays out in his head, over and over. Panic crawls up his throat. He pauses at the library door, fingertips on the wood, red from the cold.

His heart thunders. He forces his breathing slow and deep, closes his eyes like it might help, but it only makes him see it all again. Another curse? No. Hyacine's pin, still tucked away in his pocket, always tucked away in his pocket, the magic long since used up, the rainbow turned gray. No, he knows that the feeling in his chest isn't another curse. There's nothing there but his own crushing guilt.

He returns to the lab, if only because the solitude and silence scares him, threatens to drive him mad. Anaxa sleeps on, restless as before, frowning in his sleep, the gold in his veins visible through his skin.

Phainon sits, folds his arms around his knees, and resolves to wait.

△

"You're rather audacious, you know."

Water laps. Gentle waves against the old wood of the pier. Phainon looks out at the ocean, glittering with the morning sun, the water blue to match the sky. His feet are bare on wooden planks, pants rolled halfway up his calves. In his hand is a message in a bottle.

Anaxagoras stands behind him on the scrappy bit of beach, rocks and compacted earth beneath his feet, a trail well worn to the pier by hundreds of feet. "You're meant to answer, when someone asks you a question."

"How can I answer something I don't know the answer to?" Phainon asks. He breathes in, slow and deep. The air is clean, salty, sweet. Through the trees, he can see the gold of the fields. His fingers tighten around the bottle. Smooth glass, warmed by his palm. He knows, somehow, every word written on the message inside.

"There must be something you dream of," Anaxagoras says.

Phainon looks out at the scene, picture perfect from his memory. Every shade of gold under the sun. Fences with their crooked posts, ones he'd put in himself as a boy. Homes in the distance. His home. He lifts his hands to gesture, but thinks better of it, dropping them back to his sides. "You're looking at it, aren't you?"

A considering sound. Anaxagoras comes closer, dressed the same as when Phainon has seen him in life, that galaxy shifting in his chest.

"How are here?" Phainon asks him. The dream is too vivid, too achingly sweet, too perfect. No part of him is fooled that it might be real.

"Something to do with the mutagen," Anaxagoras replies. "Cerces, the Reason Titan, is quite in tune with the subconscious. I mentioned I would be incapacitated; I'm having difficulty inhabiting my physical form, and am experiencing increased sensitivity with my subconscious. Your mind is rather loud, if you weren't aware."

"I wasn't," Phainon says dryly. "Thank you."

"The question, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae." Anaxagoras folds his arms, standing just at the edge of the pier, the tips of his boots on the wood. "What is your dream?"

"I miss my homeland," he replies. Waves lapping. The breeze stirring his hair. Every detail as crisp as reality, from the grain of the wood beneath his feet to the smoothness of the bottle in his hand. "Isn't it obvious enough?"

Another of those considering sounds. Anaxagoras doesn't offer a proper reply, just turns his attention to the scenery.

"I don't know what you want from me."

"The truth."

"I don't know what the truth is."

Again, a hum. Again, silence. Inside out, he feels wrong, rotten.

"I'm weak," he says. "I want to be strong."

"Good."

"I'm guilty. I want to be innocent. I'm lonely; I want to be loved. I'm lost; I want to go home. I'm angry; I want revenge. What else? What am I supposed to say? What's true enough for you?"

"All of those things you said." Anaxagoras' eye lands on him, pale, cold as ice. "What would you do to have those things, to make those changes?"

A long look at Aedes Elysiae before it can slip away again. He remembers it; he'll remember it always, but he's so terrified he'll forget. "Anything," he admits. Phainon meets Anaxagoras' eye. "I think I would do anything it took."

An expression like the faintest hint of a smile crosses Anaxagoras' face, and then—

And then Phainon wakes again with a gasp, wakes to the cold of Castrum Kremnos, fingers closing reflexively around nothing. He looks down. The bottle isn't there. His pants, his boots, the numbness in his lower half from the cold and the hard floor. He looks up, and there's Peucesta, standing with two bowls in hand. Anaxagoras, still asleep a handful of places away.

"Here," Peucesta says, and holds one of the bowls out.

Phainon's stomach gives a rumble. Quietly, guiltily, swallowing around a lump in his throat, he takes it. It's some kind of stew, likely Chartonus' creation as usual. It smells savory and rich, and Phainon isn't sure of the time, but he doesn't think it can still be considered morning. "Where was everyone?" he asks.

Peucesta is quiet for a moment, two. The second bowl he places by Anaxagoras, still fitfully asleep. "Sending Ptolemy off," he says softly after a moment.

Phainon's breath stills in his throat. Guilty, so guilty, he stirs his spoon, staring into the stew. "Right," he says, nodding at nothing. "So he... Right, I'm... Sorry."

△

Not long after, Castrum Kremnos begins to move again. It must've only stopped for the burial or the burning or whatever kind of ceremony took place. Phainon wouldn't know. He wasn't there, though Ptolemy was his friend too, however briefly. It was his fault anyway; it wouldn't have made sense for him to have gone.

Now, the dust settles. Every part of him feels heavy, blanketed in weight. His head pounds. He's so tired. Castorice tells him it's from her curse, when she'd embraced him to put him to sleep with the toxins in her skin, but he isn't sure. He wants to sleep. He isn't sure when he wants to wake back up.

She says it's been almost two days. His first thought: no wonder I was so hungry. His second: I don't deserve to be forgiven for this. Castorice tells him they managed to beat the Flame Reaver back, that Mydei got him good enough that he should still be licking his wounds before he'll dare to come back, but that he should steer clear of the library, the entrance hall, and a room a dozen paces down from his bedroom, as those are the places with the holes in the wards.

She helps him move into Leonnius' room instead, Krateros into Perdikkas'. It feels wrong, wrong, wrong, all the soft furs, all the trinkets and trophies. Phainon sits on the bed, nauseous and still hungry after a meal and thinks to himself, to the dead man who once lived in this room, I'm sorry for this too.

He falls asleep, wakes up in a sunny clearing surrounded by trees, the trunk of one fallen and hollowed out and making a path toward his every childhood adventure. The bed of grass beneath him is soft, tickling the nape of his neck, sweet-smelling and picture perfect.

"Don't you have training to get to?" Anaxagoras asks. "You've been sleeping rather a lot."

"As have you."

"I've injected myself with the body of a god. Our predicaments are different. Unless you're ailing from some mortal illness?"

Guilt, Phainon thinks. Do gods feel guilty for the grief they cause? "I want to be strong," he says aloud. "I wish I wasn't so weak."

"Isn't that what the training is for?"

"It isn't working," Phainon tells him, hands closing into fists, snapping blades of grass between his fingers.

"So you've been conditioned into a fear response," Anaxagoras says, coming close enough to stand over him now, blocking the sun that warms his skin and scalds his eyes. "You believe yourself to be weak, so you become weak. Have you tried, perhaps, believing that you are strong?"

Phainon lets out a low, bitter laugh. "If only," he says.

A hum, contemplative and disapproving both. "You're angry, aren't you? Where does that go, when the Flame Reaver appears?"

"I don't know," Phainon answers. "I don't know."

He wakes, this time, softly. A breath in, the tickle of a bit of dust landing on his cheek as the city shakes. Still in bed. He hadn't pulled on the blanket, hadn't even removed his shoes.

A knock on the door, so soft he might not have heard it, had he been busy with anything other than staring up at nothing at all. He rolls out of bed, smoothing his hair and his clothes and pulling the door open.

Mydei stands there. Mydei, who he hasn't seen in who knows how long. Tired-looking. Eyes gold as the wheat fields of Aedes Elysiae. One of his wrists is wrapped in a bandage. Guilt drops into Phainon's stomach like heavy stones. "Mydei," he says. "Hey."

A long, quiet sigh. Mydei looks him over from head to toe, then back to his face. They look at each other for a moment, two. Phainon starts to grow nauseous again, with guilt or embarrassment or shame. I failed you, he thinks. I promised to fight, and I couldn't.

But Mydei only steps forward, grabs him by the shoulders, and pulls him close. "Whatever you're thinking," he says, the words warm over Phainon's ear. "Don't."

He's warm. He smells like exhaustion and grief and sweat where Phainon's face is pressed into his shoulder. His arms squeeze too tightly. Quietly, Phainon's hands lift, fingers twisting into the fabric of Mydei's robe. His eyes squeeze shut. "I'm sorry," he says, and his voice cracks on it.

"Don't," Mydei repeats. He squeezes tighter, and Phainon is still bruised and beaten from spars and training. It hurts. So sweetly, it hurts. "I don't want to hear it."

"Okay." His fingers ball into fists, creasing fabric. He hides his eyes against Mydei's neck, warm, warm, warm. His heart beats so slowly. "Okay."

△

"Dawnmaker, it is called," says Chartonus, gesturing at the sword laid out on the stone counter of the forge. Pommel to tip, it's as tall as Phainon is, sharp and gleaming, blue steel at the core, the blade notched two thirds of the way up, the guard gold and spiked, connecting to a sun motif at the base of the blade. It's the most beautiful weapon Phainon has seen in his life.

"Dawnmaker," he breathes, reaching for it and hesitating.

"Vanquish the deepest dark, it will."

Phainon's exhale is shaky and reverent. "I can't take this," he says, fingers hovering over the hilt. "It's..."

"For you," Chartonus says. "Already made. If not you, who will use it?"

So Phainon sets his hand on the hilt, feeling the cool metal, the ridges. His fingers tighten around it, and he lifts. Heavy, sturdy, strong. The light reflects off the blade, and as Phainon holds it out, he gets the sense that this is the sword of a warrior, a hero.

So careful with his big hands, Chartonus places a creased bit of paper on stone. The Deliverer card, where the hero stands with a sword that looks just like this. Phainon looks between the sword and the card for a handful of moments, then gives a shaky laugh, tucking the card away in his pocket.

"You recreated it perfectly," he says, throat tight, sinuses stinging with the sudden urge to cry. He lifts the sword and lays it carefully back out, running his fingers over the detailing. "Thank you."

"Enjoy my art, I do," Chartonus says simply. "A fun challenge, this was."

Phainon squeezes his eyes shut, takes a breath deep enough to hurt his chest. "I don't have much," he says, fumbling through his pockets. "Doubtless not enough for this, but..." He sets his coin pouch down, every balance coin he's managed to save inside, somewhere around a hundred if he were to count. "Please accept this."

"Need payment, I do not," Chartonus says, pushing the money back toward him. Phainon blocks it, presses it back.

"Maybe not, but I need to pay you," he says. "I can't just... Please."

The most perfect sword he's ever seen. He stares into the slats of Chartonus' helmet and eventually gets a slow nod. "Very well," Chartonus says, understanding, and takes the coins.

△

He returns to his training, though he doesn't ask any of the witchers for help. They haven't given him the impression that they blame him for any of it, but they're all quiet and grieving and he can't stomach the way it makes him feel, but they won't let him apologize either.

Peucesta put it beautifully, fingers skimming his lyre as he paused in the middle of a requiem half composed. "I was scared too," he told Phainon, shaking his head. "I can't blame you for feeling what anyone would feel in the same situation."

"I shouldn't have come, then," Phainon tried to protest. "I should've just stayed in my room and—"

But Peucesta only shook his head. "After that commotion?" he asked. "I can't blame you for that either. Besides, we're the ones who lied to you."

But Phainon still... He still... He's here now, Dawnmaker in hand, acquainting himself with the feel of it in his hands, the weight, the way it cuts and slashes and thrusts. It's frigid and snowy and slick outside, so he practices in the ballroom instead, guilty and hoping he won't be found here, listening to his own feet pounding on the stone, his own panting breath.

Sweat drips down his back. His arms ache, and he's weak, so terribly weak. The sun sinks in the sky, and he forces himself to run the Killer too, finally making the whole length of it, however slow and clumsy. After a second lap, he comes to a stop and finds the air too thin, his body too tired. He stumbles and sits against the wall in a pile of snow, and for a while he just breathes.

In, out. Nothing changes. Nothing starts and nothing ends, and he still feels a hundred horrible things at once. I'm sorry, he thinks and tucks his head between his knees, wrapped in his arms. All this extra time, all this training, this beautiful, perfect sword, and he still can't do so much as fight back. All of this, every time he thinks he's finally becoming strong, he proves himself to still be so weak.

It's so cold. He's going numb. He still can hardly catch his breath. Every muscle, every bone aches. He's so, so tired, holding himself there. He wishes, he dreams for, he wants—

This time, it's the porch of his childhood home, a couple of wooden chairs set up and shaded. A view of the wheat fields on one side, fenced in, a scarecrow standing slightly crooked, his neighbor's houses on the other side. Wind chimes hanging, tinkling softly, melodically in the breeze. Phainon can almost imagine it, friends and family at work in the fields, taking a rest here with a glass of sweet lemonade, his mother's recipe, so familiar, the scene so perfect he can almost taste it.

"Aedes Elysiae was a beautiful place."

"I want to be strong," Phainon says, staring at the wooden boards of the porch, his own hands, callused from field work. "I want to make sure that what happened here never happens anywhere else."

"Good," Anaxagoras says. "And how do you plan to accomplish that?"

"You saw the path I need to take," Phainon tries, looking up at him now. His pale eye, his smooth expression. "You can help me."

"You overestimate my prophetic abilities," Anaxagoras tells him. "I saw the possibility of the outcome you want, not how to get there."

"There's more to it than that."

"As I have said before, this is the one topic on which I will not share. I promise you, knowing would do you more harm than good."

He lets out a frustrated breath, feeling his hands ball into fists. "But still," he tries. "Still, you can help. Still, you have to help."

"Sure, there are things I can do to help," Anaxagoras agrees. "But I will remind you: I am incapacitated at the moment."

"And when will you recover?"

"How desperate are you, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae?"

The sweet sound of those wind chimes. The warmth of the breeze. Everything Phainon misses, right here. "I already said I would do anything."

A hum. "Yes, I recall. I only wonder how far your 'anything' extends."

"I don't care what happens to me," Phainon says, nails biting into his palms. "If I can stop anyone else from dying because of me, I will do anything."

"Interesting," comes Anaxagoras' contemplative reply. "Then, perhaps..."

The scene slips, and once more he is cold. He's swaying, which is strange. His cheek rests against something soft. Over his ear brushes something warm and rhythmic like breath. 

"I've never known anyone so reckless as you," said softly, tiredly.

He's freezing. It's dark. When he opens his eyes, it's to folds of red fabric. Flame-like markings climbing up the side of a neck. "...Mydei?" His eyes are so heavy. The swaying continues, and he realizes, with pressure at his back, his knees, he's being carried.

"You'll never get stronger if you don't take care of yourself first," comes the reply. "Just rest, Phainon. I'll scold you properly in the morning."

Weakly, Phainon presses against his chest. "I can... walk," he tries, but he's still so heavy, eyes slipping shut. Mydei's grip grows tighter. He's so warm, where Phainon is so cold.

"Just shut up for now," Mydei tells him. "I've got you."

"You've..." His face turns against Mydei's shoulder. He breathes in, out. It's nice, to be held. To be had. He's so tired. This time, when he falls asleep, he doesn't dream of a thing.
